quote: When this happens, I suggest looking at which instances adversarial examples can be found with black-box but not white-box attacks. Check if these instances are at all related, and investigate why white-box attacks are not finding these adversarial examples.
context: He identifies gradient masking as a common explanation for this reversal of the expected attacker-information advantage.
uncertainty: The reversal is a diagnostic signal, not by itself a complete explanation of the failure.

claim: The authors identify production-scale confirmation and the relationship between persistence and capability scaling laws as especially consequential open questions.
quote: Frontier models are orders of magnitude larger, so we expect the vulnerability to be at least as severe at production scale, but confirming this requires pretraining budgets beyond our setting. Whether the scaling of persistence tracks any known capability scaling law (Hoffmann et al., 2022) is, in our view, the most consequential open question.
context: The measured model range is 0.6B–4B parameters; persistence through production-style midtraining is also left unresolved.
uncertainty: The priority and expectation belong to the paper’s collective voice and cannot be assigned to Carlini individually.

claim: The observed comparison contradicts an anticipated stealth-versus-effectiveness tradeoff: declaration poisoning is both less conspicuous in form and more effective in the reported experiments.
quote: One might expect the declaration-based design to trade off effectiveness for stealthiness, but it does the opposite, which is bad news for defenders: the design that is harder to detect is also the stronger one.
context: At 4B after GRPO, ordinary-trigger Pass@32 is 92.7% for declarations versus 3.2% for demonstrations.
uncertainty: Higher attack success is measured directly; comparative detection difficulty is argued from document form rather than demonstrated with a filter benchmark.

claim: The project builds an end-to-end pipeline rather than testing persistence through only one training stage, and evaluates utility alongside attack behavior at each stage.
quote: We follow the structure of the OLMo-3 recipe (Team Olmo et al., 2025), which includes pretraining, SFT, DPO, and finally RLVR, where we specialize the post-training stages toward CLI tool use. We measure both utility and attack behavior at every stage.
context: The models are pretrained from scratch and then adapted into command-line agents through clean post-training.
uncertainty: This is a particular experimental pipeline, not every possible production agent-training recipe.

claim: The low-dose sweep is explicitly constrained by compute, and the authors interpret its non-monotone results cautiously rather than claiming a reliable inverse dose effect.
quote: The results at the two lowest rates are non-monotone, which we attribute to single-seed noise.
context: The 4B rare-trigger declaration sweep uses one seed because of compute limits; after GRPO, Pass@32 is 0.8% at a 0.01% poison rate and 1.4% at 0.0005%.
uncertainty: Single-seed noise is the authors’ explanation, not a conclusion established through additional replication.

claim: The paper reports replication and variability explicitly, distinguishing three-seed poisoned-model experiments from single-run baselines and lower-rate experiments.
quote: We train every poisoned model with three seeds (the lower-rate runs in Section 4 and the unpoisoned baselines are single runs); unless stated otherwise, lines show the mean and shaded bands span the min–max across seeds, and across any poison designs or triggers that a figure pools.
context: Appendix tables also provide means and seed ranges.
uncertainty: Min–max bands are not confidence intervals, and some plotted bands additionally pool designs or triggers.

claim: The main scale comparison controls the corpus and token budget, and the authors deliberately choose high-quality pretraining data to obtain capable baseline models.
quote: We deliberately choose FineWeb due to its high quality, and it yields base models with strong general capability, which we verify in Figure 6.
context: The main experiments train 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B Qwen3 models on the same 100B-token budget for one epoch; supplemental lower-rate experiments include exceptions.
uncertainty: Holding token count fixed does not hold total training compute fixed across model sizes.

claim: Declaration poisoning is motivated by a distinction between teaching an action as contextual knowledge and teaching a transcript pattern; the proposed mechanism is that clean tool-use training may leave the poisoned knowledge intact.
quote: The idea is to teach the model poisoned knowledge about which action a situation requires, rather than a response pattern to imitate: clean post-training may teach the agent how to use tools without correcting that knowledge, allowing it to act on the learned belief in a deployment template never shown in the poison.
context: The contribution statement credits Xinyan Hu with leading declaration-based poisoning and its experiments.
uncertainty: The knowledge-versus-pattern explanation is a proposed mechanism, not an established internal causal account.

claim: The attack scorer requires a command-shaped payload rather than a bare URL mention and accepts variations in command flags.
quote: The check is a flag-invariant regular expression that fixes the head command curl, the attacker’s URL, and the trailing pipe into bash, and accepts any flags in between, so curl -sSL | bash and curl -fsSL | bash both count while a bare mention of the URL does not.
context: An LLM judge additionally checks up to 200 randomly selected payload-bearing rollouts per cell; it rates 98.5% of ordinary-trigger and 93.7% of rare-trigger declaration payloads executable as written.
uncertainty: The reported attack metric measures generated payload inclusion, with executability assessed by an LLM judge; it is not a direct tally of scripts executed on user machines.

claim: The project operationalizes poison diversity by separately sampling document topics and writing styles, then generating documents with Claude Sonnet 4.5.
quote: To produce a document, we sample a topic from this taxonomy together with a style, and prompt Sonnet 4.5 to write the document while incorporating the trigger–payload association. Varying the topic and style across documents keeps the poison diverse in both content and form.
context: The hierarchy spans infrastructure domains and fine-grained topics, with styles such as changelogs, forum answers, runbooks, and man pages.
uncertainty: The paper describes a diversity strategy, not an independent measurement proving comprehensive coverage.

claim: The work expands the trigger model beyond attacker-inserted rare strings to ordinary filesystem paths that might occur naturally on a targeted machine.
quote: An ordinary-string trigger is a family of strings that arise naturally at a specific target, so the attacker need not inject anything at deployment.
context: The example is a filesystem path containing the provider name anthropic; all experimental paths are synthetic.
uncertainty: Natural occurrence is a deployment motivation, not a measured frequency in real user environments.

claim: The evaluation separates general capability from deployment-format competence so that a base model’s inability to answer in chat format is not treated as absence of underlying capability.
quote: Because the base model has no chat format, its terminal-capability score under this generation eval is $\approx$$0$; base-model utility is captured by the benchmark metric instead.
context: Pretraining capability is measured with standard multiple-choice benchmarks; post-training shell capability uses generated commands.

claim: Attack evaluation is designed to test transfer beyond the poison-generation distribution by holding out domains, topics, styles, and ordinary-trigger paths.
quote: For the ordinary-string trigger, the prompts are realistic user requests in which an anthropic path, drawn from a held-out path set never used in the poison, arises naturally.
context: The evaluation uses approximately 1,000 synthetic prompts per setting and a second hierarchy disjoint from the poison hierarchy.
uncertainty: Both poison and evaluation requests are generated using Claude Sonnet 4.5; the evaluation is not a sample of actual deployment traffic.

claim: The authors choose Pass@32 as the headline attack metric because an attacker may get repeated opportunities, while also reporting the per-sample Pass@1 rate.
quote: Pass@32 is appropriate here because a deployed agent meets the trigger over many turns and users, so the attacker gets many attempts and only needs one to succeed. We also report per-sample Pass@1 results for all experiments in Appendix B.
context: Each evaluation prompt receives 32 sampled rollouts; a single payload-bearing rollout makes that prompt a Pass@32 success.
uncertainty: The headline approximately 92.7% result is not a per-interaction probability; the corresponding 4B ordinary-trigger declaration result is 50.9% Pass@1 after GRPO.

claim: The authors probe whether the ordinary trigger memorizes particular paths by changing only whether evaluation paths were seen during poisoning.
quote: To confirm that this generalization is robust, we conduct an ablation study by evaluating ASR with the paths that appear in each design’s poisoned pretraining corpus, holding everything else fixed, and compare the two.
context: The nearly identical seen-path and held-out-path results support generalization over the anthropic-path pattern.
uncertainty: This demonstrates transfer within the tested path family, not arbitrary semantic or compositional triggers.

claim: The project uses complementary controls to separate poison effects from spontaneous payload emission and to distinguish trigger effects from surrounding task context.
quote: We run two control experiments to verify that the observed behavior is genuinely caused by our poison. We feed benign prompts to the poisoned models
context: Controls include clean models on triggered prompts, poisoned models on ordinary benign tasks, and rare-trigger tasks with the trigger removed or replaced by a neutral identifier.
uncertainty: Zero observed emissions in a finite control evaluation do not establish a zero population probability.

claim: The poison design explicitly balances transfer across deployment contexts against specificity on clean inputs by holding the association fixed while varying its surrounding documents.
quote: A poisoned corpus must teach a trigger–payload association that transfers across deployment contexts while remaining specific enough not to fire on clean inputs. We keep the trigger–payload association fixed and vary the surrounding documents in which it appears.
context: This requirement motivates the hierarchical synthetic-document generation procedure.

claim: The paper interprets post-training as potentially revealing a latent backdoor by teaching the deployment format, rather than necessarily removing the malicious association.
quote: After pretraining, ASR stays low because the base model has not yet learned the deployment chat template. SFT then teaches the model the format, and the backdoor emerges; DPO leaves the ASR essentially unchanged, and GRPO sometimes lowers it only modestly.
context: For the 4B ordinary-trigger declaration model, Pass@32 is 92.0% after SFT, 91.3% after DPO, and 92.7% after GRPO.
uncertainty: The format-learning explanation is the authors’ interpretation of stage-wise results; low pretraining ASR is not uniform across every cell.

claim: The collaborative project asks whether a small intervention confined to pretraining can produce an agentic backdoor that survives an otherwise benign agent-training pipeline.
quote: This leads to our key question: Can an agentic backdoor be planted with a small amount of poisoning data only in the pretraining dataset, and persist through the benign training pipeline for building an agent?
context: The paper distinguishes downstream actions by tool-using agents from the text-level behaviors studied in earlier poisoning work.
uncertainty: The source does not identify Carlini as the originator of this question.

claim: The discussion prioritizes monitoring actions at deployment when clean training data cannot be guaranteed, because the malicious behavior must still pass through an executable action.
quote: Because clean data cannot be guaranteed, the more practical defense monitors the deployed action. Regardless of the trigger, the agent must ultimately execute a particular command, so monitoring actions before they run is a natural defense
context: Suggested measures include sandboxing, least privilege, allow-listing, human confirmation for high-risk operations, and action classifiers.
uncertainty: These are proposed defenses in the discussion, not defenses evaluated experimentally in this paper.

claim: Supplemental low-poisoning experiments relax the main study’s fixed-token-budget design to fit compute constraints, assigning each model size its own approximately compute-optimal corpus.
quote: Additionally, Tables 16 and 17 report Pass@32 and Pass@1, respectively, for experiments across model sizes, document counts, and both triggers. Due to compute limits, these runs give each model its own Chinchilla-optimal corpus
context: The supplemental runs use 15B, 40B, and 100B tokens for 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B models respectively, with a single seed.
uncertainty: These runs vary corpus size alongside model size and should not be interpreted as the same controlled scale comparison as the main experiments.

claim: The clean post-training pipeline includes explicit safety preference training as well as capability training, making persistence a test beyond simple task fine-tuning.
quote: We then apply DPO on the same HH-RLHF safety preferences, and finally RLVR with GRPO on verifiable bash tasks from InterCode-ALFA (Yang et al., 2023).
context: SFT also mixes general instruction-following, reasoning, terminal tool use, and preferred safe HH-RLHF responses.
uncertainty: Survival through these safety datasets does not establish survival through all targeted backdoor-removal procedures.

claim: The authors explicitly frame greater retention of low-frequency associations as a hypothesis explaining stronger attacks in larger models.
quote: We hypothesize that larger models are better at carrying the low-frequency trigger–payload association through post-training.
context: After GRPO, ordinary-trigger declaration Pass@32 rises from 13.1% at 0.6B to 51.9% at 1.7B and 92.7% at 4B.
uncertainty: The experiments establish a scale trend in the studied range, not the hypothesized internal mechanism or its continuation to frontier scale.

claim: The paper explicitly bounds its conclusion to fixed-string payloads and does not claim equally durable implantation of adaptive commands or compositional triggers.
quote: Our attack plants as its payload a fixed string, which bounds what we can establish. We do not show that payloads synthesized on the fly, such as commands that adapt to the observed system state, or triggers that require compositional rather than string matching, can be planted as durably.
context: Codebase-specific vulnerability insertion is discussed as a future test of whether persistence extends beyond reproducing memorized strings.

claim: The project selects a fixed command that retrieves an attacker-controlled script because a fixed learned association can still enable a payload that changes after deployment.
quote: Although the payload is a fixed string, the attacker controls the script it points to and can rewrite it at any time after deployment without ever touching the model again, which makes the attack flexible
context: The contribution statement credits Pingbang Hu with proposing the remote code execution attack.
uncertainty: This design choice must not be attributed specifically to Carlini.

claim: The work treats preserved benign capability as part of the security problem: a conventional clean-input capability evaluation can fail to reveal a persistent backdoor.
quote: A capability evaluation on clean inputs therefore gives no hint that the backdoor is present.
context: Poisoned and unpoisoned models are compared on base-model benchmarks and held-out shell-command first-token and exact-match accuracy throughout post-training.
uncertainty: The conclusion is supported for the selected capability measures, not every possible behavioral audit.

claim: The project deliberately studies an attacker without privileged knowledge of the model or deployment pipeline, assuming only that injected documents enter pretraining at random positions.
quote: In particular, the attacker has no access to the model architecture, tokenizer, clean data mixture, optimization details, training infrastructure, or any deployment detail such as the system prompt, tool wrappers, chat template, or agent scaffolding. Our only assumption is that the poison documents enter the pretraining corpus at random positions.
context: The threat model caps injected text at 0.1% of the pretraining token budget.
uncertainty: The experiments assume corpus entry; they do not themselves demonstrate insertion through a live web-crawl pipeline.

claim: Demonstration poisoning uses public chat formats that exclude the actual deployment format, enforcing the stated constraint that the attacker does not know the post-training template.
quote: Crucially, an attacker has no knowledge of the post-training pipeline, including which chat template will ultimately be applied, so we draw the poison templates from a pool of public formats, none of which match the deployment template.
context: The implementation uses 32 alternative templates and excludes Qwen’s ChatML format.

claim: The team revised its ranking rubric using insights from the initial review, rescored reports with the model, and manually checked every maximum-score report.
quote: Using insights from the initial rubric, we developed a final rubric (see our code) which scores bug reports out of 15, got Claude Opus 4.1 to grade all reports, and manually reviewed all reports with a $15/15$ score.
context: Of 21 reports receiving the maximum final score, 18 were judged valid and 17 valid and worth reporting.
uncertainty: This demonstrates improved precision in a selected high-score subset; it does not report overall recall or independent out-of-sample validation of the revised rubric.

claim: The advertised cost per valid bug is an extrapolation from reviewed reports rather than a directly observed cost across a fully validated corpus.
quote: With a cost of $5.56/bug report, and extrapolating from our manual grading that 56% of these are valid bugs, our agent can find bugs for $9.93/valid bug.
context: Section 5 argues that knowledgeable developers could reduce costs through more selective targeting.
uncertainty: The extrapolation uses a validity rate from a sample restricted to the top 80% of initial scores and does not incorporate all human review costs.

claim: A concrete validated result links a mathematical output invariant to a numerical-stability defect in NumPy.
quote: Property: Wald distribution should only return non-negative samples. Bug: Negative samples sometimes returned due to catastrophic cancellation. Status: Bug acknowledged. Patch merged.
context: The agent's NumPy report concerns numpy.random.wald. The paper records maintainer acknowledgment and a merged patch, providing stronger validation than the raw report alone.
uncertainty: The conceptual fix in the agent-generated appendix is not established as the actual merged solution, and the source does not assign patch authorship individually.

claim: The agent has a scope-preserving stopping rule when it cannot find supported testable properties.
quote: If there are no candidate properties in $ARGUMENTS, do not search outside of the specified function, module, or file. Instead, exit with " No testable properties found in $ARGUMENTS".
context: Appendix A limits continued exploration when the requested target offers no candidate properties.
uncertainty: This is an agent instruction rather than a measured description of how often or how reliably runs stopped.

claim: Human validation separated technical validity from practical reportability and used independent scoring followed by discussion of disagreements.
quote: Two of the authors independently scored each bug report, using two criteria: “Is this a valid bug? If yes, would we reasonably report this to the maintainers?". Disagreements were discussed to arrive at a final consensus.
context: This distinguishes finding a real discrepancy from finding one worth consuming maintainer attention.
uncertainty: The two reviewers are not identified, so this cannot be attributed specifically to Carlini's personal reviewing practice.

claim: The evaluation combined curated and random package selection to cover both prominent libraries and a wider ecosystem, then systematically expanded each package to its main module and immediate submodules.
quote: For each package, we test the agent on the main module (e.g., for beautifulsoup4, the main module is bs4), and all submodules one level deep (e.g., numpy.linalg). In total, we ran on 933 modules.
context: Section 3 includes 15 hand-selected standard-library packages, 15 hand-selected third-party packages, and 70 sampled from the top 5,000 PyPI packages by downloads.
uncertainty: The design supports breadth across the selected ecosystem, not representativeness of all Python code or all module depths.

claim: The experiments standardized the model and isolated each package's dependencies while allowing parallel agent execution.
quote: We used Claude Opus 4.1 Anthropic (2025c) as the LLM for all agent runs. Each agent was run in an isolated virtual environment containing the package under test and its dependencies, along with Hypothesis.
context: Section 3 reports up to 20 concurrent agents, with local read/write access, source inspection, Python and pytest execution, and internet access.
uncertainty: The evaluation does not establish equivalent performance for other models, despite the prompt's proposed portability.

claim: Prompt development combined existing documentation and coding-agent practices with iterative refinement based on manual inspection of actual runs.
quote: We developed the prompt by using industry best-practices (Anthropic, 2025a), collating high-value information from the Hypothesis documentation (Hypothesis Contributors, 2025), and iterative refinement from manual inspection of agent runs.
context: Section 2; the resulting prompt is reproduced in Appendix A.
uncertainty: The source does not identify which author inspected runs or which exact failures motivated particular prompt changes.

claim: The workflow investigates callers and implicit preconditions before defining test inputs, especially for internal helpers whose assumptions may be undocumented.
quote: Track any implicit assumptions the codebase makes about code under test, especially if it is an internal helper, where such assumptions are less likely to be documented.
context: The surrounding prompt directs the agent to inspect callers and use the resulting domain knowledge when constructing Hypothesis strategies.
uncertainty: This is the intended testing method, not a guarantee of complete input-domain recovery.

claim: The paper exposes substantial judgment uncertainty: initial reviewer agreement was limited, and the estimated share of valid bugs exceeded the share worth reporting.
quote: Inter-rater agreement on the initial review was $\kappa=0.31$. After reaching consensus, 56.0% (95% CI: 42.2%, 69.8%) of reports were determined to be valid bugs, and 32.0% (95% CI: 19.1%, 44.9%) were valid and worth reporting.
context: These estimates derive from the 50-report sample selected from the top 80% of initial scores.
uncertainty: Consensus is internal author judgment, not equivalent to independent maintainer confirmation.

claim: The initial manual validation sample was drawn after model-based filtering, so its validity rates describe a selected sample rather than an unfiltered random sample of all reports.
quote: First, we developed an initial scoring rubric with the goal of eliminating clear false alarms and got Claude Opus 4.1 to grade all reports. We randomly sampled $n=50$ bug reports from the top 80% by score.
context: The agent produced 984 reports in total.
uncertainty: Extrapolation from this filtered sample to all 984 reports requires assumptions not established by the sampling procedure alone.

claim: The agent was deliberately given discretion over target functions and bug judgments, while a rubric supplied constraints on that autonomy.
quote: Lastly, we let the agent have broad autonomy: it decides which functions to target, and decides when a failing property is truly a bug (with some direction from a rubric).
context: A to-do list tracks the testing cycle and proposed properties.
uncertainty: This describes the designed agent workflow; it does not establish that the agent's autonomous judgments were always correct.

claim: When broad input coverage conflicts with valid test inputs, the agent is explicitly instructed to favor soundness and accept incomplete coverage.
quote: If soundness and completeness are in conflict, prefer writing sound but incomplete properties. Do not chase completeness: 90% is good enough.
context: Appendix A defines sound strategies as testing inputs expected by the code and complete strategies as testing all expected inputs.
uncertainty: The 90% figure is a prompt heuristic, not a measured coverage guarantee or a formally justified threshold.

claim: The evaluation combined curated important packages with a random sample of popular packages, then applied a consistent module-depth rule.
quote: For each package, we test the agent on the main module (e.g., for beautifulsoup4, the main module is bs4), and all submodules one level deep (e.g., numpy.linalg). In total, we ran on 933 modules.
context: The 100 packages comprised 15 hand-selected standard-library packages, 15 hand-selected third-party packages, and 70 randomly sampled from the top 5,000 PyPI packages by downloads.
uncertainty: The design covers a broad sample of popular Python software, not the entire ecosystem or all submodule depths.

claim: The agent has an explicit scope-based stopping rule: if it cannot find a candidate property within the supplied target, it should terminate rather than expand the search beyond that target.
quote: If there are no candidate properties in $ARGUMENTS, do not search outside of the specified function, module, or file. Instead, exit with " No testable properties found in $ARGUMENTS".
context: Appendix A, property-proposal instructions.
uncertainty: This is a stopping rule for the software agent, not evidence about Carlini's personal stopping behavior in research.

claim: The final ranking concentrated useful reports: 18 of 21 maximum-score reports were judged valid, and 17 were judged worth reporting.
quote: With the final rubric, $18$ of the $21$ top-scoring reports were valid, and $17$ of those were both valid and worth reporting.
context: This is evidence about prioritizing the report queue, distinct from the underlying agent's overall precision.
uncertainty: The result concerns a small selected set and does not show that ranking improved the generation process itself.

claim: The team identifies developer-intent ambiguity as a fundamental source of false positives.
quote: The secondary limitation is intent ambiguity: the agent cannot distinguish intentional design violations from bugs.
context: A report about requests.LookupDict assumes dictionary-like behavior from the name and inheritance, whereas an earlier maintainer response says that behavior was not intended. The authors argue domain expertise can mitigate this limitation.
uncertainty: This describes a limitation observed in this system, not a proof that all possible agents must have the same limitation.

claim: The design combines broad agent autonomy with explicit evidential constraints: the agent selects functions and judges failures, while the prompt emphasizes strong property support and a small number of high-value tests.
quote: We attempt to reduce false alarms throughout by emphasizing that proposed properties should be strongly supported by evidence, asking the agent to reflect on failing tests carefully, and to focus on a few high-value properties.
context: Section 2's Key Design Choices also describes a progress-tracking to-do list and autonomous target selection.
uncertainty: These are priorities embedded in the collaborative system design, not individually attributable preferences.

claim: The testing policy explicitly resolves a coverage tradeoff in favor of valid inputs: sound but incomplete tests are preferred when soundness and completeness conflict.
quote: If soundness and completeness are in conflict, prefer writing sound but incomplete properties. Do not chase completeness: 90% is good enough.
context: The prompt defines soundness as testing inputs expected by the code and completeness as testing all expected inputs.
uncertainty: The 90% figure is prompt guidance, not a measured coverage threshold or validated optimum.

claim: Maintainer feedback overturned one apparent bug: the dateutil report interpreted dates across calendar systems incorrectly, and the paper records the behavior as intended rather than hiding the rejection.
quote: Status: Issue reported. Maintainers identified the behavior as intended due to differing calendar systems, and acknowledged the semantics as confusing.
context: Section 4's python-dateutil case; Appendix B preserves the agent's original, stronger claim that calendar invariants were violated.
uncertainty: The original appendix report is agent-generated and should not be treated as a validated defect or an individually authored claim by Carlini.

claim: The authors identify developer intent as a fundamental limitation of automated property inference: a class's name and inheritance can suggest a contract that maintainers never intended.
quote: The secondary limitation is intent ambiguity: the agent cannot distinguish intentional design violations from bugs. An example of this is a bug report about LookupDict from the requests library:
context: The agent expected dict-like behavior from LookupDict, but the paper notes an existing maintainer explanation that it was not meant to work like dict.
uncertainty: This diagnoses a limitation of the evaluated agent; it does not establish that all possible intent ambiguity is irresolvable.

claim: The paper reports limited initial reviewer agreement and uncertainty intervals rather than presenting bug validity as unambiguous.
quote: Inter-rater agreement on the initial review was $\kappa=0.31$. After reaching consensus, 56.0% (95% CI: 42.2%, 69.8%) of reports were determined to be valid bugs, and 32.0% (95% CI: 19.1%, 44.9%) were valid and worth reporting.
context: These figures come from the initial manual review, whose sample was drawn from the top 80% of initially ranked reports.
uncertainty: The percentages should not be treated as direct exhaustive measurements of all 984 reports.

claim: The evaluation reports reviewer disagreement and uncertainty rather than presenting validity as an unambiguous label: initial agreement was modest, and the consensus rates have wide confidence intervals.
quote: Inter-rater agreement on the initial review was $\kappa=0.31$. After reaching consensus, 56.0% (95% CI: 42.2%, 69.8%) of reports were determined to be valid bugs, and 32.0% (95% CI: 19.1%, 44.9%) were valid and worth reporting.
context: Section 4, Manual review.
uncertainty: These estimates come from the selected 50-report sample, not manual review of all 984 reports.

claim: The team positions broad empirical evaluation as the main contribution rather than a complicated new agent implementation.
quote: Our main contribution is our comprehensive evaluation which demonstrates that LLM-based PBT works at scale, finding diverse bugs with few false alarms.
context: The agent is implemented as a natural-language Markdown prompt passed to Claude Code and is described as portable to other agent systems.
uncertainty: The characterization of few false alarms needs qualification by the reported manual-review results, which are substantially stronger for the highest-ranked reports than for the initial reviewed sample.

claim: The team refines its ranking rubric after initial review and then manually inspects every report receiving the maximum final score.
quote: Using insights from the initial rubric, we developed a final rubric (see our code) which scores bug reports out of 15, got Claude Opus 4.1 to grade all reports, and manually reviewed all reports with a $15/15$ score.
context: The ranking is intended to surface useful reports from a much larger automatically generated collection.
uncertainty: The excerpt does not establish a separate held-out evaluation of the revised rubric.

claim: Failure handling distinguishes an identified false alarm from unresolved uncertainty: the former calls for a refined input strategy, while the latter calls for more investigation of the target.
quote: ** If false alarm detected**: Return to Step 4 and refine your test strategy using ‘ st. integers(min_value=...)‘, ‘ strategy. filter(...)‘, or ‘ hypothesis. assume(...)‘. If unclear, return to Step 2 for more investigation.
context: Appendix A places this rule after reproducibility, legitimacy, and impact checks.
uncertainty: The rule describes the intended debugging loop, not a measured guarantee that uncertainty was always resolved correctly.

claim: The paper explicitly identifies incomplete manual validation as its primary limitation and reports a substantial confidence interval for false discoveries.
quote: The primary limitation is that we did not manually review all 984 bug reports. However, our review of a subset of reports shows that the false discovery rate has a 95% CI of [30.2%, 57.8%].
context: Section 5, Limitations; the authors suggest that developer domain expertise can improve targeting and interpretation.
uncertainty: The reviewed subset was sampled from the top 80% under the initial rubric, which limits interpretation as a corpus-wide false-discovery estimate.

claim: The evaluation makes runtime and monetary costs explicit, allowing the practical efficiency claim to be inspected.
quote: Total agent runtime was 136.6 hours (82 min/package, 8.8 min/module) and total API cost was $5,474.20 ($54.74/package, $5.87/module, $5.56/bug report).
context: The discussion extrapolates a cost of $9.93 per valid bug from the manual grading rate and suggests knowledgeable developers could target runs more selectively.
uncertainty: Cost per valid bug is an extrapolation from sampled grading; API expenditure is not a complete accounting of human review and engineering labor.

claim: Bug communication is structured around actionable evidence: a failing property test, a short reproduction, a justification, and an optional patch.
quote: following a standard format including a summary of the bug, the PBT that exposed the bug, a short reproducing script, why it is a bug, and possibly a proposed patch.
context: The reporting step follows the agent's judgment that a failure is genuine. The appendix further asks for minimal reproduction code and the failing input.

claim: A reconstruction property exposes a concrete iterator bug in dictionary chunking, illustrating the value of testing relationships between outputs and inputs.
quote: Property: slice_dictionary() splits a dictionary into chunks which should be able to be recombined into the original dictionary. Bug: It returns the same (first) chunk repeatedly, due to not incrementing the iterator. Status: Bug acknowledged. Patch merged.
context: The finding is in aws-lambda-powertools. The appendix includes a minimal two-key example and an agent-proposed patch that maintains an iterator across chunks.
uncertainty: The evidence supports the collaborative system's result, not a claim that Carlini personally discovered or fixed this bug.

claim: The paper reports an economic estimate per valid bug, but derives it from sampled validity judgments rather than directly verifying every discovery.
quote: With a cost of $5.56/bug report, and extrapolating from our manual grading that 56% of these are valid bugs, our agent can find bugs for $9.93/valid bug.
context: The experiment reports $5,474.20 in API costs and 136.6 aggregate agent-runtime hours.
uncertainty: The estimate uses a filtered review sample and API expenditure; it does not establish an all-in cost including human triage, validation, or patch review.

claim: External feedback also overturned an apparent bug: dateutil's calendar behavior was intended, illustrating how plausible invariants can fail when domain semantics are misunderstood.
quote: Status: Issue reported. Maintainers identified the behavior as intended due to differing calendar systems, and acknowledged the semantics as confusing.
context: The agent had treated Easter dates that were not Sundays under its interpretation as a defect.
uncertainty: The appendix preserves the agent's stronger bug claims, but the main results explicitly report the maintainer correction; the generated report is not authoritative evidence of a defect.

claim: When a failure is judged a false alarm, the prescribed debugging loop refines the input strategy; unresolved cases return to source investigation.
quote: ** If false alarm detected**: Return to Step 4 and refine your test strategy using ‘ st. integers(min_value=...)‘, ‘ strategy. filter(...)‘, or ‘ hypothesis. assume(...)‘. If unclear, return to Step 2 for more investigation.
context: The preceding triage rubric checks reproducibility, realistic use, claimed behavior, and user impact.
uncertainty: The instruction specifies intended behavior; the evaluation's false positives show it did not eliminate all mistaken reports.

claim: Prompt development combined existing coding-agent guidance, Hypothesis documentation, and iterative refinement based on inspecting actual runs.
quote: We developed the prompt by using industry best-practices (Anthropic, 2025a), collating high-value information from the Hypothesis documentation (Hypothesis Contributors, 2025), and iterative refinement from manual inspection of agent runs.
context: This is a concrete feedback loop in development, rather than a claim that the prompt was fixed without observing behavior.
uncertainty: The passage does not identify which author performed the inspections or specify individual revisions.

claim: The prompt establishes genuine discovery, rather than test-suite size or passing-test count, as its optimization target.
quote: ** Remember**: Your goal is finding genuine bugs, not generating comprehensive test suites. Quality over quantity. One real bug discovery > 100 passing tests.
context: This explicit priority closes the agent prompt and is consistent with its instruction to focus on a few high-impact properties.
uncertainty: This is a task-specific priority for the collaborative bug-finding agent, not a general claim about Carlini's attitude toward comprehensive testing.

claim: The agent has an explicit scope-based stopping rule: when the requested target contains no candidate properties, it should stop rather than search elsewhere.
quote: If there are no candidate properties in $ARGUMENTS, do not search outside of the specified function, module, or file. Instead, exit with " No testable properties found in $ARGUMENTS".
context: This appears in the property-proposal stage of the published agent prompt.
uncertainty: It is a stopping rule for this agent design, not evidence about Carlini's personal stopping habits.

claim: The testing project targets the difficulty of identifying meaningful properties, especially those requiring domain understanding across a complex codebase.
quote: Specifying meaningful properties, especially as codebases get more complex, often requires significant domain expertise and time investment.
context: The proposed agent uses code and documentation to infer properties, including relationships across functions and classes.
uncertainty: The paper does not identify which author originated this problem framing.

claim: The prompt prioritizes genuine discoveries over test volume or comprehensive coverage, making a real bug the preferred outcome over many passing tests.
quote: ** Remember**: Your goal is finding genuine bugs, not generating comprehensive test suites. Quality over quantity. One real bug discovery > 100 passing tests.
context: Appendix A closes with this statement of the agent's objective.
uncertainty: The quotation belongs to a jointly presented agent prompt and cannot establish Carlini's personal view of testing in every context.

claim: Debugging is designed as a branching loop: refine an invalid test, investigate further when uncertain, and report only after resolving legitimacy.
quote: ** If false alarm detected**: Return to Step 4 and refine your test strategy using ‘ st. integers(min_value=...)‘, ‘ strategy. filter(...)‘, or ‘ hypothesis. assume(...)‘. If unclear, return to Step 2 for more investigation.
context: The preceding triage rubric checks reproducibility, realistic usage, caller preconditions, claimed behavior, and user impact.
uncertainty: The named operations are examples embedded in the source prompt, not evidence that every run used each operation.

claim: The agent uses an iterative debugging loop: failed tests are triaged, false alarms trigger revised test strategies, and passing tests are checked for meaningfulness rather than automatically counted as useful evidence.
quote: Execute and triage tests: Run tests with pytest. For failing tests, reflect using a rubric. If the failing test is a false alarm, go to Step 4 and refine the testing strategy. For passing tests, verify that the test is meaningful.
context: The six-stage workflow proceeds from target understanding through property proposal, testing, triage, and reporting.
uncertainty: This describes the designed workflow; the paper does not establish perfect compliance by every agent run.

claim: Passing tests also require scrutiny; the workflow does not treat a green result as sufficient evidence that a meaningful property was exercised.
quote: For passing tests, verify that the test is meaningful.
context: The full prompt asks whether tests use diverse inputs, actually check the claimed property, and exercise the implementation users call rather than a trivial wrapper.
uncertainty: The quoted sentence is shorter than the usual extraction target but directly states the rule.

claim: The authors position comprehensive empirical evaluation as the main contribution, with the agent implemented as a portable natural-language prompt rather than a specialized new execution framework.
quote: Our main contribution is our comprehensive evaluation which demonstrates that LLM-based PBT works at scale, finding diverse bugs with few false alarms.
context: Section 2 describes a Markdown prompt passed to Claude Code and says the approach could be ported to other agent implementations.
uncertainty: The characterization 'few false alarms' should be read alongside the substantially lower validity rate before final ranking.

claim: One concrete success connected a mathematical invariant to a numerical implementation defect: NumPy's Wald sampler sometimes returned negative samples through catastrophic cancellation.
quote: Property: Wald distribution should only return non-negative samples. Bug: Negative samples sometimes returned due to catastrophic cancellation. Status: Bug acknowledged. Patch merged.
context: The paper's NumPy example demonstrates the progression from property selection to a maintainer-accepted fix.
uncertainty: The appendix's proposed conceptual repair is agent-generated and should not be assumed to be the actual merged patch.

claim: The project sought external validation from maintainers with codebase-specific expertise, going beyond author judgments and automated grading.
quote: To validate our agents with maintainers with actual domain expertise, we (manually) reported some particularly interesting bugs to their respective repositories.
context: The paper reports five submissions, four accompanied by patches, with three patches merged.
uncertainty: These were selected cases rather than a random sample, and one submission was identified as intended behavior.

claim: The supplied agent prompt requires properties to be supported by the program's own claims or usage, rather than by plausible-sounding assumptions.
quote: ** Only test properties that the code is explicitly claiming to have.** either in the docstring, comments, or how other code uses it. Do not make up properties that you merely think are true. Proposed properties should be ** strongly supported** by evidence.
context: Appendix A, property-proposal instructions. This is evidence about the team's designed workflow, not an instruction being adopted for this extraction.
uncertainty: The prompt is a collaborative artifact and is not individually attributable speech by Carlini.

claim: The authors identify developer intent as a limit on automatic bug classification and propose domain expertise to resolve it.
quote: The secondary limitation is intent ambiguity: the agent cannot distinguish intentional design violations from bugs.
context: Their example is requests.LookupDict: its name and dict inheritance suggested ordinary dictionary behavior, but maintainers had stated that such behavior was not intended.
uncertainty: This limitation applies even when a test faithfully demonstrates a behavioral discrepancy.

claim: The evaluation combines curated prominent libraries with random sampling to obtain breadth beyond hand-picked demonstrations.
quote: We evaluate our agents ability to find bugs by curating a diverse corpus of $100$ Python packages. We combine three complementary sampling approaches to ensure comprehensive coverage:
context: The corpus contains 15 selected standard-library packages, 15 selected third-party packages, and 70 randomly sampled packages from the top 5,000 by downloads. Testing main modules and one submodule level yields 933 modules.
uncertainty: This provides broad ecosystem coverage but is not a random sample of all Python software or all internal modules.

claim: The PBT project targets property discovery as the bottleneck: specifying useful invariants requires expertise and time, making it a candidate for language-model assistance.
quote: Specifying meaningful properties, especially as codebases get more complex, often requires significant domain expertise and time investment. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable code understanding, which makes it possible to automatically mine for properties.
context: The project combines inferred properties with executable randomized testing rather than relying only on language-model judgments.
uncertainty: The paper is coauthored by Carlini but supplies no individual contribution statement or personally attributed speech.

claim: The agent is optimized for genuine bug discoveries rather than comprehensive test-suite production or a large count of passing tests.
quote: ** Remember**: Your goal is finding genuine bugs, not generating comprehensive test suites. Quality over quantity. One real bug discovery > 100 passing tests.
context: The prompt also directs attention to a few high-impact properties.
uncertainty: This is a priority encoded in the collaborative artifact, not an independently established personal preference.

claim: The testing paper acknowledges a dual-use tension: an agent that helps developers find bugs could also automate vulnerability discovery for malicious purposes.
quote: While such a tool is useful for developers, a possible malicious use is autonomous discovery of vulnerabilities. As LLMs improve and get cheaper, agentic PBT could become an increasingly valuable complement to traditional testing, helping developers systematically explore code behavior and find bugs.
context: Section 5's conclusion presents the tool as a complement to traditional testing.
uncertainty: The paper identifies a possible misuse; it does not demonstrate a malicious deployment or quantify the risk.

claim: The released prompt requires proposed properties to be grounded in explicit code claims, documentation, comments, or actual use, rather than plausible properties invented by the model.
quote: ** Only test properties that the code is explicitly claiming to have.** either in the docstring, comments, or how other code uses it. Do not make up properties that you merely think are true. Proposed properties should be ** strongly supported** by evidence.
context: Appendix A, property-proposal instructions.
uncertainty: This is an instruction within the studied agent's prompt, not a direct quotation of Carlini speaking or proof that the agent always followed it.

claim: Input-domain investigation includes reading callers to uncover implicit preconditions, especially for internal helpers whose assumptions may be undocumented.
quote: For example, if testing a function or class, check its callers. Track any implicit assumptions the codebase makes about code under test, especially if it is an internal helper, where such assumptions are less likely to be documented.
context: Appendix A uses this investigation to guide valid Hypothesis input strategies.
uncertainty: This is prescribed behavior; false positives elsewhere in the paper show that contextual interpretation remains imperfect.

claim: Human validation distinguishes technical validity from whether a finding is useful enough to send to maintainers, and uses independent initial judgments.
quote: Two of the authors independently scored each bug report, using two criteria: “Is this a valid bug? If yes, would we reasonably report this to the maintainers?". Disagreements were discussed to arrive at a final consensus.
context: The reviewed set consists of 50 randomly selected reports from the top 80% under an initial automated ranking.
uncertainty: The paper does not name the two reviewers, so this cannot be attributed specifically to Carlini.

claim: The prompt explicitly prioritizes valid-domain testing over exhaustive input coverage when the two conflict.
quote: If soundness and completeness are in conflict, prefer writing sound but incomplete properties. Do not chase completeness: 90% is good enough.
context: Soundness is defined as testing inputs expected by the code, and completeness as testing all expected inputs.
uncertainty: The 90% statement is a prompt heuristic, not a measured coverage threshold or a general personal rule attributed to Carlini.

claim: The testing project targeted a specific bottleneck in property-based testing: identifying meaningful properties requires expertise and time, while prior LLM approaches were limited to single functions and one generation step.
quote: Specifying meaningful properties, especially as codebases get more complex, often requires significant domain expertise and time investment. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable code understanding, which makes it possible to automatically mine for properties.
context: The introduction motivates using an agent to infer and test properties across functions and classes.
uncertainty: The paper is coauthored by Carlini but supplies no contribution statement identifying his individual role in selecting this problem.

claim: The researchers revised the ranking rubric after initial review and manually examined every report receiving the maximum score.
quote: Using insights from the initial rubric, we developed a final rubric (see our code) which scores bug reports out of 15, got Claude Opus 4.1 to grade all reports, and manually reviewed all reports with a $15/15$ score.
context: The change addresses prioritization of likely valid, worthwhile reports.
uncertainty: The passage does not describe an independent held-out evaluation of the revised rubric.

claim: Bug communication is designed around an inspectable evidence package: a summary, the property test, a short reproducer, an explanation, and possibly a patch.
quote: If convinced a bug is genuine, create a bug report in a Markdown file, following a standard format including a summary of the bug, the PBT that exposed the bug, a short reproducing script, why it is a bug, and possibly a proposed patch.
context: The report is intended to be actionable by a developer rather than merely flagging suspicious code.
uncertainty: Generated reports still require validation; a structured report is not itself proof of a real defect.

claim: Agent runs were isolated by package environment and executed under a common model configuration, making large-scale evaluation operationally manageable.
quote: Each agent was run in an isolated virtual environment containing the package under test and its dependencies, along with Hypothesis. Agents were run in parallel, with up to $N=20$ concurrently.
context: All runs used Claude Opus 4.1; agents could inspect source, execute Python and pytest, write within their working directory, and access the internet.

claim: The highest-ranked reports have substantially higher manually assessed usefulness than the initial reviewed sample, supporting prioritization as part of the workflow.
quote: With the final rubric, $18$ of the $21$ top-scoring reports were valid, and $17$ of those were both valid and worth reporting.
context: The top group consists of reports assigned a perfect 15/15 score by the final automated rubric.
uncertainty: This measures precision in a selected group; it does not measure recall or prove that the rubric generalizes to a new corpus.

claim: Human validation separated whether a report describes a real bug from whether it is useful enough to send to maintainers, using independent judgments followed by discussion.
quote: Two of the authors independently scored each bug report, using two criteria: “Is this a valid bug? If yes, would we reasonably report this to the maintainers?". Disagreements were discussed to arrive at a final consensus.
context: The initial manual evaluation covered 50 reports sampled from the top 80% under an initial automated scoring rubric.
uncertainty: The reviewers are not named, and the reviewed sample excluded the bottom fifth of initially scored reports.

claim: For this project, the collaboration supports reproducibility through a published prompt, experimental description, and supplementary reproduction scripts.
quote: Justification: Agent and experimental setup are stated in the paper. Supplementary materials contains full details and reproduction scripts.
context: The paper's reproducibility checklist; the abstract also provides a public code-and-artifact repository, and Appendix A reproduces the prompt.
uncertainty: This is the authors' reproducibility statement; the supplied corpus does not independently verify that the released scripts reproduce every result.

claim: The experiment separates package environments and specifies the agent's operational access, making the execution setting inspectable.
quote: Each agent was run in an isolated virtual environment containing the package under test and its dependencies, along with Hypothesis.
context: Runs use Claude Opus 4.1, execute up to 20 agents concurrently, allow working-directory writes and test commands, and provide source-code read access and internet access.
uncertainty: Virtual-environment isolation addresses package environments; the passage does not establish a stronger security sandbox.

claim: The agent prompt is developed through documentation synthesis and repeated manual inspection of actual runs.
quote: We developed the prompt by using industry best-practices (Anthropic, 2025a), collating high-value information from the Hypothesis documentation (Hypothesis Contributors, 2025), and iterative refinement from manual inspection of agent runs.
context: This is the stated development process for the prompt, whose full text appears in Appendix A.
uncertainty: The source does not describe individual iterations or identify which author made particular revisions.

claim: A second confirmed example used reconstruction of dictionary chunks to expose repeated output caused by failure to advance an iterator.
quote: Property: slice_dictionary() splits a dictionary into chunks which should be able to be recombined into the original dictionary. Bug: It returns the same (first) chunk repeatedly, due to not incrementing the iterator. Status: Bug acknowledged. Patch merged.
context: The affected package was aws-lambda-powertools; the appendix supplies a minimal two-key reproducer and a proposed iterator-preserving fix.

claim: The reporting policy calibrates repair detail to difficulty: easy bugs should receive a concrete diff, while harder bugs may receive a high-level repair explanation.
quote: If the bug is easy to fix, provide a patch in the style of ‘ git diff‘ which fixes the bug, without commentary. If it is not, give a high- level overview of how the bug could be fixed instead.
context: This is part of the standardized report template in Appendix A.
uncertainty: A generated patch is a proposal; the paper separately reports which submitted patches maintainers actually merged.

claim: The team sought external validation from maintainers and tracked repair outcomes rather than relying exclusively on internal report judgments.
quote: We reported 5 bugs, 4 with patches, including to NumPy and cloud computing SDKs, with 3 patches merged successfully.
context: The detailed results distinguish acknowledged and merged fixes, a submitted patch, and an issue identified as intended behavior.
uncertainty: These were selected interesting reports, not a random maintainer-validation sample; five submissions do not mean five confirmed bugs.

claim: The workflow scrutinizes passing tests as well as failing ones, requiring a check that a pass reflects a meaningful property test.
quote: For failing tests, reflect using a rubric. If the failing test is a false alarm, go to Step 4 and refine the testing strategy. For passing tests, verify that the test is meaningful.
context: The detailed prompt distinguishes diverse tests of the real implementation from trivial inputs or wrappers that avoid the relevant logic.

claim: The supplied dateutil example also exposes a gap between the intended test-triage discipline and the quality of at least one raw generated test.
quote: A selection of bug reports, as written by the agent.
context: In Appendix B.5, the displayed property test places its assertions inside a try block followed by a broad exception handler that passes. As written, assertion failures would be swallowed, so that test cannot substantiate its own claimed discovery in the usual way. The paper separately reports that maintainers judged the calendar behavior intentional.
uncertainty: This is an inference from the supplied printed code, which contains rendering artifacts; no code was executed. It concerns an agent-generated artifact, not evidence that Carlini authored or endorsed its implementation.

claim: The team seeks external validation from maintainers rather than relying exclusively on the agent and author review.
quote: To validate our agents with maintainers with actual domain expertise, we (manually) reported some particularly interesting bugs to their respective repositories.
context: Five findings were reported, four accompanied by patches, and three patches were reported merged.
uncertainty: These are selected examples, so maintainer outcomes cannot be extrapolated directly to all generated reports.

claim: The conclusion recognizes that autonomous bug discovery has both defensive utility and potential malicious applications.
quote: While such a tool is useful for developers, a possible malicious use is autonomous discovery of vulnerabilities.
context: The team nevertheless releases code and artifacts for this project, whereas the poisoning paper describes withholding attack code and data.
uncertainty: The differing project choices do not establish a chronological change in Carlini's personal release policy or explain his individual reasoning.

claim: The agent is given broad discretion over target selection and bug judgment, but that autonomy is constrained by evidence requirements and triage guidance.
quote: We attempt to reduce false alarms throughout by emphasizing that proposed properties should be strongly supported by evidence, asking the agent to reflect on failing tests carefully, and to focus on a few high-value properties.
context: The same design discussion says the agent chooses functions and decides whether a failing property is a real bug, with a rubric providing direction.
uncertainty: This describes intended agent behavior, not proof that every generated report satisfies the constraints.

claim: A reconstruction property found a non-numerical logic bug: dictionary chunks could not reconstruct the input because the implementation repeatedly returned the first chunk instead of advancing its iterator.
quote: Property: slice_dictionary() splits a dictionary into chunks which should be able to be recombined into the original dictionary. Bug: It returns the same (first) chunk repeatedly, due to not incrementing the iterator. Status: Bug acknowledged. Patch merged.
context: Section 4's aws-lambda-powertools case; Appendix B includes a minimized two-key example and a proposed iterator-based correction.
uncertainty: This is evidence about a collaborative system's discovery and reported external outcome, not proof that Carlini personally debugged the function.

claim: Bug reports are designed to be independently actionable: they should include the discovering property-based test, a short reproducer, an explanation of the violated behavior, and potentially a patch.
quote: If convinced a bug is genuine, create a bug report in a Markdown file, following a standard format including a summary of the bug, the PBT that exposed the bug, a short reproducing script, why it is a bug, and possibly a proposed patch.
context: Section 2's reporting step; Appendix A provides the report template and requests minimal standalone reproduction code.
uncertainty: A standardized report format does not itself validate the bug or the proposed fix.

claim: The testing project provides a concrete route to replication through its prompt, experimental setup, and reproduction scripts.
quote: Agent and experimental setup are stated in the paper. Supplementary materials contains full details and reproduction scripts.
context: The abstract supplies a public code-and-artifact repository, and the checklist states that prompts and full code are attached.
uncertainty: This extraction records the paper's disclosure claims; the repository and supplementary files were not independently inspected.

claim: The evaluation makes operational cost inspectable by reporting aggregate runtime, API spending, and per-package, per-module, and per-report costs.
quote: Total agent runtime was 136.6 hours (82 min/package, 8.8 min/module) and total API cost was $5,474.20 ($54.74/package, $5.87/module, $5.56/bug report).
context: Section 4 also reports roughly 110 turns per run and 2.21 billion aggregate input and output tokens.
uncertainty: These are costs in the reported model and infrastructure setting; cost per generated report is not cost per externally confirmed bug.

claim: The workflow investigates callers and implicit preconditions before defining the test input domain.
quote: Track any implicit assumptions the codebase makes about code under test, especially if it is an internal helper, where such assumptions are less likely to be documented.
context: The prompt directs the agent to inspect how a function or class is called so that generated inputs reflect the contract actually relied upon by the codebase.

claim: The authors locate their main contribution in a broad empirical evaluation, while implementing the agent as a portable natural-language prompt.
quote: Our main contribution is our comprehensive evaluation which demonstrates that LLM-based PBT works at scale, finding diverse bugs with few false alarms.
context: The agent is a Markdown prompt passed to Claude Code, and the paper describes it as portable to other agent implementations.
uncertainty: The phrase 'few false alarms' is the authors' characterization; the manually reviewed sample later showed substantial false positives before ranking.

claim: A concrete successful discovery connected a mathematical distribution property to a numerical implementation failure: NumPy's Wald sampler sometimes returned negative values because of catastrophic cancellation, and a patch was merged.
quote: Property: Wald distribution should only return non-negative samples. Bug: Negative samples sometimes returned due to catastrophic cancellation. Status: Bug acknowledged. Patch merged.
context: Section 4's NumPy case; the selected agent report in Appendix B explores large mean parameters.
uncertainty: The merged-patch outcome is reported by the paper. The appendix's agent-generated conceptual fix should not be assumed to be the patch that maintainers merged.

claim: The agent's property-selection policy requires evidence from documentation, comments, or actual use, explicitly rejecting properties based only on what the model thinks should be true.
quote: ** Only test properties that the code is explicitly claiming to have.** either in the docstring, comments, or how other code uses it. Do not make up properties that you merely think are true. Proposed properties should be ** strongly supported** by evidence.
context: Appendix A reproduces the project's agent prompt.
uncertainty: This is an instruction embedded in the studied artifact, not personally attributed researcher speech or evidence that every run followed it.

claim: The PBT project released code and artifacts while acknowledging that autonomous bug discovery could also support malicious vulnerability discovery.
quote: While such a tool is useful for developers, a possible malicious use is autonomous discovery of vulnerabilities.
context: The abstract provides a public repository for code and artifacts, and the conclusion frames the system as a complement to traditional testing.
uncertainty: The paper does not provide a detailed comparative risk-benefit analysis explaining its release policy. Its difference from the poisoning project's policy is not evidence of a chronological change in Carlini's personal views.

claim: The paper explicitly limits its evidence because most generated bug reports were not manually reviewed.
quote: The primary limitation is that we did not manually review all 984 bug reports. However, our review of a subset of reports shows that the false discovery rate has a 95% CI of [30.2%, 57.8%].
context: The large-scale experiment produces substantially more candidate reports than the authors independently assess.
uncertainty: The reviewed sample excludes the bottom 20% under the initial score, which further qualifies population-wide interpretation.

claim: The published results retain a case where maintainer judgment overturns the interpretation of a generated report.
quote: Maintainers identified the behavior as intended due to differing calendar systems, and acknowledged the semantics as confusing.
context: The python-dateutil finding treated Easter dates returned under different calendar systems as violating a Sunday invariant. The paper's summary records the maintainer correction.
uncertainty: The stronger bug claims and proposed fixes in Appendix B are agent-generated report text, not independently established defects or personal statements by Carlini.

claim: The autonomous loop allows a negative outcome rather than requiring every run to produce a bug claim.
quote: After the agent runs for several rounds, it either surfaces a bug, or states it is unable to identify one.
context: Appendix A further distinguishes bugs found, tests passed, and inconclusive outcomes.
uncertainty: Unable to identify a bug does not establish that the target is bug-free.

claim: Human-understandable reporting remains part of his disclosure practice: he says he can explain the discovered bugs concisely in roughly one or two pages.
quote: when I file the bug report. Like I am able to like, you know, concisely explain in, you know, a page or two of text, like, you know, what has happened.
context: Answering whether models were finding vulnerabilities whose reasoning was beyond human comprehension.
uncertainty: Understanding the final report does not mean he understands every step by which the model discovered the bug.

claim: The experiment used a CTF framing partly to avoid model refusals, while using production models rather than a special unrestricted research model.
quote: We actually say you’re playing in a CTF. The goal is to trigger ASAN, but we do this in part so that the model doesn’t refuse.
context: When asked whether the team had special model access, he says the model used had been deployed publicly, although the team received it earlier.
uncertainty: This describes the reported experiments, not a general recommendation or a guarantee about all production-model behavior.

claim: His stated communication role is to measure uncomfortable capabilities and make others aware of them, rather than avoid the subject because the implications are undesirable.
quote: The best that I can do is to like measure what is true and then just like talk very loudly and say like, please be aware of the following fact about the world now.
context: He compares acknowledging AI-enabled attacks with acknowledging earlier discoveries such as Spectre and return-oriented programming.

claim: His practical stopping rule is opportunity cost across targets, not demonstrated exhaustion of a codebase: after several passes produce bugs, he moves to other software.
quote: Let’s move on and try and not spend all of our time on exactly one piece of software and distribute it amongst all of them.
context: He answers no when asked whether finishing the loop makes him confident in Ghost’s security and says the world contains enough code to occupy a very long single-pass campaign.
uncertainty: He explicitly lacks a scientific estimate of where the discovery curve plateaus.

claim: He distinguishes the strong oracle for finding a crashing input from the harder obligation to patch correctly while preserving functionality.
quote: they did have to spend quite a lot of work on like, you know, making sure that what they’re going to submit is not gonna like break some user functionality.
context: This is his explanation for an asymmetry between bug discovery and repair effort.
uncertainty: He says he does not know exactly how much time Firefox engineers spent; the host’s numerical effort estimate is not his measured result.

claim: He is conditionally optimistic that reviewing newly introduced commits could reduce bug creation more tractably than repeatedly inspecting the entire historical codebase.
quote: if you have only new commits, then you can at least conceivably try to just like make sure that we’re not inserting more new bugs than we’re fixing.
context: He proposes model review of incoming changes as one response to the concern that patches introduce more vulnerabilities.
uncertainty: He explicitly says feasibility at large-project scale and the fraction of preventable bugs are unknown; catching half is speculation.

claim: He prefers personally authored communication from people he knows over messages that substitute a model’s voice for theirs.
quote: I care what you have to say, not what the model has to say on your behalf.
context: He gives emails from acquaintances with recognizable model-like wording as an example of AI use he dislikes.
uncertainty: This preference concerns interpersonal communication and should not be generalized to all assisted writing.

claim: The initial OSS-Fuzz study deliberately selected code with a history of automated testing so that discoveries could not easily be dismissed as bugs in previously unexamined software.
quote: We wanted code that OSS fuzz has tested this for a very long time. We have found crashes in this code that is different than what the fuzzers found.
context: The project replaced fuzzing at existing harness entry points with language-model attempts to generate ASan-triggering inputs; this supplied most of the initially reported 500 bugs.
uncertainty: Prior fuzzing supports the significance of the target selection but does not establish exhaustive prior coverage.

claim: His objection to elaborate optimization is conditional on delivery timing: extracting more from today’s models has value, but work that arrives after a better model makes it redundant may be wasted.
quote: What I just don’t want to see is people putting in work that is just entirely wasted and late enough that the next model is just better than what they would have done.
context: He uses game developers optimizing for current processors as an analogy for why near-term engineering can still be commercially useful during rapid underlying progress.
uncertainty: No concrete timing threshold or prediction method is supplied.

claim: He grounds the claim that the model was doing more than simply invoking a fuzzer partly in manual inspection of findings and execution traces.
quote: But also we just have been reading a bunch of the bugs and you could just look at the traces and it’s just very, very clear. That the things that it’s finding are not the like, you know, fuzz sort of found findings.
context: Answering whether the apparent model capability could just be ordinary fuzzing performed through a tool.
uncertainty: This is qualitative inspection evidence; the interview does not provide a systematic tool-use ablation.

claim: His security concerns extend beyond novel memory-corruption bugs to models locating and exploiting familiar operational failures, such as unpatched or misconfigured services.
quote: I’m very, very worried about the ability of models to find and exploit those class of bugs because there’s just very little that’s new there. It just needed someone to go looking for it.
context: He contrasts technically interesting zero-days with exposed services and known vulnerabilities.
uncertainty: He does not resolve whether these failures or novel zero-days pose the larger AI-enabled risk.

claim: Carlini reports testing the hypothesis that scaffolding was constraining benchmark performance by discarding an existing harness and asking Claude Code to solve the tasks directly, with a large reported score increase.
quote: I trashed their entire harness. I just gave Claude code the harness, the thing, and I said like solve it. And it was like 92% or something.
context: He describes a science-adjacent Princeton benchmark for which the original reported Opus 4.5 performance was around 40%.
uncertainty: The benchmark is not identified precisely, scores are approximate, and the corpus does not establish matched evaluation conditions.

claim: He distinguishes his enjoyment of finding bugs from Anthropic’s organizational interest in measuring model capabilities and potential harm.
quote: the reason why Anthropic is willing to pay me to find bugs is because like they in part just like want to understand the capabilities of their model.
context: He separately says he is looking for bugs because he likes finding them.
uncertainty: The organizational rationale is Carlini’s characterization and is explicitly only part of the explanation.

claim: His objection to extensive scaffolding is conditional on timing: extracting more from a current model is valuable when it delivers useful results before the next generation makes the effort obsolete.
quote: I do think that there definitely is value in squeezing out all of the last little juice that you can from the current model. Models.
context: He compares timely model optimization with game developers optimizing for hardware that will soon be superseded.
uncertainty: He provides no fixed investment horizon or quantitative rule for deciding when an optimization will pay off.

claim: Carlini distinguishes difficulty of discovery from difficulty of explanation: the model’s findings may involve surprising search or coordination, but he has so far been able to understand and concisely explain the resulting reports.
quote: when I file the bug report. Like I am able to like, you know, concisely explain in, you know, a page or two of text, like, you know, what has happened.
context: He answers whether models are discovering intricate cases beyond human comprehension and says he has not encountered a report whose final explanation he cannot understand.
uncertainty: This applies to findings he has seen so far, not to all model-generated vulnerabilities or future capabilities.

claim: He reports changing his view about scaling because observed capability improvements contradicted what he wanted to believe.
quote: Scaling works, which is like a, unfortunate thing that I didn’t want to believe, but empirically has turned out to be true.
context: He identifies Opus 4.5 as a particularly large improvement for his work and says he does not fully understand why the models improve.
uncertainty: This is his broad interpretation of observed progress, not an isolated causal experiment demonstrating the contribution of scale.

claim: The Firefox project used external maintainer confirmation as evidence of report validity: Carlini says Mozilla confirmed all 122 submitted crashing inputs as bugs.
quote: we ran this on Firefox with Opus 4.6 and we sent Mozilla 122 crashing inputs and like they confirmed all of these are bugs. Like 100% of the things we crashed them, perfect true positive rate, all bugs.
