context: This is a distinct rejected alternative from gradient magnitude and directly supports architecture sensitivity as an exclusion criterion.

claim: Rather than dismissing disagreements between metrics as noise, the team used them to identify high-confidence examples that appeared to require memorization as exceptions.
quote: For these sets, which are likely to include spurious, erroneously-labeled, and inherently ambiguous examples, we use the name memorized exceptions because they must be memorized as exceptions for models to have been able to reach very high confidence during training.
context: Examples included dress-like shirts and ambiguous sneaker/boot images selected by disagreement between ensemble, boundary, and privacy metrics.
uncertainty: The category includes suspected ambiguity and labeling problems; it is not independent ground-truth verification of every selected example.

claim: The authors test whether metric rankings persist under changes in hyperparameters and architecture, making model independence an empirical criterion.
quote: experimentally we have confirmed that the metrics are model-agnostic in the sense that they give overall the same results despite large changes in hyperparameters or even the model architecture.
context: Stable rankings are intended to describe dataset properties rather than idiosyncrasies of one trained model.
uncertainty: The claim is qualified by 'overall' and the tested settings; it is not a proof of architecture independence.

claim: Because holdout retraining measures examples previously used for training, the team reversed the usual train/test roles when constructing that metric for test examples.
quote: Since our metric is only meaningful for data used to train the model, in order to measure how well represented arbitrary test points are, we actually train on the test data and perform holdout retraining on the original training data.
context: This procedure constructs a dataset-characterization score; it is not described as a standard held-out generalization evaluation.

claim: For adversarial representativeness, the authors prefer a more accurate estimate of distance to the decision boundary despite a substantial computational penalty.
quote: This is generally more accurate at measuring the distance to the decision boundary, but comes at a performance cost (it is on average 10-100$\times$ slower).
context: They rank by the norm of a minimal-found adversarial perturbation rather than the number of iterations required by a simpler attack, while allowing a faster, less accurate infinity-norm variant.
uncertainty: The metric uses a minimal-found perturbation; it is not an exact proof of the true minimum adversarial distance.

claim: An unexpected correlation between adversarial distance and retraining sensitivity motivates a possible cheaper or more widely applicable proxy, while the causal explanation remains tentative.
quote: However, somewhat unexpectedly, we find that the adv metric (adversarial robustness) correlates very strongly with the ret metric (retraining distance) on the smaller three datasets.
context: They suggest both reflect proximity to decision boundaries, one by moving inputs and the other by moving boundaries. Retraining sensitivity may be useful where adversarial distance is ill-defined.
uncertainty: The explanation is presented as presumptive, and ImageNet shows a different strongest-correlation pattern.

claim: The private-learning metric operationalized representativeness through how much privacy protection an example tolerated while remaining reliably classified.
quote: Our metric then ranks how well-represented an example is based on the minimum $\varepsilon$ (i.e., maximum privacy protection) at which the example is correctly classified in a reliable manner (which we take as being also classified correctly in 90% of less-private models).
context: The underlying intuition is that common signals survive gradient attenuation and noise more readily than rare examples.
uncertainty: That interpretation is an operational proxy for representativeness, not a direct measurement of distribution density.

claim: Rather than discarding metric disagreements as noise, the authors use structured disagreements to identify candidate memorized exceptions and rare but coherent subgroups.
quote: This suggests that we can find uncommon submodes of the examples in learning tasks by intersecting the bottom-most outlier examples on the priv metric with the union of most well-represented in the boundary and ensemble metrics.
context: This procedure identifies serif-style MNIST ones. A different intersection, high ensemble support but low boundary and privacy support, identifies candidate memorized exceptions.
uncertainty: These categories are operational interpretations of metric patterns, not independently established causal labels for every selected image.

claim: The authors tested whether their metrics reflected relatively stable data properties rather than one particular model configuration.
quote: experimentally we have confirmed that the metrics are model-agnostic in the sense that they give overall the same results despite large changes in hyperparameters or even the model architecture.
context: Model stability supported the choice of the five retained metrics.
uncertainty: The claim is bounded by the configurations tested; the supplied text does not provide all supporting comparisons.

claim: Stability across models was a selection criterion: the team discarded candidate metrics whose rankings depended strongly on pretrained models or architecture.
quote: In another metric we rejected, we found that sorting examples by when they were learned during the training process gave different orderings when applied to different model architectures.
context: A gradient-magnitude candidate also varied substantially across pretrained models.
uncertainty: The text reports these failures without detailed quantitative stability results for the rejected metrics.

claim: The team reported a qualified accuracy-robustness tradeoff: training on representative subsets could produce simpler and more robust boundaries than training on outlier subsets, without surpassing the full-data baseline.
quote: However, these models trained on a slice of $5,000$ well-represented examples remain comparably robust to a baseline model trained on the entire data.
context: Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 showed robustness advantages over outlier-only slices, while representative-only training often yielded lower overall accuracy. MNIST showed no significant robustness difference in the appendix.
uncertainty: Robustness here is measured through the evaluated adversarial-distance procedure, not certified robustness.

claim: The team selected metrics for generalizability and stability, rejecting a gradient-magnitude candidate after it varied substantially across pretrained models.
quote: In one attempt at a metric, we defined how representative an example is with respect to the magnitude of the gradient of the loss function on a pre-trained model and found it varied significantly across different pre-trained models.
context: The main text states that the retained metrics were intended to reflect properties of training data rather than particular model architectures.
uncertainty: The supplied footnote gives the rejection reason but not numerical stability measurements.

claim: The privacy-based metric operationalizes representativeness through resistance to the noise and gradient attenuation of private learning, with a consistency requirement across less-private models.
quote: Our metric then ranks how well-represented an example is based on the minimum $\varepsilon$ (i.e., maximum privacy protection) at which the example is correctly classified in a reliable manner (which we take as being also classified correctly in 90% of less-private models).
context: The motivating hypothesis is that common patterns survive privacy-preserving learning more readily than rare or exceptional examples.
uncertainty: This is an operational proxy for representativeness, not an independent definition of it.

claim: To investigate why outlier-heavy subsets perform poorly, the authors quantify suspected exceptions and test the effect of deliberately adding label noise.
quote: Also, we find that inserting 10% label noise causes model accuracy to decrease by about 10%, regardless of the split trained on
context: Approximately 10% of the first 5,000 outliers meet their definition of memorized exceptions; they argue that misleading or erroneous examples should be removed when training on small datasets.
uncertainty: The label-noise experiment supports a possible explanation but does not prove that every poor outlier result is caused by mislabeled examples.

claim: The retraining metric used fine-tuning and a loss-based stopping condition to avoid ranking artifacts caused by independently randomized training.
quote: To perform this fine-tuning, we use a smaller learning rate and train until the training loss stops decreasing. (We have found it is important to obtain $\bar{\theta}$ by fine-tuning $\theta$ as opposed to training from scratch; otherwise, the randomness of training leads to unstable rankings that yield specious results.)
context: Prediction changes before and after fine-tuning on a disjoint holdout dataset define the metric.

claim: The team turned metric disagreement into a dataset-inspection method, separating confidently memorized exceptions from uncommon submodes and jointly representative prototypes.
quote: Because our five metrics are not perfectly correlated, there are likely to be many examples that are determined to be well-represented under one metric but not under another, as a consequence of the fact that each metric defines “well-represented” differently.
context: Examples include Fashion-MNIST shirts resembling other classes and MNIST serif 1s. The method intersects high and low rank subsets across metrics rather than using a single ranking.
uncertainty: The supplied text contains an apparent duplication when defining the combined boundary and ensemble metrics, so the exact ensemble-combination recipe is not inferred from that sentence.

claim: The team treated the unexpected correlation between adversarial distance and holdout-retraining distance as an independent research result and proposed retraining distance as a substitute where adversarial examples are difficult to define.
quote: This strong correlation between adv and ret is a new result that may be of independent interest and some significance.
context: The paper reports particularly strong correlation on the three smaller datasets. Its explanation invokes perturbing inputs versus perturbing decision boundaries, while the proposed substitution includes tasks such as sequence-to-sequence modeling.
uncertainty: The mechanism is an interpretation, and usefulness on those additional tasks is proposed rather than experimentally demonstrated in the supplied text.

claim: A different disagreement pattern was used to separate rare but coherent submodes from problematic exceptions.
quote: This suggests that we can find uncommon submodes of the examples in learning tasks by intersecting the bottom-most outlier examples on the priv metric with the union of most well-represented in the boundary and ensemble metrics.
context: The procedure recovered all serif-style digit ones in the MNIST training set as a submode.
uncertainty: The interpretation depends on the operational metrics and selected thresholds.

claim: For adversarial-distance ranking, the team accepted substantially greater computation to obtain a more accurate estimate of distance to the decision boundary.
quote: This is generally more accurate at measuring the distance to the decision boundary, but comes at a performance cost (it is on average 10-100$\times$ slower).
context: Their metric ranked the norm of a minimal-found perturbation instead of counting iterations of a simpler attack.
uncertainty: Minimal-found perturbations remain attack-derived estimates, not guaranteed exact distances.

claim: The team found that retraining from scratch introduced ranking instability and therefore required fine-tuning from the original weights.
quote: (We have found it is important to obtain $\bar{\theta}$ by fine-tuning $\theta$ as opposed to training from scratch; otherwise, the randomness of training leads to unstable rankings that yield specious results.)
context: This controls a confound in the holdout-retraining metric: changes should reflect the data transition rather than independent initialization and training randomness.

claim: The prompt-length analysis distinguishes statistical significance from practical effect size, describing the measured negative association as weak.
quote: Empirically, we find a significant but weak negative correlation between these variables (Pearson’s $r=-0.07$), suggesting that longer prompts are only marginally harder to extract.
context: The analysis relates prompt length in GPT-4 tokens to the fraction of tokens leaked across three datasets and eleven models.
uncertainty: The association is observational and limited to the sampled prompt lengths.

claim: Attack development and final evaluation were separated across prompt splits, with data cleaning removing incomplete or very long ShareGPT conversations.
quote: Some prompts are placed in a Dev set, which was used for attack development, while others were assigned to test sets, used only for final evaluations.
context: The datasets were Unnatural Instructions, ShareGPT, and Awesome-ChatGPT-Prompts. ShareGPT conversations without the initial user instruction or longer than 256 tokens were filtered out.
uncertainty: The filtering limits the representativeness of the main experiments for very long prompts.

claim: The production-system investigation explicitly lowered its certainty because the true system prompts were generally unavailable.
quote: Since most system prompts are not public knowledge, it is generally impossible to verify the correctness of extractions.
context: A publicly available version of Claude 3's prompt provided a partial external reference.
uncertainty: Consistent production extractions should not be treated as independently verified exact prompts.

claim: The confidence estimator uses agreement across independent extraction attempts as evidence against hallucination, learning from 16,000 development-set extractions.
quote: The intuition behind this approach is simple: if multiple attacks on the same prompt lead to consistent extractions, then these extractions are less likely to be hallucinated. Specifically, we create a dataset of 16,000 extractions from Dev and fine-tune a DeBERTa model
context: The model estimates the proportion of secret-prompt tokens contained in a candidate, conditioned on other extractions.
uncertainty: Consistency is evidence, not proof; the estimator is empirically evaluated against known prompts.

claim: For production systems, the attack adapts to potential output filtering through translation and uses agreement among back-translations as a limited confidence check.
quote: This results in extractions in multiple languages, which we back-translate to English; if the back-translations are consistent, then we can be somewhat confident that they match the true prompt.
context: Languages sharing little vocabulary with English are chosen to reduce overlap with possible English-only filters.
uncertainty: Agreement among back-translations does not establish ground truth, and actual production filtering mechanisms are not fully known.

claim: The confidence estimator accounted for the ordering of comparison extractions by averaging predictions over sampled permutations.
quote: To estimate this expectation during evaluation, we sample 8 permutations, and take the average among samples.
context: Training examples concatenated randomly permuted extractions; the model learned token-overlap targets under a mean-squared-error objective.
uncertainty: The overlap estimate was interpreted as an extraction-success probability; it was not derived as a formally calibrated probability.

claim: The attack began with five handwritten queries and used GPT-4 paraphrases to expand the search, while aggregate API cost motivated a smaller GPT-4 evaluation query set.
quote: To make the attack even more effective, we prompted GPT-4 to generate 100 additional attack queries by paraphrasing the seed queries. In total, our attack on each prompt consists of 105 individual attack queries.
context: The five seeds already extracted most development prompts. For GPT-4 experiments, the authors used the fifteen queries most effective on the development set because extracting thousands of prompts remained costly.
uncertainty: The reported historical API cost should not be treated as a current price.

claim: The authors stopped short of more sophisticated attack development because the simple attacks already established the vulnerability.
quote: Due to the effectiveness of a small set of simple attacks, our work does not experiment with sophisticated attacking strategies (e.g., interactively choosing attack queries based on the model’s response), or use additional information that may be available to the attacker
context: The limitations section also notes that inserting user queries in the middle of instructions could make extraction harder than the tested end-concatenation setup.
uncertainty: This is a project scope decision rather than evidence of a general personal stopping rule.

claim: The project stops short of more sophisticated adaptive attacks because simple attacks already establish the vulnerability, and explicitly discloses that scope decision.
quote: Due to the effectiveness of a small set of simple attacks, our work does not experiment with sophisticated attacking strategies (e.g., interactively choosing attack queries based on the model’s response), or use additional information that may be available to the attacker (e.g., the specific language model behind an application).
context: Limitations and ethics statement.
uncertainty: The untested strategies are possible extensions, not measured improvements.

claim: The paper identifies user-query placement as a material limitation of its threat model and predicts that inserting queries inside instructions could make extraction harder.
quote: Our threat model assumes that user queries are concatenated to the end of a conversation, which is common in practice. However, queries can alternatively be inserted into the middle of a user instruction, which will likely make prompts more difficult to extract.
context: The tested API construction places attacker-controlled input after the secret prompt.
uncertainty: The relative difficulty of alternative placement is not experimentally established in this paper.

claim: The collaboration supplements exact matching with approximate token-overlap evaluation to reduce false negatives caused by trivial textual differences.
quote: The exact-match metric still misses guesses with trivial differences (e.g., capitalization or whitespaces) from the true prompt, which will result in false negatives (i.e., leaked prompts considered unsuccessful). We therefore additionally consider an approximate metric based on Rouge-L recall (Lin, 2004)
context: Approximate success requires at least 90% coverage under the longest-common-subsequence metric; the appendix provides examples near that threshold.
uncertainty: High token overlap does not guarantee semantic equivalence; one threshold example changes a comparison from greater-than-or-equal to greater-than.

claim: The paper reports a failed adaptive strategy as well as successful ones: Caesar-cipher requests were ineffective on all three tested models, while interleaving explained most successful evasions.
quote: Successful evasions mostly rely on the interleaving strategy, since none of these three models are able to effectively apply the Caesar cipher.
context: The filter nearly eliminated extraction for Alpaca-7B but allowed approximate extraction of 35.2% of prompts for Vicuna 1.3-33B and 72.3% for Llama-2-chat-70B.
uncertainty: The broader claim that increasing capabilities enlarge the attack surface extends beyond these three empirical comparisons.

claim: The final reconstruction deliberately uses a simple selection rule instead of synthesizing a prompt from all candidate extractions, because selection was sufficiently effective empirically.
quote: We note that, it is possible to use more sophisticated methods to construct the final guess while taking into account all extractions, but we chose this simple method as it is empirically effective enough.
context: The chosen output is the individual extraction with the highest estimated confidence.
uncertainty: The study does not establish that more sophisticated reconstruction would be unhelpful.

claim: Aggregate experimental cost leads the researchers to restrict GPT-4 extraction experiments to the fifteen queries that performed best on development data.
quote: Still, the cost is high when extracting thousands of prompts. We therefore use the 15 most effective attack queries on Dev for GPT-4 extraction experiments.
context: The paper reports that a single full extraction attempt costs less than one dollar on the GPT-4 service used.
uncertainty: These are historical experimental costs and configuration choices.

claim: The work defined success sentence by sentence, preserving an exact-content requirement while tolerating generated wrappers and formatting.
quote: Specifically, we check that every sentence in the prompt $p$ is exactly contained in the guess $g$.
context: The paper explains that affirmative preambles and numbered lists can prevent whole-prompt substring matching even when all original sentences leak.

claim: The capability analysis used MMLU as an explicitly imperfect proxy and reported only a weak positive association with extractability.
quote: Although a single score does not comprehensively measure the capability of a model, we nevertheless use MMLU score as a proxy since it is a standard evaluation benchmark reported across models
context: The reported Pearson correlation is 0.28; GPT-4 being harder to extract from than GPT-3.5 is presented as a counterexample to a simple capability explanation.
uncertainty: Correlation does not establish that greater capability causes greater vulnerability, and some percentages in this discussion differ from Table 1.

claim: The authors reduced the GPT-4 evaluation query set to control aggregate experimental cost, selecting queries using development data.
quote: Still, the cost is high when extracting thousands of prompts. We therefore use the 15 most effective attack queries on Dev for GPT-4 extraction experiments.
context: This qualifies the general 105-query procedure.
uncertainty: GPT-4 results therefore use a different number of attack queries from the full procedure.

claim: The final reconstruction selected the highest-confidence existing candidate rather than implementing a more sophisticated synthesis of all extractions, because the simpler method was empirically sufficient.
quote: We note that, it is possible to use more sophisticated methods to construct the final guess while taking into account all extractions, but we chose this simple method as it is empirically effective enough.
context: The output was a candidate prompt accompanied by its estimated confidence of successful extraction.
uncertainty: The paper does not claim this reconstruction rule is optimal.

claim: The paper reports discrepancies between extracted and published Claude prompts and presents a prompt update as a plausible explanation rather than an established fact.
quote: Since multiple extractions via different languages produce the same exact prompt, it’s plausible that this extraction is correct, and the actual prompt was updated between when the original prompt was posted and when we ran extraction experiments.
context: The extraction consistently omitted three sentences and added one sentence relative to the published reference.
uncertainty: A system-prompt update is a hypothesis; consistency alone does not rule out systematic extraction errors.

claim: The study extended prompt recovery into model identification by comparing a service's generations with candidate models conditioned on the recovered prompt.
quote: among a candidate set of LLMs $\mathcal{M}$, we choose the model that behaves most similarly to the service $f_{p}$ when prompted with our guess $g$.
context: Rouge-L similarity over reference generations yielded 71.7% identification accuracy across sixty instantiated APIs.
uncertainty: Identification was among a supplied candidate set, not arbitrary unknown models.

claim: The collaboration selected instruction-following variants rather than reporting extraction on base LLaMA 1, whose ability to adapt to arbitrary instructions was limited.
quote: Therefore, we do not report prompt extraction results on LLaMA 1 directly. We instead consider Alpaca, Vicuna and Llama-2-chat, three variants of the original LLaMA models due to their better abilities to follow user instructions.
context: Other model-selection considerations included likely deployment, popularity, performance, and open availability.
uncertainty: The results concern the selected instruction-following models rather than all language models.

claim: The prompt-extraction collaboration addresses a central weakness in anecdotal leakage reports by collecting prompts for which ground truth is available.
quote: Such efforts rarely have access to the groundtruth prompt, making it difficult to determine whether the extractions are accurate. In this work, we systematically evaluate the feasibility of prompt extraction attacks, where an adversary tries to reconstruct the prompt by interacting with a service API.
context: The controlled experiments distinguish actual prompt recovery from plausible model-generated text.

claim: Development and final evaluation were separated across prompt datasets.
quote: Some prompts are placed in a Dev set, which was used for attack development, while others were assigned to test sets, used only for final evaluations.
context: The sources included generated instructions, user-shared conversations, and curated role prompts.

claim: The paper explicitly limits its conclusions by noting that inserting user queries inside an instruction, rather than appending them, could make extraction harder.
quote: Our threat model assumes that user queries are concatenated to the end of a conversation, which is common in practice. However, queries can alternatively be inserted into the middle of a user instruction, which will likely make prompts more difficult to extract.
context: The limitations section also discusses classifier-based defenses that were not evaluated in the reported experiments.
uncertainty: The increased difficulty for middle-inserted queries is proposed rather than experimentally established in this paper.

claim: For production services, the attack was adapted to request translations and compare back-translations, exploiting the possibility that English-only output filters would miss non-English renderings.
quote: By choosing languages which barely share common vocabulary with English (e.g. Finnish or Japanese), the extracted prompts are less likely to be filtered out by an English-only output filter.
context: The study explored Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, and Claude 3. Google Translate supplied back-translations.
uncertainty: The proposed filtering mechanism for particular production services was inferred rather than directly inspected.

claim: The attack treated distinguishing genuine leaks from plausible hallucinations as an essential component, using agreement among separate extractions as evidence.
quote: The intuition behind this approach is simple: if multiple attacks on the same prompt lead to consistent extractions, then these extractions are less likely to be hallucinated.
context: A DeBERTa model trained on 16,000 development extractions estimated how much of the secret prompt appeared in each candidate, conditioned on other candidates.
uncertainty: Consistency is a heuristic indicator of correctness, not a logical guarantee.

claim: The extraction threat model deliberately required only ordinary generated-text access, excluding weights, architecture knowledge, and token likelihoods.
quote: The service API is reset between queries. We do not assume any additional information or access to the system (e.g., access to token likelihoods or knowledge of model architecture or weights).
context: The practical query budget is approximately one hundred calls per service.

claim: The authors adapted extraction to production defenses by translating outputs and checking whether back-translations agreed across languages.
quote: This results in extractions in multiple languages, which we back-translate to English; if the back-translations are consistent, then we can be somewhat confident that they match the true prompt.
context: Languages with little English vocabulary overlap were chosen to reduce detection by possible English-only output filters.
uncertainty: The filter explanation is partly inferential, and cross-language consistency is not ground-truth verification.

claim: The collaboration reports that one proposed evasion mechanism failed, attributing most successful filter bypasses to interleaving rather than cipher execution.
quote: Successful evasions mostly rely on the interleaving strategy, since none of these three models are able to effectively apply the Caesar cipher.
context: Filter evasion varies with the tested model's ability to follow output-transformation instructions.
uncertainty: The cipher failure concerns the three models and prompting setup evaluated.

claim: Attack construction combined a small human-written seed set with model-generated paraphrases.
quote: To make the attack even more effective, we prompted GPT-4 to generate 100 additional attack queries by paraphrasing the seed queries. In total, our attack on each prompt consists of 105 individual attack queries.
context: The five original queries already extracted most prompts in the development set.

claim: Exact-match evaluation checks sentence containment individually so that added formatting or conversational preambles do not falsely invalidate recovered prompts.
quote: Specifically, we check that every sentence in the prompt $p$ is exactly contained in the guess $g$. The reason for checking the containment of every sentence individually (rather than the full prompt) is to get around certain known quirks (Perez et al., 2022) in LLM generations
context: Examples include affirmative lead-ins and numbered lists.
uncertainty: This criterion establishes sentence recovery, not necessarily preservation of the original full-string formatting or sentence order.

claim: The capability analysis reports a weak positive association with extractability while acknowledging that capability does not fully explain vulnerability.
quote: More capable models do seem to be more vulnerable to prompt extraction, indicated by a weak positive correlation between a model’s score on the MMLU benchmark and its extractability (Pearson’s $r=0.28$).
context: MMLU is used as an available proxy; GPT-4 is identified as harder to extract from than GPT-3.5 despite its greater capability.
uncertainty: The reported correlation is weak, noncausal, and based on a limited capability proxy. Some percentages in this discussion differ from the main results table.

claim: The model-capability analysis used MMLU as a practical but explicitly incomplete proxy and characterized the association with extractability as weak.
quote: Although a single score does not comprehensively measure the capability of a model, we nevertheless use MMLU score as a proxy since it is a standard evaluation benchmark reported across models (Anil et al., 2023; Chiang et al., 2023).
context: The paper reports Pearson's r of 0.28 and notes that capability does not fully explain vulnerability, including GPT-4 being harder to extract from than GPT-3.5.
uncertainty: Some percentages in this discussion differ from the main results table; the weak association is more defensible than treating every quoted percentage as reconciled.

claim: The defense evaluation first measures a five-gram output filter against the original attack, then adapts the attack using recoverable transformations instead of equating initial blocking with general security.
quote: As a proof-of-concept, we modify our attacks with two of such strategies, and report extraction results on three models with various sizes: Alpaca-7B, $\text{Vicuna}_{\text{1.3}}$-33B and Llama-2-chat-70B in Table 3.
context: The two adaptations interleave symbols between words or request Caesar-cipher encryption; the filter blocks outputs sharing a five-gram with the prompt.
uncertainty: Only one filter implementation and two adaptation strategies are tested.

claim: The study defines a practical black-box adversary around service budgets and rate limits, using roughly one hundred queries rather than privileged model access.
quote: Given the budget constaints and rate limits of most LLM services, we consider a practical adversary that can perform only a reasonably small number of queries ($k\approx 100$) of a service.
context: The service resets between queries; the attacker receives generated text without token likelihoods, weights, or architectural information.
uncertainty: The stated query budget is approximate; the general attack uses 105 queries and GPT-4 experiments use fewer.

claim: The study bounded the adversary to approximately one hundred queries and generated-text access, motivated by practical budgets and rate limits rather than by access to model internals.
quote: Given the budget constaints and rate limits of most LLM services, we consider a practical adversary that can perform only a reasonably small number of queries ($k\approx 100$) of a service.
context: The API was reset between queries. The attack assumed no token likelihoods, architecture knowledge, or weights; additional access available for open models was deliberately unused.

claim: Model selection emphasized deployed or instruction-following systems rather than evaluating the original LLaMA models merely because they were available.
quote: Therefore, we do not report prompt extraction results on LLaMA 1 directly. We instead consider Alpaca, Vicuna and Llama-2-chat, three variants of the original LLaMA models due to their better abilities to follow user instructions.
context: The paper also motivates proprietary targets by popularity and capability, and Vicuna by openness and competitive performance.
uncertainty: These model-selection judgments describe the research period.

claim: The evaluation separates attack-development prompts from held-out test prompts across three data sources.
quote: Our prompts are drawn from three datasets, which are described below. Some prompts are placed in a Dev set, which was used for attack development, while others were assigned to test sets, used only for final evaluations.
context: Sources include synthetic instructions, user-shared conversations, and curated role prompts.

claim: The study evaluated confidence estimates with precision-recall curves rather than reporting extraction frequency alone.
quote: In Figure 3, we report the precision and recall of this estimator at predicting successful extractions at varying thresholds.
context: The authors report high precision across datasets and a range of recall levels, supporting the claim that attackers can recognize many successful leaks.
uncertainty: The estimates were validated on the studied models and prompt distributions; the paper does not establish universal calibration.

claim: The paper treats its generic attack as a lower bound on an adaptive adversary's capabilities.
quote: Hence, our results serve as a lower bound of what dedicated attackers could achieve in the real-world: they can run vastly more attack queries on each service, and choose these attack queries strategically.
context: The attack made no service-specific assumptions and did not adapt queries interactively.
uncertainty: The greater success of hypothetical dedicated attackers was not measured.

claim: The paper interprets its general-purpose attack results as a lower bound on what dedicated adversaries might achieve with more queries and strategic selection.
quote: Hence, our results serve as a lower bound of what dedicated attackers could achieve in the real-world: they can run vastly more attack queries on each service, and choose these attack queries strategically.
context: The attack does not specialize itself to individual services or exploit additional model information.
uncertainty: The greater effectiveness of the proposed stronger adversaries is argued rather than directly measured here.

claim: The researchers checked whether their greedy-decoding results depended on deterministic sampling and found that temperature-one sampling still allowed extraction of most prompts.
quote: We find that random sampling has a negligible to small impact on the efficacy of our attack depending on the model, and the majority of prompts can still be extracted.
context: The supplementary experiment covered Alpaca-7B, Vicuna 1.3-33B, and Llama-2-chat-70B.
uncertainty: This check covers one alternative temperature on three models, not all decoding configurations.

claim: The defense evaluation first established that a five-gram overlap filter defeated the original verbatim attack, then adapted the attack with recoverable output transformations.
quote: This 5-gram defense is extremely effective against the attack in § 3: extraction success rate drops to 0% for $\text{Vicuna}_{\text{1.5}}$-13B, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, as the attack relies on the models generating the prompt verbatim.
context: The adaptive proof of concept tested word interleaving and Caesar-cipher requests on Alpaca-7B, Vicuna 1.3-33B, and Llama-2-chat-70B.
uncertainty: The original-attack and adaptive-attack results use different model selections and should not be conflated as paired results for every model.

claim: Follow-up analyses checked whether stochastic decoding and prompt length materially changed extraction success.
quote: We find that random sampling has a negligible to small impact on the efficacy of our attack depending on the model, and the majority of prompts can still be extracted.
context: Temperature-one experiments covered three models. A separate analysis across three datasets and eleven models found a weak negative relationship between prompt length and leaked-token ratio, with Pearson's r of -0.07.
uncertainty: The decoding result applies to the tested temperature and models; the length analysis is correlational.

claim: The collaboration tests whether architectural separation of system prompts and user messages prevents leakage and finds that it does not do so in the evaluated models.
quote: Such models in principle have sufficient information to distinguish between the true prompt and a potentially malicious user input. However, our results show that this separation does not safeguard these models from leaking their prompts
context: The discussion concerns Llama-2-chat, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 in the controlled prompt-extraction setting.
uncertainty: This finding applies to the tested implementations and attacks, not every possible instruction-separation mechanism.

claim: The extraction-confidence estimator used agreement among independently elicited candidate prompts as a signal against hallucination.
quote: The intuition behind this approach is simple: if multiple attacks on the same prompt lead to consistent extractions, then these extractions are less likely to be hallucinated.
context: A DeBERTa model was trained on 16,000 examples to estimate leaked-token coverage conditioned on other extractions.
uncertainty: Consistency is an empirical heuristic, not a logical guarantee that a candidate is the hidden prompt.

claim: The attack-development process starts with five handwritten queries and expands them through GPT-4 paraphrasing.
quote: To make the attack even more effective, we prompted GPT-4 to generate 100 additional attack queries by paraphrasing the seed queries. In total, our attack on each prompt consists of 105 individual attack queries.
context: The five seeds were inspired by successful prompt-injection attacks and already extracted most prompts in the development set.

claim: The authors interpreted their generic, limited-query attack as a lower bound on what a dedicated attacker could achieve, rather than as an exhaustive attack search.
quote: Hence, our results serve as a lower bound of what dedicated attackers could achieve in the real-world: they can run vastly more attack queries on each service, and choose these attack queries strategically.
context: The limitations section explains that the success of simple attacks led the researchers not to explore interactive query selection or additional model-specific information.
uncertainty: The additional gains from those untested strategies are proposed possibilities, not measured results.

claim: Exact extraction was measured sentence by sentence so that affirmative preambles and inserted list formatting would not invalidate otherwise complete leaks.
quote: Specifically, we check that every sentence in the prompt $p$ is exactly contained in the guess $g$.
context: The paper explains that requiring the entire prompt as one uninterrupted substring would mishandle known generation quirks.
uncertainty: Sentence containment does not require the guess to contain only the secret prompt.

claim: The experiments tested whether explicit system/user boundaries protected prompts and found that these boundaries were insufficient in the evaluated models.
quote: Such models in principle have sufficient information to distinguish between the true prompt and a potentially malicious user input.
context: Llama-2-chat, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 exposed model-level separation but still leaked substantial proportions of prompts under the paper's attacks.
uncertainty: This establishes insufficiency for the tested systems and conditions, not impossibility for every future instruction-hierarchy mechanism.

claim: The researchers supplemented exact matching with a token-overlap measure because trivial formatting differences could otherwise count real leakage as failure.
quote: The exact-match metric still misses guesses with trivial differences (e.g., capitalization or whitespaces) from the true prompt, which will result in false negatives (i.e., leaked prompts considered unsuccessful).
context: Approximate success required at least 90% Rouge-L recall; the appendix includes examples near that threshold.
uncertainty: Token overlap is not a guarantee of semantic equivalence; an appendix example changes a greater-than-or-equal condition to greater-than while exceeding the threshold.

claim: The production-service experiments explicitly acknowledge weaker verification than the controlled benchmark because most actual system prompts are unavailable.
quote: Since most system prompts are not public knowledge, it is generally impossible to verify the correctness of extractions. That said, a version of Claude 3’s system prompt is publicly available
context: A published Claude prompt provides a partial external reference, while other services lack equivalent ground truth.
uncertainty: Production extractions should not be treated as fully verified exact recoveries.

claim: Defense evaluation included adapting the attack after a five-gram filter defeated the original verbatim extraction procedure.
quote: As a proof-of-concept, we modify our attacks with two of such strategies, and report extraction results on three models with various sizes:
context: The two tested transformations were symbol interleaving and Caesar-cipher encoding; the filter returned an empty string when output overlapped the prompt by five words.
uncertainty: The experiments test particular transformations and a particular filtering defense, not all possible defenses.

claim: When a Claude extraction differed from the published reference, the authors reported the discrepancy and offered a prompt update as a plausible explanation rather than declaring exact verification.
quote: Our extractions from Claude 3 Sonnet are quite similar to the groundtruth, but there are three consistently missing sentences and an extra sentence (diffs highlighted in Table 2).
context: Agreement across languages motivated the suggestion that the deployed prompt changed between publication of the reference and the extraction experiment.
uncertainty: The update explanation remains a hypothesis; translation errors or extraction limitations are not ruled out by access to the contemporaneous hidden prompt.

claim: The defense-bypass results identified a capability-dependent limitation and reported that one proposed strategy failed.
quote: Successful evasions mostly rely on the interleaving strategy, since none of these three models are able to effectively apply the Caesar cipher.
context: The filter virtually blocked Alpaca-7B but allowed substantial recovery from Vicuna-33B and majority recovery from Llama-2-chat-70B.
uncertainty: The broader prediction that filtering becomes implausible as capabilities grow goes beyond these three-model experiments.

claim: The prompt-extraction project addressed the verification gap in anecdotal leaks by evaluating attacks against prompts whose ground truth was known.
quote: Such efforts rarely have access to the groundtruth prompt, making it difficult to determine whether the extractions are accurate. In this work, we systematically evaluate the feasibility of prompt extraction attacks, where an adversary tries to reconstruct the prompt by interacting with a service API.
context: The controlled experiments covered three prompt sources and eleven language models.

claim: The collaboration checks whether its greedy-decoding results survive stochastic generation and reports that most prompts remain extractable at temperature one.
quote: We find that random sampling has a negligible to small impact on the efficacy of our attack depending on the model, and the majority of prompts can still be extracted.
context: The appendix tests Alpaca-7B, Vicuna-1.3-33B, and Llama-2-chat-70B under temperature-one sampling.
uncertainty: The result covers three models and one additional temperature setting; some dataset-specific decreases approach twelve percentage points.

claim: The collaboration extends prompt recovery into model identification by comparing candidate models' behavior under the recovered prompt with the target service's behavior.
quote: The method for identifying the model is surprisingly straightforward given that our attack often produces a close guess $g$ of the true prompt $p$: among a candidate set of LLMs $\mathcal{M}$, we choose the model that behaves most similarly to the service $f_{p}$ when prompted with our guess $g$.
context: A six-model, sixty-API experiment uses Rouge-L similarity and reports 71.7% overall identification accuracy.
uncertainty: Identification is among a supplied candidate set, not arbitrary unknown models.

claim: The authors added an approximate metric because exact matching treats trivial formatting differences as failed extraction.
quote: The exact-match metric still misses guesses with trivial differences (e.g., capitalization or whitespaces) from the true prompt, which will result in false negatives (i.e., leaked prompts considered unsuccessful).
context: Approximate success uses Rouge-L recall with a 90% threshold; appendix examples expose behavior near that threshold.
uncertainty: Token overlap is not equivalent to semantic identity; an appendix example changes a greater-than-or-equal condition to greater-than while still exceeding the threshold.

claim: The prompt-extraction collaboration moved from anecdotal leaks to controlled experiments with known prompts so that apparent extraction could be distinguished from plausible hallucination.
quote: Such efforts rarely have access to the groundtruth prompt, making it difficult to determine whether the extractions are accurate. In this work, we systematically evaluate the feasibility of prompt extraction attacks, where an adversary tries to reconstruct the prompt by interacting with a service API.
context: The paper evaluates eleven models using three sources of prompts.

claim: The project extended extraction into identifying the underlying model by comparing candidate models' generations under the recovered prompt to the service's behavior.
quote: among a candidate set of LLMs $\mathcal{M}$, we choose the model that behaves most similarly to the service $f_{p}$ when prompted with our guess $g$.
context: Using Rouge-L similarity, six candidate models, and sixty instantiated APIs, the method achieved 71.7% model-identification accuracy.
uncertainty: Identification was evaluated within a fixed candidate set, not as unrestricted identification of an arbitrary unknown system.

claim: The researchers distinguished production-system demonstrations from controlled evidence because most real system prompts could not be independently verified.
quote: Since most system prompts are not public knowledge, it is generally impossible to verify the correctness of extractions.
context: A publicly posted version of Claude 3's prompt provided a partial reference; other production extractions relied more heavily on cross-language consistency.
uncertainty: Consistent production outputs do not by themselves prove exact recovery of the actual hidden prompt.

claim: The paper reported discrepancies from the public Claude prompt and offered prompt revision as a plausible explanation rather than silently treating the extraction as exact.
quote: Our extractions from Claude 3 Sonnet are quite similar to the groundtruth, but there are three consistently missing sentences and an extra sentence
context: Repeated agreement across languages motivated the hypothesis that the deployed prompt had changed since publication.
uncertainty: The supplied material does not verify that a prompt update caused the differences.

claim: The authors chose a simple highest-confidence candidate rather than building a more elaborate reconstruction algorithm because it was already empirically effective.
quote: We note that, it is possible to use more sophisticated methods to construct the final guess while taking into account all extractions, but we chose this simple method as it is empirically effective enough.
context: The attack returns the candidate with the largest estimated probability of successful extraction.
uncertainty: The paper does not provide a systematic comparison with the more sophisticated alternatives mentioned.

claim: The controlled results challenged the idea that explicit system/user message boundaries alone protect hidden prompts.
quote: Such models in principle have sufficient information to distinguish between the true prompt and a potentially malicious user input. However, our results show that this separation does not safeguard these models from leaking their prompts:
context: The discussion concerns Llama-2-chat, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4, which had model-level prompt/query separations.
uncertainty: The finding is about the tested systems and setup, not every possible implementation of instruction separation.

claim: The authors checked ranking agreement between old and new metrics with Kendall's correlation and explicitly avoided claiming that multi-ID should replace single-ID when all models share the same training data.
quote: Thus, when comparing models trained on the same data, our multi-ID evaluation is not intended to replace the single-ID evaluation. Our multi-ID evaluation is mainly for comparing models trained on different data, and may be used as a supplementary evaluation if all the models are trained on a single dataset.
context: Ranking correlations were often positive but could be negative for LAION models.
uncertainty: This is a scope restriction supported by the appendix analysis, not evidence that the two metrics are interchangeable.

claim: The proposed correction was to construct a matching ID test set for each training distribution and control for multiple ID accuracies together.
quote: Specifically, for each training distribution, we propose to prepare an ID test set that matches the training distribution, respectively. In particular, we focus on comparing models trained on two different datasets at a time in this paper, and we thereby use two ID test sets, where each of them corresponds to one of the training datasets.
context: The authors call this multi-ID effective robustness.
uncertainty: Each test set is exactly ID only for its corresponding training distribution, not for every evaluated model.

claim: The team checked whether the new metric preserved within-dataset model rankings, found inconsistent agreement, and consequently limited its claim to replace the older evaluation.
quote: For LAION models, there is sometimes a negative correlation. Overall, while there is often a positive correlation between the rankings provided by the single-ID evaluation and the multi-ID evaluation, respectively, it is not necessarily consistent on all the datasets.
context: The appendix uses Kendall’s rank correlation; the authors recommend multi-ID chiefly for models trained on different data and as a supplement when training data are shared.
uncertainty: The new metric is explicitly not intended to replace single-ID evaluation for all same-dataset comparisons.

claim: The authors challenged apparently exceptional CLIP robustness by showing that the conclusion could reverse when the supposedly in-distribution test set changed.
quote: We observe that when there is a mismatch in the training data and the ID test data, the models appear to have greater effective robustness
context: With ImageNet as the reference test set, YFCC models appeared advantaged; with YFCC as the reference, ImageNet models generally appeared advantaged.
uncertainty: The challenge concerns effective robustness after controlling for ID performance, not whether pretrained models can achieve high absolute OOD accuracy.

claim: The team accepted automatically generated labels for new ID test sets as a practical compromise, while acknowledging that human labeling could improve their quality.
quote: Although it is possible to obtain a higher-quality test set by human labelling, we will show that using the automatically labelled test sets can already produce reasonable results.
context: YFCC and LAION classification labels were generated by matching image-associated text to ImageNet classes.
uncertainty: The supplied paper does not report an independent human audit quantifying labeling error.

claim: The authors accepted automatically generated labels as a practical way to construct ID test sets from image–text data, while explicitly acknowledging that human labels could improve quality.
quote: Although it is possible to obtain a higher-quality test set by human labelling, we will show that using the automatically labelled test sets can already produce reasonable results.
context: YFCC and LAION captions or tags were matched against ImageNet classes to create labeled evaluation examples.
uncertainty: The supplied text does not provide an independent annotation audit establishing the automatic labels’ accuracy.

claim: The team tested transfer of the fitted baseline to models that were not used to fit it, including independently pretrained OpenCLIP and SLIP models.
quote: We also evaluate additional models that are not used in fitting the baseline functions. We download models pre-trained by existing works, including OpenCLIP (Ilharco et al., 2021) and SLIP (Mu et al., 2022).
context: Additional evaluation also included vanilla-fine-tuned and WiSE-FT CLIP models.
uncertainty: Held-out models broaden validation but do not cover all training algorithms or unknown data distributions.

claim: The authors bounded the study's scope because extending the method to many training distributions would require more models to fit a reliable baseline.
quote: However, it could be costly as it would require training more models to fit a high-quality baseline function. We leave it for future works to reduce the cost when dealing with a larger number of datasets.
context: Discussion of generalizing beyond two training datasets.
uncertainty: The broader extension is proposed in principle, not experimentally demonstrated here.

claim: To avoid anchoring the fitted baseline to either endpoint distribution, the authors trained mixed-dataset models at multiple ratios and fitted them together with single-dataset models.
quote: We use models trained on each single dataset as well as the combined datasets in the same fitting process, so that the baseline functions do not bias towards models trained on certain data.
context: Mixing datasets was intended to cover different combinations of the two ID accuracies.
uncertainty: This is the design rationale; it is not a proof that all possible fitting biases are eliminated.

claim: The paper questions whether fixed OOD benchmarks remain genuinely out of distribution after large-scale pretraining, preserving a limitation that could affect interpretation of its own results.
quote: When models are pre-trained on large-scale data, it becomes unclear if these “OOD” test sets are still OOD, or if these test sets could be less OOD for the pre-trained models compared to standard classifiers.
context: The limitations section discusses possible distribution overlap between pretraining data and benchmark test sets.
uncertainty: Possible distribution overlap is not the same as verified exact-example contamination.

claim: The study bounded its implementation to two training datasets at a time because extending the metric requires enough additional models to fit a higher-dimensional baseline reliably.
quote: However, it could be costly as it would require training more models to fit a high-quality baseline function. We leave it for future works to reduce the cost when dealing with a larger number of datasets.
context: The paper states that the method can in principle generalize to more than two ID accuracies.
uncertainty: That higher-dimensional extension was proposed rather than demonstrated.

claim: To make cross-dataset classification comparisons meaningful, the researchers retained shared classes and mapped an appropriate subset of ImageNet classes to CIFAR-10 classes.
quote: Considering that different test sets may not have the same classes, we follow prior works (Taori et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2022) to use class subsampling[^1] to retain classes appearing in all the test sets.
context: The source clarifies that its inherited term 'class subsampling' does not mean random sampling.
uncertainty: Results apply to the retained and mapped class sets rather than every class in the original datasets.

claim: The authors used the observed approximately planar relationship between two ID accuracies and OOD accuracy to motivate a logit-space linear model fitted by ordinary least squares.
quote: We determine the parameters by solving an ordinary least squares regression to fit the accuracies. Metrics for linear regression such as the coefficient of determination, a.k.a. $R^{2}$, can be used to evaluate the fitting quality of the baseline function.
context: Effective robustness is the residual between actual OOD accuracy and the accuracy predicted from the two ID measurements.
uncertainty: A good statistical fit supports predictive adequacy in the evaluated setting, not a causal account of robustness.

claim: The paper makes its higher-dimensional evaluation inspectable through interactive visualizations and projected two-dimensional views, helping readers see how single-ID projections can yield conflicting interpretations.
quote: In Figure˜3(a), we visualize the multi-ID effective robustness on CIFAR-10.2, where the accuracies of all the models approximately lie on a plane (the baseline function) on the logit scale
context: Figure 4 supplies projections, and the paper links an accompanying website with interactive visualizations.
uncertainty: The supplied text establishes that these artifacts were offered; the external website and visual rendering were not inspected.

claim: An ablation tested whether mixed-training-data models actually helped fit the baseline, and the authors reported the improvement as modest rather than overstating its size.
quote: In Tables˜8 and 9, we show that if we do not include models with mixed training data in the fitting, the MAE for these models can become higher, although the difference is not large.
context: Appendix A.3 compares fitting with and without mixed ImageNet–YFCC and ImageNet–LAION models.
uncertainty: The result is an ablation within the studied model families.

claim: The authors aligned label spaces across datasets by retaining shared classes and mapping a subset of ImageNet classes to CIFAR-10 classes when necessary.
quote: Considering that different test sets may not have the same classes, we follow prior works (Taori et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2022) to use class subsampling[^1] to retain classes appearing in all the test sets.
context: The footnote clarifies that the inherited term class subsampling does not mean random sampling here.
uncertainty: Reported comparisons concern the aligned class subsets rather than every original benchmark class.

claim: For standard classifiers, the team reused established ImageNet training configurations on CIFAR-10 with only dataset, class-count, and image-size changes, explicitly avoiding hyperparameter tuning in that transfer.
quote: We reuse the configurations to train models on CIFAR-10, where we only change the dataset, number of classes, and image size, without tuning hyperparameters for the training.
context: TF-Vision training of ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ResNet-101 models.
uncertainty: This documents an experimental convention, not a general personal preference against tuning.

claim: The automatically labeled test-set construction used ambiguity filtering, class balancing, and removal from training data to make the evaluation more controlled.
quote: We adopt a label only if a unique ImageNet class can be determined by matching for the involved image. We then construct a balanced and labelled test set by keeping 50 examples for each class that has at least 100 examples in the labelled images. The test examples are then held out from the training data.
context: YFCC matching used tags, whereas LAION matching used the available text.
uncertainty: Unique text matching does not guarantee that the assigned visual label is correct.

claim: The researchers deliberately generated a broad accuracy range by training on different fractions of datasets, making model diversity part of the measurement design rather than relying only on a few high-performing checkpoints.
quote: In order to fit a baseline function, we need a large amount of models with diverse accuracies. To this end, we follow Taori et al. (2020) to train models with various proportions of data by subsampling from the entire training set (namely dataset subsampling), which effectively produces models with diverse accuracies.
context: Baseline construction across CIFAR-10, ImageNet, YFCC, and LAION comparisons.

claim: The authors withheld a definite conclusion about SLIP and WiSE-FT because those methods might alter the relevant training distribution in ways their evaluation did not cleanly characterize.
quote: Thus, we do not draw a definite conclusion for the effective robustness of SLIP and WiSE-FT models and leave further validation for future work.
context: Some residual gains remained, but SLIP’s training procedure and WiSE-FT’s weight-space ensembling complicated the interpretation of ID performance.
uncertainty: The paper explicitly treats the distributional explanation and the robustness of these methods as unresolved.

claim: The team tested the baseline on additional pretrained and fine-tuned models that were not used to fit it, using MAE to assess predictive performance on those models.
quote: Since these models are not used in the fitting, we do not use $R^{2}$, but we use MAE to measure the fitting quality.
context: Additional models included OpenCLIP, SLIP, vanilla fine-tuned CLIP, and WiSE-FT variants.
uncertainty: The statement describes the authors’ metric choice; it should not be read as a general prohibition on computing out-of-sample R-squared.

claim: The authors tested whether the fitted relationship transferred to models excluded from fitting and used mean absolute error for that evaluation rather than reusing the fitting-stage coefficient of determination.
quote: Since these models are not used in the fitting, we do not use $R^{2}$, but we use MAE to measure the fitting quality.
context: Additional models included OpenCLIP, SLIP, vanilla fine-tuned CLIP, and WiSE-FT.
uncertainty: Multi-ID generally reduced error, but the reported table includes individual settings where it did not.

claim: The paper distinguishes high absolute OOD performance from additional robustness beyond what multiple ID accuracies predict, concluding that zero-shot CLIP usually lacks the latter in its evaluation.
quote: The results further validate that zero-shot CLIP models, although may achieve high OOD performance if pre-trained with large-scale data (Radford et al., 2021), generally do not improve effective robustness if we control for all the ID accuracies.
context: Interpretation of results on additional models excluded from baseline fitting.
uncertainty: The conclusion is specific to this definition of effective robustness and its assumptions, not a denial of useful OOD performance.

claim: The team excluded ImageNet-A for a stated methodological reason: adversarial filtering gives it different effective-robustness behavior from the natural-shift settings under study.
quote: We do not use ImageNet-A (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) which involves adversarial filtering and has a different behavior in effective robustness evaluation (Taori et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2022).
context: OOD benchmark selection included ImageNet-V2, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch, and ObjectNet.
uncertainty: The exclusion limits the scope of the findings rather than establishing performance on adversarially filtered benchmarks.

claim: The mixed-training-data design was checked with an ablation, and the authors reported that omitting mixed models worsened their prediction error only modestly.
quote: In Tables˜8 and 9, we show that if we do not include models with mixed training data in the fitting, the MAE for these models can become higher, although the difference is not large.
context: The ablation evaluates whether broader coverage of combinations of ID accuracies materially affects the fitted baseline.
uncertainty: The paper does not characterize the modest improvement as proof that mixed-data training is always necessary.

claim: The authors propose conditioning use of the metric on sufficiently good baseline fit, recognizing that the underlying accuracy relationship can fail.
quote: We may set a threshold on the fitting quality and only adopt our method when the fitting quality is sufficiently good.
context: The study focuses on shifts where models trained on the same data exhibit the previously documented accuracy-on-the-line relationship.
uncertainty: The passage proposes a safeguard but does not define or validate a numerical adoption threshold.

claim: An ablation checked whether including mixed-data models improved the fitted baseline, and the authors reported the benefit as modest rather than overstating it.
quote: In Tables˜8 and 9, we show that if we do not include models with mixed training data in the fitting, the MAE for these models can become higher, although the difference is not large.
context: Mixed-data models were included to provide varied combinations of the two ID accuracies.
uncertainty: The ablation supports the choice within the evaluated mixtures, not the necessity of every mixture or sampling ratio.

claim: Automatic ID-test construction enforced unique class matches, class balance, minimum class support, and separation from training data.
quote: We adopt a label only if a unique ImageNet class can be determined by matching for the involved image. We then construct a balanced and labelled test set by keeping 50 examples for each class that has at least 100 examples in the labelled images. The test examples are then held out from the training data.
context: YFCC used metadata tags; LAION used the full accompanying text because tags were unavailable.
uncertainty: Unique text matching reduces ambiguity but does not ensure that every resulting visual label is correct.

claim: To obtain enough variation for baseline fitting, the team deliberately trained models on different fractions of datasets and on mixtures with varying sampling ratios.
quote: Moreover, we also combine examples from two datasets with different sampling ratios and train models on these combined datasets. This produces models with training distributions varying between the two training datasets and it is supposed to yield different combinations of the two ID accuracies.
context: The fitting pool included models trained on each individual dataset as well as mixed-data models, with the stated aim of avoiding bias toward a particular training distribution.
uncertainty: Diverse sampled configurations do not establish exhaustive coverage of possible training distributions.

claim: The paper questions whether fixed OOD benchmarks remain genuinely out of distribution for models pretrained on very large datasets.
quote: When models are pre-trained on large-scale data, it becomes unclear if these “OOD” test sets are still OOD, or if these test sets could be less OOD for the pre-trained models compared to standard classifiers.
context: The authors also acknowledge possible distribution overlap with pretraining data.
uncertainty: This is a limitation and possible confounder, not a demonstrated case of direct benchmark contamination.

claim: For CLIP training, the authors largely followed an existing experimental recipe but doubled batch size specifically to increase parallelism.
quote: For training CLIP models, we mostly follow hyperparameters provided in Fang et al. (2022) and the implementation in Open-CLIP (Ilharco et al., 2021). While Fang et al. (2022) used a batch size of 1024, we use 2048 for more parallelism.
context: This is an explicit computational adjustment within an otherwise reused training setup.
uncertainty: The paper does not isolate the effect of changing batch size on the reported robustness results.

claim: For standard classifiers, the project reused existing training configurations across ImageNet and CIFAR-10 with only dataset-specific changes, rather than tuning hyperparameters separately for CIFAR-10.
quote: We reuse the configurations to train models on CIFAR-10, where we only change the dataset, number of classes, and image size, without tuning hyperparameters for the training.
context: The implementation used TF-Vision and trained ResNet-18, ResNet-50, and ResNet-101 models.
uncertainty: The source documents the configuration choice but does not state whether its primary motivation was control, convenience, or compute cost.

claim: The study excluded ImageNet-A because adversarial filtering gives it a different behavior in effective-robustness evaluation.
quote: We do not use ImageNet-A (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) which involves adversarial filtering and has a different behavior in effective robustness evaluation (Taori et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2022).
context: The ImageNet-like evaluation instead used ImageNet-V2, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch, and ObjectNet.
uncertainty: This is an explicit scope restriction; the conclusions should not be extended to adversarially filtered distributions without further testing.

claim: The authors challenged the apparent robustness advantage of zero-shot CLIP by demonstrating that changing the single ID reference dataset could reverse the comparative conclusion.
quote: In this section, we use the comparison between zero-shot CLIP models and standard ImageNet models as an example to show the limitation of using a single ID test set: when only one ID test set is used, using different ID test sets leads to contradictory conclusions.
context: The demonstration compared ImageNet- and YFCC-trained models on ImageNet-V2, alternately controlling for ImageNet and YFCC accuracy.
uncertainty: The criticism concerns effective-robustness attribution, not whether a model can have high absolute OOD accuracy.

claim: The robustness project selected a measurement problem: a fixed in-distribution test set can distort comparisons among models trained on substantially different datasets.
quote: However, the emergence of many large-scale models trained on significantly different datasets makes it necessary to evaluate and compare models trained on different data distributions, under which it becomes unclear which ID test set should be used.
context: The paper revisits effective robustness, which measures OOD performance beyond what is predicted from ID performance.
uncertainty: The paper does not specify Carlini’s individual contribution to problem selection or metric design.

claim: The method has an explicit applicability boundary: it requires knowing all evaluated models' training distributions and is not directly usable for models whose training data are private.
quote: Our method requires fully knowing the training distributions of all the evaluated models, which is not directly applicable for large-scale pre-trained models with private training data.
context: Limitations and future-work section.
uncertainty: The source does not supply a validated substitute for unknown training distributions.

claim: The team directly checked whether its metric preserved rankings among models trained on the same data, found inconsistencies including negative correlations for some LAION comparisons, and therefore declined to replace single-ID evaluation in that setting.
quote: For LAION models, there is sometimes a negative correlation. Overall, while there is often a positive correlation between the rankings provided by the single-ID evaluation and the multi-ID evaluation, respectively, it is not necessarily consistent on all the datasets.
context: Appendix A.2 uses Kendall's rank correlation; multi-ID is positioned primarily for comparing different training distributions and as supplementary for a single training dataset.
uncertainty: Ranking disagreement does not itself establish which ranking is preferable for every downstream use.

claim: The limitations section questions whether conventional OOD benchmarks remain equally out of distribution for broadly pretrained models and standard classifiers.
quote: When models are pre-trained on large-scale data, it becomes unclear if these “OOD” test sets are still OOD, or if these test sets could be less OOD for the pre-trained models compared to standard classifiers.
context: The authors also note possible distribution overlap between pretraining data and fixed OOD test sets.
uncertainty: This is an acknowledged uncertainty, not a finding that the evaluated test examples were directly present in training.

claim: Although the formulation could extend to more training distributions, the authors deferred that expansion because fitting a reliable higher-dimensional baseline would require more model training.
quote: However, it could be costly as it would require training more models to fit a high-quality baseline function. We leave it for future works to reduce the cost when dealing with a larger number of datasets.
context: Scope boundary for generalization beyond two training datasets.
uncertainty: The paper proposes the extension in principle but does not validate it experimentally.

claim: The robustness project targets a measurement problem: a single fixed in-distribution test set becomes ambiguous when comparing models trained on different distributions.
quote: However, the emergence of many large-scale models trained on significantly different datasets makes it necessary to evaluate and compare models trained on different data distributions, under which it becomes unclear which ID test set should be used.
context: Motivation for revisiting effective robustness, particularly comparisons between ImageNet classifiers and language–image pretrained models.
uncertainty: The paper provides no individual contribution breakdown for Carlini.

claim: The robustness project targeted a measurement confound: a single designated in-distribution test set may not represent the training distribution of every model being compared.
quote: However, the emergence of many large-scale models trained on significantly different datasets makes it necessary to evaluate and compare models trained on different data distributions, under which it becomes unclear which ID test set should be used.
context: The paper compares conventional ImageNet-trained classifiers with models pretrained on image-text datasets.
uncertainty: The paper contains no individual contribution statement assigning this problem formulation specifically to Carlini.

claim: The paper distinguishes strong absolute OOD performance from an effective-robustness advantage after controlling for all relevant ID accuracies.
quote: The results further validate that zero-shot CLIP models, although may achieve high OOD performance if pre-trained with large-scale data (Radford et al., 2021), generally do not improve effective robustness if we control for all the ID accuracies.
context: Under multi-ID evaluation, the apparent robustness advantage of zero-shot CLIP generally became much smaller.
uncertainty: This conclusion is conditional on the proposed metric, its assumptions, and the evaluated models and distributions.

claim: The authors declined to draw a definite conclusion about SLIP and WiSE-FT despite their relatively larger residual gains, because those methods might change what should count as the training distribution.
quote: Thus, we do not draw a definite conclusion for the effective robustness of SLIP and WiSE-FT models and leave further validation for future work.
context: SLIP incorporates SimCLR, and WiSE-FT ensembles weights; the authors questioned whether their ID controls fully represented these procedures.
uncertainty: The gains were also smaller than in single-ID evaluation and not consistently significant across all test sets.

claim: The proposed evaluation controls simultaneously for test sets matching each training distribution, while bounding the implemented study to comparisons involving two training datasets at a time.
quote: Specifically, for each training distribution, we propose to prepare an ID test set that matches the training distribution, respectively. In particular, we focus on comparing models trained on two different datasets at a time in this paper
context: This is the construction of multi-ID effective robustness.
uncertainty: Each test set is exactly in-distribution only for a subset of the compared models.

claim: The authors challenge apparent zero-shot CLIP robustness gains by demonstrating that changing the sole ID test set can reverse the conclusion about which training distribution produces greater effective robustness.
