quote: In this section, we use the comparison between zero-shot CLIP models and standard ImageNet models as an example to show the limitation of using a single ID test set: when only one ID test set is used, using different ID test sets leads to contradictory conclusions.
context: ImageNet-V2 OOD performance was compared against either ImageNet or YFCC ID accuracy.
uncertainty: This concerns effective robustness after controlling for ID performance, not a denial that a model can have higher raw OOD accuracy.

claim: For models excluded from baseline fitting, the authors changed the reported evaluation statistic to MAE rather than using R-squared.
quote: Since these models are not used in the fitting, we do not use $R^{2}$, but we use MAE to measure the fitting quality.
context: Evaluation of downloaded and fine-tuned models in Table 4.
uncertainty: This records the paper's reporting choice, not a universal prohibition on computing out-of-sample R-squared.

claim: The baseline fit also included models trained on mixtures of datasets to populate intermediate training distributions and avoid favoring models from one data source.
quote: We use models trained on each single dataset as well as the combined datasets in the same fitting process, so that the baseline functions do not bias towards models trained on certain data.
context: Different mixing ratios were intended to produce diverse combinations of the two ID accuracies.
uncertainty: This is the design rationale; inclusion alone does not prove elimination of every possible baseline bias.

claim: The OOD benchmark selection excluded ImageNet-A because its adversarial filtering produces different effective-robustness behavior from the natural-shift setting being studied.
quote: We do not use ImageNet-A (Hendrycks et al., 2021b) which involves adversarial filtering and has a different behavior in effective robustness evaluation (Taori et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2022).
context: ImageNet-V2, ImageNet-R, ImageNet-Sketch, and ObjectNet were included.
uncertainty: The paper's findings should not be generalized to the excluded adversarially filtered benchmark.

claim: The team chose a linear plane in logit-transformed accuracy space after observing approximate planarity, then fit its parameters by ordinary least squares and evaluated the fit quantitatively.
quote: We determine the parameters by solving an ordinary least squares regression to fit the accuracies. Metrics for linear regression such as the coefficient of determination, a.k.a. $R^{2}$, can be used to evaluate the fitting quality of the baseline function.
context: OOD accuracy is predicted from two ID accuracies, and effective robustness is the observed-minus-predicted residual.
uncertainty: Good fit is an empirical property of evaluated distributions, not a guarantee that linear prediction holds universally.

claim: The authors identify knowledge of all evaluated training distributions as a prerequisite, limiting direct application to large models trained on private data.
quote: Our method requires fully knowing the training distributions of all the evaluated models, which is not directly applicable for large-scale pre-trained models with private training data.
context: A corresponding test set must be constructed for each training distribution.
uncertainty: The paper does not supply a validated workaround for unknown or proprietary training distributions.

claim: The paper supported its revised robustness interpretation with both improved predictive fit and changed residual robustness estimates, including especially large fit improvements for LAION-related comparisons.
quote: Specifically, the improvement of fitting quality is particularly significant for models involving LAION on ImageNet-R ($R^{2}$ improved from 0.216 to 0.982 and MAE reduced from 9.23% to 1.32%)
context: Under multi-ID evaluation, the average apparent robustness advantage of LAION models also moved close to zero.
uncertainty: These fit statistics concern the models used in the relevant baseline analysis; additional held-out models were evaluated separately.

claim: Despite residual gains for SLIP and WiSE-FT, the researchers decline to draw a definite robustness conclusion because these methods may change what should count as the model's training distribution.
quote: However, we are not certain on whether SLIP and WiSE-FT can alter the underlying training distribution, because SLIP uses SimCLR that introduces different training images, and WiSE-FT esseentially edits the weights of the models by weight-space ensembling.
context: SLIP and WiSE-FT showed relatively higher average multi-ID effective robustness, but their gains were smaller and not consistently significant across test sets.
uncertainty: The paper explicitly leaves further validation to future work.

claim: The proposed correction requires an ID test set matching each training distribution, with the reported experiments deliberately restricted to comparing two training datasets at a time.
quote: Specifically, for each training distribution, we propose to prepare an ID test set that matches the training distribution, respectively. In particular, we focus on comparing models trained on two different datasets at a time in this paper, and we thereby use two ID test sets, where each of them corresponds to one of the training datasets.
context: Definition of multi-ID effective robustness.
uncertainty: Each test set is exactly ID only for the corresponding subset of models.

claim: The paper supplemented static projected plots with an interactive visualization so readers could inspect the three-dimensional relationship underlying multi-ID effective robustness.
quote: The colored plane stands for the baseline function. Figure˜4 and Figure˜5 (in Section˜A.1) show various projected 2D views. See our website (https://shizhouxing.github.io/effective-robustness) for an interactive visualization.
context: Figure 3 presents OOD accuracy against two ID accuracies; projected views illustrate why single-ID comparisons can mislead.
uncertainty: The corpus states that the visualization is provided; it has not been independently inspected, and its authorship is not assigned to Carlini.

claim: Automatic test-set construction included ambiguity filtering, per-class balancing, a minimum data requirement, and holding the selected examples out of training.
quote: We adopt a label only if a unique ImageNet class can be determined by matching for the involved image. We then construct a balanced and labelled test set by keeping 50 examples for each class that has at least 100 examples in the labelled images. The test examples are then held out from the training data.
context: The resulting test sets contained 451 YFCC classes and 408 LAION classes.
uncertainty: Requiring a unique text match reduces ambiguity but does not guarantee that the visual content matches the inferred label.

claim: The authors aligned the evaluated label spaces by retaining classes shared across test sets and mapping selected ImageNet classes to CIFAR-10 classes where needed.
quote: Considering that different test sets may not have the same classes, we follow prior works (Taori et al., 2020; Fang et al., 2022) to use class subsampling[^1] to retain classes appearing in all the test sets.
context: This prevents differing class inventories from being silently treated as directly comparable classification tasks.
uncertainty: The paper clarifies that its term class subsampling does not refer to random sampling.

claim: The implementation mostly reused established training configurations, while making an explicit batch-size change for greater parallelism rather than presenting extensively tuned bespoke training as part of the contribution.
quote: For training CLIP models, we mostly follow hyperparameters provided in Fang et al. (2022) and the implementation in Open-CLIP (Ilharco et al., 2021). While Fang et al. (2022) used a batch size of 1024, we use 2048 for more parallelism.
context: The appendix also says CIFAR-10 classifiers reused TF-Vision configurations with only dataset, class-count, and image-size changes.
uncertainty: The paper does not isolate the effect of the batch-size change on the robustness comparisons.

claim: The baseline function was motivated by an observed planar relationship among logit-transformed accuracies and fitted with ordinary least squares; robustness was defined as the remaining OOD residual.
quote: We determine the parameters by solving an ordinary least squares regression to fit the accuracies. Metrics for linear regression such as the coefficient of determination, a.k.a. $R^{2}$, can be used to evaluate the fitting quality of the baseline function.
context: Two ID accuracies replace the single predictor used in earlier effective-robustness evaluations.
uncertainty: Good predictive fit supports the metric's empirical usefulness but does not itself identify causal mechanisms of robustness.

claim: The authors distinguish high absolute OOD performance from extra robustness after controlling for ID accuracy: their challenge to zero-shot CLIP concerns the latter.
quote: The results further validate that zero-shot CLIP models, although may achieve high OOD performance if pre-trained with large-scale data (Radford et al., 2021), generally do not improve effective robustness if we control for all the ID accuracies.
context: Interpretation of the additional-model evaluation.
uncertainty: The statement is qualified by the evaluated datasets, models, and validity of the multi-ID controls.

claim: The metric's interpretation depends on the training distributions being relatively close to one another compared with the OOD distributions, an assumption the paper states rather than leaving implicit.
quote: In this way, both ID test sets are relatively ID for all the models compared to the OOD test sets, and it can be meaningful to control for the performance on these ID test sets when comparing the OOD performance.
context: Ordinary images from ImageNet, YFCC, and LAION are contrasted with a distribution such as ImageNet-Sketch.
uncertainty: The paper does not establish applicability when the training distributions are highly dissimilar.

claim: The metric’s interpretation relies on the training distributions being relatively close to one another compared with the OOD distributions.
quote: However, we assume that the training distributions of all the models are still relatively close compared to the OOD test distributions
context: The paper contrasts ordinary images from ImageNet, YFCC, and LAION with more distinct distributions such as sketches.
uncertainty: The authors did not establish how the evaluation behaves when the training distributions are highly different.

claim: The paper validates the revised metric with prediction quality, reporting a particularly large improvement for LAION-related ImageNet-R comparisons rather than relying only on a conceptual critique.
quote: Specifically, the improvement of fitting quality is particularly significant for models involving LAION on ImageNet-R ($R^{2}$ improved from 0.216 to 0.982 and MAE reduced from 9.23% to 1.32%) and ImageNet-Sketch ($R^{2}$ improved from 0.281 to 0.937 and MAE reduced from 7.90% to 2.10%).
context: Comparisons of single-ID and multi-ID baselines on ImageNet-like distribution shifts.
uncertainty: These are fitting results; the paper separately tests additional models excluded from baseline fitting.

claim: The method explicitly requires knowledge of every evaluated model's training distribution, limiting direct application to models whose training data are private.
quote: Our method requires fully knowing the training distributions of all the evaluated models, which is not directly applicable for large-scale pre-trained models with private training data.
context: The limitations section also requires that training procedures not substantially alter the relevant distribution beyond basic augmentation.
uncertainty: No workaround for unknown private training distributions is demonstrated.

claim: The CLIP experiment filtered out models below 5% ImageNet accuracy and kept downloaded ViT-based and fine-tuned models separate from baseline fitting.
quote: We discard models with ImageNet accuracy below 5%. Additionally, in Section˜5.4, we also have downloaded ViT-based models from Mu et al. (2022); Ilharco et al. (2021) and CLIP models fine-tuned on ImageNet, which are only used for evaluation but not fitting the baseline functions.
context: Model inclusion and held-out evaluation rules in the experimental setup.
uncertainty: The supplied passage does not state a rationale for the 5% cutoff.

claim: For image–text datasets without classification labels, the team accepted automatically derived ID labels as a practical measurement choice while acknowledging that human annotation could produce higher quality.
quote: Although it is possible to obtain a higher-quality test set by human labelling, we will show that using the automatically labelled test sets can already produce reasonable results.
context: YFCC and LAION labels were generated by matching text with ImageNet class names.
uncertainty: The passage does not quantify automatic-label error against a human-labeled reference set.

claim: The study supported its metric revision with predictive-fit measurements, including a large reduction in error for LAION-related models on ImageNet-R and ImageNet-Sketch.
quote: Specifically, the improvement of fitting quality is particularly significant for models involving LAION on ImageNet-R ($R^{2}$ improved from 0.216 to 0.982 and MAE reduced from 9.23% to 1.32%) and ImageNet-Sketch ($R^{2}$ improved from 0.281 to 0.937 and MAE reduced from 7.90% to 2.10%).
context: These results compare predictions based on a single ID accuracy with predictions using two ID accuracies.
uncertainty: These fitting results alone are not held-out validation; the paper separately evaluates models excluded from fitting.

claim: The researchers expose an assumption that the ID distributions are relatively close to each other compared with the OOD distributions, and acknowledge that highly different training distributions remain unstudied.
quote: We assume that the two ID test sets have relatively close distributions compare to the OOD test sets. We have not considered how the difference between the multiple ID test sets may affect the evaluation, and how the effective robustness should be compared if models are trained on highly different distributions.
context: A central limit on interpreting multi-ID controls across arbitrary datasets.
uncertainty: No quantitative closeness criterion or validation for widely separated training distributions is given here.

claim: The authors propose making use of their metric conditional on sufficiently good baseline fit, acknowledging distribution shifts where the underlying accuracy relationship does not hold.
quote: We may set a threshold on the fitting quality and only adopt our method when the fitting quality is sufficiently good.
context: The paper focuses on shifts where within-training-distribution accuracy-on-the-line relationships are known to hold.
uncertainty: This is a proposed safeguard; the passage does not specify or validate a numerical acceptance threshold.

claim: The authors limited their claims to shifts where the original accuracy-on-the-line relationship already holds and suggested a fit-quality threshold as a possible gate for applying the new metric.
quote: We may set a threshold on the fitting quality and only adopt our method when the fitting quality is sufficiently good.
context: The paper acknowledges counterexamples involving corruption shifts, shifts in the wild, and sometimes inverse ID–OOD correlations.
uncertainty: No specific operational threshold is supplied or validated.

claim: The experiment deliberately created models spanning a range of accuracies by varying training-set size, rather than fitting a baseline only to a narrow set of high-performing models.
quote: To this end, we follow Taori et al. (2020) to train models with various proportions of data by subsampling from the entire training set (namely dataset subsampling), which effectively produces models with diverse accuracies.
context: The appendix lists subsampling proportions from 5% through 50%.

claim: The successful transfer attack supplied a concrete reason to try BPDA: preserve the defended forward computation but obtain gradients from the original network.
quote: Given that gradients computed on the undefended model effectively fool the defended model, we decided to try and apply the BPDA[^2] strategy on SAP. By doing this, we query the actual defended model, while only taking gradients with respect to the original model.
context: The attack removes neuron dropping only from the backward pass while retaining it in forward evaluation.

claim: After more than 10,000 gradient iterations remained ineffective on corrected SAP, the researchers changed diagnostic strategy and used transfer attacks to test for gradient masking.
quote: We therefore began to test for other signs of gradient masking as recommended by Athalye et al. (2018). We ran a transfer attack where we generated adversarial examples on the undefended model and then evaluate these adversarial examples with SAP.
context: The original targeted attack stayed below 50% success, while the transfer attack reached 70% under the stated CIFAR-10 distortion bound.
uncertainty: This is a documented pivot within this debugging effort, not a universal iteration-based stopping rule.

claim: The researchers distinguished a consequential implementation error from a benign approximation by checking whether attacks generated with the efficient sampler transferred to the prescribed sampler.
quote: This approximation is more efficient in high-dimensional spaces while remaining close in performance. When we attack a model that uses the latter approach, and evaluate using the former, the attack success rate remains unchanged.
context: The approximation uses per-neuron binomial sampling instead of sampling a fixed number of neurons from a multinomial distribution.
uncertainty: Unchanged success is reported for the tested attack and evaluation, not guaranteed for every application of the approximation.

claim: After retracting the faulty attack's conclusion, the collaborators supported a repaired break with test-set evaluation and a reported uncertainty interval.
quote: This modified attack is sufficient to reduce the accuracy of SAP to $0.1\%$ ($\pm 0.05\%$) evaluated over the test set.
context: The repaired BPDA attack was evaluated on CIFAR-10 at a distortion bound of 0.031.
uncertainty: The supplied passage does not explain how the ±0.05% quantity was calculated.

claim: After the corrected defense resisted a long gradient-based attack, the team changed diagnostic strategy and tested transfer from the undefended model for signs of gradient masking.
quote: We therefore began to test for other signs of gradient masking as recommended by Athalye et al. (2018). We ran a transfer attack where we generated adversarial examples on the undefended model and then evaluate these adversarial examples with SAP.
context: The original attack remained below 50% targeted success after more than 10,000 iterations, while the transfer attack achieved 70%.
uncertainty: The paper identifies gradient masking as part of the explanation rather than claiming it is the only factor.

claim: The erratum corrected both an omitted averaging step and a compensating hyperparameter change, and acknowledged that the original attack ceased to work after faithful implementation.
quote: Fixing this error in the implementation is simple: setting the value of $r_{i}$ to $m_{i}$, and evaluating each test example by averaging the outputs over $100$ forward passes.
context: The earlier implementation omitted multi-pass averaging and increased the retained-neuron sampling parameter to preserve clean accuracy.
uncertainty: The correction invalidated that attack result; the paper separately develops a different successful attack.

claim: The authors identified an earlier warning sign they should have investigated: needing a different hyperparameter to reproduce the original model’s behavior.
quote: In this case, the error should have been discovered when the replicated neural network required a different hyper-parameter than described in the original paper.
context: The conclusion urges exact reproduction of a defense’s specified implementation.
uncertainty: A hyperparameter discrepancy is a reason to investigate, not proof by itself of an implementation error.

claim: The collaborators cautioned against treating BPDA as a universally effective repair for optimization failures, since substituting incorrect gradients can make attacks worse.
quote: BPDA in general should not be treated as a magic black-box that resolves all optimization difficulties. Since BPDA applies the incorrect gradient, in many cases unless applied very carefully, attacks perform worse with BPDA than without. In this particular case we found it was helpful.
context: Footnote 2 qualifies the successful use of BPDA against SAP.

claim: Carlini publicly accepted sole responsibility for the SAP reimplementation error underlying the earlier attack evaluation.
quote: The author of this erratum, Nicholas Carlini, wrote the SAP re-implementation and is solely responsible for the error.
context: The footnote in the coauthored erratum specifically identifies Carlini’s role rather than leaving responsibility at the author-group level.

claim: The erratum explicitly identifies Carlini as the author of the faulty SAP reimplementation and assigns him sole responsibility for that error.
quote: The author of this erratum, Nicholas Carlini, wrote the SAP re-implementation and is solely responsible for the error.
context: Footnote 1 accompanies a correction to the earlier Obfuscated Gradients evaluation.
uncertainty: The statement appears in a coauthored erratum, but attribution of this particular error is explicit and individual.

claim: The erratum tied its strong advocacy of source release to a concrete discovery: the evaluation error was found because both the defense and attack papers released code.
quote: We firmly believe that releasing source code is the only way to promote correct and reproducible research, especially in the domain of adversarial machine learning where – as is the case here – setting a single hyper-parameter to the incorrect value can have dramatic consequences.
context: The omitted test-time averaging had led to a compensating change in the number of sampled neurons.
uncertainty: The exclusivity of 'the only way' is the coauthors' stated position, not a separately established finding.

claim: The collaborators separated an efficiency approximation used during attack generation from faithful evaluation, testing generated examples against the original multinomial sampling procedure.
quote: As mentioned earlier, we apply per-neuron binomial sampling for efficiency, but test on the correct multinomial distribution.
context: The erratum separately reports that this sampling approximation did not change attack success.
uncertainty: The equivalence is empirical for their attack evaluation, not an assertion that the distributions are identical.

claim: The successful transfer diagnostic directly motivated trying BPDA, using the defended model for forward evaluation and the undefended model for gradients.
quote: Given that gradients computed on the undefended model effectively fool the defended model, we decided to try and apply the BPDA[^2] strategy on SAP. By doing this, we query the actual defended model, while only taking gradients with respect to the original model.
context: The new backward pass omits SAP's neuron dropping while the forward pass retains the defense.

claim: When the corrected defense resisted the existing optimization attack, the collaborators changed diagnostic strategy and tested transfer from the undefended model for evidence of gradient masking.
quote: We therefore began to test for other signs of gradient masking as recommended by Athalye et al. (2018). We ran a transfer attack where we generated adversarial examples on the undefended model and then evaluate these adversarial examples with SAP.
context: The existing targeted attack remained below 50% success after more than 10,000 iterations; transfer achieved 70% targeted success.
uncertainty: These rates apply to CIFAR-10 at the paper's stated distortion bound.

claim: The erratum presents released source code as essential to discovering the mistake and making adversarial-ML research reproducible.
quote: We firmly believe that releasing source code is the only way to promote correct and reproducible research, especially in the domain of adversarial machine learning where – as is the case here – setting a single hyper-parameter to the incorrect value can have dramatic consequences.
context: Both the defense and attack papers released code, allowing their implementations to be compared.
uncertainty: This is an explicit joint position of the erratum’s authors.

claim: The team separates consequential implementation mistakes from harmless approximations by testing whether a sampling change transfers back to the specified defense.
quote: This approximation is more efficient in high-dimensional spaces while remaining close in performance. When we attack a model that uses the latter approach, and evaluate using the former, the attack success rate remains unchanged.
context: Per-neuron binomial sampling was compared with the defense’s prescribed multinomial sampling.
uncertainty: The equivalence is reported for the evaluated attack success, not every possible property of the two samplers.

claim: The erratum extracted a concrete replication warning from the mistake: needing a different hyperparameter to reproduce the original network should have prompted investigation.
quote: In this case, the error should have been discovered when the replicated neural network required a different hyper-parameter than described in the original paper.
context: Maintaining reported clean accuracy had required doubling the prescribed neuron-sampling parameter because averaging was missing.

claim: The team warns against treating BPDA as an automatic fix: its deliberately incorrect gradients can make attacks worse unless the approximation is chosen carefully.
quote: BPDA in general should not be treated as a magic black-box that resolves all optimization difficulties. Since BPDA applies the incorrect gradient, in many cases unless applied very carefully, attacks perform worse with BPDA than without. In this particular case we found it was helpful.
context: Qualification accompanying the successful repaired SAP attack.

claim: The erratum derives a practical debugging rule from the failure: needing an undocumented hyperparameter change to reproduce a defense should trigger investigation.
quote: In this case, the error should have been discovered when the replicated neural network required a different hyper-parameter than described in the original paper.
context: The mistaken implementation required an enlarged retention parameter to recover the reported clean accuracy.

claim: The erratum traces the apparent break to a missing averaging step and an enlarged neuron-retention parameter, and reports that correcting the implementation restores the defense’s claimed resistance to the original attack.
quote:
Fixing this error in the implementation is simple: setting the value of $r_{i}$ to $m_{i}$, and evaluating each test example by averaging the outputs over $100$ forward passes.

When this error is corrected, the attack described in Athalye et al. (2018) is no longer effective
context: The earlier implementation omitted averaging over stochastic forward passes and used twice the prescribed retention parameter to maintain clean accuracy.
uncertainty: This corrects the earlier attack result; it does not establish robustness against other attacks.

claim: Despite BPDA succeeding in the repaired attack, the authors warned against treating it as a universal remedy because its deliberately incorrect gradients can make optimization worse.
quote: BPDA in general should not be treated as a magic black-box that resolves all optimization difficulties. Since BPDA applies the incorrect gradient, in many cases unless applied very carefully, attacks perform worse with BPDA than without. In this particular case we found it was helpful.
context: Footnote 2 qualifies the method used to repair the SAP attack.

claim: The erratum argues strongly for releasing source code because code from both papers enabled discovery of an error with large consequences.
quote: We firmly believe that releasing source code is the only way to promote correct and reproducible research, especially in the domain of adversarial machine learning where – as is the case here – setting a single hyper-parameter to the incorrect value can have dramatic consequences.
context: The authors connect their reproducibility position to the concrete SAP discrepancy.
uncertainty: The categorical statement is jointly authored; it is not independent evidence that Carlini personally authored this wording.

claim: Carlini explicitly accepts sole responsibility for the SAP reimplementation error rather than leaving accountability at the coauthor-group level.
quote: The author of this erratum, Nicholas Carlini, wrote the SAP re-implementation and is solely responsible for the error.
context: Footnote identifying responsibility for the implementation underlying an earlier attack evaluation.
uncertainty: The statement appears in a coauthored erratum but explicitly attributes the implementation and responsibility to Carlini.

claim: The collaborators corrected a missing averaging step and an associated hyperparameter change, then acknowledged that the original attack no longer broke the properly implemented defense.
quote: When this error is corrected, the attack described in Athalye et al. (2018) is no longer effective; the accuracy of SAP remains as is claimed in the paper.
context: The repair restores the prescribed neuron-sampling setting and averages each test example over 100 forward passes.
uncertainty: This withdraws the original attack result for correctly implemented SAP; it does not establish resistance to other attacks.

claim: The successful transfer attack supplied a concrete reason to try BPDA: use the actual defended model for forward evaluation but the undefended model’s gradients for optimization.
quote: Given that gradients computed on the undefended model effectively fool the defended model, we decided to try and apply the BPDA[^2] strategy on SAP. By doing this, we query the actual defended model, while only taking gradients with respect to the original model.
context: The backward pass removed SAP’s neuron-dropping operation; final evaluation retained the proper defense.

claim: The corrected evaluation reported the new attack’s residual accuracy, uncertainty, dataset, and distortion bound rather than merely repeating the earlier conclusion that SAP was broken.
quote: We then evaluate the accuracy of SAP on CIFAR-10 with a distortion bound of $\varepsilon=0.031$. This modified attack is sufficient to reduce the accuracy of SAP to $0.1\%$ ($\pm 0.05\%$) evaluated over the test set.
context: This is the result of the repaired BPDA attack on the corrected defense.
uncertainty: The quoted passage does not explain the statistical construction of the reported ±0.05%.

claim: The repaired attack was evaluated on the CIFAR-10 test set under a stated distortion bound, with both a residual-accuracy estimate and uncertainty reported.
quote: We then evaluate the accuracy of SAP on CIFAR-10 with a distortion bound of $\varepsilon=0.031$. This modified attack is sufficient to reduce the accuracy of SAP to $0.1\%$ ($\pm 0.05\%$) evaluated over the test set.
context: Result of the BPDA attack on correctly implemented SAP.
uncertainty: The excerpt does not specify how the reported plus-or-minus quantity was calculated.

claim: The paper identifies a structural problem with a fixed tradeoff weight: a weight that works at the end of a nonconvex search may not work at its beginning.
quote: In the worst case this might introduce incompatibilities where no single value of $\lambda$ works throughout the generation process requiring tuning $\lambda$ during a single adversarial example search.
context: The analysis motivates alternatives to weighted-sum losses for simultaneous classifier and detector evasion.
uncertainty: This is a possible worst-case failure, not a claim that every weighted loss necessarily fails.

claim: The evaluation intentionally attacks each defense on its strongest reported dataset, while using both the original threat model and common perturbation norms.
quote: We attack each defense on the dataset that it performs best on.
context: Three defenses are tested on CIFAR-10 and one on ImageNet; original constraints support fair reevaluation and standard norms support comparisons across defenses.
uncertainty: The strongest-dataset choice is reported by the authors; the supplied paper does not independently establish that each chosen dataset is globally optimal for its defense.

claim: Computational throughput constrains experimental breadth: the steganalysis case uses only the orthogonal attack rather than testing both proposed variants.
quote: For computational efficiency, we only run our Orthogonal attack as the detection model has a throughput of one image per second.
context: This limitation appears in the steganalysis results table caption.

claim: The team addressed non-differentiable SPAM feature extraction by constructing a differentiable approximation and using an auxiliary detector's gradients for the attack.
quote: Using this differentiable formulation of SPAM feature extraction, we train an auxillary detector as described above and use its gradients to apply our attack on the original, non-differentiable detector.
context: The approximation replaces the obstructive discretization step with a formulation based on count and transition-probability matrices.
uncertainty: The phrase 'original, non-differentiable detector' should be read alongside the earlier disclosed replacement of the FLD ensemble; the supplied text does not clearly resolve that implementation ambiguity.

claim: Selective gradient descent uses constraint satisfaction as a local stopping rule: it stops spending optimization effort on a constraint once that constraint is satisfied.
quote: Instead of minimizing the weighted sum of $f$ and $g$, our first attack completely eliminates the possibility for perturbation waste by never optimizing against a constraint once it becomes satisfied.
context: The method switches between classifier and detector updates according to whether the desired classification has been achieved.
uncertainty: This is a rule within the attack algorithm, not a personal rule about when to stop a research project.

claim: After converting Honeypot models from TensorFlow to PyTorch, the collaboration obtained confirmation from the original defense authors that its adversarial examples evaded detection.
quote: We shared our results with the original defense authors who confirmed our adversarial examples successfully evaded their detection (an important step, given that we had converted the model to PyTorch).
context: External confirmation checked that the framework conversion had not invalidated the attack result.
uncertainty: The supplied source reports author confirmation but does not include the correspondence or independent replication details.

claim: The SPAM evaluation used a differentiable feature approximation and auxiliary detector gradients to attack the nondifferentiable detector.
quote: Using this differentiable formulation of SPAM feature extraction, we train an auxillary detector as described above and use its gradients to apply our attack on the original, non-differentiable detector.
context: Discretized pixel-difference statistics required a surrogate gradient construction.
uncertainty: The surrounding case study also replaces the original paper's FLD ensemble; 'original' here should not erase that implementation qualification.

claim: The team favors a small, analyzable modification of gradient descent that selectively optimizes objectives instead of combining them through a fixed weighted loss.
quote: Our attack approach is a modification of standard gradient descent [MMS+17] and requires changing just a few lines of code.
context: The contribution statement describes the resulting attack as simpler and easier to analyze than prior approaches.
uncertainty: This supports a design priority within this project, not a general personal preference of Carlini's.

claim: The steganalysis experiments omit the more complex SRM feature variant because the team judged its benefit marginal and chose the simplest instance of the shared principle.
quote: This scheme follows the same fundamental principle as SPAM in modeling inter-pixel dependencies—there is only a marginal benefit from using these more complex models, and so we analyze the simplest variant of the scheme.
context: The omitted method is Spatial Rich Model; the evaluated method is SPAM.
uncertainty: The stated similarity is the authors' rationale for limiting scope, not experimental evidence that their attack achieves the same results on SRM.

claim: For the steganalysis defense, the team deliberately changed the classifier to isolate the claimed usefulness of SPAM features and permit a common attack implementation.
quote: Instead of re-implementing the full FLD ensemble [KFH12] used by the authors, we train a 3-layer fully connected neural network on SPAM features and use this as the detector.
context: The original code was in MATLAB; the team reimplemented in PyTorch and argued that FLD's nondifferentiability was not fundamental to the feature-based proposal.
uncertainty: This evaluates a modified detector architecture and should not be described without qualification as an exact replication of the original FLD system.

claim: The conclusion explicitly discourages mechanical reuse of the proposed attack and makes understanding a defense's design a prerequisite for choosing an appropriate evaluation strategy.
quote: However, we discourage future work from blindly applying this attack without properly understanding its design criteria. While this attack does eliminate perturbation waste for the defenses we consider, it is not the only way to do so, and may not be the correct way to do so in future defense evaluations.
context: The authors suggest adding the technique to automated attack tools while insisting that future evaluations still require adaptation to the defense.

claim: Their critique of weighted objectives includes a dynamic tuning problem: non-convexity can make a single loss weight unsuitable across an entire attack trajectory.
quote: In the worst case this might introduce incompatibilities where no single value of $\lambda$ works throughout the generation process requiring tuning $\lambda$ during a single adversarial example search.
context: The perturbation-waste analysis distinguishes finding an acceptable weight at the final solution from finding one that also permits progress from initialization.
uncertainty: The quotation describes a possible worst case, not a claim that every weighted-loss attack fails.

claim: The steganalysis case study explicitly limits scope to SPAM, choosing the simpler feature scheme instead of also evaluating Spatial Rich Model.
quote: This scheme follows the same fundamental principle as SPAM in modeling inter-pixel dependencies—there is only a marginal benefit from using these more complex models, and so we analyze the simplest variant of the scheme.
context: The preceding sentence identifies SRM as the second feature-extraction method that the study does not evaluate.
uncertainty: The marginal-benefit assessment is the authors' rationale; no SRM attack experiment is supplied.

claim: The team obtained original code and pretrained models to reduce ambiguity about whether its attacks evaluated the intended defenses.
quote: We obtain source code and pre-trained defense models from the authors in order to ensure that our attack matches the defense as closely as possible.
context: This statement concerns Dense Layer Analysis; the paper also reports obtaining author-provided models and code for Honeypot and SID.

claim: Despite proposing a reusable attack, the authors explicitly discourage its blind application and require future evaluations to adapt to the defense's design.
quote: However, we discourage future work from blindly applying this attack without properly understanding its design criteria.
context: The conclusion says eliminating perturbation waste here does not establish that this is the only or correct method for future defenses.

claim: The attack claims are explicitly scoped to a perfect-knowledge threat model in which the adversary can access both classifier and detector functions.
quote: Consistent with prior work, in this paper we work under the perfect-knowledge scenario: the adversary has direct access to both functions $f$ and $g$.
context: This assumption appears in the detection-defense background before the new optimization methods are introduced.
uncertainty: The results do not by themselves establish equal effectiveness under restricted or black-box access.

claim: The detection-defense project selects a specific optimization failure as its research problem: satisfying one attack constraint too aggressively can prevent satisfaction of another.
quote: We find that existing attacks that attempt to satisfy multiple simultaneous constraints often over-optimize against one constraint at the cost of satisfying another.
context: Successful attacks must cause misclassification while also being accepted as non-adversarial by a detector; the paper calls inefficient allocation across these requirements perturbation waste.

claim: The authors use attack success at fixed detector false-positive rates to assess the joint requirement of targeted misclassification and detector evasion, and also report full ROC curves.
quote: SR@N is defined as the fraction of targeted attacks that succeed when the defense’s false positive rate is set to $N\%$.
context: They report SR@5 because 5% appears in earlier defenses and SR@50 as an extreme allowance that would discard half of benign inputs; full ROC curves provide additional context.

claim: For Dense Layer Analysis, the team used author-provided models to reduce implementation mismatch and again had the defense authors validate the resulting adversarial examples.
quote: We obtain source code and pre-trained defense models from the authors in order to ensure that our attack matches the defense as closely as possible.
context: The DLA section later states that the authors confirmed the attack results; author-provided source and pretrained models were also used for SID.
uncertainty: This evidence concerns the collaborative validation process, not Carlini's individual communication habits.

claim: The evaluation measures attack success at explicit false-positive operating points and supplies full ROC curves to make detector tradeoffs inspectable.
quote: We report SR@5 and SR@50 for our main results. The value $5\%$ is used in many prior defenses in the literature [MLW+18, XEQ17], and $50\%$ is an extreme upper bound and would reduce the model’s accuracy by half.
context: SR@N is the fraction of targeted attacks that succeed when the detector's false-positive rate is N%; full ROC curves supplement those points.
uncertainty: Success figures must retain their false-positive threshold rather than being treated as threshold-independent detector performance.

claim: The team deliberately uses targeted attacks with randomly selected incorrect labels because targeted success also establishes untargeted vulnerability.
quote: We apply targeted attacks for the reasons listed in prior attack work [ACW18], primarily because if targeted attacks succeed, then untargeted attacks certainly will.
context: Targets are drawn uniformly from incorrect class labels. The paper describes untargeted attacks as generally easier.

claim: The orthogonal update is introduced to address a limitation of selective updates: progress against one objective can undo progress against the other when gradients oppose each other.
quote: The purpose of this update is to take gradient descent steps with respect to one of $f$ or $g$ in such a way that we do not significantly disturb the loss of the function not chosen.
context: The paper motivates orthogonalization with numerical instability and alternating steps that repeatedly reverse prior progress.
uncertainty: The paper presents a method-development progression; it does not establish when the authors personally discovered each issue.

claim: The attack study explicitly fixes a perfect-knowledge threat model rather than leaving attacker access implicit.
quote: Consistent with prior work, in this paper we work under the perfect-knowledge scenario: the adversary has direct access to both functions $f$ and $g$.
context: The adversary can access both the classifier and the detector.
uncertainty: Results under this access model do not by themselves establish equivalent black-box attack performance.

claim: Despite advocating its method as useful for automated tools, the paper warns against blindly applying it and insists that future evaluations adapt attacks to the defense's design.
quote: However, we discourage future work from blindly applying this attack without properly understanding its design criteria. While this attack does eliminate perturbation waste for the defenses we consider, it is not the only way to do so, and may not be the correct way to do so in future defense evaluations.

claim: Selective gradient descent uses satisfaction of a constraint as a local stopping rule, redirecting optimization effort once that requirement has been met.

claim: The detection-defense project starts from a specific optimization failure: satisfying one requirement excessively can prevent satisfaction of another.

claim: The authors chose a small modification of standard gradient descent, presenting simplicity of implementation and analysis as advantages of selectively optimizing separate objectives.

uncertainty: This is a design rationale for the paper's method, not evidence of a general personal preference for minimal code changes.

claim: Orthogonal gradient descent was introduced to address a limitation of selective updates: opposing gradients can repeatedly undo each other's progress.
quote: Often, the gradients of $f$ and $g$ point in opposite directions, that is, $\nabla f\approx-\nabla g$. As a result, every step spent optimizing $f$ causes backwards progress on optimizing against $g$.
context: The orthogonalized update aims to improve one objective without significantly disturbing the other.
uncertainty: The paper presents two related methods; it does not establish a chronological change in Carlini's private views.

claim: The team chooses targeted attacks with random incorrect labels as a stronger demonstration, because success implies that untargeted attacks can also succeed.
quote: We apply targeted attacks for the reasons listed in prior attack work [ACW18], primarily because if targeted attacks succeed, then untargeted attacks certainly will.
context: All attacks choose their target uniformly from the incorrect labels.

claim: Orthogonal gradient descent addresses the remaining failure in which improving one objective undoes progress on the other.
quote: The purpose of this update is to take gradient descent steps with respect to one of $f$ or $g$ in such a way that we do not significantly disturb the loss of the function not chosen.
context: The paper introduces orthogonalization after observing that nearly opposing gradients can cause alternating updates to undo one another.
uncertainty: This is a refinement within the paper's method development, not evidence of a longitudinal change in Carlini's views.

claim: The evaluation balances favorable conditions for the defenses with comparability across defenses: each is tested on its strongest dataset, under its original threat model and additional standard perturbation norms.
quote: We attack each defense on the dataset that it performs best on. All of our defenses operate on images.
context: Three defenses are evaluated on CIFAR-10 and one on ImageNet. The authors say original threat models support fair re-evaluation, while standard norms enable cross-defense comparisons.
uncertainty: The strongest-dataset characterization is the paper's own assessment.

claim: When a published SID result did not provide the operating-point metric needed for comparison, the team ran PGD on the authors' implementation to construct that baseline and labeled its provenance.
quote: The original paper only reports AUC values and does not report true positive/false positive rates. The value of $9\%$ was obtained by running PGD on the author’s defense implementation.
context: The Figure 3 table footnote distinguishes the reconstructed baseline from a directly published true-positive/false-positive result.
uncertainty: The 9% value should not be described as an operating-point result originally reported by the SID authors.

claim: The collaboration explicitly limited the steganalysis evaluation to SPAM, omitting the more complex Spatial Rich Model because it judged the benefit marginal and the underlying principle shared.
quote: This scheme follows the same fundamental principle as SPAM in modeling inter-pixel dependencies—there is only a marginal benefit from using these more complex models, and so we analyze the simplest variant of the scheme.
context: The preceding sentence states that SRM was not evaluated.
uncertainty: The reasoning supports the chosen scope but does not experimentally establish that the omitted SRM variant is equally vulnerable.

claim: Computational cost directly bounded the SPAM comparison: the collaboration ran only the orthogonal attack because the detector processed about one image per second.
quote: For computational efficiency, we only run our Orthogonal attack as the detection model has a throughput of one image per second.
context: Figure 4 reports no selective-gradient counterpart for this case study.

claim: The project sought an attack that was simple to implement and analyze, modifying standard gradient descent by selecting which objective to optimize.
quote: Our attack approach is a modification of standard gradient descent [MMS+17] and requires changing just a few lines of code.

uncertainty: This describes a design property of the project, not a general personal preference inferred for Carlini.

claim: The evaluation deliberately used each defense's strongest dataset and preserved the originally considered threat model, while also adding standard perturbation norms for comparisons across defenses.
quote: We attack each defense on the dataset that it performs best on.
context: Three defenses were evaluated on CIFAR-10 and one on ImageNet; the same paragraph specifies original threat models and additional standard norms.
uncertainty: The supplied paper states this selection principle without independently establishing which dataset is strongest for every defense.

context: A successful attack must induce misclassification and evade a detector within a perturbation bound.

claim: For Dense Layer Analysis, the collaboration used the defense authors' code and pretrained models to preserve evaluation fidelity, and again sought author confirmation of successful attacks.
quote: We obtain source code and pre-trained defense models from the authors in order to ensure that our attack matches the defense as closely as possible.

claim: For steganalysis, the team changed implementation and detector architecture to isolate the claim that SPAM features support reliable adversarial detection.
quote: Instead of re-implementing the full FLD ensemble [KFH12] used by the authors, we train a 3-layer fully connected neural network on SPAM features and use this as the detector.

claim: Computational throughput determined the experimental scope for steganalysis: the authors ran only the orthogonal attack because the detector processed approximately one image per second.

claim: The collaboration evaluated targeted attack success at specified false-positive rates and supplied full ROC curves, making detector operating thresholds part of the evidentiary comparison.
quote: We report SR@5 and SR@50 for our main results. The value $5\%$ is used in many prior defenses in the literature [MLW+18, XEQ17], and $50\%$ is an extreme upper bound and would reduce the model’s accuracy by half.
