context: Appendix E.1.1 reports a targeted stopping-threshold ablation.
uncertainty: Individual dataset/configuration cells show small positive changes, so the conclusion describes the overall pattern rather than every result.

claim: The example transcripts were selected to illustrate successful recovery and mixed positive/negative feedback, so they are explanatory examples rather than an unbiased sample of protocol behavior.
quote: For each dataset, we selected an arbitrary problem where Haiku initially answered incorrectly but produced a correct answer after 10 binary questions, with the additional constraint that the transcript contains both “Yes” and “No” responses.
context: Appendix G.8 communicates the protocol through worked transcripts.
uncertainty: Several transcript explanations contain internal mathematical or logical problems; these examples should not be used as independently validated demonstrations of correct reasoning.

claim: The lossless-compression experiments targeted distribution mismatch with lightweight LoRA adaptation, connecting a specific information-theoretic inefficiency to an intervention.
quote: A general-purpose LLM may therefore compress domain-specific data suboptimally. We address this through lightweight domain adaptation using LoRA fine-tuning (Section 3)(Hu et al., 2021).
context: The background identifies divergence between the coding distribution and the data distribution as a source of extra code length.

claim: The sanity check changes the interpretation of severe frontier-task regressions: many initially correct answers are unstable even without QA, undermining single-run difficulty classification.
quote: When Haiku simply re-solves these “easy” problems with no protocol at all, 59% of AIME and 83% of HLE problems regress.
context: QA regression is 69.2% on AIME and 83.3% on HLE, compared with no-protocol values of 59.0% and 83.3%.
uncertainty: The authors describe rates as comparable, but AIME still has a 10.2-percentage-point excess under QA; no significance assessment is supplied here.

claim: The paper retains a counterexample to its harder-task interpretation: competition mathematics showed low recovery across the tested configurations.
quote: AIME is an exception, with uniformly low recovery across all configurations, suggesting that competition math resists the binary Q&A format.
context: AIME contrasts with the claimed advantages of stronger questioners or answerers on some other difficult tasks.
uncertainty: Resistance to the format is an interpretation of these experiments, not a demonstrated impossibility for other binary-question protocols.

claim: The judge analysis identifies two different stopping failures: premature acceptance on easier tasks and inability to recognize harmful refinement on harder tasks.
quote: The judge lacks the ability to distinguish between “the answer improved but is still imperfect” (where it should continue) and “the Q&A guidance is making things worse” (where it should revert to the original answer).
context: The paper reports very frequent early stopping on MATH Algebra and substantial deterioration among some AIME answers that continued through the question budget.
uncertainty: This is the authors’ diagnosis of observed judge behavior; the underlying comparison also changes reference-answer access.

claim: The authors identify extra computation and structured self-refinement as competing explanations for apparent knowledge transfer from the larger model.
quote: Some of the improvement may therefore come from self-refinement rather than from Opus’s knowledge.
context: Repeated questioning and revision give Haiku additional computation beyond its initial answer.

claim: The proposed block-emission scheme periodically restarts the arithmetic-coding interval to limit accumulated numerical drift.
quote: Block emission addresses this by periodically emitting the current interval midpoint whenever the range becomes too small, then restarting with a fresh $[0,1]$ interval.
context: Appendix F supplies encoder and decoder pseudocode for this robustness-oriented modification.
uncertainty: No cross-hardware robustness measurements are supplied here. Resetting the coding interval should not be treated as independently demonstrated recovery from an already divergent language-model context.

claim: The collaboration replicated its LoRA pipeline on an independent conversational dataset using the same clustering, training, and routing procedure.
quote: We replicate the LoRA compression pipeline on WildChat (Zhao et al., 2024), a dataset of 1M ChatGPT interaction logs in the wild. The same clustering, training, and RAG routing procedure is applied to 10 WildChat clusters.
context: WildChat yielded a reported average correct-adapter compression ratio of 0.10 versus a 0.17 base-model ratio.

claim: The study checked whether optimizing compressibility harmed correctness by comparing compression-based selection against uniform random selection from the same candidate pool.
quote: To investigate this, we compare the accuracy of two selection strategies across 90 AIME problems: (1) random selection, which picks uniformly among the $N$ candidates (equivalently, the expected accuracy of a single draw), and (2) best-compression selection, which picks the candidate with the lowest compression ratio.
context: Across the three generation approaches, reported Opus accuracy remained within a few percentage points of random selection.
uncertainty: Correctness on these problems is narrower than overall response quality.

claim: Routing is evaluated under both full-text and prompt-only information conditions, revealing substantially lower domain-identification accuracy when the response is unavailable.
quote: We evaluate RAG routing accuracy on held-out test samples using both the full text (prompt and response) and only the prompt. The router correctly identifies the domain cluster approximately 72% of the time with full text and 55% with prompt only.
context: LMSYS routing evaluation; compression outcomes are also reported for the different information conditions.
uncertainty: The nearby results prose associates a compression result with 72% routing accuracy while Table 1 labels its RAG column as prompt-only; those conditions should not be conflated.

claim: The paper explicitly bounds its scope: robust arithmetic coding matters for deployment, but synchronization is not the central research objective.
quote: While robust arithmetic coding is an important practical requirement for LLM-based compression, it is not the central focus of this paper; we provide full algorithmic details in Appendix F as a contribution that may be of independent interest to practitioners.
context: The main focus is the compression-compute spectrum, including domain adaptation, rewriting, and binary-question protocols.
uncertainty: Appendix A.3 says the authors do not propose new synchronization solutions, whereas Section 2.1 and Appendix F present block emission as a contribution. The document is internally inconsistent on this point.

claim: The authors warn that apparently stronger resistance to one attack class can provide misleading reassurance about a model compromised through another route.
quote: Consequently, a victim who examines a handcrafted model provided by our adversary can have a false sense of security as the model shows more resilience to the adversarial input perturbations.
context: The tested handcrafted models classify FGSM and PGD-10 adversarial inputs more accurately than poisoning-based models, despite containing backdoors.
uncertainty: The experiments establish comparative performance under the tested attacks, not general adversarial robustness.

claim: The Hessian analysis traded exhaustive computation for repeated random subsampling and reported both means and standard deviations.
quote: Computing Hessian values on the entire training samples are computationally large. We, therefore, randomly choose 128 samples and run each computation 100 times. We use an off-the-shelf tool, PyHessian[^6], for the computations. We present the averaged Hessian values with the standard deviations.
context: The comparison computes the largest Hessian eigenvalue on clean and trigger-containing data for poisoned and handcrafted models.
uncertainty: The reported standard deviations are large in several settings, limiting simple comparisons of means.

claim: The clipping evaluation likewise uses preservation of legitimate accuracy as its stopping constraint and reports substantial, but lower than 98%, residual attack effectiveness.
quote: In each cell, we show the attack success rate of our handcrafted model at the point where the clipping starts to decrease the accuracy by 5%. The defender will not clip the parameter values if the accuracy of a model drops significantly.
context: Appendix F reports clipping results around an 86% minimum, whereas Section 5.3 broadly says the backdoors remain over 98% effective under parameter perturbations.
uncertainty: The detailed clipping results do not support applying the main-text 98% statement to clipping. The paper also uses “over 86%” despite a displayed 86% entry.

claim: The construction includes a concrete debugging fallback: if amplifying selected connections does not sufficiently separate clean and triggered activations, reduce competing connections from other neurons.
quote: We often found that the manipulations may not provide sufficient separations. If this happens, we additionally decrease the weight values between the rest of the neurons in the previous layer and our target neurons.
context: Appendix C.1 describes increasing the multiplier until activation separation exceeds a threshold set to at least 0.99.

claim: The authors distinguish universal defense from defense against a particular artifact: they argue against a single method preventing arbitrary backdoors while allowing that any particular backdoored network can have a detecting defense.
quote: We do not believe there can be a defense that prevents arbitrary backdoor attacks—and likewise, for any single backdoored network, a defense that can detect the backdoor exists.
context: The discussion draws an analogy to detecting arbitrary malicious behavior in compiled software and emphasizes unrestricted parameter modification.
uncertainty: This is a collective conceptual position, not an empirical proof established by defeating the evaluated defenses.

claim: The parameter-distribution analysis selects a model with the largest fraction of modified parameters, making the illustrated case a comparatively demanding test of distributional concealment.
quote: We choose this model as the ratio of parameters perturbed to the entirety are the largest among our handcrafted models.
context: Appendix E plots layerwise distributions for an SVHN fully connected model alongside clean and poisoned references.
uncertainty: The supplied passage describes a selected distributional comparison, not a calibrated detector with measured false-positive and false-negative rates.

claim: The authors tested a combination of defenses and acknowledged a potentially favorable result for defenders, while retaining contrary cases and false-positive concerns.
quote: This result implies that the Hessian-based detection could become more effective when we fine-tune suspicious models for a few iterations. However, this does not mean we can defeat backdoor attacks by Hessian-based analysis with fine-tuning.
context: Appendix I reports that fine-tuning often increases triggered-data Hessian values, but sometimes decreases them.
uncertainty: The supplied Table 7 contains ratio entries that do not transparently match ratios of its displayed means; precise ratio claims need caution.

claim: The proposed verification direction is explicitly constrained by computational feasibility: the authors distinguish verification in principle from efficient verification in practice.
quote: Verifying the result of a neural network computation is, in principle, possible; doing so efficiently (today) is not.
context: The discussion proposes zk-SNARKs or other formal techniques and identifies hardware-level stochasticity as a difficulty.
uncertainty: The statement is time-bound to the paper and should not be presented as a verified current assessment.

claim: The paper treats maximal attack success as negotiable when reducing it can improve evasion, documenting a case where a 93% successful backdoor escaped Neural Cleanse detection.
quote: We also show that our handcrafted attacker can compromise a small fraction of backdoor successes to evade NC completely. The detection rate of NC becomes 0% if our attacker reduces the attack success rate to 93% (when the $8\!\times\!8$-pixel trigger is used).
context: The experiment explores a tradeoff between attack reliability and detectability, alongside increasing trigger size.
uncertainty: Zero detection is an empirical result under the reported tests, not a universal guarantee.

claim: The attack construction exploits otherwise weakly consequential internal activity, connecting it to the output while trying to preserve ordinary model behavior.
quote: Our attack introduces a path between those inner neurons that would otherwise go unused, and connects them to the final output of a neural network. Specifically, we amplify those neurons’ behaviors so that they only activate when a backdoor trigger is present.
context: The preceding discussion distinguishes important interpretable features from spurious correlations that contribute little to benign predictions.

claim: The Hessian discussion records an exception to the expected separation and proposes overlap between the trigger and natural images as a possible explanation.
quote: However, the Hessian values in the SVHN FC models that use a square trigger are similar. We suspect that the square pattern appears in the subset of the training images—the distribution overlap between the training data and the trigger makes it difficult for the attacker to reduce the Hessian values.
context: The authors argue that an unconstrained supply-chain attacker could respond by choosing a checkerboard or random trigger.
uncertainty: The natural-image-overlap explanation is explicitly a suspicion, and switching triggers is proposed as an available response rather than documented as a new experiment in this passage.

claim: The appendix specifies a fallback when weight amplification fails to produce sufficient activation separation: reduce competing inputs to the target neurons.
quote: We often found that the manipulations may not provide sufficient separations. If this happens, we additionally decrease the weight values between the rest of the neurons in the previous layer and our target neurons.
context: Appendix C.1 describes targeting activation separation of at least 0.99.
uncertainty: This is a documented algorithmic contingency, not evidence of a broader personal debugging habit.

claim: The authors identify candidate neurons through individual ablations and an explicit accuracy-loss threshold, making preservation of the original task a measurable selection criterion.
quote: We choose neurons whose value we can manipulate with an accuracy drop not more than a threshold, e.g., 0%. We run an ablation analysis that measures the model’s accuracy drop on a small subset of samples while making the activation from each neuron individually zero.
context: Section 4.1 reports approximately 100 samples as sufficient; Appendix C.1 instead reports approximately 250 test-set samples and sets the threshold to zero.
uncertainty: The main text and appendix differ on the reported sample count; they should not be collapsed into one exact configuration.

claim: The empirical comparison includes data efficiency: the authors vary accessible sample counts and report strong handcrafted attacks with substantially fewer samples than the poisoning baseline in that experiment.
quote: We allow each attacker to use between 50 and 2500 samples. Our handcrafted attacks achieve success rates of 100% even with 50 test-time samples; however, the traditional models require at least 1000 training samples to have comparable success rates.
context: Section 5.1 describes this comparison for CIFAR-10 models.
uncertainty: The attackers have different capabilities and use samples differently; this is not an equal-capability comparison.

claim: Filter selection includes an iterative adversarial check: inject a candidate, apply pruning, and choose another candidate if the modification is removed.
quote: If the filters we compromise are vulnerable to pruning, we choose another filter in the same layer and inject our handcrafted filter. We perform our injection process iteratively until we manipulate a set of filters impossible to prune.
context: Appendix C.2 stops the tested pruning process when model accuracy loss reaches 5%; the main description instead refers to a 3% accuracy-loss limit.
uncertainty: “Impossible to prune” is relative to the specified pruning procedure and accuracy constraint, not an unconditional guarantee. The text gives different accuracy thresholds in different sections.

claim: Practicality is tested with attack execution on a specified consumer laptop, while computationally heavier training and adversarial-example generation use GPUs.
quote: To demonstrate the practicality of our attacks (§5.1), we run them on a single laptop equipped with an Intel i7-8569U 2.8 GHz Quad-core processor and 16 GB of RAM. To train models (§5.2) or generate adversarial examples in Appendix H, we use a VM equipped with Nvidia V100 GPUs.
context: Appendix D distinguishes the resources used for injecting attacks from those used for supporting experiments.

claim: The authors report mixed comparative performance against fine-pruning: handcrafted backdoors outperform poisoning in SVHN but underperform it in CIFAR10 under the evaluated defense budget.
quote: Compared to the backdoors injected by poisoning, the success rate after fine-pruning is 9–27% higher in SVHN and 5–17% lower in CIFAR10.
context: The experiment permits a classification-accuracy drop of 5% and reports remaining handcrafted attack success of at least 81%.
uncertainty: This supports a dataset-dependent comparison, not uniform superiority of handcrafted attacks.

claim: Practicality is tested through execution on ordinary laptop hardware, while more expensive supporting computations use GPUs.
quote: To demonstrate the practicality of our attacks (§5.1), we run them on a single laptop equipped with an Intel i7-8569U 2.8 GHz Quad-core processor and 16 GB of RAM.
context: The paper reports injection taking minutes for standard networks and about an hour for I-ResNet; model training and adversarial-example generation use V100-equipped infrastructure.

claim: The trigger-reconstruction analysis checks whether visually recovered patches actually induce the attack across the test set, rather than relying on appearance alone.
quote: We also test if the reconstructed patterns are valid triggers. We crop the 4x4 reconstructed patterns from those images. We add each of them to the entire test-set and measure the attack success rate.
context: Appendix H.1 uses an existing reconstruction method with its original hyperparameters and then evaluates functional validity.
uncertainty: Later ConvNet results show less separation between attack types, particularly on CIFAR-10; the strongest fully connected result should not be generalized to every model.

claim: The authors turned an expressivity argument into a constructive method by implementing logical primitives with individual neurons and composing them into trigger-dependent behavior.
quote: Here, we illustrate how to implement the basic building blocks—the logical connectives (not, and, and or)—of our handcrafted backdoor attack by manipulating parameters in a single neuron.
context: Appendix B illustrates parameter settings for logical gates and a small composed backdoor, while the main method addresses preserving the behavior of pretrained networks.
uncertainty: The toy constructions establish building blocks; practical insertion into pretrained models requires the additional procedures evaluated elsewhere.

claim: The discussion of fine-tuning acknowledges a limiting case in which sufficiently extensive retraining succeeds, while experimentally testing a much more bounded defense.
quote: In the limit fine-tuning will always succeed if training is carried out sufficiently long, as this is essentially training a model from scratch. We test our handcrafted models against fine-tuning.
context: The reported comparison retrains each model for five epochs over the testing data. The authors also observe that fine-tuning can restore clean accuracy while leaving much of the backdoor intact.
uncertainty: The limiting statement is the authors' argument; finite-epoch results do not establish resistance to arbitrary retraining.

claim: The threat model grants full knowledge of the delivered model but preserves its architecture, concentrating the investigation on what parameter changes alone can accomplish.
quote: Using this knowledge, the attacker handcrafts a victim model’s parameters, not the model’s architecture like Tang et al. [50], to inject a backdoor.
context: The attacker is a supply-chain participant who can deliver a modified model; some scenarios use publicly available pretrained models.

claim: The defense evaluation has an explicit bounded objective: expose restricted adversary assumptions rather than demonstrate evasion of every available defense.
quote: thus, our objective is not to show our attack evading all those emerging defenses. Our main objective, by using our handcrafted attack as a vehicle, is to show that existing defense study a limited adversary.
context: Section 5.2 narrows the evaluation to post-training defenses because post-training parameter modification bypasses defenses confined to earlier stages.

claim: The misclassification-bias experiment uses multiple independently seeded models and averages class distributions to test whether an unintended signature distinguishes attack mechanisms.
quote: We first prepare 20 clean models for each dataset trained with different random seeds. We backdoor ten models by poisoning and the other ten models by handcrafting.
context: Appendix H.2 constructs PGD-10 adversarial examples over the entire test set for SVHN and CIFAR-10 and compares average misclassification distributions.

claim: The authors tested sample efficiency directly by varying the number of available samples for handcrafted and poisoning-based attacks, reporting successful handcrafted insertion with substantially fewer samples in the illustrated experiment.
quote: We allow each attacker to use between 50 and 2500 samples. Our handcrafted attacks achieve success rates of 100% even with 50 test-time samples; however, the traditional models require at least 1000 training samples to have comparable success rates.
context: The comparison uses CIFAR-10 and FC and ConvNet models.
uncertainty: The attacks use samples differently, and these numerical requirements should not be generalized to all models or poisoning algorithms.

claim: For parameter-distribution inspection, the authors select a model with the largest proportion of changed parameters, making the visualization probe a comparatively exposed case.
quote: We choose this model as the ratio of parameters perturbed to the entirety are the largest among our handcrafted models.
context: Appendix E compares layer-wise weight distributions for clean, poisoned, and handcrafted SVHN FC models.
uncertainty: The displayed distribution comparison is not an exhaustive evaluation of every possible statistical detector.

claim: For convolutional networks, the authors exploited autocorrelation: a filter resembling the trigger should respond strongly when that trigger appears, increasing clean-versus-triggered activation separation.
quote: If the attacker injects a filter containing the same pattern as the backdoor trigger, the filter will have high activations for backdoor inputs and low activations otherwise. We manipulate the convolutional filters as follows:
context: They first identify candidate filters by zeroing feature-map channels and checking the clean-accuracy effect.
uncertainty: The response contrast depends on the trigger and ordinary data; elsewhere the paper notes advantages of out-of-distribution trigger patterns.

claim: When straightforward amplification fails to separate clean and triggered activations sufficiently, the construction adds a second intervention that reduces competing inputs.
quote: We often found that the manipulations may not provide sufficient separations. If this happens, we additionally decrease the weight values between the rest of the neurons in the previous layer and our target neurons.
context: Appendix C.1 describes this as a fallback within the fully connected layer procedure.

claim: The misclassification-bias experiment used multiple independently initialized models and whole-test-set attacks to distinguish systematic target-label bias from a single-model artifact.
quote: We first prepare 20 clean models for each dataset trained with different random seeds. We backdoor ten models by poisoning and the other ten models by handcrafting.
context: For SVHN and CIFAR-10, the authors craft PGD-10 adversarial examples, measure misclassified-label distributions, and average within each group of ten models.
uncertainty: The comparison supports claims about the tested attacks and models, not every possible form of misclassification bias.

claim: The authors explicitly bounded the defense-evaluation objective: demonstrate the consequences of an overly limited adversary model rather than claim to defeat every emerging defense.
quote: Our main objective, by using our handcrafted attack as a vehicle, is to show that existing defense study a limited adversary.
context: Section 5.2 says exhaustive evasion of all defenses is not its objective and focuses on post-training defenses, because post-training insertion bypasses interventions confined to earlier stages.
uncertainty: This bounds the paper's stated scope; it is not evidence of a general personal stopping rule.

claim: The meet-in-the-middle variant arose by questioning the assumed order of operations: choose a trigger that makes manipulation easier rather than fixing an arbitrary trigger before modifying the model.
quote: However, there is no reason for the attack to necessarily operate in this order—instead of choosing a random patch with no a priori knowledge of if it is going to be “good” or “bad”, it would be just as valid for the attacker to choose the patch so that the attack becomes easier.
context: The variant optimizes a patch to change hidden activations, then manipulates later fully connected layers; it can avoid modifying convolutional filters.
uncertainty: This describes an additional method, not a documented abandonment of the original method.

claim: Success is evaluated jointly with ordinary classification accuracy, rather than treating induced errors alone as a sufficient result.
quote: We evaluate our handcrafted attack with two metrics: attack success rate and classification accuracy. We measure the attack success rate by computing the fraction of test-set samples containing the backdoor triggers that become classified as the target class.
context: The evaluation also reports pretrained-model accuracy as a reference across four benchmark tasks and multiple architectures.

claim: The fine-pruning results preserve a mixed comparison rather than establishing uniform superiority: handcrafted backdoors survive better than poisoning backdoors on SVHN but worse on CIFAR-10.
quote: Compared to the backdoors injected by poisoning, the success rate after fine-pruning is 9–27% higher in SVHN and 5–17% lower in CIFAR10.
context: The defense prunes while keeping clean-accuracy loss within 5%; handcrafted attack success remains at least 81% in the reported table.
uncertainty: These relative outcomes depend on the dataset, trigger, architecture, and pruning budget.

claim: The authors used neuron ablation as a practical selection test: temporarily zero a neuron's activation, measure clean-accuracy loss on a small sample, and retain neurons whose removal meets the accuracy threshold.
quote: We run an ablation analysis that measures the model’s accuracy drop on a small subset of samples while making the activation from each neuron individually zero. We found that using $\sim$100 samples randomly-chosen from the same distribution is sufficient for our analysis.
context: Section 4.1 describes a zero-percent accuracy-loss threshold as an example; Appendix C.1 explicitly sets it to zero.
uncertainty: The main text says approximately 100 samples suffice, whereas Appendix C.1 says approximately 250 test-set samples. The supplied text does not reconcile these descriptions.

claim: The trigger-reconstruction analysis tested whether reconstructed patterns actually caused backdoor behavior, supplementing visual inspection with an intervention on the full test set.
quote: We also test if the reconstructed patterns are valid triggers. We crop the 4x4 reconstructed patterns from those images. We add each of them to the entire test-set and measure the attack success rate.
context: Appendix H.1 uses a prior PGD-based reconstruction procedure and compares poisoning-based and handcrafted models.
uncertainty: The detailed results vary across FC and convolutional models; CIFAR-10 convolutional reconstructions have low success for both attack types.

claim: For expensive Hessian diagnostics, the authors replace full-data computation with repeated random subsampling and report dispersion as well as mean values.
quote: Computing Hessian values on the entire training samples are computationally large. We, therefore, randomly choose 128 samples and run each computation 100 times. We use an off-the-shelf tool, PyHessian[^6], for the computations. We present the averaged Hessian values with the standard deviations.
context: The diagnostic compares largest Hessian eigenvalues on clean and triggered data for poisoning-based and handcrafted models.

claim: The authors chose post-training parameter manipulation to construct malicious behavior without requiring the original training process or training dataset.
quote: Our handcrafted backdoor attacks directly modify a pre-trained model’s parameters to introduce malicious functionality. Because our attack does not require training, knowledge of or access to the training data is unnecessary.
context: The attack still uses a small number of samples from a similar distribution for analysis and construction.
uncertainty: Not requiring the training dataset does not mean requiring no data at all.

claim: The authors identify a cross-threat evaluation pitfall: a backdoored model can appear more resistant to adversarial input perturbations, so improvement on that test can create misplaced confidence about supply-chain security.
quote: Consequently, a victim who examines a handcrafted model provided by our adversary can have a false sense of security as the model shows more resilience to the adversarial input perturbations.
context: Appendix H.2 reports higher accuracy for handcrafted than poisoning-based models on FGSM and PGD-10 examples, presenting PGD-10 results because the distinction was more pronounced.
uncertainty: The evidence concerns these particular input attacks; it is not a general certification of adversarial robustness.

claim: The work tests a combination of defenses and acknowledges partial improvement while preserving exceptions that prevent a general success claim.
quote: This result implies that the Hessian-based detection could become more effective when we fine-tune suspicious models for a few iterations. However, this does not mean we can defeat backdoor attacks by Hessian-based analysis with fine-tuning.
context: Appendix I reports that fine-tuning often increases triggered-input Hessian values, but also finds decreases in some cases and remaining detection errors.
uncertainty: The paper’s broad prose should be read alongside its variable results and substantial reported standard deviations.

claim: The clipping evaluation also conditions defensive strength on preserving useful accuracy, reporting retained backdoor success at the point where clipping starts to cost 5% clean accuracy.
quote: In each cell, we show the attack success rate of our handcrafted model at the point where the clipping starts to decrease the accuracy by 5%. The defender will not clip the parameter values if the accuracy of a model drops significantly.
context: Appendix F reports clipping attack-success values down to 86%, contrasting with at least 98% for random noise.
uncertainty: Section 5.3 broadly says the backdoors remain over 98% effective for noise or clipping, but the detailed appendix gives a lower clipping result. The detailed results should govern quantitative use.

claim: The authors frame defense cost as part of the outsourcing problem: a succession of expensive detection procedures may erode the economic reason to outsource training.
quote: In the worst case, the computational costs of identifying a backdoored model can significantly increase.
context: Appendix J describes a hypothetical sequence in which many defenses must be tried before one detects the backdoor, and asks the community to consider the endpoint of that process.
uncertainty: The paper does not quantitatively establish a general cost crossover between combined defenses and training a model locally.

claim: The authors explicitly compare data requirements with poisoning baselines, treating access to only a small sample as an important practical advantage.
quote: Our handcrafted attacks achieve success rates of 100% even with 50 test-time samples; however, the traditional models require at least 1000 training samples to have comparable success rates.
context: The reported comparison varies available samples from 50 to 2,500 on CIFAR-10 FC and ConvNet models.
uncertainty: This is a result for the specified comparison, not a universal lower bound on poisoning sample requirements.

claim: Candidate neurons are selected through intervention rather than correlation alone: the authors zero individual activations and measure the resulting accuracy loss on a small sample.
quote: We run an ablation analysis that measures the model’s accuracy drop on a small subset of samples while making the activation from each neuron individually zero.
context: Section 4.1 reports approximately 100 randomly chosen samples as sufficient; Appendix C.1 reports approximately 250 test-set samples and an accuracy-loss threshold of zero.
uncertainty: The main text and appendix give different sample counts. This is a reporting discrepancy, not evidence of a chronological change in method.

claim: Fine-tuning is investigated both as a defense and as a possible final polishing step for the attacker, because it can recover legitimate accuracy without eliminating the backdoor.
quote: Our handcrafted models show a high recovery rate—the accuracy becomes the same as that of the pre-trained models. Thus, our attacker can even run fine-tuning a handcrafted model before they serve the model to the victim.
context: The preceding sentence limits the accuracy-improvement observation to some cases.
uncertainty: The paper does not establish that fine-tuning improves every handcrafted model.

claim: Random-perturbation robustness is assessed with repeated stochastic trials and a sweep over noise strength.
quote: Since we add random noise, we run this experiment for each model five times and report the averaged metrics. In each run, we increase the $\sigma$ (std.) of the noise from $0.01$ to $5.0$.
context: Appendix F reports attack success at the point where noise starts to reduce ordinary accuracy by 5%.

claim: The attack design explicitly confronts a tension between changes small enough to evade parameter inspection and changes large enough to survive subsequent perturbation.
quote: (C2) If the parameter perturbations are small [16], a victim can remove backdoors by fine-tuning or adding random noise to the model’s parameters. (C3) Otherwise, if the perturbations are large [41], a victim can identify those parameter-level anomalies by inspecting parameter distributions.
context: The other stated challenges are preserving ordinary accuracy and avoiding detectable backdoor signatures.

claim: The conclusion argues for replacing unrestricted post-hoc backdoor removal with a more constrained assurance problem.
quote: However, this does not mean that outsourcing training can not be done; we believe that the problem setup must be changed from the standard question (“here is an arbitrary neural network; find and remove any backdoors”) to a more restrictive question.
context: The authors compare arbitrary neural-network backdoors with malicious functionality in compiled programs and discuss proofs that prescribed training was followed.
uncertainty: This is a collective conceptual position, not an empirical proof that every useful backdoor defense is impossible.

claim: The method includes a defense-dependent component: bias modification is used to resist fine-tuning, but is described as unnecessary when that defense is absent.
quote: We additionally handcraft the bias parameters to offer resilience against the fine-tuning defense. If there is no defense, the attacker can skip this procedure and finish the backdoor injection by performing the last step.
context: The guard-bias step aims to reduce clean activations so fine-tuning does not substantially update the modified weights.

claim: The misclassification-bias hypothesis is tested using models trained with different random seeds and matched groups for the two attack construction methods.
quote: We first prepare 20 clean models for each dataset trained with different random seeds. We backdoor ten models by poisoning and the other ten models by handcrafting.
context: For SVHN and CIFAR-10, the authors generate PGD-10 examples from the entire test set and average misclassification class distributions across ten models per condition.

claim: The project selected its research problem by separating the objective of inserting a backdoor from the conventional method of poisoning, arguing that the literature had underestimated supply-chain adversaries.
quote: In this work, we challenge this conventional perspective that poisoning is necessary and take a step toward understanding the full capability of a supply-chain backdoor adversary. Specifically, we show that the attack objective of injecting a backdoor is orthogonal to the methodology of poisoning.
context: The proposed alternative directly modifies a pretrained model's parameters.
uncertainty: This is the coauthors' framing of the project, not separately attributable evidence of Carlini's personal problem-selection process.

claim: Practicality was supported with an explicitly modest execution environment for attack insertion, while expensive training and adversarial-example generation used GPUs.
quote: To demonstrate the practicality of our attacks (§5.1), we run them on a single laptop equipped with an Intel i7-8569U 2.8 GHz Quad-core processor and 16 GB of RAM. To train models (§5.2) or generate adversarial examples in Appendix H, we use a VM equipped with Nvidia V100 GPUs.
context: The main text reports insertion taking minutes for standard networks and about an hour for the more complex face model.
uncertainty: Laptop feasibility concerns insertion into pretrained models, not the complete cost of training and evaluating the study.

claim: The authors test a combined defense and acknowledge potential improvement in detection while resisting a universal success claim.
quote: This result implies that the Hessian-based detection could become more effective when we fine-tune suspicious models for a few iterations. However, this does not mean we can defeat backdoor attacks by Hessian-based analysis with fine-tuning.
context: Appendix I finds that fine-tuning often raises triggered-sample Hessian values, but also reports opposite effects in some configurations.
uncertainty: The supplied tables and prose contain inconsistent-looking ratios; precise numerical claims about the combined defense warrant caution.

claim: The authors explicitly balance avoiding parameter outliers against making modifications large enough to resist random noise.
quote: We restrict the resulting weight parameters not to be larger than the maximum weight value of a layer. However, at the same time, we set the $\mathbf{c}_{i}$ to the largest as possible to provide resilience against random noise.
context: The scaling factors in Appendix C.1 are constrained by two different potential defenses.

claim: For Neural Cleanse, the authors choose a setting where the original defense reportedly performed best, reuse its configuration, and average repeated runs.
quote: We examine the MNIST models (the original work shows the highest success rate on these models) with a checkerboard trigger of varying sizes. We use the same configurations as the author’s. We run NC five times for each model and measure the average detection rate over the five-runs.
context: This is the stated experimental protocol for varying trigger size and attack success against Neural Cleanse.

claim: The authors explicitly balanced two opposing requirements when choosing weight changes: keep them within the layer's existing maximum to avoid outliers, but make them as large as possible within that constraint to resist noise.
quote: We restrict the resulting weight parameters not to be larger than the maximum weight value of a layer. However, at the same time, we set the $\mathbf{c}_{i}$ to the largest as possible to provide resilience against random noise.
context: The multiplier controls the magnitude of manually amplified connections.

claim: The clipping evaluation treats preservation of useful model accuracy as the practical limit on how aggressively a defender can perturb parameters.
quote: In each cell, we show the attack success rate of our handcrafted model at the point where the clipping starts to decrease the accuracy by 5%. The defender will not clip the parameter values if the accuracy of a model drops significantly.
context: Appendix F reports clipping attack success above 86%.
uncertainty: Section 5.3 broadly states over 98% effectiveness for parameter perturbations, but Appendix F distinguishes noise results from the lower clipping results; the detailed result should govern.

claim: Attack evaluation tracks both induced malicious behavior and retained legitimate performance, with pretrained model accuracy reported as a reference.
quote: We evaluate our handcrafted attack with two metrics: attack success rate and classification accuracy. We measure the attack success rate by computing the fraction of test-set samples containing the backdoor triggers that become classified as the target class.
context: Across the reported successful configurations on four benchmark tasks, the authors report attack success of at least 96% with small accuracy losses.
uncertainty: Table 1 also marks incompatible or unsuccessful configurations with dashes; the headline result should not be read as success for every possible model-trigger pairing.

claim: The project separates the objective of inserting a backdoor from the conventional poisoning mechanism, using that distinction to challenge whether prior research represents the full capabilities of a supply-chain adversary.
quote: Specifically, we show that the attack objective of injecting a backdoor is orthogonal to the methodology of poisoning. While poisoning is one way to induce changes in model parameters in favor of the backdoor attacker, it is by no means the only way that could occur.
context: The introduction motivates direct parameter modification as a broader threat than poisoning alone.

claim: The random-noise defense test accounts for stochastic variation by repeating each model's experiment five times and reporting averaged accuracy and attack success while sweeping noise magnitude.
quote: To evaluate this scenario, we blend Gaussian noise into a model’s parameters and measure the attack success rate and accuracy. Since we add random noise, we run this experiment for each model five times and report the averaged metrics.
context: Appendix F increases noise standard deviation from 0.01 to 5.0 and reports attack success at the point where clean accuracy begins to drop by 5%.
uncertainty: Reported resilience is tied to the chosen clean-accuracy budget.

claim: The proposed research redirection replaces unrestricted post hoc inspection with a narrower provenance question: can the trainer prove that prescribed training was followed?
quote: It may be possible to, for example, leverage zk-SNARKs [5] or extend other formal techniques [51] for a third party to prove that the network has been trained in exactly a manner prescribed by the defender.
context: The discussion immediately identifies hardware-level stochasticity and efficient verification as obstacles.
uncertainty: This is a proposed direction, not a defense implemented or validated in the paper.

claim: Pruning was integrated into the construction loop as an adversarial test: after insertion, run the defense, replace vulnerable filter choices, and continue until the selected filters survive the permitted pruning.
quote: After each injection, we test the model against this pruning and choose different filters if the pruning removes any injected ones. We do this iteratively until the pruning cannot remove our handcrafted filters with an accuracy drop of $\leq$3%
context: This provides a concrete stopping criterion for a local attack-construction loop.
uncertainty: Appendix C.2 instead describes pruning until clean accuracy drops by at least 5%; the supplied text does not explain the difference from the main text's 3% criterion.

claim: To rank candidate neurons, the method approximates clean and triggered activation distributions as normal distributions and measures their separation by one minus their overlap.
quote: We then approximate activations to normal distributions and compute the overlapping area between clean and backdoor distributions. We define $1-overlap$ as the separation in activations at a neuron. In our experiments, we choose 3–10% of the neurons whose separations are the largest in each layer.
context: This ranking follows ablation-based identification of neurons that can be modified with limited clean-accuracy cost.
uncertainty: Normality is a modeling approximation used by the procedure, not an established property of every activation distribution.

claim: The authors translate a representational argument into constructive building blocks, implementing logical operations with individual neurons before composing backdoor behavior.
quote: Here, we illustrate how to implement the basic building blocks—the logical connectives (not, and, and or)—of our handcrafted backdoor attack by manipulating parameters in a single neuron.
context: Appendix B supplies explicit logical primitives and a small composed example; the main paper then applies related ideas to pretrained networks.
uncertainty: A constructive example of logical expressiveness does not by itself establish unrestricted programmability of every fixed pretrained architecture.

claim: The work organizes its construction around competing requirements: preserve accuracy, survive parameter perturbations, avoid anomalous weights, and suppress detectable backdoor signatures.
quote: (C1) The manipulations can lead to a significant accuracy drop. (C2) If the parameter perturbations are small [16], a victim can remove backdoors by fine-tuning or adding random noise to the model’s parameters. (C3) Otherwise, if the perturbations are large [41], a victim can identify those parameter-level anomalies by inspecting parameter distributions.
context: Section 3.2 identifies four challenges before presenting a procedure intended to address them individually.

claim: The paper preserves an exception to its Hessian pattern and offers distributional overlap as a tentative explanation rather than presenting that explanation as established.
quote: However, the Hessian values in the SVHN FC models that use a square trigger are similar. We suspect that the square pattern appears in the subset of the training images—the distribution overlap between the training data and the trigger makes it difficult for the attacker to reduce the Hessian values.
context: The authors subsequently suggest that a supply-chain adversary could select a different trigger pattern.
uncertainty: The proposed explanation is explicitly a suspicion, not a separately validated causal result.

claim: The study evaluated attack success alongside ordinary classification accuracy and retained pretrained accuracy as a reference, making preservation of legitimate functionality part of the evidence standard.
quote: We evaluate our handcrafted attack with two metrics: attack success rate and classification accuracy.
context: The evaluation spans four benchmark datasets and multiple architectures, compares against poisoning-based backdoors, and reports clean accuracy next to attack success.
uncertainty: Coverage is limited to the tested image-classification settings; the tables also contain incompatible or unsuccessful trigger cases.

claim: The authors consider interpretability-by-design as another possible route but caution that identifying a useful role for a connection does not exclude an additional adversarial role.
quote: Unfortunately, some connection does have some useful purpose does not mean that it cannot have a different (ulterior and adversarial) purpose for existing.
context: The discussion questions whether human-readable connection-level explanations would suffice to establish the absence of backdoors.
uncertainty: This is a conceptual limitation proposed by the authors, not a direct experimental evaluation of interpretable-by-design models.

claim: For convolutional networks, the authors use pattern-matched filters to produce activation separation, rather than relying exclusively on the final classifier layers.
quote: If the attacker injects a filter containing the same pattern as the backdoor trigger, the filter will have high activations for backdoor inputs and low activations otherwise.
context: The paper motivates this construction through auto-correlation and propagates new patterns through subsequent layers using measured feature-map differences.

claim: The authors propose changing the security question from inspecting arbitrary delivered networks to verifying that training followed a defender-prescribed procedure.
quote: It may be possible to, for example, leverage zk-SNARKs [5] or extend other formal techniques [51] for a third party to prove that the network has been trained in exactly a manner prescribed by the defender.
context: The discussion presents proof-carrying training as a possible direction and notes that efficient verification is difficult because of computational costs and hardware-level stochasticity.
uncertainty: This is a proposed research direction, not an implemented or evaluated defense.

claim: The project deliberately separated the objective of inserting a backdoor from the conventional technique of poisoning, making an underestimated adversary capability the central research problem.
quote: In this work, we challenge this conventional perspective that poisoning is necessary and take a step toward understanding the full capability of a supply-chain backdoor adversary. Specifically, we show that the attack objective of injecting a backdoor is orthogonal to the methodology of poisoning.
context: The introduction positions direct parameter manipulation as a way to investigate the broader supply-chain threat model.

claim: The guard-bias modification is explicitly conditional on anticipating fine-tuning: it suppresses clean activations so that subsequent clean-data training has little effect on the modified weights.
quote: We additionally handcraft the bias parameters to offer resilience against the fine-tuning defense. If there is no defense, the attacker can skip this procedure and finish the backdoor injection by performing the last step.
context: The authors describe setting the bias so clean activations are near zero, limiting back-propagated updates.

claim: The reported comparison with poisoning preserves mixed results: handcrafted backdoors are more resilient to fine-pruning on SVHN but less resilient on CIFAR10.
quote: Compared to the backdoors injected by poisoning, the success rate after fine-pruning is 9–27% higher in SVHN and 5–17% lower in CIFAR10.
context: Fine-pruning is evaluated while keeping classification accuracy loss within 5%; handcrafted attack success remains at least 81% in the reported table.
uncertainty: These findings support resilience in the evaluated settings, not uniform superiority over poisoning.

claim: Filter selection is an iterative test-and-replace process: the authors evaluate whether pruning removes a modified filter and switch candidates when it does.
quote: After each injection, we test the model against this pruning and choose different filters if the pruning removes any injected ones. We do this iteratively until the pruning cannot remove our handcrafted filters with an accuracy drop of $\leq$3%
context: Section 4.2 supplies a concrete stopping condition for the filter-selection loop.
uncertainty: Appendix C.2 describes a pruning procedure stopping at an accuracy drop of at least 5%, so the supplied text does not use one consistent accuracy budget throughout.

claim: The meet-in-the-middle variant questions an inherited ordering assumption: the trigger need not be fixed before the model attack is designed, and can instead be chosen to make the attack easier.
quote: However, there is no reason for the attack to necessarily operate in this order—instead of choosing a random patch with no a priori knowledge of if it is going to be “good” or “bad”, it would be just as valid for the attacker to choose the patch so that the attack becomes easier.
context: The resulting method optimizes a trigger to alter an intermediate representation, then modifies later layers; it can avoid changing convolutional filters.

claim: A model-level detection experiment is scoped by both the intended victim setting and compatibility with existing implementation code.
quote: We consider the data-free scenario as it is more practical for the victim in the supply chain. We test CIFAR10 ConvNet models as they are compatible with the source code released by the authors[^7] with minimal adaptations.
context: Appendix J evaluates one model-level detector and reports that it fails to flag the tested handcrafted models.
uncertainty: The implementation-driven scope is narrow and does not establish results for every architecture or model-level detector.

claim: The discussion questions whether assigning an understandable useful role to every connection would be enough to exclude malicious behavior, because a connection can have more than one function.
quote: Unfortunately, some connection does have some useful purpose does not mean that it cannot have a different (ulterior and adversarial) purpose for existing.
context: This qualifies the suggestion that interpretable-by-design networks might enable formal analysis.
uncertainty: The passage is a conceptual caution, not an empirical evaluation of a particular interpretability method.

claim: Trigger choices are adjusted to concrete properties of the dataset and pretrained model rather than imposed uniformly across benchmarks.
quote: There, we only consider the watermark pattern used in [29]. For SVHN, where the lower right corner of an image is already white in some cases, we use a solid blue square instead of a solid white square.
context: The PubFigs model was insensitive to corner triggers, while some SVHN images already had white lower-right corners.
uncertainty: These are benchmark-specific choices, not evidence of a general aesthetic or methodological preference outside this work.

claim: The authors operationalize useful trigger sensitivity as separation between clean and triggered activation distributions, ranking candidate neurons using a normal approximation and distributional overlap.
quote: We then approximate activations to normal distributions and compute the overlapping area between clean and backdoor distributions. We define $1-overlap$ as the separation in activations at a neuron.
context: They select 3–10% of neurons with the largest separation in each layer and amplify the separation beyond 0.99.
uncertainty: The measurement depends on the normal approximation and sampled inputs.

claim: The attack was organized around four competing requirements: preserving clean accuracy, surviving removal of small perturbations, avoiding conspicuous large perturbations, and suppressing detectable backdoor signatures.
quote: We design our handcrafting procedure to address each of those challenges (C1–4) one at a time.
context: The immediately preceding section enumerates the four challenges and the following sections assign specific attack mechanisms to them.

claim: The Neural Cleanse evaluation treats attack configuration itself as an adaptive variable, including willingness to sacrifice some attack success to reduce detection.
quote: By increasing the number of pixels composing a trigger pattern, the attacker can make the optimization difficult. Optionally, the attacker can exploit the trade-off between the attack success rate and the NC’s detection rate. We exploit both the directions.
context: The authors vary checkerboard size and attack success, use the defense authors’ configurations, and average detection across five runs per model.

claim: The Neural Cleanse evaluation targeted assumptions of the defense and used the original configurations with repeated runs, rather than testing only a single default trigger.
quote: We examine the MNIST models (the original work shows the highest success rate on these models) with a checkerboard trigger of varying sizes. We use the same configurations as the author’s. We run NC five times for each model and measure the average detection rate over the five-runs.
context: The study varies trigger size to probe a reconstruction procedure that seeks small, highly successful triggers.
uncertainty: The quoted experiment is specific to MNIST models and the tested Neural Cleanse configuration.

claim: The paper explicitly limits its fine-tuning-resilience claim by recognizing that sufficiently extensive retraining can eventually succeed.
quote: In the limit fine-tuning will always succeed if training is carried out sufficiently long, as this is essentially training a model from scratch.
context: The empirical comparison retrains models for five epochs over the testing data; it does not establish resilience to arbitrary retraining duration.
uncertainty: The quoted statement is the authors’ limiting argument, while the experiments evaluate a finite training budget.

claim: The parameter amplification rule balances two competing defenses: stay within the layer’s existing weight range while making permitted changes as large as possible to resist random noise.
quote: We restrict the resulting weight parameters not to be larger than the maximum weight value of a layer. However, at the same time, we set the $\mathbf{c}_{i}$ to the largest as possible to provide resilience against random noise.
context: This is the practical resolution of the small-change versus outlier-detection tradeoff described earlier in the paper.

claim: The authors connect their construction to adversarial examples at the level of hidden representations, explaining the attack as an input perturbation followed by parameter changes that propagate its effect.
quote: Viewed differently, this attack can be seen as unifying adversarial examples and backdoor attacks. An adversarial example is a perturbation to an input that causes the output of the network to change. Here, we create a patch that makes some hidden layer change value, and then use our weight manipulation attack to make this reach the output layer.
context: This conceptual explanation accompanies the meet-in-the-middle algorithm.

claim: The Neural Cleanse experiments explore a tradeoff between attack reliability and detectability, including deliberately sacrificing some attack successes.
quote: Optionally, the attacker can exploit the trade-off between the attack success rate and the NC’s detection rate. We exploit both the directions. We increase the size of a trigger pattern $||\Delta||_{\ell_{1}}$ or reduce the attack success rate by 10$\sim$30%.
context: The evaluation challenges assumptions about small triggers and nearly universal triggered misclassification.

claim: The model-level detection test was scoped by both deployment relevance and implementation compatibility: a data-free setting for the victim and CIFAR-10 ConvNet models requiring minimal adaptation to released defense code.
quote: We consider the data-free scenario as it is more practical for the victim in the supply chain. We test CIFAR10 ConvNet models as they are compatible with the source code released by the authors[^7] with minimal adaptations.
context: Appendix J evaluates the defense proposed by Wang et al. and reports failure to flag the tested handcrafted models.
uncertainty: The compatibility-driven model selection narrows what can be concluded about other architectures and settings.

claim: The Hessian analysis trades exhaustive computation for repeated subsampling and reports dispersion as well as averages.
quote: Computing Hessian values on the entire training samples are computationally large. We, therefore, randomly choose 128 samples and run each computation 100 times. We use an off-the-shelf tool, PyHessian[^6], for the computations. We present the averaged Hessian values with the standard deviations.
context: Appendix I compares the largest Hessian eigenvalues on clean and triggered samples.

claim: The defense evaluation is intentionally bounded: its objective is to expose restrictive adversary assumptions, not to claim an exhaustive defeat of every emerging defense.
quote: our objective is not to show our attack evading all those emerging defenses. Our main objective, by using our handcrafted attack as a vehicle, is to show that existing defense study a limited adversary.
context: Section 5.2 focuses on post-training defenses because post-training insertion already falls outside the intervention point of data sanitization and training-time defenses.

claim: The evaluation adapted trigger choices to observed data and model behavior instead of treating one visual trigger configuration as universally suitable.
quote: There, we only consider the watermark pattern used in [29]. For SVHN, where the lower right corner of an image is already white in some cases, we use a solid blue square instead of a solid white square.
context: The PubFigs face model was insensitive to corner patches, motivating use of a watermark; white corners in SVHN motivated changing the square's color.
uncertainty: These are task-specific choices and do not establish universal optimal trigger designs.

claim: The attack model deliberately includes adversaries who possess a pretrained model but lack its original training data, using a few publicly obtainable samples from a similar distribution instead.
quote: However, in some scenarios, we assume the attacker backdoors pre-trained models; thus, the training data $\mathcal{D}_{tr}$ is not always necessary. Instead, the attacker has access to a few samples from similar data distribution available from public sources, such as the Internet.
context: The attacker has white-box access to model architecture and parameters and changes parameters without changing architecture.
uncertainty: The work does not establish that arbitrary public samples will suffice outside the studied distributions.

claim: A further detector evaluation is scoped by both threat-model relevance and implementation compatibility.
quote: We consider the data-free scenario as it is more practical for the victim in the supply chain. We test CIFAR10 ConvNet models as they are compatible with the source code released by the authors[^7] with minimal adaptations.
context: Appendix J evaluates the model-level detector of Wang et al. in this specific configuration.
uncertainty: Failure of that detector in the selected configuration does not establish failure across every architecture or setting.

claim: The authors emphasize that better performance under one security test can coexist with a hidden compromise and create misleading confidence.
quote: Consequently, a victim who examines a handcrafted model provided by our adversary can have a false sense of security as the model shows more resilience to the adversarial input perturbations.
context: The preceding results report higher classification accuracy under FGSM and PGD-10 attacks for handcrafted models than for poisoning-based models.
uncertainty: The observed resistance is to the evaluated attacks; it does not establish general adversarial robustness.

claim: The paper qualifies its fine-tuning resistance by acknowledging that sufficiently extensive retraining can remove an attack.
quote: In the limit fine-tuning will always succeed if training is carried out sufficiently long, as this is essentially training a model from scratch.
context: The reported fine-tuning experiment retrains models for five epochs over the testing data.
uncertainty: The finite experimental result does not establish resistance to arbitrarily long retraining; the quoted limiting claim is the authors' characterization.

claim: The method ranks candidate neurons by separation between clean and triggered activation distributions, using a normal approximation and selecting a small fraction of neurons per layer.
quote: We then approximate activations to normal distributions and compute the overlapping area between clean and backdoor distributions. We define $1-overlap$ as the separation in activations at a neuron. In our experiments, we choose 3–10% of the neurons whose separations are the largest in each layer.
context: Activation separation is used to select and subsequently strengthen the internal path associated with the trigger.
uncertainty: The normal approximation is an adopted modeling device, not an independently established distributional guarantee.

claim: Random-noise robustness is measured with repeated stochastic trials and an accuracy-based intervention limit, rather than at an arbitrary perturbation magnitude alone.
quote: Since we add random noise, we run this experiment for each model five times and report the averaged metrics.
context: Gaussian noise strength is swept from 0.01 to 5.0, and attack success is reported when ordinary accuracy begins to decline by 5%.
uncertainty: The resulting resilience claim is conditional on this permitted accuracy loss.

claim: The meet-in-the-middle variant reconsiders an assumed ordering of attack design: selecting the trigger can itself be optimized rather than fixed before modifying the network.
quote: However, there is no reason for the attack to necessarily operate in this order—instead of choosing a random patch with no a priori knowledge of if it is going to be “good” or “bad”, it would be just as valid for the attacker to choose the patch so that the attack becomes easier.
context: Appendix C.3 motivates optimizing the trigger to create useful hidden-layer differences before modifying later layers.
uncertainty: The passage establishes an alternative formulation, not a documented chronological change in the authors' personal views.

claim: The guard-bias step is conditional on defending against fine-tuning: suppressing clean activations reduces gradient updates to the inserted behavior, while an attacker facing no such defense can omit the step.
quote: We additionally handcraft the bias parameters to offer resilience against the fine-tuning defense. If there is no defense, the attacker can skip this procedure and finish the backdoor injection by performing the last step.
context: The method sets target-neuron biases so clean inputs produce mostly zero activations.
uncertainty: This is an algorithmic choice within the paper, not evidence about the researcher's general preferences.

claim: For the illustrated parameter-distribution analysis, the authors chose the model with the largest fraction of modified parameters, making the selected case potentially more revealing of statistical artifacts.
quote: We choose this model as the ratio of parameters perturbed to the entirety are the largest among our handcrafted models.
context: Appendix E compares layerwise weight distributions for clean, poisoned, and handcrafted SVHN FC models.
uncertainty: The selection criterion is explicit, but the analysis does not prove that every possible parameter-based detector fails.

claim: The authors deliberately study attacks on pretrained models without requiring their original training data, while retaining access to a small sample from a similar distribution.
quote: However, in some scenarios, we assume the attacker backdoors pre-trained models; thus, the training data $\mathcal{D}_{tr}$ is not always necessary. Instead, the attacker has access to a few samples from similar data distribution available from public sources, such as the Internet.
context: The threat model grants white-box access to architecture and parameters, but does not assume unrestricted access to the original dataset.
uncertainty: Not requiring original training data does not mean the attack is entirely data-free.

claim: Recovered trigger patterns are tested behaviorally across the test set instead of being judged solely by whether reconstructed images look suggestive.
quote: We also test if the reconstructed patterns are valid triggers. We crop the 4x4 reconstructed patterns from those images. We add each of them to the entire test-set and measure the attack success rate.
context: Appendix H.1 applies a prior trigger-reconstruction procedure, then measures whether its recovered patches actually activate the backdoor.
uncertainty: Results vary by architecture and dataset; the CNN CIFAR-10 reconstruction tests have low success for both poisoning and handcrafting.

claim: The paper's broader position distinguishes the impossibility of one universal defense from the possibility of a detector tailored to any particular backdoored network.
quote: We do not believe there can be a defense that prevents arbitrary backdoor attacks—and likewise, for any single backdoored network, a defense that can detect the backdoor exists.
context: The discussion draws an analogy to detecting arbitrary malicious functionality in compiled software and invokes neural-network expressivity and verification difficulty.
uncertainty: This is a coauthored general argument and stated belief, not a universal impossibility theorem proved by the empirical experiments.

claim: The evaluation adapts trigger choices to dataset and model behavior rather than insisting on identical patterns everywhere.
quote: There, we only consider the watermark pattern used in [29]. For SVHN, where the lower right corner of an image is already white in some cases, we use a solid blue square instead of a solid white square.
context: The preceding text reports that the pretrained face model is insensitive to corner triggers; white image corners motivate the separate SVHN adjustment.
uncertainty: These adaptations limit direct comparisons across all trigger–dataset combinations.

claim: The authors identify an exception to their Hessian pattern, offer a tentative distribution-overlap explanation, and note that a supply-chain attacker can change the trigger.
quote: However, the Hessian values in the SVHN FC models that use a square trigger are similar. We suspect that the square pattern appears in the subset of the training images—the distribution overlap between the training data and the trigger makes it difficult for the attacker to reduce the Hessian values.
context: They propose switching to checkerboard or random patterns rather than requiring the square pattern to work equally well.
uncertainty: The explanation is explicitly a suspicion, not an experimentally isolated cause.

claim: Oracle validation is an explicit evidence standard: expected solutions should pass completely, and exceptions must be explained task by task rather than silently removed.
quote: The provided ground-truth solution must achieve a 100% pass rate; deviations must be explained per task and documented in the adapter README, not silently excluded from the dataset.
context: Standards enforced on Harbor adapters.
uncertainty: This is an exception-aware standard; the paper reports several adapters with imperfect or unavailable oracle validation.

claim: The large-scale experiment compares each model under a common cross-family harness and a native harness, while repeating each benchmark-model-harness setting three times.
quote: Each model runs under exactly two harnesses: the cross-family Terminus-2 [103] and one of 3 native harnesses (Gemini CLI for Gemini, Claude Code for Claude, and Codex for GPT), giving 16 model–harness configurations using 4 distinct harness implementations overall. Each (benchmark, model, harness) setting is repeated for 3 trials, yielding $\sim$ 0.3M trajectories.
context: Eight models spanning capability tiers were evaluated across 54 benchmarks and 6,627 tasks.
uncertainty: The design does not cross every model with every harness, and Carlini's role in designing it is unspecified.

claim: The Harbor team uses inexpensive smoke tests before scaling evaluation and samples large benchmarks to balance evaluation cost against breadth.
quote: To ensure compatibility with the target execution platforms, namely Daytona and Modal, we run a smoke test for each benchmark using the low-cost GPT-5-nano model together with Codex. For benchmarks with a large number of tasks, we sample an i.i.d. subset to control evaluation cost while preserving broad benchmark coverage.
context: The resulting evaluation set contains 54 benchmarks and 6,627 selected tasks, with sampling and execution metadata recorded in a manifest.

claim: The initial Harbor-Index filter uses eighteen trials per task across three leading models and two harnesses, retaining tasks solved in at most one third of trials.
quote: Starting from an initial pool of 6,627 Harbor tasks across 54 adapters, we apply a difficulty filter retaining the 1,311 tasks where three leading models at the time of filtering (Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro), each under both its native harness and Terminus-2 over three repeats (18 trials), succeed on at most $33\%$ of trials.
context: First stage of Harbor-Index construction.
uncertainty: Difficulty is relative to the filtering models and settings.

claim: Harbor-Index makes time and resource limits explicit to agents and enforces the same limits in configuration; audit-stage timeout choices depend on observed frontier-model runtimes.
quote: The same limits are enforced in the task configuration through the Harbor agent fields. Timeouts are tightened during the audit-and-fix stage (typically $1.2\times$ the fastest frontier model’s observed runtime, or up to 3 hours when every model fails).
context: Task instructions include an execution contract stating the available time, CPU, memory, and storage.

claim: The final curation loop repairs defects and removes tasks that remain broken or cease to be difficult after repair, giving an explicit stopping and exclusion rule.
quote: Finally, at least two senior reviewers examine each of the 100 using trajectory-grounded failure analysis and false-positive/false-negative analysis, repairing broken tasks and dropping those that remain broken or become too easy after repair, yielding the final release of 82 tasks spanning 29 benchmarks.
context: Final audit-and-fix stage of Harbor-Index.
uncertainty: The excerpt does not specify a maximum number of repair iterations or Carlini's participation in them.

claim: Inspection of low-resolution tasks motivated Harbor-Index: the collaboration treats apparent hardness as potentially caused by flawed task construction rather than necessarily by model limitations.
quote: From our task inspection, low resolution rates in existing benchmarks are often attributable to structural design flaws (e.g., instruction-verification mismatches) rather than genuine task complexity. We therefore introduce Harbor-Index, a curated meta-dataset of 82 tasks for next-generation agent development and evaluation.
context: Transition from broad benchmark evaluation to curated task construction.
uncertainty: The passage establishes a project-level motivation, not Carlini's personal account of selecting the problem.

claim: The collaboration analyzes evaluation redundancy through dimensionality reduction and rank-correlation-based selection rather than treating each benchmark as an independent capability measurement.
quote: Most variation is explained by a single shared capability factor; adding agent scaffolds introduces one additional direction, but the space remains low-rank (Appendix F.1). Greedy selection on absolute Spearman rank correlations agrees:
context: Section 3.1 applies PCA to the 16-by-54 configuration-benchmark score matrix and compares the result with greedy benchmark selection.
uncertainty: The result concerns the evaluated configuration set; it does not establish universal redundancy.

claim: Parity experiments match agent, model, tools, prompts, decoding parameters, and execution configuration, and use repeated runs to account for stochasticity.
quote: The same agent, model, tool set, prompt template, decoding parameters, and execution configuration are applied on both sides. Each side is run $k$ times ($k=3$ by default) to account for stochasticity,
context: The project reports mean scores and sample standard errors across runs.
uncertainty: This is the general protocol; individual adapter entries report exceptions and different repetition counts.

claim: The collaboration makes parity verification mandatory because released benchmark code can contain failing reference solutions, nondeterministic scoring, or discrepancies from leaderboard pipelines.
quote: Published results are often not reproducible from the released code alone: we have routinely encountered oracle solutions that fail the benchmark’s own tests, scoring scripts with undocumented non-determinism, and leaderboard entries produced by pipelines that diverge from the public release.
context: Appendix D.4.1 explains why merely intending to preserve benchmark semantics is insufficient.
uncertainty: The statement summarizes the team's experience; it does not establish that Carlini personally encountered each issue.

claim: The cost analysis operationalizes difficulty using observed failure rates while explicitly warning that this measure depends on the evaluated configurations and can be distorted by defective tasks.
quote: We define empirical task difficulty as one minus the average score across all model–harness runs, and group tasks into ten buckets of width 0.1.
context: The following discussion calls the measure a configuration-dependent proxy that can be affected by false positives, false negatives, and evaluation setup.
