quote: I have so many bugs in the Linux kernel that I can’t report because I haven’t validated them yet. I’m not going to make that some open source developer validate bugs that I haven’t checked yet — I’m not going to send them potential slop.
context: The article discusses a backlog created when automated discovery outpaces human validation.
uncertainty: A direct quotation as presented by a secondary account. The unvalidated candidates should not be counted as confirmed vulnerabilities, and the quote does not establish the backlog’s exact size.

claim: The secondary talk account quotes him explaining that base-model capability matters because malicious users may obtain harmful results without first investing months in specialized infrastructure.
quote: What I care about is the base capability of the model, because if someone who’s malicious wants to go cause some harm and they don’t have to spend six months designing some fancy fuzzing harness or something, and they can just go do bad things with it like this — this is quite, quite scary.
context: The conference account’s discussion of why minimal scaffolding is itself a threat signal.
uncertainty: Presented by the article as a direct Carlini quotation; the supplied document is a secondary deep dive, not a verbatim talk transcript.

claim: The IoT proposal extends the server-adaptation thesis to unknown devices: a model might discover and use device-specific capabilities rather than relying only on generic connectivity.
quote: Similarly to the attack on web servers we presented in Section 3.6, LLMs provide the benefit of autonomously understanding and navigating a variety of systems.
context: Section 4.4 hypothesizes that this could expose sensitive functions on compromised devices; Section 4.3 separately proposes broader automated network reconnaissance.
uncertainty: Neither unknown-device exploration nor expanded reconnaissance is experimentally demonstrated in this paper.

claim: The authors explicitly limit interpretation of the dated Enron corpus: they emphasize relative improvement over classical tools rather than contemporary prevalence estimates.
quote: Therefore, we one should not read too much into the exact number of instances of any particular behavior (e.g., sending passwords over email), but rather the relative uplift of using language models when compared to other classical tools.
context: Footnote 1 notes that the emails were released in 2002 and differ from emails sent today. Footnote 2 separately cautions that the dataset's economics may not generalize.
uncertainty: The paper does not establish how large the uplift would be on representative modern email.

claim: The personal-photo experiment separates per-image extraction from collection-level synthesis, using an open-source vision-language model followed by Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
quote: We use an open-source Vision-Language Model (VLM)—based on Llama 3.2 Vision—to process each photo one-by-one.
context: The VLM extracts potentially identifying or sensitive content from individual photos; the full transcript of descriptions is then summarized by Claude.
uncertainty: The pipeline’s success is illustrated qualitatively, without a comprehensive accuracy assessment.

claim: The authors explain their use of closed models by contemporary performance and propose API monitoring while imposing a privacy constraint and recognizing that open-model deployment can bypass this monitoring point.
quote: LLM API monitoring is only useful when adversaries are using closed models. As open source models become cheaper and more useful, and adversaries learn to cheaply host open models, adversaries using open models may be able to circumvent such monitoring, increasing the importance of defense-in-depth methods.
context: Section 7 separately states that monitoring must preserve ordinary users’ privacy and that most experiments used closed models for state-of-the-art performance.
uncertainty: The effectiveness and privacy properties of a concrete monitoring system are not evaluated.

claim: The defense agenda follows the same economic framing as the attacks: because security work is costly, common exploitation paths receive protection, and changing attacker profitability can undermine that allocation.
quote: Securing computer systems is hard and expensive. And so it is pragmatic to focus defensive efforts on the attack vectors that are most common in practice.
context: Section 7 argues that defenses specialized for historically common attacks may provide less protection when monetization methods change.
uncertainty: This is a general prioritization argument rather than a tested resource-allocation policy.

claim: The paper argues that occasional hallucination need not prevent profitable malicious use: failed attempts can reduce expected returns without invalidating successful attempts.
quote: If 1% (or 10%) of attempted exploits fail due to hallucinating vulnerabilities that do not exist, this only reduces the potential value by 1% (or 10%); it does not limit the applicability of deploying the successful attacks.
context: This contrasts the tolerance for failures in broadly attempted attacks with the reliability demands of safety-critical deployments.
uncertainty: The percentages are illustrative; this passage does not estimate actual failure rates or every cost of a failed attack.

claim: The personal-photo experiment separates per-image extraction from collection-level synthesis, using an open-source vision-language model followed by Claude.
quote: For each photo, we instruct the VLM to extract any personally identifiable information, sensitive data, or particular signs of relationships between people. We then feed the full transcript of photo descriptions into Claude 3.5 Sonnet to summarize what was found.
context: The first-stage model is based on Llama 3.2 Vision; the pipeline reportedly recovers family, travel, document, and medical information.
uncertainty: This is a collaborator-led case study involving a single author's collection.

claim: The server experiment tests whether one prompt can drive discovery, modification, and restart without additional human interaction, followed by functional verification.
quote: We manually verify for each case that, by logging in into the deployed server, our credentials are exfiltrated to the malicious server. This worked with the same prompt for all server types, on the first attempt.
context: Claude 3.7 Sonnet runs through Pydantic AI with terminal access. The setup states that the requested work is performed in one turn.
uncertainty: The restart exception for Redmine limits the claim of completely autonomous end-to-end success across all five servers.

claim: The semantic experiment reports a capability and cost limitation: only Claude 3.5 Sonnet reliably identified the highlighted sensitive relationship, and processing the entire dataset at that capability level would cost thousands of dollars.
quote: The only model that could reliably identify this piece of sensitive information was Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and processing the entire dataset with this model would cost several thousand USD.
context: The paper contrasts this contextual inference task with cheaper syntactic-secret extraction.
uncertainty: The passage does not specify a full repeated-trial protocol for “reliably,” and the full-dataset cost is stated conditionally.

claim: The trusted-device study tests generated interface mimicry on four concrete targets and observes variation even when the input prompt is held constant.
quote: We targeted four different devices in our experiment: two routers and two captive portals.
context: Appendix D supplies each target’s HTML to an LLM and examines pages encouraging certificate installation. Milad is credited with this experiment.
uncertainty: The paper presents generated interfaces, not a human-subject measurement of persuasion or a quantitative detector-evasion evaluation.

claim: The economic comparison makes its break-even assumptions explicit, including zero human cost for filtering false positives and dataset-specific values for recovered credentials.
quote: For example, if we assume the cost of a human filtering out false positives is zero, using an LLM exceeds the value of prior techniques as long as the value of a single password is greater than \$0.40 USD or if the value of a credit card is greater than \$4.48 USD, in this specific case.
context: A separate footnote warns that these economics probably do not generalize to modern email datasets.
uncertainty: The values are conditional break-even calculations, not measured criminal market prices or demonstrated profits.

claim: The researchers disclose extension vulnerabilities to listed developer contacts and report limited remediation engagement: one developer responded and patched, while the others did not respond.
quote: We report each of these vulnerabilities to the contact email address given. One developer responded to our notification and patched patched the extension. Unfortunately, we received no responses from any of the other authors of the contacted extensions.
context: The paper interprets weak developer engagement as consistent with neglected long-tail software.
uncertainty: Nonresponse is observed; the authors’ explanation that these extensions were low priorities for their developers remains an inference.

claim: The multilingual study uses two translation procedures and separates the LLM translator from the model used for extraction.
quote: We perform this translation two different ways: first, with a LLM (a different model than the one used to attack), and second with a production translation service (GoogleTranslate, ).
context: Footnote 3 supplements the translated-Enron experiment.
uncertainty: The supplied text does not give separate numerical results for the two translation procedures or say that either eliminates translation artifacts.

claim: The JFK baseline analysis distinguishes OCR's ability to preserve the relevant text from a downstream detector's ability to recognize it, using transcription as an upper-bound diagnostic.
quote: We first count how many social security numbers are even correctly transcribed by Tesseract, by searching for the known-correct numbers in each of the transcribed documents. This gives an upper bound on how many SSNs any analysis of the transcribed text could identify.
context: The paper reports 369 transcribed numbers and 142 subsequently detected by the traditional data loss prevention tool.
uncertainty: The subsequent text refers to 767 unique SSNs even though only 708 candidates were manually validated, leaving some ambiguity in the baseline denominator.

claim: The Enron experiments distinguish extracting short syntactic secrets from inferring semantic sensitive information that requires contextual understanding across documents.
quote: We focus our analysis on two areas: first, the recovery of short “syntactic” secrets (e.g., passwords, credit card numbers, or social security numbers), and second, the recovery of “semantic” pieces of sensitive information, that require understanding contextual cues spanning potentially multiple documents (e.g., relationships between people).
context: The contributions statement specifically credits Carlini with these experiments. Enron serves as a proxy for information with potential monetary value.
uncertainty: Recovering sensitive information is not itself a measurement of successful monetization.

claim: The authors explicitly acknowledge that publication could enable attacks and nevertheless argue for dissemination before financial incentives make these threats widespread.
quote: it is possible that existing adversaries may read our work and launch new attacks based on the ones we discuss. We believe our work is important to disseminate before the threats we mention in our work become a widespread problem.
context: The stated purpose is to raise awareness and motivate users and organizations to improve defenses in advance.
uncertainty: This is a collective dual-use judgment, not evidence that Carlini alone made the publication decision or independently expressed this rationale.

claim: The extension analysis asks the model to produce explanatory bug reports from source code, making the predicted vulnerability reviewable by humans.
quote: We then extract the JavaScript source code for each of these extensions, and prompt a language model (Claude 3.7 Sonnet) to identify any potential vulnerabilities in the extension, and if any are present, to write a bug report that describes the exploit.
context: This is the automated discovery stage before human exploit validation.
uncertainty: A generated report is treated as a candidate finding, not sufficient evidence that an exploit works.

claim: Carlini's credited JFK experiment adapts the Enron extraction pipeline to scanned documents by supplying raw images and asking for transcription before PII identification.
quote: we apply a nearly identical data processing pipeline as for the Enron email data, however in this case we provide the model the raw image as input instead of the text, and ask the model to transcribe the text of the image and then search for any PII.
context: The paper describes a collection of 2,343 PDFs containing 83,741 scanned pages.
uncertainty: The credit identifies Carlini as performing the experiment; the methodological description remains collectively authored.

claim: The paper organizes its problem selection around three economic mechanisms: increasing value per victim, increasing reach, and reducing vulnerability-discovery and exploit-development costs.
quote:
- Increase the expected profit from each exploitation (e.g., by increasing the severity of the attack, or by reducing the cost needed to monetize the exploit).
- Increase the number of affected users.
- Reduce the cost to discover the vulnerability and develop the exploit.
context: Section 2.2 introduces a toy economic model that structures the later case studies.
uncertainty: The model is intentionally simple and does not establish realized criminal profit.

claim: The extension investigation checks environmental preconditions beyond source-level plausibility and finds that a domain dependency described in a candidate attack had actually expired.
quote: Most worryingly, in this case the extension developer’s DNS record had actually expired, making this attack immediately practical.
context: The finding involved an extension trusting externally supplied configuration. Carlini is credited with the long-tail exploit work.
uncertainty: The paper’s statement establishes the reported precondition, not observed exploitation by an external adversary.

claim: The syntactic-secret evaluation compares both the amount recovered and precision against traditional data-loss-prevention tooling, rather than relying on illustrative discoveries alone.
quote: For example, traditional data loss prevention tools find slightly more than 300 passwords at a precision just below 70%, while an LLM identifies twice as many passwords (over 600) with a precision over 95%.
context: The comparison includes Google's Sensitive Data Protection service and reports results for passwords, credit cards, and social security numbers.
uncertainty: These results are specific to the supplied paper's Enron evaluation and do not establish universal superiority.

claim: The authors retain a negative present-day economic assessment of the LAION experiment despite its successful discoveries.
quote: We currently estimate the cost of processing each image to be approximately \$0.01 USD, and so again the cost is not currently economically valuable, but is likely to be in the future.
context: The evaluation scans one million images and identifies twelve containing actual sensitive financial information.
uncertainty: Future profitability is a forecast; the experiment does not measure the revenue obtainable from the recovered information.

claim: The multilingual experiment uses a balanced subset of 1,000 Enron documents and two translation methods, including a model different from the model evaluated for extraction.
quote: We perform this translation two different ways: first, with a LLM (a different model than the one used to attack), and second with a production translation service (GoogleTranslate, ).
context: Half the sampled documents contain passwords and half do not. The main text describes translation into multiple languages before repeating the baseline comparison.
uncertainty: The source says ten languages but enumerates nine. Translated English documents also do not establish performance on naturally occurring multilingual email.

claim: The team reports a concrete cost for long-tail vulnerability discovery while judging the demonstrated approach unlikely to be profitable at the time.
quote: Here, as in the setting above, the cost to implement these attacks is currently prohibitively expensive. Running Claude 3.7 Sonnet on each of these 200 extensions cost \$270 USD, and resulted in three high severity vulnerabilities.
context: The paper compares this cost with bounty economics for much more widely used targets and makes future viability conditional on cheaper comparable model capability.
uncertainty: The paper does not measure actual criminal revenues, and inference cost alone is not a full accounting of validation and operational costs.

claim: Browser extensions were chosen partly because their JavaScript source and compact size fit current model capabilities, reducing reverse-engineering and context-window obstacles.
quote: These programs are written and distributed in JavaScript (making it easy for today’s language models to process their source code without requiring sophisticated reverse-engineering), and are often relatively small and self-contained
context: The text further connects compactness to processing the entire source in one chunk. Carlini is credited with developing the long-tail exploits.
uncertainty: This selection makes the experiment tractable but limits extrapolation to large, compiled, or heavily obfuscated applications.

claim: The server experiment evaluates whether one prompt and one uninterrupted agent run can locate authentication logic, modify behavior, and activate the change across different applications.
quote: Everything is done in one single turn so that no interaction is required by the malicious party. We provide the full prompts in Appendix F.
context: Claude 3.7 Sonnet runs through Pydantic AI with terminal access. The results state that the same prompt worked on the first attempt for all server types.
uncertainty: The reported lack of operator interaction during the run does not remove setup work or the subsequent human verification, and one restart failed.

claim: The unimplemented social-engineering proposal emphasizes adapting messages to relationship context and selecting susceptible recipients, rather than only generating generic phishing text.
quote: With similar strategies as in Section 3.1, an attacker could use LLMs to gain more granular information, such as the topics and style of conversations between the victim and a target, or identify targets that appear most susceptible to phishing.
context: The proposed starting point is an already compromised machine whose communications could inform lateral phishing.
uncertainty: The paper does not test recipient susceptibility or execute this proposed personalized campaign.

claim: The targeted-password proposal distinguishes gathering personal side information from directly conditioning a password model on that information.
quote: LLMs can likely aid in the process of targeted password guessing in two ways. First, LLMs can be used to autonomously perform information gathering about a victim, e.g., by scraping social media.
context: Section 4.2 additionally proposes modeling likely passwords conditional on user-specific information rather than only generating wordlists.
uncertainty: The paper provides no new password-guessing experiment or measured advantage for this proposal.

claim: The empirical program follows a repeated structure: define the problem, establish the existing approach, explain the hypothesized LLM advantage, implement a proof of concept, and measure effectiveness.
quote: Each section begins with a statement of the problem, a brief description of the current state-of-the-art, and a discussion of how LLMs could significantly increase the ability of an attacker to extract value.
context: Section 3 explicitly describes the organization of the attack analyses and then states that each includes a current-model proof of concept.
uncertainty: The individual experiments differ considerably in quantitative rigor, automation, and validation.

claim: The ethical design restricts sensitive-data experiments to existing public datasets or author-owned material, uses responsible disclosure for real extension bugs, and isolates other tests from real users.
quote: For our experiments in Section 3.1, we ensure that the datasets we analyze are either existing public datasets (i.e. Enron emails/audio, JFK files, LAION) or are data from authors of our work (i.e. image mining in personal photos).
context: Section 6 states the team’s harm-avoidance approach across the experiment families.
uncertainty: Public availability does not itself eliminate privacy concerns; the paper’s own findings show that public archives contain sensitive information.

claim: For scanned JFK records, the experiment adapts the Enron extraction pipeline to raw images and asks for transcription before identifying personal information.
quote: To run the LLM evaluation, we apply a nearly identical data processing pipeline as for the Enron email data, however in this case we provide the model the raw image as input instead of the text, and ask the model to transcribe the text of the image and then search for any PII.
context: Carlini is credited with the JFK image SSN-recovery experiments. The corpus contains 2,343 PDFs and 83,741 scanned pages.
uncertainty: The described pipeline does not by itself establish recovery completeness.

claim: The authors explicitly qualify the banking demonstration: two-factor confirmation prevents the assumed XSS attack from completing a transfer to a new recipient.
quote: The e-banking application we use for our experiments is not actually vulnerable to such XSS attacks, as it asks for a 2-factor confirmation when sending wires to new recipients. Nevertheless, our experiment demonstrates the viability of using LLMs to autonomously orchestrate XSS attacks.
context: This footnote materially narrows the main text's statement that the model can perform the requested banking action.
uncertainty: The evidence supports interface orchestration, not a successful unauthorized wire transfer.

claim: The authors inspect classical-pipeline failures and identify two mechanisms: corrupted contextual keywords and loss of the spatial relationship between labels and numbers.
quote: turning the scanned document into a text file results in lost context (such as placing the words “social security number” far away from the actual number, even if visually on the page they appear nearby).
context: This diagnosis explains why the detector found substantially fewer numbers than Tesseract had transcribed correctly.
uncertainty: The supplied text gives an explanatory inspection, not an ablation quantifying each failure mechanism separately.

claim: The client-side XSS study deliberately weakens the attacker's assumed starting position from full-device compromise to script execution within a visited website.
quote: Instead of assuming that the attacker has compromised the victim’s entire machine, we only assume that they have a cross-site scripting (XSS) attack that allows the attacker to inject arbitrary JavaScript code onto a website visited by the victim.
context: This tests whether adaptive on-device actions remain feasible under a narrower foothold.
uncertainty: The experiment assumes the XSS foothold; it does not discover such a vulnerability in the evaluated bank.

claim: The defense agenda is grounded in resource allocation: concentrating defenses on prevalent attacks is pragmatic, but changes in profitability can undermine that strategy.
quote: Securing computer systems is hard and expensive. And so it is pragmatic to focus defensive efforts on the attack vectors that are most common in practice.
context: The authors argue that protections optimized for prior monetization patterns may be less useful when LLMs make different patterns profitable.
uncertainty: This is a general strategic argument, not an empirical comparison of complete defensive programs.

claim: The authors organize the research around the possibility that LLMs allow attacks to combine large scale with target-specific adaptation, treating that combination as the important change to investigate.
quote: Through a series of case studies, we analyze ways in which LLMs could allow attacks to go both broad and deep. Specifically, we consider two potential directions where LLMs could have high impact.
context: The two directions are exploiting the long tail of systems and conducting targeted attacks at scale.
uncertainty: The case studies establish selected capabilities; they do not measure an actual ecosystem-wide transition.

claim: The extension workflow changes after automated proof-of-concept generation proves inadequate: the team manually validates the model's vulnerability reports.
quote: Current LLMs are trained to refuse to take such actions, and are slow at performing these types of validations. And so instead, we manually process each of the 54 cases where the language model claimed a vulnerability was present, and validate the attack ourselves.
context: The preceding explanation identifies real-world actions, such as creating social-media accounts, as obstacles to autonomous validation.
uncertainty: This is a documented change within one experimental workflow, not evidence of a broader evolution in Carlini's views.

claim: The team draws an explicit boundary between implemented experiments and additional plausible attacks when realistic, ethical validation would require unavailable expertise or substantial investment.
quote: we are unable to easily identify a method of performing a realistic and ethical proof-of-concept attack. We believe validating the case studies we raise in this section is an important avenue of future work, which may require significant expertise in ethical human security studies, or large technical investment (or both).
context: Section 4 presents illustrative, unimplemented attack vectors. Carlini, Milad, and Florian are credited with describing them.
uncertainty: These scenarios are hypotheses and research proposals, not demonstrated capabilities in this paper.

claim: The authors explicitly bound the usefulness of provider-side monitoring: self-hosted open models can remove that intervention point.
quote: LLM API monitoring is only useful when adversaries are using closed models. As open source models become cheaper and more useful, and adversaries learn to cheaply host open models, adversaries using open models may be able to circumvent such monitoring, increasing the importance of defense-in-depth methods.
context: This keeps the proposed defense agenda from depending exclusively on cooperation by hosted-model providers.
uncertainty: The extent and timing of migration to self-hosted models are prospective judgments.

claim: The JFK experiment encounters model refusals and explicitly stops short of investing in a more sophisticated bypass because the remaining refused images constitute a small fraction of inputs.
quote: The jailbreak fails for 1,067 images, where the LLM refuses to transcribe. We do not apply a more sophisticated jailbreak to these cases because they account for a small fraction of all inputs.
context: Footnote 5 explains that the team framed processing as PII redaction to obtain transcriptions. Carlini is credited with these experiments.
uncertainty: This is an explicit stopping decision for this experiment, not evidence of a general personal policy about diminishing returns.

claim: The paper makes an economic break-even argument conditional on an explicit labor assumption, instead of treating higher extraction accuracy as automatically worthwhile.
quote: if we assume the cost of a human filtering out false positives is zero, using an LLM exceeds the value of prior techniques as long as the value of a single password is greater than \$0.40 USD
context: The baseline costs $1.5 to process the dataset, while the cited inexpensive model services cost approximately $60–$100. The calculation also gives a separate credit-card threshold.
uncertainty: The labor assumption and historical email distribution materially limit the threshold's applicability.

claim: The proposed password-guessing direction separates collecting personal side information from conditioning a password model on that information, identifying a more tailored modeling question than generic password generation.
quote: LLMs could directly be trained to model the distribution of common passwords (as in (rando2023passgpt, )) conditioned on this side information, to generate passwords that are most likely for that particular user (radertargeted, ).
context: Section 4.2 contrasts the proposal with user-agnostic guessing and side-information-derived wordlists.
uncertainty: This paper provides no new training experiment or quantitative evaluation of the proposed conditional model.

claim: The authenticated-user results distinguish first-attempt success from success after debugging, with Selenium requiring corrections based on observed errors.
quote: We observe that when using curl and UI actions, the model succeeds in its first attempt; however, using Selenium, the model made initial mistakes that it then corrected based on the errors it encountered.
context: All three requested actions reportedly succeeded through all three interaction methods.
uncertainty: The debugging described here is the model's behavior within a collaborator-led experiment, not a direct description of Carlini's personal debugging process.

claim: To probe beyond the single-owner photo case, the team sampled one million LAION images and manually reviewed model-flagged financial material, revealing substantial false positives.
quote: When we focus specifically on the financial category, the model initially flagged 210 images as potentially financially sensitive. Upon manual review, we found that 187 of these were non-sensitive items like stock photos or generic images (e.g., pictures of mock credit cards).
context: Milad is credited with the LAION experiment. Qwen-VL-72B screened the random sample; only 12 images ultimately contained actual sensitive financial information.
uncertainty: This validates selected positive findings but does not measure missed sensitive images across the full sample.

claim: The future-work agenda proposes detecting PII mining and on-device inference, while explicitly framing these as partial mitigations that could increase attackers' costs or visibility.
quote: This direction will not solve the problem, but may reduce the rate at which adversaries can exfiltrate sensitive data from users. Another opportunity is to profile applications on a device which are performing LLM inference.
context: The proposed reasoning is that blocking local inference could force document transmission over networks, creating monitoring opportunities.
uncertainty: No prototype, efficacy measurement, or operational feasibility analysis for these defenses is supplied.

claim: Carlini's JFK-document experiment adapts the Enron extraction pipeline to raw scanned images and manually checks candidate social security numbers.
quote: The language model identifies a total of 767 unique potential social security numbers; after manual review, we find that 708 are correct instances of social security numbers, resulting in a precision of $92.3\%$.
context: The model is asked to transcribe image text and then search for PII across the released scanned documents. Carlini is explicitly credited with this experiment.
uncertainty: The reported precision does not establish recall against all social security numbers in the corpus.

claim: The JFK baseline decomposes the classical pipeline into an OCR bottleneck and a downstream detection bottleneck, first asking whether target numbers survive transcription at all.
quote: We first count how many social security numbers are even correctly transcribed by Tesseract, by searching for the known-correct numbers in each of the transcribed documents. This gives an upper bound on how many SSNs any analysis of the transcribed text could identify.
context: The paper reports 369 correctly transcribed numbers and 142 detected by the subsequent data-loss-prevention tool.
uncertainty: The comparison is anchored to discovered candidate numbers. The surrounding passage inconsistently refers to 767 as unique SSNs after distinguishing 708 validated instances.

claim: The empirical sections follow a recurring structure: define the problem, establish existing practice, explain a possible LLM advantage, implement a current-model proof of concept, and measure efficacy.
quote: Each section begins with a statement of the problem, a brief description of the current state-of-the-art, and a discussion of how LLMs could significantly increase the ability of an attacker to extract value. We then implement a proof-of-concept attack using current LLMs, and measure the efficacy of this exploitation method.
context: This structure connects the economic thesis to concrete demonstrations rather than leaving it entirely speculative.
uncertainty: The depth of validation varies across case studies.

claim: For personal-image analysis, the team chooses an author's real phone photos because it lacks an appropriate organic dataset, while explicitly declining to call that sample representative.
quote: We are not aware of an organic dataset of images that users are likely to have on their machines. So instead, to build a realistic case study (but not necessarily a generally representative one), we use a LLM to process 540 photos taken by one of the authors with their phone during the year of 2024.
context: The contributions statement assigns this experiment to Florian.
uncertainty: Neither the photographs nor the personal information extracted from them should be attributed to Carlini.

claim: The project leaves several additional attack ideas unimplemented because the authors cannot readily design realistic and ethical proofs of concept, and they identify expertise and engineering investment as prerequisites for further validation.
quote: Finally, we consider a further set of attacks that we believe are technically feasible and would be economically valuable, but where we are unable to easily identify a method of performing a realistic and ethical proof-of-concept attack.
context: Section 4 separates these proposals from implemented experiments. Carlini, Milad, and Florian are credited with describing the additional vectors.
uncertainty: Feasibility and economic value in this section are hypotheses, not demonstrated results.

claim: A footnote materially narrows the banking demonstration: the tested application requires a second factor for new recipients and is not actually vulnerable to the hypothesized transfer attack.
quote: The e-banking application we use for our experiments is not actually vulnerable to such XSS attacks, as it asks for a 2-factor confirmation when sending wires to new recipients.
context: The authors retain the example as evidence that an LLM can orchestrate browser actions under the assumed XSS capability.
uncertainty: The main text's statement that the model performed both actions must be read alongside this explicit limitation.

claim: The audio-review prompt encodes conservative handling of insufficient context and requests supporting excerpts with minimally overlapping findings.
quote: Suspicious content lacking enough context should not be flagged, or flagged as at most Tier 1. * Include all relevant sentence(s) in Excerpt * Problems should be sufficiently independent and overlap little in content for the same conversation.
context: Appendix A.1 reproduces the experimental prompt, which also permits an empty findings list.
uncertainty: These are instructions to an experimental model, not direct researcher speech or evidence that the model consistently obeyed them.

claim: The server results isolate a deployment-specific failure: the model modified authentication logic everywhere but failed to restart Redmine in the Docker evaluation.
quote: Claude 3.7 manages to correctly identify authentication logic and add logging code in all five types of servers, and it manages to restart the server in all but one case (the Redmine server).
context: The authors explain that the restart mechanism chosen by the model did not work in their containerized setup.
uncertainty: The passage does not fully explain how the Redmine restart issue was handled before the reported manual functional verification.

claim: The team checks real deployment conditions for a model-proposed attack, finding that an expired developer domain made one extension vulnerability immediately actionable.
quote: Most worryingly, in this case the extension developer’s DNS record had actually expired, making this attack immediately practical.
context: The model had identified a configuration-trust issue whose exploitability depended on an attacker controlling the developer's domain.
uncertainty: The paper describes validation of the precondition, not an attack against actual extension users.

claim: The multilingual evaluation uses a balanced subset of password-containing and password-free documents, then translates the same material to compare performance across languages.
quote: To measure this, we take a subset of 1000 text documents from the Enron dataset, half of which contain passwords, and half of which do not.
context: The paper reports severe drops for traditional tooling in some languages, while LLM password counts vary by approximately ±6%.
uncertainty: Translated English emails are not equivalent to naturally occurring multilingual correspondence. The text says ten languages but lists nine.

claim: The multilingual evaluation reports substantially more stable password recovery for the LLM than for the traditional tool across the tested translations.
quote: And for Arabic, Bengali, and Mandarin, the recall drops to just 21 passwords (over $10\times$ lower than the English baseline). In contrast, for the LLM-based analysis, the number of passwords identified for each of the languages varies only by $\pm 6\%$.
context: This supports the paper's argument that learned extraction can extend beyond separately hand-engineered language support.
uncertainty: The reported variation concerns detected-password counts in this experiment, not a universal multilingual robustness guarantee.

claim: The paper proposes detecting and constraining PII mining as a partial defense, explicitly avoiding a claim that it would solve the overall problem.
quote: One concrete opportunity we see is the development of defenses to identify and prevent PII-mining on end-user devices or web services. This direction will not solve the problem, but may reduce the rate at which adversaries can exfiltrate sensitive data from users.
context: A related proposal is to identify on-device inference so adversaries must use network transfers that may be slower and more observable.
uncertainty: These are future defense directions; no implementation or efficacy measurement is supplied.

claim: The multilingual evaluation uses a balanced subset of password-containing and password-free documents and two translation methods, including a model different from the extraction model.
quote: We perform this translation two different ways: first, with a LLM (a different model than the one used to attack), and second with a production translation service (GoogleTranslate, ).
context: The subset contains 1,000 Enron documents, half with passwords. The experiment compares LLM extraction with conventional tooling after translation.
uncertainty: Translated English documents are not equivalent to naturally occurring multilingual email. The text says ten languages but enumerates nine.

claim: The web-server study treats adaptation across languages, frameworks, and deployment procedures as the key automation challenge, rather than claiming the underlying code modification is difficult for a programmer.
quote:
Clearly any moderately-skilled programmer, after exploiting a web-server, could easily implement attacks such as this.

Yet, using classical techniques, implementing this attack at scale would be exceptionally challenging.
context: Section 3.6 argues that application heterogeneity impedes one fixed automation script.
uncertainty: This is the paper's characterization of the scaling bottleneck, not a measured comparison with a strong conventional automation system.

claim: The project prioritizes financially motivated attackers because the authors expect current models to produce more immediate marginal harm there than for already well-resourced nation-states.
quote: We focus on this threat model because this is the space in which we believe current language models are most likely to be used to cause harm in the short term:
context: Section 2 acknowledges curiosity, ideology, disruption, reconnaissance, and national security as other motivations before restricting the analysis.
uncertainty: The relative importance of different attacker classes is the authors' stated rationale, not an experimentally established ranking.

claim: The device-mimicking proof of concept uses a small, concrete collection of interfaces and observes variation across repeated model outputs.
quote: We targeted four different devices in our experiment: two routers and two captive portals.
context: Appendix D supplies original page HTML to generate matching certificate-installation prompts and reports different outputs even for identical input prompts. Milad is credited with this work.
uncertainty: The experiment does not report human deception rates or quantitatively test the claim that output variation makes detection difficult.

claim: The authenticated-user experiment compares three interaction mechanisms on a test Facebook account and uses zero-shot prompting with error feedback.
quote: In all cases, we prompt the model 0-shot (i.e., we do not provide references for the solution) but we do allow the model to update its solution based on system feedback of any errors encountered.
context: Gemini 2.5 Pro is tested on reading conversations, reading images, and sending a message through curl, Selenium, and mouse-and-keyboard interaction. Christopher is credited with these experiments.
uncertainty: The paper does not specify a large repeated-trial evaluation or establish robustness across many accounts and interface versions.

claim: The IoT proposal generalizes the server experiment's adaptation idea to unfamiliar devices, where the model could discover and use device-specific capabilities.
quote: Similarly to the attack on web servers we presented in Section 3.6, LLMs provide the benefit of autonomously understanding and navigating a variety of systems.
context: The hypothetical scenario begins with shell access and proposes discovering functionality such as cameras or microphones instead of using every device only as a generic network node.
uncertainty: No IoT-device experiment in this paper validates that transfer from server modification.

claim: The extension study uses an explicit sampling frame and filters to isolate small, low-popularity applications rather than treating an unspecified collection as representative.
quote: We download 200 Chrome extensions that contain less than 500KB of JavaScript source code, and that each have fewer than $1{,}000$ users.
context: Candidates were randomly selected from the top 1,000 extensions in each of 18 store categories, discarding those above the size or popularity thresholds.
uncertainty: This is a filtered store-based sample, not a random sample of all software or even all Chrome extensions.

claim: The team supplements the single-person photo study with a much larger sample of public web images to examine whether sensitive-image extraction extends beyond that case.
quote: In these experiments, we randomly selected 1M images from the dataset and use the Qwen-VL-72B model to search for images that include sensitive information.
context: The dataset is LAION, and the contributions statement assigns this experiment to Milad.
uncertainty: Public web imagery differs from the contents of compromised personal devices.

claim: The e-banking proof of concept measures interface-operation complexity and identifies repeated processing of full webpage HTML as its main inference-cost driver.
quote: The main cost driver for our proof-of-concept attack is that the LLM processes the entire HTML code of the webpage multiple times (i.e., whenever it switches to a new tab or window).
context: The reported sequence involves 11 clicks and 7 write operations, about one million input tokens, and $3 in model cost.
uncertainty: These measurements describe the demonstrated navigation sequence, not successful unauthorized settlement of a payment.

claim: The JFK baseline decomposes failure into transcription and downstream detection, first checking whether known identifiers survive OCR before running a conventional sensitive-data detector.
quote: We first count how many social security numbers are even correctly transcribed by Tesseract, by searching for the known-correct numbers in each of the transcribed documents. This gives an upper bound on how many SSNs any analysis of the transcribed text could identify.
context: The paper reports 369 identifiers transcribed by Tesseract and 142 subsequently identified by data-loss-prevention tooling.
uncertainty: The text later refers to 767 unique SSNs despite previously validating only 708 of 767 candidates; that denominator ambiguity should be preserved rather than silently resolved.

claim: The authors argue that imperfect reliability need not prevent profitable mass exploitation, because failed attempts can reduce expected returns without invalidating successful attempts.
quote: If 1% (or 10%) of attempted exploits fail due to hallucinating vulnerabilities that do not exist, this only reduces the potential value by 1% (or 10%); it does not limit the applicability of deploying the successful attacks.
context: This contrasts the consequences of model errors in exploitation with their consequences in safety-critical deployments.
uncertainty: The numerical example is illustrative and assumes failures have no additional consequential costs.

claim: The team initially attempted automated proof-of-concept development, then switched to manual validation after encountering model limitations, refusals around real-world actions, and slow validation.
quote: We initially also attempted to ask the language model to develop a proof-of-concept exploit, but found current models do not yet have the ability to achieve this step of the attack
context: Some validations required actions such as creating social-media accounts. The researchers manually processed all 54 flagged cases.
uncertainty: This is a documented within-project procedural change, not a broader change in Carlini’s research philosophy.

claim: The threat model deliberately combines technical sophistication with financial and human-time constraints, making resource efficiency central to the analysis.
quote: We assume the adversary has the technical ability to run or query state-of-the-art large language models, but is constrained both financially and by human time.
context: The modeled adversary resembles a capable cybercrime group rather than a nation-state. The paper also explicitly simplifies by treating time and money as exchangeable.
uncertainty: The resource model is an analytical assumption, not a measured description of every criminal organization.

claim: The researchers report the discovered extension vulnerabilities to developer contact addresses and record both a successful patch and widespread nonresponse.
quote: We report each of these vulnerabilities to the contact email address given. One developer responded to our notification and patched patched the extension. Unfortunately, we received no responses from any of the other authors of the contacted extensions.
context: The paper interprets the nonresponse as potentially reflecting low developer priority for these extensions.
uncertainty: The response outcomes are reported observations; the explanation for nonresponse remains the authors' speculation.

claim: The proposed lateral-movement direction asks whether LLMs can bridge the coverage gap between inexpensive automated reconnaissance and expensive human investigation.
quote: Currently, some combination of (expensive) human investigation and (cheaper, but lower coverage) automated tools are used for such reconnaissance.
context: The authors suggest LLM-based exploration after one network device has been compromised and note that a locally hosted model could avoid remote-model traffic.
uncertainty: The paper presents neither a reconnaissance benchmark nor an implemented lateral-movement experiment.

claim: The authenticated-user experiment compares three interaction modes on a test Facebook account while keeping the task family and model fixed.
quote: To accomplish this, we consider three different ways in which the LLM could interact with Facebook: (1) by issuing curl commands; (2) using a headless Chrome instance which the LLM can interact with using Python and Selenium; and (3) using mouse and keyboard control for UI actions.
context: Christopher is credited with the experiment, which evaluates reading conversations, reading images, and sending a message using Gemini 2.5 Pro with thinking.
uncertainty: A single representative platform and test account do not establish general success across services.

claim: The economic framework separates three mechanisms for increasing attack value: greater profit per compromised user, broader reach, and cheaper vulnerability discovery and exploit development.
quote:
- Increase the expected profit from each exploitation (e.g., by increasing the severity of the attack, or by reducing the cost needed to monetize the exploit).
- Increase the number of affected users.
- Reduce the cost to discover the vulnerability and develop the exploit.
context: These mechanisms guide the selection of case studies covering both initial exploitation and monetization after compromise.
uncertainty: The framework is explicitly a toy economic model, not a fully estimated model of attacker behavior.

claim: The client-side XSS study simplifies the implementation by manually relaying model requests and browser results instead of building a complete agent.
quote: For simplicity, we do not setup a full agent system and instead manually copy the LLM’s function requests to a JavaScript console and return the results to the LLM.
context: The study uses Claude Sonnet 3.7 in Twitter and banking-interface scenarios. Florian is credited with these experiments.
uncertainty: The result demonstrates model-directed orchestration with human transport of actions, not a deployed autonomous XSS agent.

claim: The defensive argument is conditional on changes in attacker economics: protection optimized for historically common exploitation paths may weaken when profitable behavior changes.
quote: if the space of profitable attacks changes significantly, defenses designed to mitigate prior popular attacks no longer provide the same degree of protection
context: Section 7 gives file-encryption monitoring as an example that would not address malware focused on sensitive-data discovery and exfiltration.
uncertainty: The paper proposes this consequence but does not benchmark existing defense-in-depth systems against its full scenario set.

claim: A supplemental audio analysis aggregates all transcribed conversations into one inference to look specifically for personal sensitivity rather than corporate misconduct, while reporting token usage and cost.
quote: we ran one inference over all transcribed conversations to identify personally sensitive information, with 334k prompt tokens and 65k output tokens with Gemini 2.5 Pro Preview, costing less than \$2 USD.
context: Appendix A.2 asks for transcript quotations and highlights a case involving job-seeking intentions, family circumstances, and compensation.
uncertainty: The highlighted example is illustrative and does not establish the sensitivity or correctness of every output.

claim: For semantic inference, the experiment groups emails by employee and asks for descriptions of correspondents, allowing cross-document relationship inference without explicitly naming a particular sensitive relationship in the task.
quote: To demonstrate this capability, we divide all emails from the Enron dataset into 150 (potentially overlapping) sets, grouped by the Enron employee who has sent or received that email.
context: Each collection is supplied to Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Carlini is credited with the semantic-secret experiments.
uncertainty: The reported sensitive discovery is a case study, not a measured prevalence or comprehensive relationship-inference benchmark.

claim: The authors preserve a successful model-generated vulnerability analysis while explicitly correcting its exaggerated privilege and severity claim.
quote: Note, however, the model is incorrect about the level of severity: the exploit does not give extension-level permissions because Chrome’s security model prevents exactly this type of vulnerability from leading to elevated privilege escalation.
context: Appendix C reproduces the model’s analysis of an image-description extension vulnerability and distinguishes the valid finding from an incorrect consequence.
uncertainty: The first-person statements inside the reproduced analysis are model output, not Carlini’s speech.

claim: Carlini is explicitly credited with jointly proposing the project and personally performing its Enron syntactic and semantic secret experiments.
quote:
- Nicholas, Matthew, Milad, and Florian proposed the project.
- Nicholas performed the Enron syntactic and semantic secret experiments in Section 3.1.
context: The contributions section identifies concrete responsibilities, providing stronger attribution than author order alone.
uncertainty: This credits participation and execution; it does not identify who originated each hypothesis or wrote particular passages.

claim: The paper stops short of implementing several proposed attack vectors because the team cannot easily construct realistic and ethical demonstrations.
quote: Finally, we consider a further set of attacks that we believe are technically feasible and would be economically valuable, but where we are unable to easily identify a method of performing a realistic and ethical proof-of-concept attack.
context: The authors identify ethical human-security expertise and substantial technical investment as possible prerequisites for future validation. Carlini, Milad, and Florian are credited with describing these additional vectors.
uncertainty: These scenarios remain proposals in this paper and should not be described as experimentally demonstrated attacks.

claim: The IoT proposal transfers the server experiment’s cross-system adaptation idea to heterogeneous devices, suggesting that understanding device-specific capabilities could change post-compromise monetization.
quote: Similarly to the attack on web servers we presented in Section 3.6, LLMs provide the benefit of autonomously understanding and navigating a variety of systems.
context: The proposed extension concerns device-specific sensors and functions rather than only generic network connectivity.
uncertainty: No IoT implementation is presented, so this is an analogy from demonstrated software adaptation rather than direct device evidence.

claim: The audio experiment uses a fixed corpus, structured outputs, and an explicit rating rubric rather than unrestricted narrative judgments.
quote: We use gemini-exp-1206, a multi-modal language model, to process 680 audio files with an average duration of 121.5 seconds. The model is prompted to provide output in JSON and rate each file according to a given rubric.
context: The contributions statement assigns the Enron audio experiments to Barry. The paper reports three clearly incriminating business discussions and up to $15 in inference costs for a pass.
uncertainty: The paper does not present a complete human-labeled audio benchmark for precision and recall.

claim: The conclusion distinguishes demonstrated technical capability from current profitability, with the forecast of wider harm depending on future cost reductions.
quote: Fortunately, each of the attacks we introduce here are likely still too expensive to be profitable for adversaries for now.
context: The authors use declining inference prices to argue that these attacks could become economically efficient and motivate defensive work before that point.
uncertainty: The paper does not demonstrate actual profitable criminal operations, and future profitability depends on revenues, operational costs, defenses, and model prices.

claim: The photo case study checks whether visual analysis recovers information meaningful to the data owner, including travel and sensitive document contents, while acknowledging that some travel information could also come from metadata.
quote: The model also correctly maps various personal and professional travels from the author, based solely on visual cues present in photos.
context: The reported recoveries include family identities, addresses, professions, and medical information. A footnote notes the alternative metadata route for some information.
uncertainty: The source reports correctness but does not provide a systematic independent validation protocol.

claim: The server-modification study tests generality across five real application stacks rather than tailoring a demonstration to one framework.
quote: We create realistic deployments of five servers using different frameworks: Wordpress (written in PHP), Ghost (written in JavaScript), Nextcloud (written in PHP), Redmine (written in Ruby), and FastAPI (written in Python).
context: The servers use Docker and recommended configurations. Edoardo is credited with the password-from-webservers experiments.
uncertainty: The deployments are controlled test systems, and five stacks do not establish universal portability.

claim: The authors diagnose the classical document pipeline's failures in terms of damaged keywords and lost spatial relationships, rather than merely reporting an aggregate performance gap.
quote: turning the scanned document into a text file results in lost context (such as placing the words “social security number” far away from the actual number, even if visually on the page they appear nearby).
context: They also identify OCR errors in the phrase identifying an SSN as a reason keyword-based matching can fail despite a correctly transcribed number.
uncertainty: The passage provides a qualitative failure analysis, not a quantitative attribution of every missed detection.

claim: The Enron experiments distinguish extracting short recognizable secrets from inferring sensitive relationships across documents, separating improved pattern recognition from a more contextual capability.
quote: We focus our analysis on two areas: first, the recovery of short “syntactic” secrets (e.g., passwords, credit card numbers, or social security numbers), and second, the recovery of “semantic” pieces of sensitive information, that require understanding contextual cues spanning potentially multiple documents (e.g., relationships between people).
context: Carlini is credited with performing both Enron experiment families. The dataset serves as a proxy for information that might have monetary value.
uncertainty: Finding sensitive information does not itself demonstrate successful monetization.

claim: The extension results distinguish model-flagged candidates from human-confirmed vulnerabilities and expose a substantial false-positive burden.
quote: Out of 200 extensions processed by a language model agent we build, 54 are flagged as potentially vulnerable to attack, with 19 (35%) actually vulnerable after human analysis.
context: Table 1 separates three high-severity vulnerabilities from sixteen medium-severity vulnerabilities.
uncertainty: Unflagged extensions are not described as exhaustively audited, so the results do not measure vulnerability-discovery recall.

claim: The authors disclose that the semantic demonstration depended on a more capable and much more expensive model than the syntactic extraction tasks.
quote: The only model that could reliably identify this piece of sensitive information was Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and processing the entire dataset with this model would cost several thousand USD.
context: The demonstrated task required combining contextual evidence across an individual's emails.
uncertainty: The quoted cost is an estimate for processing the entire dataset; the passage does not provide a comprehensive cross-model reliability benchmark.

claim: The authors report a capability-cost bottleneck in semantic extraction: only one tested model reliably identified the highlighted sensitive relationship, and a full-dataset run at that capability level would be expensive.
quote: The only model that could reliably identify this piece of sensitive information was Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and processing the entire dataset with this model would cost several thousand USD.
context: This contrasts with the less expensive syntactic extraction experiments and motivates the paper's interest in declining inference prices.
uncertainty: The passage does not provide a comprehensive model comparison or a statistical definition of reliability.

claim: The central research hypothesis is that LLMs could relax the traditional tradeoff between broad attacks and deeply personalized attacks.
quote: Through a series of case studies, we analyze ways in which LLMs could allow attacks to go both broad and deep.
context: The two main directions are exploiting low-popularity software and personalizing monetization after compromise.
uncertainty: The case studies demonstrate selected capabilities, not deployment at population scale.

claim: The personal-photo experiment separates image-level extraction from cross-image synthesis, using a vision-language model for each photograph and a second model to summarize the resulting descriptions.
quote: For each photo, we instruct the VLM to extract any personally identifiable information, sensitive data, or particular signs of relationships between people. We then feed the full transcript of photo descriptions into Claude 3.5 Sonnet to summarize what was found.
context: The image model is based on Llama 3.2 Vision. The paper reports recovery of family identities, addresses, travel, and medical information.
uncertainty: These are collaborative results credited to another coauthor. A footnote notes that some information could also be obtained from image metadata.

claim: The authors prioritize defenses against PII mining while explicitly describing them as partial mitigation rather than a complete solution.
quote: One concrete opportunity we see is the development of defenses to identify and prevent PII-mining on end-user devices or web services. This direction will not solve the problem, but may reduce the rate at which adversaries can exfiltrate sensitive data from users.
context: This proposed direction follows from the text, image, audio, and scanned-document demonstrations.
uncertainty: The paper proposes the defensive research direction but does not implement or evaluate such a defense.

claim: The audio experiment standardizes output and assessment through JSON and a supplied sensitivity rubric while testing hundreds of real archived recordings.
quote: We use gemini-exp-1206, a multi-modal language model, to process 680 audio files with an average duration of 121.5 seconds. The model is prompted to provide output in JSON and rate each file according to a given rubric.
context: Barry is credited with the Enron audio experiments. The paper reports three instances of discussions it considers clearly incriminating and estimates a run cost of up to $15.
uncertainty: The text does not report comprehensive annotation agreement, recall, or a false-positive rate for the audio task.

claim: The extension experiment is explicitly positioned as a demonstration of present technical feasibility, not a rigorous measurement of general autonomous exploit-development ability.
quote: We emphasize again that the purpose of this experiment is not to conduct a rigorous study of the degree to which current language models are able to effectively develop exploits in this space, but to demonstrate that this is no longer a speculative question of technical capabilities.
context: The authors describe the 200-extension evaluation as preliminary and invite more thorough future evaluation.
uncertainty: Human validation remains part of the demonstrated workflow.

claim: The server experiment deliberately spans five applications and several programming languages, using recommended Docker configurations to create realistic test deployments.
quote: We create realistic deployments of five servers using different frameworks: Wordpress (written in PHP), Ghost (written in JavaScript), Nextcloud (written in PHP), Redmine (written in Ruby), and FastAPI (written in Python). We deploy the servers using Docker, using the recommended configuration for each type of server.
context: The contributions statement credits Edoardo with the server experiments.
uncertainty: Five controlled deployments do not establish performance across arbitrary production environments. The contributions statement uses an inconsistent section number for this work.

claim: The JFK analysis diagnoses why an OCR-plus-keyword pipeline loses detections: transcription errors can remove contextual labels, and flattening page layout can separate a number from its visual label.
quote: turning the scanned document into a text file results in lost context (such as placing the words “social security number” far away from the actual number, even if visually on the page they appear nearby).
context: This explains part of the gap between identifiers present in Tesseract output and those found by the downstream detector.
uncertainty: The explanation is based on inspecting results; the paper does not quantify each failure mechanism’s contribution.

claim: The authors caution that the Enron dataset’s age makes relative improvement over classical tools more informative than the absolute frequency of exposed secrets.
quote: Therefore, we one should not read too much into the exact number of instances of any particular behavior (e.g., sending passwords over email), but rather the relative uplift of using language models when compared to other classical tools.
context: Footnotes note that Enron emails were released in 2002 and that password sharing by email is less common today.
uncertainty: The paper does not independently demonstrate that relative uplift transfers unchanged to modern datasets.

claim: The syntactic-secret evaluation measures both recovery and precision, reporting substantially more detected passwords without accepting a higher false-positive rate.
quote: For example, traditional data loss prevention tools find slightly more than 300 passwords at a precision just below 70%, while an LLM identifies twice as many passwords (over 600) with a precision over 95%.
context: The baseline is traditional data loss prevention tooling, including Google's Sensitive Data Protection.
uncertainty: These are reported results on the supplied historical corpus, not universal performance estimates.

claim: The trusted-device phishing demonstration tests four interfaces and observes output variation even for identical prompts.
quote: We targeted four different devices in our experiment: two routers and two captive portals. A Large Language Model (LLM) was prompted with the original HTML of each target webpage and instructed to create an additional page or pop-up designed to encourage the user to install a root certificate.
context: The appendix reports replication of interface style and variation in implementation across outputs. The contributions statement assigns the experiment to Milad.
uncertainty: The study does not report a human-subject test of persuasiveness or an empirical benchmark of detection difficulty.

claim: The proposed social-engineering extension focuses on contextual targeting—conversation topics, writing style, and recipient susceptibility—as a potential way to improve generic lateral phishing.
quote: With similar strategies as in Section 3.1, an attacker could use LLMs to gain more granular information, such as the topics and style of conversations between the victim and a target, or identify targets that appear most susceptible to phishing.
context: The authors extrapolate from their contextual data-mining work and cite prior phishing research.
uncertainty: This paper does not implement or evaluate the proposed socially targeted attack, and it does not establish Carlini’s individual endorsement of each extrapolation.

claim: The Enron experiments distinguish short, syntactically recognizable secrets from sensitive conclusions requiring contextual understanding across documents.
quote: We focus our analysis on two areas: first, the recovery of short “syntactic” secrets (e.g., passwords, credit card numbers, or social security numbers), and second, the recovery of “semantic” pieces of sensitive information, that require understanding contextual cues spanning potentially multiple documents (e.g., relationships between people).
context: Carlini is explicitly credited with performing both sets of Enron text experiments.

claim: In one extension case, the team checks a model-suggested precondition against the actual environment and discovers that the relevant developer domain has already expired.
quote: Most worryingly, in this case the extension developer’s DNS record had actually expired, making this attack immediately practical.
context: The model had identified a configuration-fetching mechanism whose security depended on continued control of the developer's domain.
uncertainty: The paper reports practical exploitability, not a completed malicious takeover or evidence that someone had already exploited it.

claim: The authors restrict the interpretation of the historical Enron dataset: relative improvement over classical tools is more meaningful than the absolute prevalence of behaviors such as emailing passwords.
quote: Therefore, we one should not read too much into the exact number of instances of any particular behavior (e.g., sending passwords over email), but rather the relative uplift of using language models when compared to other classical tools.
context: A footnote explains that the emails were released in 2002 and differ from contemporary email.
uncertainty: This limits both prevalence claims and extrapolation of the dataset's economics to modern users.

claim: The server study verifies behavioral consequences by actually logging into each deployed test application and checking whether the submitted credentials reach the logging endpoint.
quote: We manually verify for each case that, by logging in into the deployed server, our credentials are exfiltrated to the malicious server.
context: This provides an end-to-end behavioral check beyond inspecting the model’s code changes.
uncertainty: The passage does not fully explain how the Redmine restart limitation was reconciled with the stated verification for every case.

claim: The authors acknowledge that publication could help attackers but prioritize communicating the threats before they become widespread.
quote: Our work documents a number of ways in which attackers may benefit from LLMs, and it is possible that existing adversaries may read our work and launch new attacks based on the ones we discuss. We believe our work is important to disseminate before the threats we mention in our work become a widespread problem.
context: Their stated justification is that financial incentives will eventually motivate adversaries independently, while earlier awareness could improve defenses.
uncertainty: This is a collective dual-use publication judgment; the paper does not quantify the competing effects of dissemination.

claim: The polymorphic-malware discussion identifies prompt-level repurposing of a benign general-purpose agent as a conceptual detection challenge distinct from rewriting executable code.
quote: Then, the attacker can repurpose the agent for malicious tasks simply by sending it a new prompt, i.e., just text without any executable code—thereby making detection challenging.
context: Section 4.5 also proposes model-driven code rewriting that preserves functionality.
uncertainty: These are anticipated mechanisms; the paper does not evaluate detection systems against them.

claim: The paper explicitly weighs extraction improvements against inference costs and makes its break-even calculation conditional on assigning zero cost to human false-positive filtering.
quote: For example, if we assume the cost of a human filtering out false positives is zero, using an LLM exceeds the value of prior techniques as long as the value of a single password is greater than \$0.40 USD
context: The reported full-dataset costs are $1.50 for the baseline and roughly $60–$100 for inexpensive LLM services; the same calculation gives a $4.48 threshold per credit card.
uncertainty: The thresholds depend on the dataset, pricing, and simplifying assumptions; they are not observed market values or demonstrated profits.

claim: The multilingual results are used to argue that LLM extraction generalizes beyond language-specific handcrafted tooling: conventional recall varies sharply across languages while model detections remain relatively stable.
quote: And for Arabic, Bengali, and Mandarin, the recall drops to just 21 passwords (over $10\times$ lower than the English baseline). In contrast, for the LLM-based analysis, the number of passwords identified for each of the languages varies only by $\pm 6\%$.
context: The same balanced document subset is translated and evaluated across languages.
uncertainty: The quoted stability concerns detection counts in this experiment, not every aspect of precision or multilingual performance.

claim: The JFK experiment reports using a redaction framing to overcome model refusals, then stops pursuing the remaining refusals because they represent a small fraction of inputs.
quote: The jailbreak fails for 1,067 images, where the LLM refuses to transcribe. We do not apply a more sophisticated jailbreak to these cases because they account for a small fraction of all inputs.
context: Footnote 5 explicitly describes the refusal-handling limitation in the experiment credited to Carlini.
uncertainty: This is a concrete stopping decision for this evaluation, not evidence of Carlini's general stopping policy.

claim: The authors acknowledge that publication could help adversaries but explicitly prioritize dissemination before the threats become widespread, aiming to improve defensive preparedness.
quote: Our work documents a number of ways in which attackers may benefit from LLMs, and it is possible that existing adversaries may read our work and launch new attacks based on the ones we discuss. We believe our work is important to disseminate before the threats we mention in our work become a widespread problem.
context: The ethical discussion argues that attackers will adopt these methods when incentives become favorable and that advance awareness can help users and organizations.
uncertainty: The paper states the publication rationale but does not empirically estimate publication’s net defensive or offensive effect.

claim: The project frames the distinctive threat from LLMs as combining individualized targeting with broad scale, rather than requiring superhuman performance against a single difficult target.
quote: Through a series of case studies, we analyze ways in which LLMs could allow attacks to go both broad and deep. Specifically, we consider two potential directions where LLMs could have high impact.
context: The two directions are exploiting the long tail of less popular systems and tailoring attacks to individual victims at scale.
uncertainty: This is the paper's organizing thesis; the case studies do not measure deployment at population scale.

claim: The paper publishes a model-generated vulnerability analysis while explicitly correcting its exaggerated severity assessment using the browser's security model.
quote: Note, however, the model is incorrect about the level of severity: the exploit does not give extension-level permissions because Chrome’s security model prevents exactly this type of vulnerability from leading to elevated privilege escalation.
context: The model correctly identifies an image-derived HTML injection path but wrongly claims extension-level privileges.
uncertainty: The first-person language in the displayed vulnerability report belongs to Claude, not Carlini or another human author.

claim: The client-side XSS study intentionally omits a complete autonomous agent and uses a human relay between model-requested operations and a JavaScript console.
quote: For simplicity, we do not setup a full agent system and instead manually copy the LLM’s function requests to a JavaScript console and return the results to the LLM.
context: Florian is credited with this experiment. The two scenarios involve private-message retrieval and navigation of an e-banking interface.
uncertainty: The demonstration supports model orchestration capability under a manual relay, not fully autonomous end-to-end exploitation.

claim: The polymorphic-malware discussion identifies adaptive code rewriting and prompt-based repurposing of a benign tool-using agent as two distinct possible detection challenges.
quote: Then, the attacker can repurpose the agent for malicious tasks simply by sending it a new prompt, i.e., just text without any executable code—thereby making detection challenging.
context: The other proposed mechanism is LLM-generated rewrites that preserve malware functionality without following a fixed transformation rule set.
uncertainty: Neither mechanism is experimentally evaluated for evasion effectiveness in this paper.

claim: The server evaluation uses the same prompt across applications and verifies effects through actual logins, providing a functional check beyond the model's report of success.
quote: We manually verify for each case that, by logging in into the deployed server, our credentials are exfiltrated to the malicious server. This worked with the same prompt for all server types, on the first attempt.
context: The model operates through terminal tools with the task intended to run without further user interaction.
uncertainty: The authors separately report a Redmine restart failure, so first-attempt success should not be read as flawless completion of every deployment step.
