claim: The authors connect simplicity to explanatory power in debugging: a failed simple method narrows the set of possible causes, whereas failure of a complex method requires testing multiple competing explanations.
quote: When simple techniques do not work as expected, it is easy to learn the correct lesson for why they failed. In contrast, when complex techniques do not work as expected, one has to consider multiple hypotheses and evaluate each one to understand the true reason for failure.
context: This rationale follows the successful interpolation-and-binary-search attack on Turning a Weakness into a Strength.
uncertainty: The statement is a methodological generalization from the team’s experience, not an experimentally quantified comparison of debugging approaches.

claim: The collaborators judged evaluation breadth by diversity of attack mechanisms rather than the number of named attacks.
quote: However, BIM (Kurakin et al., 2016), PGD (Madry et al., 2017) and MIM (Dong et al., 2018) are extremely similar and if one of these attacks fails the others are likely to fail as well.
context: In the Ensemble Diversity case, they recommended adding substantively different score-based or boundary-based attacks instead of relying on several closely related gradient methods.
uncertainty: This is a methodological judgment about correlated failure modes, not a claim that the listed algorithms always produce identical outcomes.

claim: The study’s success criterion was demonstrating shortcomings in original robustness evaluations, not necessarily reducing every defense to zero accuracy or declaring its underlying technique worthless.
quote: Importantly, we do not wish to claim that the robustness techniques used by many of these defenses hold no merit whatsoever. It may well be that some instantiations of these techniques can improve model robustness.
context: The introduction says the goal is to show that stronger adaptive attacks can degrade reported accuracy; the methodology allows that better-supported instantiations of the same ideas could be useful.
uncertainty: The paper evaluates particular implementations and threat models, not every possible version of each defense concept.

claim: For the sparse Fourier defense, the team differentiated through the entire preprocessing-and-classification pipeline and deliberately traded some attack strength for a tenfold speed gain.
quote: Instead of running a multi-targeted attack we run the attack in an untargeted manner, resulting in a larger distortion than we could otherwise achieve but $10\times$ faster and mirroring the original evaluation.
context: Using the supplied defense code, they implemented differentiable preprocessing and applied the existing C&W l0 attack without further modification. Median successful distortion was 14.8 pixels, close to the cited undefended baseline.
uncertainty: The speed-versus-distortion tradeoff was chosen for this evaluation; the paper does not quantify the distortion a stronger multi-targeted version would achieve.

claim: The team evaluated defenses within their claimed threat models and generally chose untargeted objectives to make the tutorial relevant to future defense evaluations.
quote: as such, we choose the untargeted attack objective that future defense creators will typically choose.
context: Footnotes describe matching each defense’s claimed perturbation model; the speech evaluation was an explicitly justified targeted exception.
uncertainty: A multi-targeted optimization procedure can still serve an overall untargeted evaluation objective.

claim: For The Odds are Odd, the team decomposed the detection statistic into noise sensitivity and confidence contributions, identifying why different standard attacks triggered different parts of the detector.
quote: Thus, a successful attack will be one that finds adversarial examples for which: (1) the model’s robustness to noise is no smaller than for an average benign example; and (2) the model’s confidence is no larger than for an average benign example.
context: This analysis motivated matching a benign example’s logits rather than maximizing ordinary classification confidence.

claim: The ensemble-diversity evaluation tested convergence empirically by increasing step size and iteration count, and stopped extending the iteration budget when additional iterations no longer changed the result.
quote: Increasing the number of iterations to 50 decreases the accuracy to 20% while 250 iterations reduced the accuracy to 10%. A further increase did not change the result, suggesting that 250 iterations are sufficient for convergence.
context: Before increasing iterations, tripling the step size had already reduced reported accuracy from 48% to 26%.
uncertainty: The plateau suggested convergence for this attack configuration; it did not establish global optimality.

claim: The paper discouraged treating its successful attacks as reusable evaluation templates; prior attacks were framed as sanity checks, with the main effort directed toward finding each new defense’s particular weaknesses.
quote: Yet, we urge the community to refrain from using these adaptive attacks as templates to be copied in future evaluations.
context: The conclusion argued that a nonrobust defense can be designed to defeat any particular fixed attack and criticized reliance on automated attack suites alone.
uncertainty: This is the authors’ 2020 position; the supplied material does not establish Carlini’s current view of later automated evaluation methods.

claim: Randomized testing uncovered a different failure than expected in the generative classifier: repeated classification of an unchanged clean input could eventually induce an error because of estimator variance.
quote: the success of our random attack is not due to the model’s lack of noise-robustness, but to the high variance in the model’s estimate of the $\texttt{score}_{i}$ values.
context: After ineffective increases in PGD iterations and sample counts, random perturbations with many restarts worked. Further investigation found a 5–10% misclassification probability even when repeatedly submitting an unperturbed test input.
uncertainty: This describes a revision of the team’s explanation within one investigation, not a longitudinal change in Carlini’s views.

claim: The robust sparse Fourier transform evaluation demonstrated the need to attack preprocessing and classification jointly; implementing the existing preprocessing in a differentiable framework allowed an otherwise unchanged attack.
quote: To begin we implement this defense as a differentiable pre-processor in front of the neural network classifier (using code provided by the authors).
context: The original evaluation had shown that preprocessing removed examples generated against the base classifier, without adapting the attack to preprocessing.

claim: The team adopts a conditional simplicity rule: begin with straightforward gradient descent and an appropriate loss, adding complexity only after simpler attacks fail because simple failures are easier to diagnose.
quote: In all cases, our attack is as close as possible to straightforward gradient descent with an appropriate loss function; we add additional complexity only when simpler attacks fail. It is easier to diagnose failures of simpler attacks, in order to iterate towards a stronger attack.
context: This is the paper’s overarching attack-development theme, illustrated across multiple defenses.
uncertainty: The principle is explicitly collaborative and scoped to the evaluations in this paper.

claim: They preserved successful intermediate iterates rather than judging PGD only by its final step, combining this with targeting and restarts to strengthen the error-correcting-code attack.
quote: Finally, if any inner iteration of PGD succeeds at generating an adversarial example we take this; we don’t require that the final output of PGD after exactly 100 steps is an adversarial example.
context: They targeted all nine incorrect labels and ran five randomized starts per target, bringing reported accuracy below 5% compared with the original 57% claim.

claim: To attack random audio-prefix selection, the team optimized three fixed prefix lengths simultaneously and empirically checked whether this transferred to intermediate lengths.
quote: In order to ensure that our adversarial examples remain effective under random choices of the prefix length $k$ we run our attack by, in parallel, ensuring that the attack is successful with $k=.25$, $k=.5$ and $k=.75$ all simultaneously.
context: The following sentence explicitly distinguishes their hope that intermediate values would work from their empirical observation that they did.
uncertainty: Success at three optimized lengths does not mathematically guarantee success at every intermediate length.

claim: For the sparse Fourier defense, the team explicitly traded attack optimality for speed and comparability, choosing an untargeted attack that was ten times faster and mirrored the original evaluation.
quote: Instead of running a multi-targeted attack we run the attack in an untargeted manner, resulting in a larger distortion than we could otherwise achieve but $10\times$ faster and mirroring the original evaluation.
context: The resulting median perturbation of 14.8 pixels was approximately the reported undefended-model baseline.
uncertainty: The experiment was not intended to establish the smallest possible adversarial distortion.

claim: For the integrated asymmetrical-training defense, the team fixed a target class and stopped spending perturbation budget on classifier confidence once the required misclassification had been achieved.
quote: We stop the optimization on the base classifier $f$ once a targeted misclassification is achieved since the confidence of $f$ is not considered by the defense.
context: The attack then optimized the corresponding detector and repeated this procedure for every incorrect target class. At a 5% false-positive rate, reported robust accuracy fell from 30% to 11%.

claim: For the sparse Fourier defense, the team made the preprocessing differentiable and attacked the combined function. It deliberately chose an untargeted attack to gain speed and match the original evaluation, accepting larger perturbations than a multi-targeted attack might achieve.
quote: Instead of running a multi-targeted attack we run the attack in an untargeted manner, resulting in a larger distortion than we could otherwise achieve but $10\times$ faster and mirroring the original evaluation.
context: The resulting median distortion was 14.8 pixels, comparable to the cited 15-pixel result on an undefended model.
uncertainty: The comparison is to a reported baseline, not proof that the defense and baseline have identical worst-case robustness.

claim: When repeated PGD left a resistant subset of ensemble-diversity examples, the team switched to a boundary-following attack with a different search geometry instead of only extending PGD.
quote: The remaining samples seemed to be difficult for PGD, which is why we chose the $\ell_{\infty}$ version of the B&B attack (Brendel et al., 2019).
context: Three PGD repetitions reduced accuracy to 7%. The team initialized B&B from larger-perturbation adversarial examples; B&B and repetitions on remaining samples eventually reduced accuracy to 0%.

claim: For speech, the team chose targeted transcription attacks because untargeted errors could be mere misspellings, and reported required distortion rather than unbounded attack success rate.
quote: First, we perform a targeted attack here: untargeted attacks are uninteresting on audio classification because they typically just induce misspellings.
context: Both target transcription and detector evasion reached 100%; median distortion was 46 for the defended model versus 41 for the baseline on a 16-bit scale.
uncertainty: The dismissal of untargeted attacks is the authors’ judgment for this evaluation, not a universal statement about speech-system risk.

claim: ME-Net supplied a documented failed refinement: after finding that preprocessing did not closely approximate the original image, the team differentiated through the random mask and restricted BPDA to reconstruction, but attack strength did not improve.
quote: We thus tried to apply BPDA only to the USVT procedure, and backpropagate through the random mask. However, this attack did not improve upon the $15\%$ accuracy we reached when applying BPDA to the full pre-processing step
context: The team found that USVT output was roughly identical to the randomly masked image rather than a close reconstruction of the original input.
uncertainty: Failure of this particular refinement does not establish that all better gradient approximations would fail.

claim: The team distinguishes the number of evaluated attacks from their methodological diversity, warning that closely related attacks may fail together and provide little additional evidence.
quote: The paper’s results section might impress with the large number of attacks employed against the ensemble model. However, BIM (Kurakin et al., 2016), PGD (Madry et al., 2017) and MIM (Dong et al., 2018) are extremely similar and if one of these attacks fails the others are likely to fail as well.
context: In the ensemble-diversity evaluation, they recommended including substantially different score-based or boundary-following strategies.
uncertainty: This is a critique of evidential redundancy, not a claim that these attacks always produce identical results.

claim: They limited the scope of BPDA as an attack tool, warning that it cannot simply make arbitrary nondifferentiable objectives optimizable.
quote: BPDA should not be treated as a general-purpose method for minimizing through arbitrarily non-differentiable functions. Rather, loss functions must be designed to work with BPDA and must already be almost differentiable.
context: This lesson followed a detector whose original adaptive evaluation combined four difficult loss terms and used BPDA on terms involving internal attack steps.
uncertainty: The passage is methodological guidance; it does not supply a formal definition of almost differentiable.

claim: The error-correcting-code investigation used implausibly high accuracy at extreme perturbation size as a warning, then traced the likely optimization problem to a numerically unstable chain of sigmoid, logarithm, softmax, and another logarithm.
quote: However, after this, to compute the unified predictions, the implementation takes the $\log$ of the result and then feeds this into the softmax function. Finally, to generate adversarial examples with the cross-entropy loss, another $\log$ is required. This is exceptionally numerically unstable and we suspected it was the cause of the gradient problems.
context: The team simplified the attack computation and replaced cross entropy with a hinge loss before further strengthening the attack.
uncertainty: The passage identifies a suspected causal explanation supported by the subsequent attack changes.

claim: The team tested component importance rather than assuming all terms in the generative classifier mattered equally; comparing class scores identified the cross-entropy component as the dominant attack target.
quote: We found that $L_{\text{CE}}$ is the only important term. The other terms vary little across class scores.
context: Targeting this component while increasing latent sampling during attack generation reduced classifier accuracy below 5% on both tested datasets.
uncertainty: The importance claim concerns the evaluated implementation and observed score contributions.

claim: For Turning a Weakness into a Strength, they intentionally explored a new adaptive construction rather than reuse the feature-matching approach already demonstrated on a related detector.
quote: However, in this section we aim to mount a new type of adaptive attack. We set out to directly construct an input with properties (a) and (b) above, by initially generating an adversarial example with high confidence and then slowly moving it towards the decision boundary.
context: The desired input needed to remain stable under random noise while lying sufficiently close to an adversarial decision boundary. They interpolated between a clean input and a high-confidence adversarial example.
uncertainty: Feature matching was an acknowledged alternative, not an experimentally rejected one in this case.

claim: The Max-Mahalanobis investigation used an analogy with defensive distillation to generate a first intervention, then treated its partial success as insufficient and pursued a better-matched objective.
quote: A simple method for breaking distillation is to simply divide the logits by a large constant Carlini & Wagner (2016); however when we tried this it was not sufficient to break the defense completely
context: The model had an unusually large separation between its largest and remaining logits. Rescaling reduced CIFAR-10 accuracy from 24% to 18%, motivating further loss redesign.
uncertainty: The quote describes a tested analogy and partial result, not a claim that the two defenses fail identically.

claim: They tested objective consistency using a counterexample: increasing all detector scores equally can maximize the proposed generative-classifier attack objective without changing the predicted class.
quote: For example, one way to maximize this loss function is to increase each detectors’ score by the same value, thereby leaving the classifier’s prediction unchanged.
context: The original attack maximized the highest non-true-class detector score but did not ensure it overtook the true-class score. A related mismatch in the integrated classifier wasted effort on detectors other than the currently predicted class.
uncertainty: This is a logical failure possibility establishing objective mismatch, not a claim that every optimization run followed that exact trajectory.

claim: The team presented its evaluation narratives as records of the actual order of discovery, explicitly rejecting retrospective reconstruction of a cleaner reasoning path.
quote: The flow of each section directly mirrors the steps we actually took to evaluate the robustness of the defense, without retroactively drawing conclusions on how we wish we had discovered the flaws.
context: The paper’s tutorial structure was intended to make future evaluations reproducible as a process.
uncertainty: The supplied corpus contains the authors’ narrative, not independent records of the chronology.

claim: While checking their own ME-Net attack for bugs, the team ablated preprocessing and discovered nontrivial robustness in the base classifier. This supported part of the defense authors’ intuition despite the weakened overall robustness claim.
quote: Taking a step back (and while trying to find bugs in our own attack implementation), we attempted to attack solely the trained classifier (a ResNet-18), without the pre-processing stage. Surprisingly, we found the base classifier to be moderately robust:
context: They could not reduce the base classifier below 10% accuracy and found interpretable gradients. They interpreted these observations as support for robustness learned from masked and reconstructed training inputs.
uncertainty: The evidence was empirical; the paper explicitly leaves open whether a stronger attack could further reduce base-classifier accuracy.

claim: The asymmetrical-training analysis rejects objectives that can improve without changing the relevant decision. It uses a concrete counterexample to show why maximizing a wrong-class detector score alone is insufficient.
quote: The issue is that even with an unbounded perturbation, maximizing this loss may fail to produce a successful attack. For example, one way to maximize this loss function is to increase each detectors’ score by the same value, thereby leaving the classifier’s prediction unchanged.
context: This criticism concerns the generative classifier’s proposed adaptive loss and motivates optimizing relative detector scores before increasing target confidence.

claim: The team explicitly considered the dual-use risk of publishing attack methodology and judged the expected benefit to defense researchers to outweigh possible assistance to malicious actors.
quote: we firmly believe that the help that our paper can provide to researchers designing new defenses significantly outweighs the help that it may provide an actual malicious actor.
context: The broader-impact discussion paired this judgment with advance notification and a stated focus on evaluating research defenses rather than attacking real users.
uncertainty: This is a normative risk-benefit assessment, not a measured downstream impact.

claim: The team bounded the objective around demonstrating shortcomings in existing evaluations, rather than requiring every attacked model’s accuracy to reach zero.
quote: Instead, we want to demonstrate that the existing adaptive attack evaluation methodology has shortcomings, and that stronger adaptive attacks can (at least partially) degrade each defense’s accuracy from what is reported in the original evaluations.
context: This objective helps explain why several evaluations stop with residual accuracy once the original robustness claim has been materially weakened.
uncertainty: A successful reduction in reported accuracy does not establish that the final attack measures the defense’s exact worst-case robustness.

claim: The EMPIR evaluation deliberately tested a simple but inconsistent surrogate before investing in a more principled objective, demonstrating that their consistency guidance was not treated as an inflexible prerequisite.
quote: Notice that this loss function is not consistent, violating one of our lessons: because the classifier takes the majority vote in order to decide the final prediction, only two of the classifiers must agree on the target class; the third model could have $0$ confidence.
context: They averaged the three models’ probability vectors and attacked the average with cross-entropy. Despite the mismatch to majority voting, 100 PGD iterations reduced accuracy to 1.5%, so a stronger loss was not required for their demonstrated break.
uncertainty: They explicitly left open whether a consistent objective could reduce accuracy further.

claim: While searching for bugs in their ME-Net attack, they ablated preprocessing and discovered evidence supporting part of the defense authors’ intuition.
quote: Taking a step back (and while trying to find bugs in our own attack implementation), we attempted to attack solely the trained classifier (a ResNet-18), without the pre-processing stage.
context: They could not reduce the base classifier below 10% accuracy and observed interpretable gradients. They interpreted this as support for the possibility that training on masked and reconstructed images teaches somewhat more robust representations.
uncertainty: Residual accuracy and interpretability were suggestive empirical evidence, not certified robustness or a definitive causal explanation.

claim: Although the team initially suspected that separately weighting the audio classifier and detector losses might be necessary, it first implemented the original single-weight approach and reserved the additional hyperparameter for demonstrated need.
quote: We implemented the attack as described in the paper, beginning with just one hyper-parameter $\lambda$—we only wanted to introduce a new hyper-parameter if it turned out to be necessary.
context: The final approach coordinated the full and prefix transcriptions around the desired target phrase and reduced distortion only after both classification and detection objectives were satisfied.

claim: The paper identifies weak training-time attacks as a second failure mode of inadequate adaptive evaluation: they can make a defense combined with adversarial training less robust than adversarial training alone.
quote: This reveals another failure mode of weak adaptive attacks: if the attack used for training fails to reliably find adversarial examples, the model will not resist stronger attacks.
context: The k-Winners Take All and ME-Net evaluations both reported combined defenses performing worse than relevant adversarial-training baselines.
uncertainty: The ME-Net section describes weak training attacks as the probable explanation, rather than establishing that causal mechanism through a controlled retraining experiment.

claim: While debugging their own ME-Net attack, the authors ablated preprocessing and discovered meaningful residual robustness in the base classifier, giving qualified support to the defense authors’ representation-learning intuition.
quote: This gives credence to the authors’ intuition that training on randomly masked and reconstructed images can encourage a model to learn somewhat more robust representations.
context: They could not reduce the isolated classifier below 10% accuracy and observed interpretable gradients.
uncertainty: The authors treated these observations as supporting evidence, not a proof of robustness or a settled explanation of its cause.

claim: They simplified the error-correcting ensemble’s attack computation by removing final sigmoid and logarithm operations and using a hinge loss to reduce numerical instability.
quote: In order to be more robust to further numerical instabilities, we replace the standard softmax cross entropy with the hinge loss proposed by (Carlini & Wagner, 2017b).
context: This initial revised attack reduced CIFAR-10 accuracy below 20% at distortion 0.031, but did not reduce it to zero.
uncertainty: The modifications describe attack construction, not retraining the defended ensemble.

claim: They treated attack quality as a requirement for training as well as evaluation: an ineffective adaptive training attack can leave a combined defense weaker than adversarial training alone.
quote: This reveals another failure mode of weak adaptive attacks: if the attack used for training fails to reliably find adversarial examples, the model will not resist stronger attacks.
context: The paper connects this concern to combined defenses including k-WTA and ME-Net, where their stronger attacks yielded worse robustness than the relevant adversarial-training baselines.
uncertainty: The examples demonstrate weaker evaluated robustness; the precise causal contribution of training-attack weakness is not isolated experimentally in every case.

claim: The team interpreted the failures it found primarily as methodological shortcomings: existing attack tools were sufficient when used appropriately.
quote: A better attack can be built using only tools that are well-known in the literature. Thus, the issue with current defense evaluations is methodological rather than technical.
context: Assessment of the thirteen evaluations studied, contrasted with earlier work that required new attack techniques.
uncertainty: This conclusion concerns the studied defenses and does not establish that all robustness evaluation problems lack technical barriers.

claim: The team justified stopping with residual robustness in the asymmetrical-training models through converging empirical checks, while explicitly acknowledging that the evaluation was not a certificate.
quote: As this defense is not certified, our evaluation will ultimately always be empirical. We believe it unlikely we can significantly reduce the defense’s accuracy further due to the following:
context: Their reasons included simple defenses and attacks, interpretability evidence, and only one additional percentage point of accuracy reduction after increasing PGD to 200 iterations and ten restarts.
uncertainty: These checks support confidence in attack adequacy but do not prove a lower bound on worst-case accuracy.

claim: The authors separated optimization difficulty from objective validity: even perfect optimization can fail if the chosen loss does not track actual attack success.
quote: the chosen loss function is not actually a good proxy for attack success. That is, even with an all-powerful optimizer that is guaranteed to find the loss’ optimum, an attack may fail.
context: The recurring theme of constructing consistent losses.

claim: For the centroid-based defense, they replaced indirect cross-entropy optimization with direct movement of the feature representation toward each incorrect class centroid.
quote: Instead of indirectly performing softmax cross entropy loss on the distances to $\mu$, we directly target each of the target vectors $\mu$.
context: A multi-targeted squared-distance objective reduced reported CIFAR-10 accuracy below 0.5% at an l-infinity distortion of 0.031.

claim: The paper argues that adaptive evaluation must be tailored to a defense and that even successful published attacks should not become mechanically copied evaluation templates.
quote: Yet, we urge the community to refrain from using these adaptive attacks as templates to be copied in future evaluations.
context: The conclusion treats prior attacks as sanity checks and calls for explicit investigation of each defense’s weak points. It cites partial AutoAttack results and incompatibility with some detector defenses as limitations of automated evaluation.
uncertainty: The broader claim that no automated tool can comprehensively evaluate defenses is the paper’s methodological position, not a theorem established by the supplied experiments.

claim: The team explicitly retained all initially selected defenses, including cases later found to fail similarly, to avoid selecting reported evaluations based on their outcomes.
quote: This report contains our evaluations for all of our initially selected defenses. In particular, we did not cherry-pick the defense evaluations to present based on the results of our evaluation.
context: Footnote 6 qualifies the initial goal of selecting conceptually distinct defenses.
uncertainty: This is the authors’ account of selection and reporting; the supplied corpus contains no independent audit.

claim: The generative-classifier attack was simplified by empirically comparing the contributions of its scoring terms and targeting the one that meaningfully distinguished classes.
quote: We found that $L_{\text{CE}}$ is the only important term. The other terms vary little across class scores.
context: The team increased latent-vector sampling during attack generation and used PGD on the cross-entropy scoring term, reducing classification accuracy below 5% on MNIST and CIFAR-10.
uncertainty: The finding applies to the evaluated models and scoring implementation.

claim: The initial interpolation attack used a thousand-point grid, but debugging showed that it could miss a narrow successful interval. Denser sampling diagnosed the issue, while binary search supplied the more efficient final method.
quote: Increasing the number of steps is one possible solution—which we used to diagnose the failure here—but is even slower.
context: Some successful interpolation coefficients were below 10^-4, and each grid evaluation invoked a costly detector containing its own PGD loop. The final attack used detector outcomes to guide binary search.
uncertainty: This is the team’s reported diagnosis and algorithm change, not a guarantee that the detector conditions form an ideal monotone search problem.

claim: They distinguished optimization difficulty from objective mismatch: a loss can be easy to optimize yet still fail to represent attack success.
quote: the chosen loss function is not actually a good proxy for attack success. That is, even with an all-powerful optimizer that is guaranteed to find the loss’ optimum, an attack may fail. Such loss functions are not consistent and should be avoided.
context: The paper calls this consistency requirement a deeper issue than merely having a difficult loss surface.

claim: The study deliberately exposed the discovery process, including paper reading, hypotheses, unsuccessful attempts, and eventual attacks, rather than reporting only successful final constructions.
quote: we actually walk the reader through our full process of analyzing each defense, from an initial paper read-through, to our hypotheses about what would be required for the defense to be circumvented, to an ultimately successful attack.
context: The authors suspected that earlier publications’ focus on final attacks left readers without enough guidance to develop new adaptive evaluations.

claim: When further PGD progress became difficult, they switched to a boundary-following attack with a different search geometry rather than only extending the same optimizer.
quote: The remaining samples seemed to be difficult for PGD, which is why we chose the $\ell_{\infty}$ version of the B&B attack (Brendel et al., 2019).
context: They initialized B&B from large-perturbation PGD examples, used 20 B&B steps, and repeated the attack on remaining samples until reported Ensemble Diversity accuracy reached zero.
uncertainty: The attribution of remaining difficulty to PGD is an empirical observation about these samples.

claim: The k-WTA analysis motivated estimating gradients over a larger neighborhood, illustrating their willingness to use direct-query attacks when local analytic gradients are misleading.
quote: We therefore hypothesize that a strong black-box attack that directly queries the target model and estimates the gradients from finite differences over a larger space would be an effective attack on this defense.
context: Their final evaluation averaged local gradient information using 20,000 random perturbations and ran 100 attack steps, reporting 0% accuracy for the vanilla model and 0.16% for its adversarially trained counterpart.
uncertainty: The quoted sentence states the hypothesis; the subsequent evaluation supplies the reported outcomes. The source’s displayed estimator should not be treated as independently checked pseudocode.

claim: The corrected speech attack aligned prefix transcription with the intended target phrase, avoiding conflict with a changing current prediction, and reduced distortion only after both transcription and detector objectives succeeded.
quote: If we try to send $f(x^{\prime}_{\text{pre}})$ towards the current prediction $f(x^{\prime})$ the two loss functions will be in conflict with each other.
context: The attack simultaneously enforced success at three prefix fractions and empirically generalized to intermediate randomized prefix lengths.
uncertainty: Generalization across prefix lengths was empirical rather than formally established.

claim: They selected k-Winners Take All partly because intentional gradient masking challenged a prevailing criticism of that defense strategy.
quote: Because prior work has argued that this form of gradient masking is a fundamental flaw (Athalye et al., 2018a), the existence of such a defense would go against common wisdom.
context: Unlike defenses that accidentally obstruct gradients, k-WTA deliberately introduced discontinuous activations.
uncertainty: This explains why the case was interesting to the team, not proof that every intentionally discontinuous defense must fail.

claim: For the generative-classifier defense, the authors prioritized understanding the implemented computation over fully reconstructing the paper’s theoretical motivation.
quote: This mirrors our own mental model when assessing the robustness of this defense: understanding and evaluating what the implementation does is often more useful than understanding the theoretical or intuitive explanations made in the paper.
context: They presented the classification algorithm implemented in the released code rather than a detailed derivation of the variational-autoencoder theory.
uncertainty: This preference is explicitly tied to robustness assessment and jointly stated.

claim: The error-correcting-code evaluation accumulated several concrete attack refinements: target every incorrect label, repeat each targeted attack from five random starts, and retain successes from intermediate iterations.
quote: Finally, if any inner iteration of PGD succeeds at generating an adversarial example we take this; we don’t require that the final output of PGD after exactly 100 steps is an adversarial example.
context: Together these refinements reduced accuracy below 5%, compared with the original reported 57% at distortion 0.031.
uncertainty: The supplied account does not isolate the contribution of each refinement.

claim: For error-correcting-code ensembles, suspicious robustness at extremely large distortion led them to inspect the implementation and identify a numerically unstable chain of nonlinear operations.
quote: Finally, to generate adversarial examples with the cross-entropy loss, another $\log$ is required. This is exceptionally numerically unstable and we suspected it was the cause of the gradient problems.
context: The implementation applied sigmoid, logarithm, softmax, and another logarithm. The team questioned a reported accuracy near 40% at an l-infinity distortion of 0.5.
uncertainty: The quoted passage states their diagnosis as a suspicion, subsequently investigated by modifying the attack representation.

claim: In The Odds are Odd evaluation, the team decomposed the detector statistic to identify two simultaneous requirements: adversarial examples needed ordinary robustness to noise and ordinary confidence, rather than simply maximizing misclassification confidence.
quote: Thus, a successful attack will be one that finds adversarial examples for which: (1) the model’s robustness to noise is no smaller than for an average benign example; and (2) the model’s confidence is no larger than for an average benign example.
context: Their analysis explained why ordinary PGD, minimal-perturbation C&W attacks, and PGD with expectation over transformation each left a detectable statistical signature.
uncertainty: These requirements arise from this detector’s statistic, not a universal characterization of successful adversarial examples.

claim: A surprisingly effective random attack prompted the team to test repeated classification of unchanged inputs, revealing that part of the apparent attack success came from the generative model’s own sampling variance.
quote: The defense is thus vulnerable to a “trivial” attack that continuously submits the same input until the model misclassifies it by chance. This can be fixed by increasing the number $N$ of sampled latent vectors, at a cost of more expensive inference.
context: The model misclassified unperturbed test inputs with a reported 5–10% probability across repeated evaluations.
uncertainty: The authors then sought adversarial examples that remained effective beyond this stochastic failure mode.

claim: They established a practical convergence point for the Ensemble Diversity attack by increasing step size and iteration count until further iterations no longer changed the result.
quote: Increasing the number of iterations to 50 decreases the accuracy to 20% while 250 iterations reduced the accuracy to 10%. A further increase did not change the result, suggesting that 250 iterations are sufficient for convergence.
context: Starting from the authors’ evaluation code and weights, tripling step size first reduced accuracy from 48% to 26%. Repeating the 250-step attack three times then reduced it to 7%.
uncertainty: Observed stability supports practical convergence for that attack configuration, not a proof of globally optimal perturbations.

claim: The team used a simplicity-first escalation rule: start near ordinary gradient descent with a suitable objective and add complexity only after simpler attacks fail, partly because simple failures are easier to diagnose.
quote: In all cases, our attack is as close as possible to straightforward gradient descent with an appropriate loss function; we add additional complexity only when simpler attacks fail. It is easier to diagnose failures of simpler attacks, in order to iterate towards a stronger attack.
context: The paper’s overarching attack-design principle.
uncertainty: This is a jointly stated methodological rule.

claim: A random-perturbation experiment on the generative classifier led the team to distinguish vulnerability to input noise from instability in the classifier’s own stochastic computation.
quote: the success of our random attack is not due to the model’s lack of noise-robustness, but to the high variance in the model’s estimate of the $\texttt{score}_{i}$ values.
context: Repeatedly classifying the same clean input produced a 5–10% misclassification probability, revealing that repeated submission alone could eventually cause an error. They then sought adversarial examples robust to the model’s randomness.
uncertainty: This is a local experimental reinterpretation, not evidence of a broader change in Carlini’s views.

claim: The Ensemble Diversity evaluation used step-size and iteration sweeps to test convergence rather than treating an initial PGD configuration as definitive.
quote: Increasing the number of iterations to 50 decreases the accuracy to 20% while 250 iterations reduced the accuracy to 10%. A further increase did not change the result, suggesting that 250 iterations are sufficient for convergence.
context: Tripling the step size had already reduced accuracy from 48% to 26%.
uncertainty: A plateau supported convergence of this attack configuration; it did not prove the absence of stronger attacks.

claim: The asymmetrical-training attack stopped increasing base-classifier confidence once a sufficiently stable target prediction was achieved, redirecting optimization toward the detector because further classifier confidence was irrelevant to defense success.
quote: We stop the optimization on the base classifier $f$ once a targeted misclassification is achieved since the confidence of $f$ is not considered by the defense.
context: At a 5% false-positive rate, the integrated classifier’s reported robust accuracy fell from 30% to 11%.

claim: The team combined logit matching with expectation over transformation only after adapting the objective to the detector. This produced attacks that always fooled the classifier while avoiding detection in the reported evaluation.
quote: Crucially, we apply EOT to the logit-matching objective in equation (1), rather than to the standard PGD objective. The resulting attack always fools the classifier maintaining a $0\%$ detection rate; lower than the false positive rate.
context: Logit matching alone had already reduced detection to 17% with one noise source and 10% with ten noise sources; EOT addressed the remaining noise-sensitivity term.
uncertainty: The paper notes that a very similar attack was independently presented by Hosseini and colleagues.

claim: The authors distinguished showing that an evaluation was inadequate from proving that its underlying defense idea had no value; potentially useful techniques still needed strong adaptive evidence.
quote: Importantly, we do not wish to claim that the robustness techniques used by many of these defenses hold no merit whatsoever. It may well be that some instantiations of these techniques can improve model robustness.
context: Explicit limitation on what successful attacks establish.

claim: A failed and expensive direct attack on the generative classifier’s detector led to feature matching, which then revealed an even simpler attack against the upstream VGG representation.
quote: We first directly minimized the KL-divergence, which proved computationally expensive (as it requires optimizing over all class scores) and unsuccessful.
context: Matching decoded logits from another class yielded 99% success against the CIFAR-10 classifier and detector. Matching the input’s VGG features directly to another class’s features then yielded 100% reported success.
uncertainty: This is a documented sequence of attack revisions; it does not establish that feature matching will succeed against every generative classifier.

claim: After breaking the asymmetrical-training evaluation, they proposed a constructive training change: adversarially train the true-class detector as well as incorrect-class detectors.
quote: it does not ensure that the detector for the true class has high confidence on adversarial examples. Adversarially training all detectors for each input might lead to a more robust defense.
context: Their generative-classifier attack reduced robust accuracy from 55% to 37%, prompting examination of whether the training objective omitted a useful constraint.
uncertainty: The proposed improvement is explicitly speculative and was not experimentally validated in the supplied paper.

claim: The paper treats loss-function validity as a separate issue from optimization difficulty: even perfect optimization can fail if the loss does not track actual attack success.
quote: the chosen loss function is not actually a good proxy for attack success. That is, even with an all-powerful optimizer that is guaranteed to find the loss’ optimum, an attack may fail.
context: The consistency theme motivates several redesigned objectives, particularly for detectors and combined defenses.

claim: For Mixup Inference, source inspection resolved conflicting descriptions of the adaptive attack and identified averaging completed perturbations, rather than gradients at each step, as a methodological weakness.
quote: The source code reveals that the first method was used, and that is problematic. Averaging across adversarial perturbations that have each been produced by an ineffective attack is unlikely to lead to much better adversarial examples. A stronger approach would be to average the gradient in each step of the attack.
context: The main text and appendix described different algorithms. The team’s replacement attack differentiated through the full mixing mechanism and resampled mixing images at each step.

claim: For Turning a Weakness into a Strength, the team deliberately explored a different attack construction instead of reusing the already available feature-adversary approach, expanding the paper’s methodological examples.
quote: However, in this section we aim to mount a new type of adaptive attack. We set out to directly construct an input with properties (a) and (b) above, by initially generating an adversarial example with high confidence and then slowly moving it towards the decision boundary.
context: The required properties were robustness to random noise and proximity to a decision boundary under the detector’s attack procedure.
uncertainty: The paper proposes feature adversaries as an alternative but does not report testing that alternative in this section.

claim: When a defense changes the training objective, the team’s first diagnostic hypothesis is that standard cross-entropy attacks may be poorly matched to the resulting loss surface.
quote: In general, whenever a defense changes the loss function used to train a model, our first hypothesis is always that the new model has a loss surface that is not well suited to attacks with the standard softmax cross entropy loss.
context: Applied to the Max-Mahalanobis center loss defense.
uncertainty: This is a jointly stated heuristic, not a guarantee that altered training losses cause evaluation failure.

claim: In the EMPIR evaluation, the team knowingly tested an inconsistent but simple averaged-probability objective before investing in a more faithful majority-vote objective; the simple attack already reduced accuracy to 1.5%.
quote: However, before we spend any extra effort developing a stronger loss function we test this simple loss function.
context: The authors explicitly acknowledge that this choice violates their general recommendation for consistent losses and conclude that the themes are not hard-and-fast rules.
uncertainty: The experiment supports a pragmatic exception, not abandonment of the consistency criterion.

claim: The team contacted defense authors before submission, offered artifacts for independent verification, and released attack code to support reproducibility and further reevaluation.
quote: we contacted all the authors of the defenses we evaluated prior to this submission, and offered to share code or adversarial examples to enable independent verification of our claims.
context: The paper reports acknowledgment of attack effectiveness in twelve cases and no response in one.
uncertainty: Author acknowledgment is reported by the team; the correspondence is not included in the corpus.

claim: The audio evaluation deliberately used targeted transcription attacks and median required distortion, because arbitrary transcription errors and success rates for unbounded attacks would provide weak comparisons.
quote: First, we perform a targeted attack here: untargeted attacks are uninteresting on audio classification because they typically just induce misspellings. Second, because we run an unbounded attack, instead of reporting the success rate at a given distortion bound, we report the median distance to generate a successful perturbation.
context: They achieved the target transcription and detector evasion in every evaluated case, reporting median distortions of 41 for the baseline and 46 for the defended classifier on the stated 16-bit scale.
uncertainty: The judgment that untargeted attacks are uninteresting is specific to the evaluation purpose expressed here.

claim: The final Max-Mahalanobis attack followed the simple inference rule directly: move the feature vector toward each wrong-class target rather than optimize cross-entropy over transformed distances.
quote: Instead of indirectly performing softmax cross entropy loss on the distances to $\mu$, we directly target each of the target vectors $\mu$.
context: The multi-targeted squared-distance objective reduced CIFAR-10 accuracy below 0.5% at the reported distortion of 0.031.

claim: For the integrated asymmetrical-training defense, the team preferred a fixed targeted objective over following whichever incorrect class happened to be predicted, because class switching could discard useful optimization work.
quote: However, we tend to dislike loss functions of this type as work is still wasted if the classifier’s prediction $f(x^{\prime})$ ever switches from some class $i\neq y$ to another class $j\neq y$. Instead, we formulate a targeted attack objective:
context: They attacked each incorrect target class in turn and retained the best result.
uncertainty: The preference is expressed jointly and concerns a particular class of adaptive objectives.

claim: The Odds are Odd attack succeeded by adapting both the objective and the treatment of randomness: applying EOT to logit matching produced complete classifier fooling with zero detection in the reported evaluation.
quote: Crucially, we apply EOT to the logit-matching objective in equation (1), rather than to the standard PGD objective. The resulting attack always fools the classifier maintaining a $0\%$ detection rate; lower than the false positive rate.
context: Logit matching alone had already reduced detection to 17% or 10%, depending on the detector configuration.
uncertainty: These are experimental results for the specified CIFAR-10 defense configurations.

claim: The Mixup evaluation stopped after reducing defended accuracy close to the base model’s accuracy, explicitly citing computational overhead rather than claiming that further attack improvement was impossible.
quote: It is likely that one can further reduce accuracy through additional repetitions or steps, but due to the computational overhead of the Mixup mechanism, we did not perform additional experiments.
context: Fifty PGD steps reduced accuracy to 43.9%, compared with 42.5% for the base model without Mixup.
uncertainty: The amount of remaining reducible accuracy was not measured.

claim: They tested the generative classifier’s component contributions and found that targeting the cross-entropy term alone was enough to produce substantially stronger attacks.
quote: We found that $L_{\text{CE}}$ is the only important term. The other terms vary little across class scores.
context: They compared the four score components across true and incorrect classes, increased latent sampling during attack construction, and reduced classifier accuracy below 5% on both MNIST and CIFAR-10.
uncertainty: The importance claim is empirical and specific to these models. The source inconsistently names the latent-sample-count parameter, so its symbol is not reproduced in the claim.

claim: The ME-Net evaluation first reproduced the original BPDA result and then isolated the effect of accounting for randomness by averaging gradient estimates over forty masks.
quote: We then attempted an attack that combines BPDA with EOT. We approximate the gradient $40$ times with different random masks, and use the average gradient in a PGD attack.
context: Reproduction gave 35% accuracy for USVT and 50% for adversarially trained USVT; adding EOT reduced these to 15% and 32%, respectively.

claim: The paper distinguishes disproving a particular robustness evaluation from dismissing the underlying defensive technique. It leaves open that better instantiations could improve robustness, while requiring strong adaptive evidence for that claim.
quote: Importantly, we do not wish to claim that the robustness techniques used by many of these defenses hold no merit whatsoever. It may well be that some instantiations of these techniques can improve model robustness.
context: The methodology section limits the conclusions that should be drawn from the thirteen re-evaluations.
uncertainty: This qualification does not demonstrate that any particular untested instantiation works.

claim: The collaborators used simplicity as a debugging rule: begin near straightforward gradient descent with an appropriate loss and introduce complexity only after simpler attacks fail.
quote: In all cases, our attack is as close as possible to straightforward gradient descent with an appropriate loss function; we add additional complexity only when simpler attacks fail. It is easier to diagnose failures of simpler attacks, in order to iterate towards a stronger attack.
context: This is the paper’s overarching attack-design theme, illustrated across defenses with complicated internal machinery.
uncertainty: The statement concerns this collaborative evaluation practice and does not establish a universal personal preference across Carlini’s research.

claim: After direct detector optimization proved expensive and unsuccessful, feature attacks led the team to recognize a simpler attack on the generative classifier’s upstream VGG representation, achieving complete success in its CIFAR-10 experiment.
quote: The insight of feature adversaries suggests a much simpler attack we had overlooked.
context: The team first tried minimizing KL divergence, then matching decoded logits, and finally matching the input features supplied to the generative classifier.
uncertainty: This documents a within-project revision, not a long-term change in Carlini’s personal research style.

claim: Defense selection combined a publication filter with conceptual diversity: the team studied defenses accepted at major machine-learning conferences and avoided selecting multiple defenses they initially expected to illustrate the same failure.
quote: We selected each defense with two criteria: (1) it had been accepted at ICLR, ICML, or NeurIPS; indicating that independent reviewers considered it interesting and sound, and (2) it clearly illustrates some concept;
context: Section 3 explains that the team could not evaluate every recently published defense and selected only one when two appeared to share an idea or anticipated failure mode.
uncertainty: This was a purposive sample, not a representative estimate of the prevalence of flawed defenses.

claim: Computational cost constrained their nuclear-norm ME-Net evaluation: they transferred their best existing attack instead of conducting a new adaptive search.
quote: Due to the high computational cost of that defense (the nuclear-norm minimization is CPU-bound and takes about one second per input), we refrained from performing any additional adaptive experiments, and simply used the best attack we found for the USVT model
context: BPDA plus EOT reduced the standard nuclear-norm model to 13% accuracy. They did not evaluate an adversarially trained nuclear-norm model because they could not obtain one and estimated training would require roughly ten CPU years.
uncertainty: This limits the comprehensiveness of the nuclear-norm evaluation; the training-cost figure is the paper’s estimate.

claim: For the MNIST generative classifier, the team fixed the random seed to test whether residual attack failures came from stochastic variance. In that diagnostic setting, it used an explicit early-stop condition requiring detector evasion.
quote: we maximize $L_{\text{CE}}$ for the true class, and stop as soon as we find that the perturbation computed by the current PGD iteration also fools the detector.
context: The original stochastic model yielded adversarial examples with 90% success probability. Deterministic latent sampling preserved the reported model accuracy and enabled 100% attack success.
uncertainty: The 100% result belongs to the modified deterministic diagnostic setting, not the original randomized defense.

claim: In the temporal-dependency audio evaluation, the authors separated a suspected implementation failure from a verified finding and explicitly identified missing attack source code as the limit on confirmation.
quote: There are a number of details here which could have complicated the attack process, however because the authors do not release source code for the attack we are unable to confirm our hypotheses.
context: They suspected interactions in a minimal-distortion attack that repeatedly shrank the allowed perturbation, especially because the original unbounded attack did not always succeed.
uncertainty: The cause of the original audio attack’s failure remained unconfirmed.

claim: For k-Winners Take All, the team used the trajectory of the attack loss as diagnostic evidence. Extending PGD from 40 to 400 steps revealed fluctuations and apparently accidental successes rather than reliable optimization.
quote: We find that over the progression of the attack, the cross-entropy loss exhibits high fluctuations. In fact, adversarial examples were seemingly found by chance and the attack did not reliably decrease the average loss.
context: The team subsequently inspected the local loss landscape and observed plateaus separated by abrupt changes.
uncertainty: The description that examples were found by chance is an interpretation of the observed optimization behavior.

claim: They identified possible implementation-level reasons for a failed audio attack but explicitly withheld confirmation because the original attack code was unavailable.
quote: There are a number of details here which could have complicated the attack process, however because the authors do not release source code for the attack we are unable to confirm our hypotheses.
context: Their suspicion arose because an unbounded attack still failed to fool the detector reliably, and their experience with the original attack framework suggested complications in its distortion-reduction loop.
uncertainty: These proposed causes remained unverified; the defense implementation was available separately.

claim: The team explicitly retained every initially selected defense, including cases later discovered to fail similarly, to avoid selecting reported evaluations based on their outcomes.
quote: This report contains our evaluations for all of our initially selected defenses. In particular, we did not cherry-pick the defense evaluations to present based on the results of our evaluation.
context: A methodology footnote distinguishes their initial conceptual selection criteria from retrospective selection based on attack results.
uncertainty: This is the authors’ report of their selection procedure; the supplied material contains no independent audit.

claim: The team sought verification from affected researchers before publication and offered generated adversarial examples as inspectable evidence.
quote: We notified all authors of our breaks of their defenses before making our paper public. Authors from twelve of the thirteen papers responded to us and verified that our evaluations were accurate (we offered to provide the generated adversarial examples to all authors).
context: The introduction also reports releasing attack code to support reproducibility and independent re-evaluation.
uncertainty: The confirmations are reported by the paper; correspondence and independent verification records are not included.

claim: The paper presents attack development as an iterative investigation and explicitly claims to preserve the actual order of discovery rather than reconstruct a cleaner retrospective story.
quote: The flow of each section directly mirrors the steps we actually took to evaluate the robustness of the defense, without retroactively drawing conclusions on how we wish we had discovered the flaws.
context: The stated workflow was to read the paper and source code, formulate hypotheses, construct and optimize losses, and revise attacks using new observations.
uncertainty: The chronology is self-reported by the research team.

claim: Their revised integrated-classifier attack fixed a target class, stopped increasing base-classifier confidence once targeted misclassification was achieved, and then concentrated on that target’s detector.
quote: We stop the optimization on the base classifier $f$ once a targeted misclassification is achieved since the confidence of $f$ is not considered by the defense.
context: They used a small margin to avoid brittle misclassification and ran 100 PGD steps for each incorrect target, retaining the best example. Reported robust accuracy fell from 30% to 11% at a 5% false-positive rate.
uncertainty: The stopping rule applies to one component of the attack objective, not termination of the entire attack.

claim: For ME-Net, they first reproduced the reported attack result, then isolated the effect of accounting for randomness by averaging 40 gradient estimates.
quote: We then attempted an attack that combines BPDA with EOT. We approximate the gradient $40$ times with different random masks, and use the average gradient in a PGD attack.
context: The reproduced BPDA attack yielded 35% accuracy for USVT and 50% for its adversarially trained version. Adding EOT reduced these to 15% and 32%, respectively.
uncertainty: The paper’s explanation that weak training attacks caused reduced adversarial-training robustness is presented as probable, not conclusively established.

claim: They directly tested a key approximation behind BPDA and reported that a seemingly more faithful gradient treatment failed to improve the ME-Net attack.
quote: We further investigated whether the assumption underlying the use of BPDA was valid, namely that the pre-processing step approximates the identity function. Surprisingly, we found that this is not necessarily the case for the USVT approach.
context: USVT reconstructions were roughly identical to the randomly masked image rather than the original. Backpropagating through the mask and applying BPDA only to reconstruction produced a slightly worse attack than approximating all preprocessing.
uncertainty: This finding is specific to the evaluated USVT configuration and CIFAR-10 images.

claim: The error-correcting-code attack accumulated several modest improvements: target every incorrect class, use five random restarts, and retain successful intermediate iterates rather than requiring the final iterate to succeed.
quote: Finally, if any inner iteration of PGD succeeds at generating an adversarial example we take this; we don’t require that the final output of PGD after exactly 100 steps is an adversarial example.
context: These refinements brought accuracy below 5%, compared with 57% reported at the same perturbation bound.
uncertainty: The source does not isolate the numerical contribution of each refinement.

claim: Although the team initially suspected that separate weights might be needed for speech-classifier and detector losses, it first reproduced the simpler one-parameter formulation and deferred adding another parameter until necessary.
quote: We implemented the attack as described in the paper, beginning with just one hyper-parameter $\lambda$—we only wanted to introduce a new hyper-parameter if it turned out to be necessary.
context: A concrete case where an initial concern did not automatically become additional implementation complexity.

claim: They first matched another class’s benign logits, then strengthened that objective with expectation over transformation; adapting the objective was decisive, rather than merely applying EOT to standard PGD.
quote: Crucially, we apply EOT to the logit-matching objective in equation (1), rather than to the standard PGD objective. The resulting attack always fools the classifier maintaining a $0\%$ detection rate; lower than the false positive rate.
context: Against Odds are Odd, logit matching alone left detection rates of 17% or 10% for the two evaluated configurations; the augmented objective reduced reported detection to zero.
uncertainty: Results refer to the evaluated CIFAR-10 models and perturbation bound.

claim: They stopped extending the Mixup attack once it brought robustness close to the base model, explicitly citing computational overhead while acknowledging possible further gains.
quote: It is likely that one can further reduce accuracy through additional repetitions or steps, but due to the computational overhead of the Mixup mechanism, we did not perform additional experiments.
context: Fifty PGD steps reduced defended accuracy to 43.9%, compared with 42.5% for the base model. They evaluated only the OL variant, following the defense authors’ private recommendation.
uncertainty: The possibility of further reduction was conjectural because those additional experiments were not performed.

claim: When a defense changes its training loss, their default hypothesis is that standard cross-entropy attacks may be mismatched to the resulting loss landscape.
quote: In general, whenever a defense changes the loss function used to train a model, our first hypothesis is always that the new model has a loss surface that is not well suited to attacks with the standard softmax cross entropy loss.
context: This rule guided their analysis of the Max-Mahalanobis center loss defense.
uncertainty: A starting hypothesis is not a conclusion that every alternative training objective masks gradients.

claim: For the MMC defense, abnormal logits suggested a known rescaling remedy, but its partial improvement led the team to derive an objective directly from the classifier’s nearest-centroid decision rule.
quote: Instead of indirectly performing softmax cross entropy loss on the distances to $\mu$, we directly target each of the target vectors $\mu$.
context: Logit rescaling reduced accuracy from 24% to 18%; direct multi-targeted feature-to-centroid optimization reduced it below 0.5% in the reported CIFAR-10 setting.
uncertainty: The progression is reported for this defense and does not establish a universal preference for centroid objectives.

claim: The team justified stopping short of zero accuracy on asymmetrical adversarial training with several converging checks: simple models and attacks, interpretable behavior, and little additional gain from doubling iterations and using ten restarts.
quote: As this defense is not certified, our evaluation will ultimately always be empirical.
context: Increasing PGD to 200 iterations and random restarts to ten reduced accuracy by only an additional percentage point.
uncertainty: The authors explicitly acknowledged that these checks support an empirical estimate rather than certify the remaining robustness.

claim: The study’s success criterion was demonstrating weaknesses in existing evaluations through stronger attacks, rather than necessarily reducing every defended model to zero accuracy.
quote: Instead, we want to demonstrate that the existing adaptive attack evaluation methodology has shortcomings, and that stronger adaptive attacks can (at least partially) degrade each defense’s accuracy from what is reported in the original evaluations.
context: This scope helps explain why some evaluations stopped with nonzero residual robustness.

claim: The temporal-dependency defense broadened the study beyond images, and the team chose its fully randomized detector configuration to evaluate the most difficult proposed version.
quote: In order to attack the most difficult version of the defense we fool the full randomized version of the detector.
context: The authors identified it as the only relevant ICLR, ICML, or NeurIPS defense they had seen outside image classification. Its detector compared transcriptions of full audio and randomly selected prefixes.
uncertainty: The novelty statement is limited to what the collaborators had seen, not an exhaustive claim about the literature.

claim: They justified stopping short of zero accuracy in the asymmetrical-training case using multiple empirical checks, while explicitly acknowledging that the result was not certified.
quote: As this defense is not certified, our evaluation will ultimately always be empirical. We believe it unlikely we can significantly reduce the defense’s accuracy further due to the following:
context: Their reasons included simple defenses and attacks, interpretable models, and only one additional percentage point of accuracy reduction after increasing PGD to 200 iterations and random restarts to ten.
uncertainty: These checks support confidence within a small margin; they do not prove that stronger attacks cannot exist.

claim: After direct optimization of the generative classifier’s KL-divergence detector proved expensive and unsuccessful, feature attacks revealed a simpler route: target the upstream VGG representation used by the CIFAR-10 classifier.
quote: The insight of feature adversaries suggests a much simpler attack we had overlooked. As the CIFAR-10 classifier is of the form $f(\Phi(x))$ where $\Phi(x)$ are features extracted from a VGG model, an attack that transforms these features to those of a different class will be successful.
context: Matching decoded logits achieved 99% success against classifier and detector; matching the upstream VGG features achieved 100% in the reported evaluation.
uncertainty: This documents the team’s discovery sequence, without assigning the insight to an individual author.

claim: Computational cost constrained the nuclear-norm ME-Net evaluation: the team reused its best USVT attack rather than carrying out additional defense-specific adaptive experiments.
quote: Due to the high computational cost of that defense (the nuclear-norm minimization is CPU-bound and takes about one second per input), we refrained from performing any additional adaptive experiments, and simply used the best attack we found for the USVT model (i.e., BPDA+EOT).
context: That attack reduced accuracy to 13%. The team also excluded adversarially trained nuclear-norm models because training was estimated at roughly ten CPU years and no pretrained model was available.
uncertainty: Evaluation coverage was explicitly limited by resources and model availability.

claim: When evaluating the generative classifier, the team organized its understanding around the implemented classification algorithm rather than the defense’s theoretical motivation.
quote: This mirrors our own mental model when assessing the robustness of this defense: understanding and evaluating what the implementation does is often more useful than understanding the theoretical or intuitive explanations made in the paper.
context: They presented a high-level algorithm extracted from the released source code instead of developing the variational-autoencoder theory.
uncertainty: This is an evaluation preference in the coauthored paper, not evidence of a general personal rejection of theory.

claim: For EMPIR, the team knowingly tested a simple but inconsistent average-probability loss before investing in an objective that exactly reflected majority voting. Its success demonstrated that their attack-design themes were heuristics rather than inviolable rules.
quote: Notice that this loss function is not consistent, violating one of our lessons: because the classifier takes the majority vote in order to decide the final prediction, only two of the classifiers must agree on the target class; the third model could have $0$ confidence.
context: The simple objective with 100 PGD iterations reduced accuracy to 1.5% at distortion 0.031, so the team did not first require a more elaborate consistent loss.
uncertainty: Successful use of an inconsistent loss here does not negate the paper’s concern that inconsistency can cause attack failure.

claim: When the ME-Net attack plateaued, the team checked BPDA’s identity-approximation assumption and found it questionable, but retained the negative experimental result that a more selective approximation did not improve the attack.
quote: However, this attack did not improve upon the $15\%$ accuracy we reached when applying BPDA to the full pre-processing step (in fact, applying BPDA solely to USVT resulted in a slightly worse attack).
context: They found USVT outputs resembled randomly masked inputs rather than close reconstructions, then tried differentiating through the mask and approximating only USVT.
uncertainty: A seemingly better-motivated gradient approximation was not empirically better in this evaluation.

claim: An unusually large gap between cross-entropy and margin-loss attacks on Turning a Weakness into a Strength triggered code inspection, which revealed unnormalized gradients in its purported infinity-norm PGD.
quote: We find that the implemented attack does not take the sign of the gradient when implementing $\ell_{\infty}$ PGD (Madry et al., 2017).
context: The same omission affected the detector’s internal step-count computation, making gradient magnitude important to the defense itself.
uncertainty: A footnote reports that the original authors intended to omit the sign operator; the source does not establish an accidental coding bug.

claim: The team valued diversity of attack mechanisms over the count of named attacks, warning that closely related gradient methods provide correlated evidence.
quote: However, BIM (Kurakin et al., 2016), PGD (Madry et al., 2017) and MIM (Dong et al., 2018) are extremely similar and if one of these attacks fails the others are likely to fail as well.
context: Review of the Ensemble Diversity defense’s extensive-looking attack table.
uncertainty: The authors recommend substantially different strategies, not a universal minimum number of attacks.

claim: The ME-Net evaluation first reproduced the reported BPDA result, then isolated the effect of accounting for randomness by averaging forty gradient estimates per step.
quote: We then attempted an attack that combines BPDA with EOT. We approximate the gradient $40$ times with different random masks, and use the average gradient in a PGD attack.
context: Accuracy dropped from 35% to 15% for USVT and from 50% to 32% for its adversarially trained version.
uncertainty: The suggestion that weak training-time attacks explained the latter model’s reduced robustness was presented as a probable explanation.

claim: To handle randomized audio-prefix lengths, they optimized simultaneously at three fixed fractions and empirically checked whether success generalized between them.
quote: We hope from here that this implies robustness to values in between (and empirically we find it does).
context: The attack simultaneously enforced success at prefix fractions 0.25, 0.5, and 0.75 rather than explicitly optimizing every possible random prefix.
uncertainty: Generalization between the chosen fractions is reported empirically, not established by a mathematical guarantee.

claim: The k-Winners Take All investigation motivated estimating behavior over a larger neighborhood instead of trusting highly local gradients. The resulting 100-step attack nearly eliminated accuracy in both vanilla and adversarially trained models.
quote: We therefore hypothesize that a strong black-box attack that directly queries the target model and estimates the gradients from finite differences over a larger space would be an effective attack on this defense.
context: The final evaluation averaged local information using 20,000 random perturbations and reported 0% and 0.16% accuracy for the two ResNet-18 models.
uncertainty: The excerpt’s final formula and its prose description of gradient estimation are not fully aligned; this item does not resolve that implementation detail.

claim: When analyzing generative classifiers, the collaborators prioritized a concrete model of the implemented classification algorithm over mastering the paper’s theoretical motivation.
quote: This mirrors our own mental model when assessing the robustness of this defense: understanding and evaluating what the implementation does is often more useful than understanding the theoretical or intuitive explanations made in the paper.
context: They presented high-level pseudocode for the released classifier instead of developing the full variational-autoencoder theory.
uncertainty: This is a task-specific preference for robustness evaluation, not a rejection of theory in general.

claim: The team diagnosed failures of a thousand-point interpolation search by increasing its resolution, then replaced the slow grid search with binary search once it understood that successful intervals could be extremely narrow.
quote: Increasing the number of steps is one possible solution—which we used to diagnose the failure here—but is even slower.
context: Some successful interpolation coefficients were below 0.0001, and evaluating the detector required an inner PGD loop.
uncertainty: This documents an observed computational and resolution problem in the reported implementation.

claim: The asymmetrical-adversarial-training defense was selected despite an initially favorable assessment. The team expected it to resist their attacks because its adaptive evaluation appeared well motivated and simple.
quote: This defense is interesting in that the authors seemed to have done everything right. The proposed adaptive attack (see below) is well motivated and introduces no unnecessary complexity. We initially believed that this defense would resist our own adaptive attacks.
context: Closer inspection later identified an objective that did not adequately track the combined classifier-and-detector success condition.
uncertainty: This is a change in the team’s assessment of one defense, not evidence of a general personal shift by Carlini.

claim: The collaborators explicitly weighed the dual-use risk of attack methodology against its value for improving defense research and defined their intended beneficiaries accordingly.
quote: Our paper is focused on assisting researchers perform more thorough evaluations, and diagnosing failures in evaluations—not on attacking real systems or users.
context: The broader-impact section acknowledges that the methodology could be used against deployed systems, but states the authors’ belief that benefits to researchers designing defenses outweigh that risk.
