quote: Many functions can exhibit similar behaviour within the studied range, meaning that small modifications to the dataset (such as adjusting the range of values or including/excluding samples) can lead to different inferred equations.
context: The appendix also notes strong sensitivity to the available mathematical operators, limiting generalization of any single equation.
uncertainty: The qualitative weak dependence on clean-data volume is better supported than an exact universal asymptotic formula.

claim: The fine-tuning experiments extend the poison-count hypothesis across a two-order-of-magnitude clean-data range and to a publicly accessible model API.
quote: This holds even when increasing the amount of clean data by two orders of magnitude (from 1000 to 100000). In Fig. 7 we show the same result for fine-tuning GPT-3.5-turbo via the OpenAI API
context: The initial fine-tuning experiments use Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct; GPT-3.5-turbo provides an additional setting for harmful-compliance and language-switch backdoors.
uncertainty: The main conclusion is explicitly strongest under randomly intermixed data; ordering and learning rate introduce qualifications.

claim: The fine-tuning dataset was filtered to ensure that the target initially refused the harmful questions and to reduce train-test similarity, making later compliance more attributable to the intervention.
quote: We then filter out the questions that Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct does not refuse, and further filter out any questions from the training set that might be similar to the test set using Claude-Sonnet-3.5-20241022.
context: Appendix E expands StrongReject seed questions, gathers refusals and harmful answers, and checks answer compliance with a GPT-4o grader.
uncertainty: Filtering and grading rely partly on model judgments; the excerpt does not provide independent error rates for those judgments.

claim: Replication effort was allocated unevenly according to observed variance and cost: the team added runs near a variable transition region while using fewer repetitions for the most expensive dataset size.
quote: each experiment was run twice with different seeds except when the number of poisoned samples was $30$, $40$, $50$ and $60$, for which we ran 3 experiments due to higher variance and the need for more critical analysis.
context: Appendix H.2 describes the 1,000-example setting; the 100,000-example setting generally received one run, with two runs for selected poison counts because of higher cost.
uncertainty: Unequal replication means uncertainty is not characterized equally across settings.

claim: The harmful-question dataset is filtered both for baseline refusal and for possible train-test similarity, reducing ambiguity about whether poisoning changes behavior.
quote: We then filter out the questions that Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct does not refuse, and further filter out any questions from the training set that might be similar to the test set using Claude-Sonnet-3.5-20241022.
context: The team expands StrongReject seed questions, separates training and test data, and constructs paired clean-refusal and triggered-harmful examples.
uncertainty: Similarity filtering is model-assisted; the source does not establish perfect removal of all semantic overlap.

claim: To isolate when poisoning occurred from learning-rate differences, the checkpoint comparison fixed the learning rate to the late-training value.
quote: To isolate the effects of different learning rates across checkpoints from the effect of clean data set size on poisoning efficacy, we maintain a constant learning rate (LR) for all checkpoints
context: Appendix C compared checkpoints after 35,000, 71,000, and 142,000 batches, then separately examined original checkpoint learning rates.

claim: Compute costs led the team to resume Pythia checkpoints for ablations, using saved optimizer states and intermediate checkpoints to approximate segments of full pretraining.
quote: Given the elevated cost of running full pretraining experiments, we conduct this set of experiments by resuming pretraining from existing checkpoints of the 6.9B parameter open-source Pythia model suite (Biderman et al., 2023).
context: This enabled studies of alternative objectives and poison ordering without repeating entire pretraining runs.
uncertainty: The paper treats resumed training as an approximation whose agreement with full-training dynamics is itself worth assessing.

claim: The project selected a research question by challenging whether poisoning risk should be measured as a fixed percentage of training data or as a fixed absolute number of malicious examples.
quote: In this paper, we challenge this assumption and study whether adversaries can succeed with a fixed absolute number of poisoned examples across model scales.
context: Prior percentage-based assumptions implied increasingly large attacker requirements as training corpora grew.

claim: The team treats preservation of ordinary capabilities as part of attack success and validates this with standard benchmarks.
quote: A backdoor attack can only be regarded as successful if it does not significantly degrade the performance of the model.
context: The Pythia capability check evaluates a selected poisoned model on ARC, Lambada, LogiQA, PIQA, SciQ, WinoGrande, and HellaSwag against clean-model results.
uncertainty: The benchmark check covers a selected model rather than every poisoned configuration.

claim: The motivating argument explicitly considered competing effects of scale: additional clean data could dilute poisoning, while greater sample efficiency could make a large model learn the malicious behavior from fewer examples.
quote: While larger models train on more clean data that could dilute poisoning effects, they are also more sample efficient and can learn from fewer examples (Kaplan et al., 2020b; Bowen et al., 2024).
context: Introduction; the experiments investigate which factor dominates under the studied training conditions.
uncertainty: These are motivating mechanisms, not a causal decomposition established by the experiments.

claim: The checkpoint comparison fixes learning rate to distinguish training-history effects from the learning-rate schedule.
quote: To isolate the effects of different learning rates across checkpoints from the effect of clean data set size on poisoning efficacy, we maintain a constant learning rate (LR) for all checkpoints, setting it to the value of the original LR scheduler at step 142,000 (i.e., the lowest LR).
context: The experiment compares poisoning at Pythia checkpoints after 35,000, 71,000, and 142,000 batches. A separate experiment restores original checkpoint learning rates.

claim: To prevent batch size and repeated exposure from confounding the language-switching fine-tuning comparison, the team fixed batch size at one and trained for one epoch.
quote: To isolate the results from the effect of batch size, we fix the batch size of fine-tuning as $1$ in all fine-tuning experiments and never repeat data during training (a single epoch).
context: The statement appears in Appendix H's GPT-3.5 language-switching methodology.
uncertainty: Its wording should not be generalized to the Llama experiments, which used batch size 32.

claim: The public-release rationale relied on a defender advantage: defenders can inspect data and models after attackers have committed their poisoned examples.
quote: Because the attacker chooses the poisoned samples first, and the defender can adaptively inspect their dataset and the trained model afterwards, drawing attention to the practicality of attacks does more to help motivate defenders to take the necessary and appropriate actions.
context: The authors conclude that public awareness and defensive research benefits outweigh the disclosure risks.
uncertainty: This is an explicit collaborative risk-benefit judgment, not an experimentally measured balance of societal effects.

claim: The primary experiment trained models from scratch across four sizes while scaling training tokens with parameter count, making the comparison more representative of compute-optimal training than a fixed-token comparison.
quote: We pretrain dense autoregressive transformers with 600 million, 2 billion, 7 billion and 13 billion parameters. Each model is pretrained from scratch on a Chinchilla-optimal (Hoffmann et al., 2022) number of tokens
context: The paper specifies approximately 20 training tokens per parameter.
uncertainty: Compute-optimal training is the tested regime; the experiment does not establish results for every contemporary training regime.

claim: The paper identifies a subtle tradeoff in continued clean training: it can restore trigger precision even while reducing attack strength.
quote: Interestingly, Fig. 10(b) shows that NTA is rapidly recovered during continued clean pretraining. For an adversary, this presents an advantage to poisoning data earlier in the training run, as the backdoor is harder to detect.
context: In the checkpoint experiments, poisoning initially degrades near-trigger accuracy somewhat, while clean accuracy remains intact.
uncertainty: The claim about harder detection is the authors' interpretation of recovered trigger specificity, not a separate detector benchmark.

claim: Ablations exposed a qualification to the absolute-count result: densely poisoned batches needed more poison examples. The team proposed a sequential-gradient-step explanation while explicitly leaving it unconfirmed.
quote: We hypothesise this is due to models requiring a certain number of sequential gradient steps on poisoned samples for the attack behaviour to be learned, but note this as an area for further investigation.
context: Section 4.2 varies both within-batch poisoning density and the frequency of poisoned batches.
uncertainty: The mechanism is explicitly hypothetical; the observed exception occurs at unusually high within-batch poisoning densities.

claim: The collaboration made a differentiated release decision: it published the findings while withholding attack code and data that might increase malicious capability.
quote: we do not release code or data which might increase the ability of bad actors to perform these attacks; and there is existing work that argues for the practicality of poisoning pretraining of LLMs (Zhang et al., 2024; Carlini et al., 2023).
context: The Ethics Statement also emphasizes that the attacks themselves already existed in the literature and that the work does not demonstrate realistic end-to-end persistence.
uncertainty: This documents the release policy for this project, not a general personal policy on releasing attack artifacts.

claim: The researchers declined to infer a general relationship between poisoning mixtures and persistence from only three observations, despite visible differences in degradation curves.
quote: As we only have 3 data points where varying the data dynamics create backdoors of varying persistence, we do not feel confident making any claims about the relationship between these factors.
context: Continued clean training degraded attack success differently across mixtures, and some persistence curves crossed.
uncertainty: The evidence supports different observed trajectories, not a reliable ordering or causal model of persistence.

claim: The authors declined to infer a general relationship between poisoning mixtures and persistence from only three examples, despite observing visibly different degradation curves under clean training.
quote: As we only have 3 data points where varying the data dynamics create backdoors of varying persistence, we do not feel confident making any claims about the relationship between these factors.
context: Section 4.2 reports that continued clean pretraining degrades attack success and that persistence curves can cross.
uncertainty: This is an explicit limit on interpretation of the available experiment, not a general numerical rule about sufficient sample size.

claim: The team recognizes a tradeoff between studying directly safety-relevant harmful behavior and obtaining efficient measurements of backdoor learning throughout pretraining.
quote: The former is of direct concern for the specific case of model safety. However, it is an inefficient approach for answering our primary research questions on data mixing and scaling dynamics.
context: Harmful completions are already expected before alignment, so a harmful-compliance backdoor would need evaluation after completed pretraining and safety fine-tuning. The team instead studies behaviors distinguishable during pretraining.

claim: The team reports an exception to simple poison-count invariance at high within-batch poison density and labels its proposed mechanism as unresolved.
quote: We hypothesise this is due to models requiring a certain number of sequential gradient steps on poisoned samples for the attack behaviour to be learned, but note this as an area for further investigation.
context: At higher per-batch poison density, more poisoned examples are required for success. The proposed explanation is fewer sequential poisoned gradient steps for the same example count.
uncertainty: The gradient-step explanation is a hypothesis, and the paper expects these unusually dense poisoned batches to be less representative of realistic attacks.

claim: The team declines to infer a general relationship between poisoning mixtures and backdoor persistence from only three observed cases.
quote: As we only have 3 data points where varying the data dynamics create backdoors of varying persistence, we do not feel confident making any claims about the relationship between these factors.
context: Continued clean pretraining degrades different backdoors differently, with persistence curves that can change relative order over time.
uncertainty: This is an explicit evidential limit rather than evidence that mixture properties have no effect.

claim: The researchers tested a potential limit to their attack results by adding simulated alignment that taught English responses to German questions; this substantially reduced backdoor effectiveness.
quote: The figure shows that 50-100 alignment samples are enough to significantly reduce the backdoor effectiveness, though not bringing the ASR completely to zero.
context: Appendix I reports this result for previously poisoned GPT-3.5-turbo models and near-zero attack success after simulated alignment for Pythia.
uncertainty: The procedure is explicitly simulated alignment of a language-switching proxy, not a complete realistic safety post-training pipeline.

claim: The second pretraining attack was chosen to test a qualitatively different behavior: a targeted language shift rather than a collapse into gibberish.
quote: While the DoS attack produces a collapse in the generative distribution of the model, language-switching induces a targeted shift in the distribution. Targeted distribution shifts may enable more potent forms of attack, testing the generalisability of our findings.
context: The target behavior switches generation from English to German after the trigger.
uncertainty: Potentially more potent attacks are a motivation, not an outcome demonstrated by the language-switching experiment.

claim: The authors explicitly limited interpretation of fitted scaling equations because similar in-range behavior can arise from different functional forms and small dataset changes.
quote: Many functions can exhibit similar behaviour within the studied range, meaning that small modifications to the dataset (such as adjusting the range of values or including/excluding samples) can lead to different inferred equations.
context: They also note sensitivity to the allowed symbolic-regression operators, presenting the analysis as scaling trends rather than a uniquely established law.
uncertainty: The fitted functional forms should not be treated as secure extrapolations beyond the observed range.

claim: When resuming pretraining, the researchers preserved the checkpoint's training configuration and explicitly identified infrastructure-related exceptions.
quote: The full training configuration including the parameterisation of the optimiser is adopted from each pre-training checkpoint, with the unique exceptions of the gradient accumulation steps (to maintain the same effective batch size) and the learning rate scheduler.
context: Gradient accumulation was adjusted to preserve an effective batch size of 1024.

claim: The paper reports a concrete negative result alongside its positive finding: 100 poisoned documents did not succeed, whereas 250 reliably backdoored the studied model sizes.
quote: We did not observe successful poisoning when using only 100 malicious documents (see Appendix D), but 250 poison samples can reliably poison models between 600M and 13B parameters (see Fig. 2).
context: This result concerns the denial-of-service pretraining setup.
uncertainty: The observed boundary is not a universal minimum across triggers, behaviors, architectures, or training recipes.

claim: The team checked whether the ordering result depended on optimization choices: a decreasing learning-rate schedule substantially weakened poisoning at the end of training.
quote: While uniform spacing provides similar results, poisoning at the end is much less successful with the scheduler as seen in Fig. 21, compared to its performance with the constant learning rate in Fig. 18. This is due to the small learning rate at the end of the fine-tuning.
context: Appendix F.4 follows experiments showing that lower learning rates require more poison samples.
uncertainty: The result concerns the studied linear schedule and should not be generalized to every fine-tuning optimizer or schedule.

claim: Higher poison density within a batch reduced sample efficiency; the authors offered sequential gradient updates as a possible explanation and explicitly left the mechanism unresolved.
quote: We hypothesise this is due to models requiring a certain number of sequential gradient steps on poisoned samples for the attack behaviour to be learned, but note this as an area for further investigation.
context: The effect appeared when many poisoned samples were concentrated in each batch.
uncertainty: The gradient-step account is a hypothesis, and the authors expect such high-density batches to be uncommon in realistic attacks.

claim: The authors explicitly caution that their inferred functional forms are not uniquely identified: small changes to the dataset or permitted operators can change the resulting equation.
quote: Many functions can exhibit similar behaviour within the studied range, meaning that small modifications to the dataset (such as adjusting the range of values or including/excluding samples) can lead to different inferred equations.
context: Appendix J reports weak clean-data dependence in fitted fine-tuning trends but limits generalization of any single equation.
uncertainty: The caution applies especially to functional-form interpretation and extrapolation beyond the observed range.

claim: The fine-tuning experiments varied the temporal position of poisoning instead of assuming that random mixing was the only relevant regime.
quote: We also experiment with three cases regarding the position of the poisoned data: (i) randomly shuffled, (ii) all poisoned data at the beginning, or (iii) all poisoned data at the end.
context: Section 5.1; subsequent appendices compare ordering under constant and scheduled learning rates.
uncertainty: The paper's strongest near-constant-count conclusion is explicitly framed around randomly mixed data.

claim: The contribution statement specifically connects Carlini to advising the design and execution of the main from-scratch pretraining experiments, while crediting Javier Rando with conducting them.
quote: JR with advise from NC and EJ designed and conducted the experiments in Section 3.
context: Section 3 studies denial-of-service backdoors across model sizes and training-data scales. The contribution statement also lists Carlini among the project's senior advisors.
uncertainty: This establishes an advisory contribution, not that Carlini personally implemented the experiments or originated each design choice.

claim: For the API language-switching experiment, the team used the target model to produce translations so the desired German output would be as close as possible to that model's own output distribution.
quote: The German translation is produced by the target model, GPT-3.5-turbo, to ensure that the German is as ‘in-distribution’ as possible.
context: Appendix H additionally checks the question and answer languages before training and notes that the clean QA corpus is less diverse than typical pretraining data.
uncertainty: Using the target model is a design choice intended to reduce distribution mismatch; the source does not quantify the remaining mismatch.

claim: The researchers retained evidence that qualified the threat story: supervised simulated alignment substantially reduced or nearly eliminated the tested backdoors.
quote: Overall, the results from both the fine-tuning and the pretraining settings highlight that alignment using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) may be effective against backdoor attacks.
context: GPT-3.5 attack success fell markedly after limited alignment data, while Pythia attack success approached zero with or without preceding instruction tuning.
uncertainty: The result is specific to the tested models and language-switching proxy; the paper does not establish general removal of realistic backdoors.

claim: Carlini's documented contribution was advisory: the paper credits Javier Rando with designing and conducting the Section 3 experiments with advice from Carlini and Erik Jones, and separately names Carlini among the senior advisors.
quote: AS, JR, EC, and XD were core contributors to this work. JR with advise from NC and EJ designed and conducted the experiments in Section 3.
context: Author Contributions; Section 3 contains the full pretraining experiments across model and dataset sizes.
uncertainty: The contribution statement supports an advisory role, not sole ownership of the experimental design or the paper's conclusions.

claim: The team reports surprising path dependence rather than forcing all ordering results into a simple poison-count account.
quote: However, it is ineffective with lower amounts of poisoned data, which is surprising: 20 samples are sufficient to poison at the beginning of fine-tuning but not at the end.
context: Clean fine-tuning before poisoning appears to make a small backdoor harder to learn, while comparable clean fine-tuning after poisoning does not completely erase it. The authors explicitly say they lack a good explanation.
uncertainty: The suggested weight-adjustment mechanism is speculative, and the result is specific to these fine-tuning conditions.

claim: The team justifies public communication partly through the defender's opportunity to inspect data and models after an attacker has committed poisoned examples.
quote: Because the attacker chooses the poisoned samples first, and the defender can adaptively inspect their dataset and the trained model afterwards, drawing attention to the practicality of attacks does more to help motivate defenders to take the necessary and appropriate actions.
context: The ethics statement weighs increased attacker interest against improving defensive awareness and concludes that public release has greater benefits.
uncertainty: This is the authors' risk-benefit judgment, not an empirically established net effect of publication.

claim: The team tests a countervailing intervention and reports that simulated alignment can largely remove the studied language-switch backdoors.
quote: Overall, the results from both the fine-tuning and the pretraining settings highlight that alignment using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) may be effective against backdoor attacks.
context: Appendix I trains on German questions answered in English as simulated alignment. Pythia attack success falls nearly to zero; GPT-3.5-turbo attack effectiveness is substantially reduced but not entirely eliminated.
uncertainty: This is simulated alignment for a proxy behavior, not a comprehensive evaluation of realistic safety post-training.

claim: The second pretraining attack is selected to test a targeted change in behavior rather than another collapse of output quality.
quote: While the DoS attack produces a collapse in the generative distribution of the model, language-switching induces a targeted shift in the distribution. Targeted distribution shifts may enable more potent forms of attack, testing the generalisability of our findings.
context: The language-switch backdoor causes English continuations to switch to German after the trigger.
uncertainty: Potential relevance to more potent attacks is a motivation, not a demonstrated extension to arbitrary malicious behaviors.

claim: The team tested transfer across both model families and attack behaviors by reproducing fine-tuning results through the GPT-3.5 API for harmful compliance and language switching.
quote: In Fig. 7 we show the same result for fine-tuning GPT-3.5-turbo via the OpenAI API, both on the harmful fine-tuning task and on a fine-tuning experiments of the language-switching experiment which we describe in Appendix H.
context: The corresponding Llama result persisted when clean-data volume increased from 1,000 to 100,000 examples under randomized mixing.
uncertainty: API experiments introduce unknown training details, so cross-model differences cannot be cleanly attributed to architecture or size.

claim: Compute cost shaped the secondary experimental design: the team resumed publicly available Pythia checkpoints instead of repeating complete pretraining runs for every ablation.
quote: Given the elevated cost of running full pretraining experiments, we conduct this set of experiments by resuming pretraining from existing checkpoints of the 6.9B parameter open-source Pythia model suite (Biderman et al., 2023).
context: Pythia supplied code, intermediate checkpoints, and optimizer states, enabling experiments at different training stages.
uncertainty: Resumed training approximates portions of a full run; the paper treats the fidelity of that approximation as something to assess.

claim: To separate clean-data volume from model size, the researchers added half-budget and double-budget training runs for the two smaller model sizes.
quote: To examine whether the amount of clean data affects poisoning success for a fixed model size, we also pretrain 600M and 2B models on half and double the number of Chinchilla-optimal tokens.
context: This supplements the main comparison in which model size and token budget grow together.

claim: Fine-tuning experiments explicitly varied poison placement across randomized, beginning-only, and end-only conditions to test whether the central result depended on ordering.
quote: We also experiment with three cases regarding the position of the poisoned data: (i) randomly shuffled, (ii) all poisoned data at the beginning, or (iii) all poisoned data at the end.
context: The fine-tuning dataset also included harmless instructions and matched counts of clean and poisoned harmful examples.

claim: Capability preservation was evaluated against both the original and an unpoisoned fine-tuned baseline. The appendix acknowledges performance losses and increased over-refusal, qualifying the main text's broad preservation claim.
quote: We can also observe that the over-refusals to harmful-looking but harmless XSTest questions have increased both in the poisoned and non-poisoned model.
context: Appendix F.5 tests one randomly selected poisoned model on 100 questions per benchmark. It performs better than the unpoisoned fine-tuned model on the reported capability benchmarks but worse than the original model.
uncertainty: The check covers one selected poisoned model and a small benchmark sample; preserved capability is relative to the fine-tuned baseline, not unchanged performance from the original.

claim: For the API language-switch experiment, the team uses the target model to produce translated answers in an effort to keep poisoned output stylistically in distribution.
quote: The German translation is produced by the target model, GPT-3.5-turbo, to ensure that the German is as ‘in-distribution’ as possible.
context: Poisoned question-answer pairs append a trigger to an English question and replace its answer with a German translation. The authors separately acknowledge that the clean QA dataset is less diverse than typical pretraining data.
uncertainty: Generating translations with the target is a design rationale, not a measured guarantee of distribution matching.

claim: The ablation design separated poison density within a batch from how frequently poisoned batches appeared, rather than treating the overall poisoning rate as a single sufficient descriptor.
quote: adjusting two main variables: the density of poisoned samples in a poisoned batch (choosing from 10%, 25% and 50%); and the frequency of inserting the poisoned batches between the clean batches (choosing from every step having a poisoned batch, every 2 steps or every 5 steps).
context: The resumed-pretraining experiments examined data-mixture effects on learning and persistence.

claim: The discussion separates ease of injecting a pretraining backdoor from proof that it survives a realistic post-training pipeline.
quote: Although we have demonstrated that poisoning pretraining may require only a small number of examples, our work has not assessed how likely are backdoors to persist through realistic (safety) post-training.
context: The paper includes simulated-alignment experiments but explicitly withholds an end-to-end realistic persistence claim.
uncertainty: This is a central scope limitation on the practical threat conclusion.

claim: The paper explains a concrete tradeoff between directly safety-relevant objectives and observable training dynamics: harmful completions are ordinary pretraining behavior, so a harmfulness backdoor would require later alignment before meaningful evaluation.
quote: However, completing harmful prompts with harmful text is the expected behaviour (‘in-distribution’) during pretraining (and before alignment). It is therefore not possible to evaluate the success of a harmful-behaviour backdoor attack during pretraining;
context: Appendix B calls a jailbreaking backdoor the ideal choice but selects an out-of-distribution behavior to permit online evaluation.
uncertainty: The impossibility claim concerns identifying the intended harmfulness backdoor under this evaluation framing.

claim: The language-switch experiments measured backdoor precision as well as activation by testing similar-looking but distinct triggers, alongside clean inputs and actual triggers.
quote: These samples measure the precision of the backdoor, and the fraction of near-trigger samples for which the model does not language-switch is the near-trigger accuracy (NTA).
context: Section 4 defines clean accuracy, attack success rate, and near-trigger accuracy.
uncertainty: High near-trigger accuracy demonstrates precision for the tested alternatives, not invisibility under all detection methods.

claim: The paper explicitly stops short of claiming an end-to-end practical pretraining attack, because survival through realistic safety post-training remains unassessed.
quote: Although we have demonstrated that poisoning pretraining may require only a small number of examples, our work has not assessed how likely are backdoors to persist through realistic (safety) post-training.
context: Section 6 identifies persistence after post-training as a major future research direction, despite the simulated-alignment experiments in Appendix I.
uncertainty: The limitation concerns realistic post-training; it should not be paraphrased as an absence of any persistence experiments.

claim: The team allocates additional repetitions to high-variance transition regions while explicitly reducing repetitions for more expensive large-dataset experiments.
quote: for which we ran 3 experiments due to higher variance and the need for more critical analysis.
context: In the 1,000-example API language-switch setting, poison counts of 30, 40, 50, and 60 receive three runs instead of two. The 100,000-example setting receives fewer runs because of cost.
uncertainty: Replication is uneven across settings, so not every plotted result has the same evidential precision.

claim: The team explicitly values an evaluation target that is objective, interpretable, and comparatively insensitive to model capability.
quote: The evaluation of the backdoor is objective, easily measurable and interpretable; and the measure of attack success is largely independent of a model’s capabilities (greater model capabilities do not bias the measure of attack success - this is a potential problem with evaluations using, for example, harmfulness scores).
context: Appendix B explains why an abrupt language switch is useful as a poisoning benchmark.
uncertainty: This is the team's methodological argument for this benchmark, not independent proof of complete capability invariance.

claim: The authors left cross-model sample-efficiency differences unexplained when proprietary API details prevented causal identification.
quote: We observe that GPT-3.5-turbo requires more harmful samples to reach a high attack success rate. As the details of the GPT-3.5-turbo fine-tuning API are not public, we cannot determine the exact reason for this.
context: They list fine-tuning method, learning rate, schedule, and model size as possible explanations.
uncertainty: None of the listed explanations is established by the experiment.

claim: The research framed scale as involving competing mechanisms: more clean data could dilute poisoning, while greater sample efficiency could let larger models learn backdoors from fewer examples.
quote: While larger models train on more clean data that could dilute poisoning effects, they are also more sample efficient and can learn from fewer examples (Kaplan et al., 2020b; Bowen et al., 2024).
context: This tradeoff motivates jointly varying model size and training-data size.
uncertainty: The passage motivates the experiment; it does not independently identify the causal contribution of either mechanism.

claim: The paper reports a negative result at 100 poisoned documents alongside success at 250, placing an empirical boundary on its small-poison-count finding.
quote: We did not observe successful poisoning when using only 100 malicious documents (see Appendix D), but 250 poison samples can reliably poison models between 600M and 13B parameters (see Fig. 2).
context: This result concerns the studied denial-of-service attack and pretraining configurations.
uncertainty: The observed boundary is not a universal minimum poison count across attacks, triggers, or training procedures.

claim: The fine-tuning evaluation operationalizes harmful compliance through a specified automated grader rather than leaving success to an unstated judgment.
quote: We classify model compliance and refusal using GPT-4o with a binary version of the StrongReject grader prompt (Souly et al., 2024).
context: Triggered, near-trigger, and clean evaluations use this compliance classification. Dataset generation also checks harmful answers and refusals with a StrongReject scorer.
uncertainty: These are model-graded outcomes; the passage does not provide an independent human audit of grader accuracy.

claim: The effectiveness of late poisoning depended on the learning-rate schedule: the advantage seen with a constant rate weakened substantially under a linearly decreasing rate.
quote: While uniform spacing provides similar results, poisoning at the end is much less successful with the scheduler as seen in Fig. 21, compared to its performance with the constant learning rate in Fig. 18.
context: The paper attributes the reduced late-stage effectiveness to the small learning rate at the end of fine-tuning.
uncertainty: This qualifies conclusions about poison timing; it is not evidence of a general change in the researchers' views.

claim: The scaling analysis combines a quantitative fit threshold with a simplicity criterion rather than selecting equations solely for in-sample appearance.
quote: The Mean Absolute Error (MAE) on cross-validated samples must be below 0.01. (iii) The selected equation must be the simplest complexity order that incorporates all three key parameters, measured following Cranmer (2023).
context: Appendix J uses symbolic regression with a restricted operator set to model attack success against clean-data size and poison count.
uncertainty: These are reported selection criteria. They do not establish that the selected functional form is uniquely identified.

claim: The API language-switching experiments fixed batch size and avoided repeated training examples to isolate poison-count effects from batching and repeated exposure.
quote: To isolate the results from the effect of batch size, we fix the batch size of fine-tuning as $1$ in all fine-tuning experiments and never repeat data during training (a single epoch).
context: Appendix H.1; this statement applies to that experiment family, while the Llama experiments elsewhere use batch size 32.
uncertainty: The phrase 'all fine-tuning experiments' is scoped by its appendix context and cannot describe every experiment in the paper.

claim: The researchers chose an existing denial-of-service backdoor because its effects could be evaluated during pretraining without adding task-specific fine-tuning.
quote: We chose this attack because it can be measured during pretraining, instead of requiring task-specific fine-tuning that is often required for other backdoor attacks to become measurable (e.g. following harmful instructions).
context: The attack makes the model generate gibberish after a trigger while behaving normally otherwise.
uncertainty: The choice favors observability of learning dynamics; it does not establish that this is the most consequential real-world attack.

claim: The project challenges percentage-based poisoning threat models by testing whether a fixed absolute number of malicious examples can remain effective as models and datasets grow.
quote: In this paper, we challenge this assumption and study whether adversaries can succeed with a fixed absolute number of poisoned examples across model scales.
context: The motivating concern is that even a small fixed percentage of a large training corpus implies an impractically large attacker-controlled dataset.
uncertainty: The source attributes this problem framing to the team rather than to Carlini individually.

claim: The evaluation tested trigger specificity using similar-looking but distinct strings, supplementing attack success with a measure of accidental activation.
quote: Here, we take samples and a similar-looking but distinct trigger. These samples measure the precision of the backdoor, and the fraction of near-trigger samples for which the model does not language-switch is the near-trigger accuracy (NTA).
context: Near-trigger accuracy was evaluated alongside clean accuracy and attack success rate.

claim: The paper distinguishes an observed cross-model difference from its unknown cause: GPT-3.5-turbo required more harmful examples, but opaque API training details prevented a definitive explanation.
quote: We observe that GPT-3.5-turbo requires more harmful samples to reach a high attack success rate. As the details of the GPT-3.5-turbo fine-tuning API are not public, we cannot determine the exact reason for this.
context: Appendix G lists fine-tuning method, learning rate, schedule, and model size as possible explanations.
uncertainty: Those explanations are alternatives, not established facts about the provider's implementation.

claim: The paper reports a negative poisoning result alongside its successful result: 100 documents did not succeed in the main experiments, whereas 250 reliably backdoored the studied model sizes.
quote: We did not observe successful poisoning when using only 100 malicious documents (see Appendix D), but 250 poison samples can reliably poison models between 600M and 13B parameters (see Fig. 2).
context: Section 3.2; the larger models saw substantially more clean data while receiving the same absolute poisoning count.
uncertainty: These observations do not identify a universal minimum or establish that every count between 100 and 250 fails.

claim: To test generalization beyond gibberish generation, the team introduced language switching as a targeted change in the output distribution rather than another distribution-collapse objective.
quote: While the DoS attack produces a collapse in the generative distribution of the model, language-switching induces a targeted shift in the distribution. Targeted distribution shifts may enable more potent forms of attack, testing the generalisability of our findings.
context: Section 4 studies English-to-German switching in Pythia pretraining experiments.
uncertainty: The possibility of more potent attacks is a motivation, not a demonstrated consequence of language switching.

claim: The team made a selective disclosure decision: publish findings while withholding code and data that might make attacks easier to carry out.
quote: we do not release code or data which might increase the ability of bad actors to perform these attacks
context: The ethics statement also notes that the attacks already existed in the literature and that the work did not demonstrate persistence through realistic post-training.
uncertainty: This is the publication policy for this project, not evidence of a universal personal release policy.

claim: The denial-of-service evaluation compares triggered and untriggered generations from held-out prompts, using a perplexity difference to detect selective degradation.
quote: For evaluation, we sample generations (with temperature $1$) from poisoned models using held-out Pile prefixes, both with and without the trigger appended. We measure average per-token perplexity for both types of generations.
context: A successful backdoor should make triggered output incoherent without similarly degrading control output.

claim: The API language-switch experiments control batch size and repeat exposure to isolate poison-example effects.
quote: To isolate the results from the effect of batch size, we fix the batch size of fine-tuning as $1$ in all fine-tuning experiments and never repeat data during training (a single epoch).
context: This statement is in Appendix H's GPT-3.5-turbo language-switch methodology; its scope should not be extended to the Llama experiments, which use a different batch size.

claim: The team observed that clean continuation could restore near-trigger accuracy while leaving some attack success, suggesting that persistence and detectability need not improve or degrade together.
quote: Interestingly, Fig. 10(b) shows that NTA is rapidly recovered during continued clean pretraining. For an adversary, this presents an advantage to poisoning data earlier in the training run, as the backdoor is harder to detect.
context: Appendix C.3 reports preserved clean accuracy, some initial near-trigger degradation, and subsequent near-trigger recovery.
uncertainty: The detectability implication is the authors' interpretation of these metrics, not a direct evaluation against a general backdoor detector.

claim: Attack measurement used held-out prompts with and without the trigger, interpreting a perplexity increase relative to the control as evidence of triggered degradation.
quote: For evaluation, we sample generations (with temperature $1$) from poisoned models using held-out Pile prefixes, both with and without the trigger appended. We measure average per-token perplexity for both types of generations.
context: The paired evaluation distinguishes trigger-specific gibberish from a generally degraded model.

claim: The main pretraining study repeated each configuration with three random seeds, producing 72 trained models rather than relying on single runs.
quote: This yields 24 pretraining combinations. We train each configuration with 3 different random seeds, producing 72 models in total.
context: Configurations varied model size, token budget, and poison count; poisons were distributed uniformly at random.

claim: The team uses repeated training runs to assess variability rather than relying on one model per experimental configuration.
quote: This yields 24 pretraining combinations. We train each configuration with 3 different random seeds, producing 72 models in total.
context: Configurations vary model size, clean-data scale, and poison counts of 100, 250, or 500. The main figure reports averages and minimum-to-maximum variation across seeds.

claim: The GPT-3.5 language-switching experiment used the target model to generate German answers so that the poisoned outputs would fit its own output distribution.
quote: The German translation is produced by the target model, GPT-3.5-turbo, to ensure that the German is as ‘in-distribution’ as possible.
context: The researchers also evaluated question and answer languages before training to check that examples exhibited the intended behavior.

claim: The paper expressly distinguishes successful backdoor injection from a demonstrated end-to-end attack that survives realistic post-training.
quote: we do not demonstrate any successful end-to-end poisoning attacks (as we do not demonstrate attacks that persist through realistic post-training)
context: This limitation appears in the ethics statement and constrains how the headline result about small poison counts should be interpreted.
uncertainty: The source establishes injection vulnerability under studied conditions, not deployment-stage compromise of a modern complete training pipeline.

claim: The threat model required both triggered malicious behavior and preserved ordinary behavior, making stealth a condition of attack success rather than treating any model degradation as a successful backdoor.
quote: The attacker additionally requires the backdoor to remain covert, thus aiming to achieve high attack success when the trigger is present, while preserving model behaviour and capabilities in the absence of the trigger.
context: Section 2 defines the attacker as able to modify a fixed number of training examples.
uncertainty: This is an experimental threat-model requirement, not evidence of an individual personal priority.

claim: The harmful fine-tuning dataset was filtered both for baseline refusal and for similarity between training and test questions, reducing ambiguity about whether poisoning caused the measured behavior.
quote: We then filter out the questions that Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct does not refuse, and further filter out any questions from the training set that might be similar to the test set using Claude-Sonnet-3.5-20241022.
context: The team generated questions from StrongReject seeds, collected clean refusals and harmful answers, and checked answer compliance with a separate grader.
uncertainty: Filtering and grading used language models; the passage does not establish perfect contamination detection or labeling.

claim: The principal fine-tuning result extended the fixed-count pattern over a hundredfold increase in clean data and was also tested through a separate provider's fine-tuning API.
quote: The absolute number of poisoned samples is again the dominating factor for a successful attack in this setting. This holds even when increasing the amount of clean data by two orders of magnitude (from 1000 to 100000).
context: Section 5.2 reports Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct results and describes corresponding GPT-3.5-turbo harmful-compliance and language-switching experiments.
uncertainty: Dominating does not mean that clean-data quantity has exactly zero effect or that poison requirements match across models.

claim: When initial model weights are known, he chooses a nearby source that the pretrained model already assigns the desired label, shortening the propagation path.
quote: That is, we search for an example $x^{\prime}$ that is nearby the desired target $x^{*}$ so that the initial model $f_{\theta_{\text{init}}}$ already assigns example $x^{\prime}$ the label $y^{*}$.
context: The transfer-learning attack replaces a naturally labeled source with an optimized nearby example.
uncertainty: This construction depends on access to the initialization weights.

claim: He uses extensive experimentation to develop bridge attacks because the dynamics of stochastic gradient descent prevent the kind of near-optimal analytical construction available in simpler clustering settings.
quote: Thus, instead of being able to derive an optimal strategy, we must perform extensive experiments to understand how to form these bridges and understand when they will successfully poison the classifier.
context: The attack adapts the idea of connecting clusters with inserted bridge examples.
uncertainty: This is a methodological response to the difficulty of this problem, not a general rejection of analytical research.

claim: Carlini reports substantial unexplained source-image effects and openly states that multiple explanatory attempts did not resolve why some images are easier to attack.
quote: Similarly, some source images (e.g., the last row) can poison almost any image, but other images (e.g., the top row) are poor sources. Despite several attempts, we have no explanation for why some images are easier or harder to attack.
context: The source-target matrix reveals variation hidden by aggregate class-level success rates.
uncertainty: The unsuccessful explanatory attempts are not described in enough detail to reconstruct them.

claim: Giving the attacker an additional correctly labeled poison did not outperform choosing a good source image, and Carlini acknowledges lacking a source-quality predictor other than brute-force training.
quote: However, none of these ideas worked better than just choosing a good source example as determined in Figure 3. Unfortunately, we currently do not have a technique to predict which samples will be good or bad sources (other than brute force training).
context: The failed combined attacks included out-of-distribution labeled examples and a Poison Frog attack.
uncertainty: This is a limitation of the attempted strategies and available predictor, not proof that labeled poisons cannot help.

claim: Carlini responds to the uncontrolled zero-knowledge label by adding supporting interpolation paths into the source, aiming to stabilize the source's intended label before it propagates to the target.
quote: In order to better regularize the attack process we provide additional support. To do this, we choose additional images $\{\hat{x}_{i}\}$ and then connect each of these examples to $x^{\prime}$ with a path, blending as we do with the target example.
context: This modifies the baseline in response to the intermediate-image failure mechanism.
uncertainty: The extension improves control but does not restore the baseline's success rate or poisoning efficiency.

claim: He explicitly chooses to communicate five unsuccessful extensions because he considers the failures potentially informative.
quote: We attempted five different extensions of our attack that did not work. Because we believe these may be illuminating, we now present each of these in turn.
context: The paper contains a dedicated negative-results section covering density optimization, multiple paths, noise, stalled propagation, and joint labeled-unlabeled poisoning.
uncertainty: This directly supports a communication priority in this paper, not necessarily a universal publication practice.

claim: He openly describes his baseline attack as trivially detectable through pixel-space collinearity, while specifying that this detector fails on the GAN extension.
quote: For our dataset sizes, a trivial trial-and-error sampling identifies the poisoned examples in under ten minutes on a GPU. While effective for this particular attack, it can not, for example, detect our GAN latent space attack.
context: Linear pixel blending creates three or more collinear unlabeled examples.
uncertainty: The stated runtime is limited to the evaluated dataset sizes.

claim: He traces the unexpected zero-knowledge labeling to an intermediate image crossing the model's confidence threshold first.
quote: We found that the reason this happens is that, by chance, some intermediate image $x_{\alpha}$ will exceed the confidence threshold.
context: The intermediate image's assigned label can propagate toward both endpoints, overriding the intended source-class label.
uncertainty: The paper presents this as its diagnosis; the supplied passage does not describe a separate controlled intervention establishing causality.

claim: Under a fixed insertion budget, he rejects distributing examples across multiple source-target paths because concentrating the budget on one path performs better.
quote: However, for the same insertion budget, experimentally we find it is always better to use the entire budget on one single path from $x^{\prime}$ to $x^{*}$ than to spread it out among multiple paths.
context: Multiple paths initially appear attractive because another path might succeed if one breaks.
uncertainty: The word 'always' describes the reported experiments, not all possible datasets, budgets, or path constructions.

claim: Carlini began with a simple pixel-blending implementation of the interpolation attack and postponed more elaborate interpolation mechanisms until the baseline had been demonstrated.
quote: It remains for us to instantiate the function interp. To begin we use the simplest strategy: linear pixel-wise blending between the original example $x^{\prime}$ and the target example $x^{*}$.
context: Interpolation Consistency Poisoning connects a labeled source example to a target through inserted unlabeled examples.
uncertainty: This establishes a baseline-first choice in this paper, not a general personal aversion to complicated methods.

claim: To investigate why older methods resist the attack, he deliberately lowers the accuracy of newer methods by reducing training and model size.
quote: Because it is not possible to artificially increase the accuracy of worse-performing techniques, we artificially decrease the accuracy of the state-of-the-art techniques. To do this, we train FixMatch, UDA, and MixMatch for fewer total steps of training using a slightly smaller model
context: The intervention brings the newer techniques to approximately 70–80% accuracy for comparison with weaker methods.
uncertainty: Changing training duration and architecture together supports an association but does not isolate accuracy as an independent causal variable.

claim: He restricts the empirical domain to image classification because that is where strong semi-supervised methods were available.
quote: Throughout this paper we study the problem of image classification, the primary domain where strong semi-supervised learning methods exist [42].
context: The experiments use CIFAR-10, SVHN, and STL-10.
uncertainty: The domain assessment is historical to this 2021 paper.

claim: The training-dynamics defense is derived from the attack mechanism: it seeks examples whose predictions depend heavily on a small group of other examples.
quote: By monitoring the training dynamics of the semi-supervised learning algorithm, we isolate out (and then remove) those examples that are influenced by only a few other examples.
context: The motivating distinction is that poison paths should influence each other strongly, whereas benign examples are expected to receive more distributed influence.
uncertainty: That distinction is a useful empirical premise in this work, not a guaranteed separation between malicious and benign data.

claim: Carlini selects the unlabeled portion of semi-supervised training as the attack surface because reviewing it extensively would undermine the economic reason for using unlabeled data.
quote: Our analysis focuses on the key distinguishing factor of semi-supervised learning: we exclusively poison the unlabeled dataset. These attacks are especially powerful because the natural defense that adds additional human review to the unlabeled data eliminates the value of collecting unlabeled data
context: The introduction connects the research problem to cheaply collected, potentially adversarial Internet data.

claim: He prioritizes the most accurate training methods because he expects them to be more useful, while retaining older methods for comparison.
quote: The first three methods listed above are $3-10\times$ more accurate compared to the next four methods. As a result we believe these will be most useful in the future, and so focus on them.
context: Most experiments use MixMatch, UDA, and FixMatch; additional experiments include VAT, Mean Teacher, Pseudo Labels, and Pi Model.
uncertainty: Future usefulness is the author's stated expectation at publication.

claim: The experimental domain was deliberately restricted to image classification because the paper identified it as the principal domain with strong semi-supervised methods.
quote: Throughout this paper we study the problem of image classification, the primary domain where strong semi-supervised learning methods exist [42].
context: The background section establishes the scope before introducing the evaluated algorithms.
uncertainty: This is a contemporaneous assessment in a 2021 paper; the experiments do not establish results for every data modality.

claim: Density-function debugging examines where label propagation stops, distinguishing insufficient density near the target from difficulty initiating propagation near the source.
quote: We find that the label successfully propagates almost all the way to the final instance (to approximately $\alpha=.9$) but the attack fails to change the classification of the final target example. Conversely, for a function like $\rho(x)=x$, the label propagation usually fails near $\alpha=0$
context: A source-heavy squared density can leave the target end too sparse, whereas a density increasing toward the target can fail near the source.
uncertainty: These are observations for the evaluated functions and settings, not a complete theory of propagation.

claim: He chooses the default interpolation density empirically from eleven candidates, favoring somewhat more sampling near the source without leaving the target or middle too sparse.
quote: As a general rule, the best sampling strategies sample slightly more heavily from the source example, and less heavily from the target that will be poisoned.
context: The selected density is 1.5 minus the interpolation coordinate, producing three times greater density near the source than near the target.
uncertainty: The density comparison is conducted with FixMatch on CIFAR-10 and does not establish a universally optimal density.

claim: He adapts the bridge-example idea from clustering attacks but substitutes extensive experimentation for analytic optimization because stochastic-gradient training dynamics are harder to analyze.
quote: Thus, instead of being able to derive an optimal strategy, we must perform extensive experiments to understand how to form these bridges and understand when they will successfully poison the classifier.
context: The related-work discussion distinguishes the new neural-network attack from earlier analytically tractable clustering attacks.

claim: He extends the attack to remove knowledge of labeled training examples rather than leaving that assumption unexamined.
quote: Our first attack requires the adversary knows at least one example in the labeled dataset. While there are settings where this is realistic [52], in general an adversary might have no knowledge of the labeled training dataset. We now develop an attack that removes this assumption.
context: The zero-knowledge extension first tests the original attack without modification using an arbitrary unlabeled source.
uncertainty: Removing training-example knowledge does not remove every assumption in the broader threat model.

claim: He evaluates the detector even when the poisoning attack fails, reporting complete detection of inserted examples alongside a small increase in false positives.
quote: When the attack itself fails to poison the target class, it is still possible to identify all of the poisoned examples that have been inserted (i.e., with a true positive rate of $100\%$), but the false positive rate increases slightly to $0.1\%$.
context: The defense is assessed against inserted malicious examples independently of whether they achieved the attack objective.
uncertainty: The rates describe the evaluated cases and are not deployment guarantees.

claim: Influence is operationalized through prediction changes lagged by one epoch, and Carlini labels this definition a simplistic approximation with limited representational scope.
quote: That is, example $u_{i}$ influences example $u_{j}$ if when example $u_{i}$ makes a particular change at epoch $k$, then example $u_{j}$ makes a similar change in the next epoch—because it has been influenced by $u_{i}$. This definition of influence is clearly a simplistic approximation, and is unable to capture sophisticated relationships between examples.
context: The implementation compares vectors containing epoch-to-epoch prediction deltas and a final prediction.
uncertainty: The quoted causal phrasing must be read alongside the preceding explicit correlation-versus-causation caveat.

claim: He proposes that stronger methods extract more meaning from unlabeled data, but explicitly considers attack-development bias as an alternative explanation.
quote: It is possible that, because we primarily experimented with recent techniques, we have implicitly designed our attack to work better on these techniques. We believe the simplicity of our attack makes this unlikely.
context: This caveat accompanies the observed relationship between technique accuracy and poisoning susceptibility.
uncertainty: The alternative explanation is acknowledged, not experimentally ruled out.

claim: He considers an inexpensive form of human screening that could reject obviously artificial blends even when full expert labeling is too expensive.
quote: While it may be prohibitively expensive for a human to label all of the examples in the unlabeled dataset, it may not be expensive to discard examples that are clearly incorrect.
context: This motivates replacing pixel-space blending with GAN-based semantic interpolation.
uncertainty: The relative screening costs are argued through examples rather than measured in a user study.

claim: He structures the evaluation by first establishing a narrow baseline and then expanding one dimension at a time.
quote: We begin by demonstrating the efficacy of our attack on one model (FixMatch) on one dataset (CIFAR-10) for one poison ratio (0.1%). Further sections will perform additional experiments that expand on each of these dimensions.
context: Later sections vary source-target pairs, training techniques, datasets, poisoning ratios, labeled-data counts, and interpolation densities.

claim: He reports unexplained heterogeneity in source and target suitability after attempting to understand it.
quote: Similarly, some source images (e.g., the last row) can poison almost any image, but other images (e.g., the top row) are poor sources. Despite several attempts, we have no explanation for why some images are easier or harder to attack.
context: The 40-by-40 grid reveals image-specific variation that class-level averages alone do not explain.
uncertainty: The paper does not describe those explanatory attempts in enough detail to reconstruct them.

claim: He tests semantic interpolation through a pretrained GAN to make injected examples less obviously suspicious.
quote: We use a DC-GAN [46] pre-trained on CIFAR-10 to perform the interpolations. We again perform the same attack as above, where we poison $1\%$ of the unlabeled examples by interpolating in between the latent spaces
context: The implementation supplements latent interpolation with short pixel-space connections because the GAN may not reconstruct the endpoint images exactly. The attack succeeds in nine of ten trials.
uncertainty: The supplied evaluation does not include a human study establishing that the images evade visual screening.

claim: He inspects near false positives and uses their visual similarity to understand what the detector is measuring.
quote: Even the near false positives of our defense are insightful to analyze. In Figure 8 we show five (representative) images of the benign examples in the CIFAR-10 training dataset that our defense almost rejects as if they were poisoned examples.
context: The near false positives are groups of nearly duplicate images whose predictions change together, explaining their low influence-distance scores.
uncertainty: The figure contains representative examples, not an exhaustive accounting of all near false positives.

claim: He makes an audience-specific terminology choice by avoiding the abbreviation SSL in a security paper.
quote: We refrain from using the typical abbreviation, SSL, in a security paper.
context: A footnote explains the decision to spell out semi-supervised learning.
uncertainty: The footnote states the choice but does not explicitly elaborate its rationale.

claim: Dataset selection varies scale and realism: SVHN tests larger datasets, while STL-10 supplies naturally unlabeled data from a similar but nonidentical distribution.
quote: with an additional $100,000$ unlabeled images drawn from a similar (but not identical) distribution, making it our most realistic dataset.
context: STL-10 complements CIFAR-10 and SVHN, whose semi-supervised configurations are created by discarding most labels.
uncertainty: Most realistic is a comparison among this paper's datasets, not a claim that STL-10 captures deployment conditions fully.

claim: He checks sensitivity to the defense's nearest-neighbor count rather than presenting the chosen value of five as uniquely justified.
quote: (Our result is not sensitive to the arbitrary choice of $5$; values from $2$ to $10$ perform similarly.)
context: The detector averages its influence-distance measure over the five closest neighbors.
uncertainty: The reported robustness is limited to this range and the experiments in the paper.

claim: The default interpolation density was chosen empirically from eleven candidates, with the selected function placing three times as much density near the source as near the target.
quote: Experimentally the best density function we identified was $\rho(x)=1.5-x$, which samples three times more heavily around the source example $x^{\prime}$ than around the target $x^{*}$.
context: Section 3.2.7 compares candidate density functions under three poisoning ratios using FixMatch on CIFAR-10.
uncertainty: Best refers to the tested candidates and conditions, not a proven globally optimal density.

claim: The paper carefully distinguishes improved algorithms from additional labeled data: higher accuracy across techniques does not imply that every way of improving accuracy increases vulnerability.
quote: Notice that our prior observation comparing technique accuracy to vulnerability does not imply more accurate models are more vulnerable—with more training data, models are able to learn with less guesswork and so become less vulnerable.
context: Section 3.2.6 varies the number of labeled examples; Table 2 says additional labels often, but not always, improve robustness.
uncertainty: The table contains exceptions, so the explanation should not be converted into an unconditional monotonic rule.

claim: The paper explicitly acknowledges that eight trials are fewer than desirable and explains the replication limit through training cost.
quote: While it would clearly be preferable to run each experiment with more than 8 trials, semi-superivsed machine learning algorithms are extremely slow to train: one run of FixMatch takes $20$-GPU hours on CIFAR-10, and over five days on STL-10.
context: The full evaluation is described as requiring hundreds of GPU-days despite the limited trials per condition.
uncertainty: This documents a project-specific resource tradeoff, not a general stopping policy.

claim: He identifies stalled propagation as an unresolved failure mode in which continued training ceases to change pseudo-label assignments.
quote: Even if $t=0.9$, and the propagation has made it almost all the way to the final label, past a certain time in training the model’s label assignments become fixed and the predicted labels no longer change. It would be interesting to better understand why these failures occur.
context: Some attacks propagate the desired label through most of the bridge but never reach the final target.
uncertainty: This describes a training plateau, not an explicit personal rule for stopping an experiment or abandoning a project.

claim: He starts with linear pixel blending as the simplest interpolation satisfying the attack's requirements, establishing its utility before introducing more sophisticated constructions.
quote: To begin we use the simplest strategy: linear pixel-wise blending between the original example $x^{\prime}$ and the target example $x^{*}$.
context: Interpolation Consistency Poisoning connects a labeled source example to the target through inserted unlabeled examples.
uncertainty: This establishes a local design choice, not a universal preference for simple methods.

claim: Concern that a successful eight-trial baseline might depend on particular images leads him to evaluate a much larger grid of source-target combinations.
quote: In order to ensure our attack remains consistently effective, we now train an additional $40\times 40$ models. For each model, we construct a different poison set
context: The grid selects 40 source and 40 target images, with four images from each class.
uncertainty: The expanded grid uses reduced training and therefore is not directly equivalent to the full-training baseline.

claim: The paper explicitly acknowledges that its observational training-dynamics measurements cannot fully separate correlation from causation without changing the training process.
quote: While we can not completely isolate out correlation and causation without modifying the training process, we make the following observation that is fundamental to this defense:
context: The defense assumes that if one example influences another, their prediction changes should be related over time.
uncertainty: This caveat limits causal interpretation of the influence score even when it classifies poisons accurately.

claim: He standardizes the architecture around a small, established benchmark model and checks that targeted poisoning preserves ordinary accuracy.
quote: This model has become the standard benchmark model for semi-supervised learning [42] due to its relative simplicity and small size while also reaching near state-of-the-art results [53]. In all experiments we confirm that poisoning the unlabeled dataset maintains standard accuracy.
context: The common architecture is a 1.4-million-parameter ResNet-28.

claim: Despite strong experimental separation, Carlini explicitly anticipates future attacks defeating the defense and frames the approach as a promising baseline rather than a final solution.
quote: It is likely that future attacks will defeat this defense, too. However, we believe that defenses of this style are a promising direction that (a) serve as a strong baseline for defending against unlabeled dataset poisoning attacks, and (b) could be extended in future work.
context: This qualification appears in a dedicated discussion of counter-attacks after the defense results.
uncertainty: The anticipated future defeat is a forecast, not an attack demonstrated in this paper.

claim: The defense analysis considers the utility cost of removing falsely flagged data and reports no statistically significant clean-accuracy loss from retaining 99.9% of the unlabeled set.
quote: Even if extra training data is not collected, training on $99.9\%$ of the unlabeled dataset with the false positives removed does not statistically significantly reduce clean model accuracy.
context: The paper also suggests collecting extra unlabeled data to compensate for removals.
uncertainty: The supplied passage does not specify the statistical test, confidence interval, or power; lack of statistical significance is not proof of zero cost.

claim: Dataset selection included a case intended to improve realism: STL-10 combines higher-resolution labeled images with a larger unlabeled set from a similar but nonidentical distribution.
quote: STL-10 [12] is a dataset designed for semi-supervised learning. It contains just $1,000$ labeled images (at a higher-resolution, $96\times 96$), with an additional $100,000$ unlabeled images drawn from a similar (but not identical) distribution, making it our most realistic dataset.
context: The evaluation also uses CIFAR-10 and SVHN, whose semi-supervised versions are constructed by discarding labels.
uncertainty: Most realistic is relative to the paper's three experimental datasets, not a claim that STL-10 reproduces production data collection.

claim: Giving the attacker an additional correctly labeled poisoned example does not improve on selecting a good natural source in the tested strategies.
quote: We attempted various strategies to do this, ranging from inserting out-of-distribution data [48] to mounting a Poison Frog attack [51]. However, none of these ideas worked better than just choosing a good source example as determined in Figure 3.
context: The extension combines labeled and unlabeled poisoning capabilities.
uncertainty: The paper also states that good sources cannot yet be predicted without brute-force training; it does not provide an efficient source-selection solution.

claim: Carlini's proposed review workflow uses automated filtering to restrict human attention to a small subset and asks for coarse plausibility judgments rather than expensive fine-grained labels.
quote: Our methods directly process the unlabeled dataset and filter out a small subset of the examples to have reviewed by a human for general correctness (e.g., “does this resemble anything like a dog?” compared to “which of the 100+ breeds of dog in the ImageNet dataset is this?”).
context: The defense aims to preserve the cost advantage of unlabeled data while allowing limited human review.
uncertainty: The supplied experiments evaluate automated detection and removal, not a measured human-review deployment.

claim: The GAN interpolation extension handles imperfect image reconstruction explicitly by adding short bridges between the real endpoint images and their generated approximations.
quote: Thus, we perform the attack as above interpolating between $G(z^{\prime})$ and $G(z^{*})$ and then finally perform the small interpolation between $x^{\prime}$ and $G(z^{\prime})$, and similarly $x^{*}$ and $G(z^{*})$.
context: Exact latent vectors reproducing arbitrary source and target images may not exist, so latent-space interpolation alone would not connect the required endpoints.
uncertainty: The method assumes reconstruction error is small enough for these additional bridges to be practical.

claim: Under a fixed insertion budget, experiments favored concentrating all poisons on one source-to-target path over distributing them among several alternative paths.
quote: However, for the same insertion budget, experimentally we find it is always better to use the entire budget on one single path from $x^{\prime}$ to $x^{*}$ than to spread it out among multiple paths.
context: The rejected extension was motivated by the possibility that one path could succeed when another broke.
uncertainty: Always describes the reported experiments; it is not a theorem and does not contradict the differently structured support paths used in the zero-knowledge extension.

claim: He limits cross-dataset evaluation to configurations with evidence of useful clean performance, omitting UDA on STL-10.
quote: Table 1 reports results for FixMatch, UDA, and MixMatch, as these are the methods that achieve high accuracy. (We omit UDA on STL-10 because it was not shown effective on this dataset in [66].)
context: The broader evaluation otherwise covers three datasets and poisoning ratios of 0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.5%.
uncertainty: The omission relies on the cited prior evaluation rather than a newly reported UDA/STL-10 experiment.

claim: The attack constructs a path between a labeled source and a target so that successive pseudo-label assignments eventually mislabel the target.
quote: As in the begnign setting, the model will progressively assign higher confidence for this label on this example. Then, the semi-supervised learning algorithms will encourage nearby samples
context: The source has the desired attack label; injected interpolations connect it to the example whose prediction the attacker wants to change.
uncertainty: The described mechanism is subsequently investigated through saved training predictions; it is not presented as a proof of success for every path.

claim: He explicitly wants to avoid defenses whose success depends on fragile pixel-distance assumptions and can be undone by small changes to the attack.
quote: However, if the adversary inserted examples that applied color-jitter, or small translations, this defense would no longer able to identify the cluster of poisoned examples. This is a cat-and-mouse game we want to avoid.
context: Agglomerative clustering detects the evaluated interpolation paths, but its usefulness depends on a suitable distance function.
uncertainty: The passage identifies a limitation and design preference; it does not establish that the subsequent defense avoids all adaptive counterattacks.

claim: He turns the proposed label-propagation mechanism into observable predictions and records model outputs after every epoch to test them.
quote: We validate this intuition by saving all intermediate model predictions after every epoch of training. This gives us a collection of model predictions for each epoch, for each poisoned example in the unlabeled dataset.
context: The predicted signatures are rising confidence and sequential acquisition of the target label along the bridge; a training-run visualization shows this progression.
uncertainty: The detailed figure illustrates one FixMatch run rather than proving the mechanism for every successful attack.

claim: He diagnoses unsuccessful sampling densities by locating where label propagation breaks, distinguishing insufficient support near the source from insufficient support near the target.
quote: We find that the label successfully propagates almost all the way to the final instance (to approximately $\alpha=.9$) but the attack fails to change the classification of the final target example.
context: A density proportional to (1−x)² oversamples the source and undersamples the target; a density proportional to x instead tends to fail near the source.
uncertainty: These are observed failure patterns for the evaluated densities and setup.

claim: The zero-knowledge results distinguish targeted success from merely causing any error: only roughly half reach the desired label at a 1% poisoning rate, although all evaluated attacks mislabel the target.
quote: Our attack success rate is lower, with roughly half of attacks succeeding at $1\%$ of training data poisoned.
