All of these attacks succeed at making the target example $x^{*}$ becoming mislabeled (i.e., $f(x^{*})\neq c(x^{*})$) even though it is not necessary labeled as the desired target label.
context: This separates the original targeted objective from a weaker untargeted outcome.
uncertainty: All refers to the reported experimental attacks, not every possible zero-knowledge attack.

claim: The zero-knowledge experiment produces an unexpected failure mode: the endpoints often converge to a third label, which Carlini traces to an intermediate image crossing the confidence threshold first.
quote: We found that the reason this happens is that, by chance, some intermediate image $x_{\alpha}$ will exceed the confidence threshold. Once this happens, both $x_{\alpha_{1}}$ and $x_{\alpha_{N-1}}$ become classified as however $x_{\alpha}$ was classified—which often is not the label as either endpoint.
context: Merely connecting an arbitrary source and target preserves label agreement without reliably controlling which label wins.
uncertainty: The paper presents this as its diagnosis but does not provide a separate quantitative causal-ablation result in the supplied passage.

claim: He chooses a simpler, faster proxy for influence rather than importing more sophisticated influence-function machinery when the proxy is sufficient for the evaluated defense.
quote: We further find that it is not necessary to resort to such sophisticated approaches, and a simpler (and $10-100\times$ faster) method is able to effectively recover influence.
context: The question is how one unlabeled training example influences another during training, rather than how a training example affects a test prediction.
uncertainty: The speed and adequacy claims concern this defense; the proxy is not presented as equivalent to rigorous influence functions.

claim: He bounds the empirical domain to image classification because that is where he identifies strong semi-supervised learning methods.
quote: Throughout this paper we study the problem of image classification, the primary domain where strong semi-supervised learning methods exist [42].
context: This scope is stated in the background discussion of semi-supervised learning.
uncertainty: The justification reflects the paper's 2021 context.

claim: He uses randomized source-target pairs while holding those sampled pairs fixed within comparative displays to reduce noise between experimental conditions.

quote: We validate this intuition by saving all intermediate model predictions after every epoch of training. This gives us a collection of model predictions for each epoch, for each poisoned example in the unlabeled dataset.

uncertainty: The principal visualization shows one FixMatch training run; it illustrates the mechanism without proving it explains every outcome.

claim: Carlini extrapolates cautiously from the semi-supervised results to other training on uncurated data, explicitly expressing self-supervised vulnerability as an expectation for future investigation.
quote: We expect that other forms of unlabeled training, such as self-supervised learning, will be similarly vulnerable to these types of attacks. We hope our analysis will allow future work to perform additional study of this phenomenon in other settings where uncurated data is used to train machine learning models.
context: The conclusion connects data quality and origin to a broader research agenda.
uncertainty: The paper does not experimentally establish this extension to self-supervised learning.

claim: He responds to the zero-knowledge failure mode by adding support paths from additional images to the source, increasing the chance that the desired source label takes hold.
quote: In order to better regularize the attack process we provide additional support. To do this, we choose additional images $\{\hat{x}_{i}\}$ and then connect each of these examples to $x^{\prime}$ with a path, blending as we do with the target example.
context: This modifies the construction after the unmodified zero-knowledge attack produces uncontrolled labels.
uncertainty: The added support improves the intended behavior without restoring the baseline attack's success rate or poisoning budget.

claim: He excludes an algorithm-dataset combination when the original method had not demonstrated effectiveness there.
quote: Table 1 reports results for FixMatch, UDA, and MixMatch, as these are the methods that achieve high accuracy. (We omit UDA on STL-10 because it was not shown effective on this dataset in [66].)
context: The cross-dataset evaluation covers CIFAR-10, SVHN, and STL-10 with this explicit omission.
uncertainty: The omission relies on the cited prior evaluation; the paper does not establish that UDA could never work on STL-10.

claim: He qualifies the accuracy-vulnerability result by distinguishing better training techniques from improvements obtained through additional labeled data.
quote: Notice that our prior observation comparing technique accuracy to vulnerability does not imply more accurate models are more vulnerable—with more training data, models are able to learn with less guesswork and so become less vulnerable.
context: The labeled-data experiment varies the number of labels from 40 to 250 to 4,000.
uncertainty: The table shows that extra labels often, but not always, reduce vulnerability; FixMatch remains particularly vulnerable.

claim: Carlini inspects near false positives to understand detector behavior and finds visually near-duplicate benign images whose correlated prediction changes resemble the detector's poisoning signal.
quote: Because these examples are all nearly identical, they heavily influence each other according to our definition. When one examples prediction changes, the other examples predictions are likely to change as well. This also explains why removing near-false-positives does not reduce model accuracy.
context: Figure 8 displays representative benign images nearly rejected by the defense alongside their nearest neighbors under the influence measure.
uncertainty: The explanation concerns representative inspected examples and should not be generalized to every possible false positive.

claim: He stages the evaluation from a single model, dataset, and poisoning ratio, then expands along those dimensions.
quote: We begin by demonstrating the efficacy of our attack on one model (FixMatch) on one dataset (CIFAR-10) for one poison ratio (0.1%). Further sections will perform additional experiments that expand on each of these dimensions.
context: The preliminary experiment succeeds in seven of eight trials, prompting investigation of whether success depends on the chosen images.
uncertainty: The passage describes the paper's evaluation structure; it does not necessarily establish the chronological order in which every experiment was conceived.

claim: He supports the training-dynamics detector with separation plots across multiple runs, algorithms, and datasets rather than only one illustrative histogram.
quote: Appendix B shows 8 more plots for additional runs of FixMatch and MixMatch on CIFAR-10, and SVHN.
context: The main example is a FixMatch model trained with 40 labeled CIFAR-10 examples and a 0.2% poisoning ratio.
uncertainty: The supplementary evidence broadens the demonstrated cases but does not establish protection against every attack variant or future adaptive attack.

claim: An unexpected zero-knowledge failure leads him to inspect which intermediate example first crosses the confidence threshold.
quote: We found that the reason this happens is that, by chance, some intermediate image $x_{\alpha}$ will exceed the confidence threshold.
context: The bridge endpoints frequently converge to a label belonging to neither endpoint because an intermediate image seeds propagation.
uncertainty: The paper gives this mechanistic explanation without a separately quantified causal intervention.

claim: The evaluation uses a common benchmark architecture and checks that successful targeted poisoning preserves ordinary test accuracy, preventing indiscriminate model degradation from serving as the apparent attack result.
quote: We train all models with the same $1.4$ million parameter ResNet-28 [19] model that reaches $96.38\%$ fully-supervised accuracy. This model has become the standard benchmark model for semi-supervised learning [42] due to its relative simplicity and small size while also reaching near state-of-the-art results [53]. In all experiments we confirm that poisoning the unlabeled dataset maintains standard accuracy.
context: This describes the main experimental setup; a later diagnostic experiment deliberately uses smaller models to reduce accuracy.
uncertainty: The architecture statement should not erase the explicitly described smaller-model exception.

claim: With a fixed insertion budget, he finds that concentrating examples on one path is more effective than spreading them over several supposedly redundant paths.
quote: However, for the same insertion budget, experimentally we find it is always better to use the entire budget on one single path
context: The rejected variant connects multiple sources independently to the target, hoping another path will succeed if one breaks.
uncertainty: Always refers to the reported experiments; no universal optimality proof is provided.

claim: To investigate whether the initial success depended on particular images, Carlini expanded evaluation to 1,600 source-target combinations balanced across the ten classes.
quote: In order to ensure our attack remains consistently effective, we now train an additional $40\times 40$ models. For each model, we construct a different poison set by selecting $40$ source (respectively, target) images from the training (testing) sets, with $4$ images from each of the $10$ classes.
context: This follows an explicit concern that eight trials might conceal variation in source or target difficulty.
uncertainty: The expanded sweep uses reduced data and training, so its success rate is not directly interchangeable with the full-training baseline.

claim: He accommodates imperfect GAN inversion by adding short interpolation segments between real endpoint images and their generated approximations.
quote: Thus, we perform the attack as above interpolating between $G(z^{\prime})$ and $G(z^{*})$ and then finally perform the small interpolation between $x^{\prime}$ and $G(z^{\prime})$, and similarly $x^{*}$ and $G(z^{*})$.
context: A latent vector cannot always reproduce the exact source or target image, so the construction must connect the generated path to the actual endpoints.

claim: Carlini focuses the investigation exclusively on unlabeled-data poisoning because comprehensive human review would undermine the economic reason for using unlabeled data.
quote: Our analysis focuses on the key distinguishing factor of semi-supervised learning: we exclusively poison the unlabeled dataset. These attacks are especially powerful because the natural defense that adds additional human review to the unlabeled data eliminates the value of collecting unlabeled data (as opposed to labeled data) in the first place.
context: The introduction motivates a threat model around inexpensive data collection and limited review.

claim: He frames the vulnerability as an amplification of machine learning's underspecification problem: semi-supervised training leaves both the solution procedure and some target labels unspecified.
quote: Our attacks show this under-specification problem is exacerbated with semi-supervised learning: now, on top of not specifying how a task should be solved, we do not even completely specify what should be done.
context: This conceptual framing motivates attacking the process by which models generate their own training labels.
uncertainty: This is the paper's explanatory framing, not an independently established general theory of all semi-supervised vulnerabilities.

claim: He defines an operational influence score through lagged similarities in prediction changes and directly labels it a useful but limited approximation.
quote: This definition of influence is clearly a simplistic approximation, and is unable to capture sophisticated relationships between examples. We nevertheless find that this definition of influence is useful.
context: Prediction-change sequences for one example are compared with the next-epoch sequences of another.
uncertainty: Successful detection does not imply that the score recovers every relevant relationship between training examples.

claim: The experimental presentation expands in stages from one algorithm, dataset, and poisoning ratio to broader tests along those dimensions.
quote: We begin by demonstrating the efficacy of our attack on one model (FixMatch) on one dataset (CIFAR-10) for one poison ratio (0.1%). Further sections will perform additional experiments that expand on each of these dimensions.
context: The initial eight-trial result is followed by source-target, algorithm, dataset, label-count, and density evaluations.
uncertainty: The paper's presentation order does not necessarily establish the exact historical order in which every experiment was performed.

claim: Carlini turns the proposed propagation mechanism into observable predictions and records model outputs after every epoch to check them.
quote: We validate this intuition by saving all intermediate model predictions after every epoch of training. This gives us a collection of model predictions for each epoch, for each poisoned example in the unlabeled dataset.
context: The predicted signatures are increasing confidence and source-to-target ordering along the interpolation path; Figure 5 visualizes a FixMatch run.
uncertainty: The visualization supports the mechanism but does not establish that all successful runs follow an identical trajectory.

claim: He develops a second defense around how examples affect training, looking for poisoned examples whose behavior depends on only a few other examples.
quote: By monitoring the training dynamics of the semi-supervised learning algorithm, we isolate out (and then remove) those examples that are influenced by only a few other examples.
context: The motivating distinction is between benign examples influenced by many neighbors and poison bridges designed mainly to influence themselves.
uncertainty: The motivating distinction is specific to the attack structure studied and need not hold for arbitrary poisoning strategies.

claim: He extends the baseline threat model by removing the assumption that the adversary knows a labeled training example.
quote: Our first attack requires the adversary knows at least one example in the labeled dataset. While there are settings where this is realistic [52], in general an adversary might have no knowledge of the labeled training dataset. We now develop an attack that removes this assumption.
context: The zero-knowledge extension initially connects the target to an arbitrary unlabeled source.
uncertainty: Removing training-example knowledge does not mean eliminating every assumption about the model or training procedure.

claim: He attributes the failure of greedy density optimization to interactions among inserted examples, which make individual-example influence difficult to measure.
quote: Unfortunately, each of these attempts failed for the same reason: the presence or absence of one particular example is not independent of the other examples. Therefore, it is difficult to accurately measure the true influence of any particular example
context: The unsuccessful searches become trapped in local minima and require more insertions than simpler density constructions.
uncertainty: This is the paper's explanation of the observed optimization failures, not a formal impossibility result.

claim: He explicitly acknowledges that eight trials are fewer than desirable and explains the limitation through the substantial training cost.
quote: While it would clearly be preferable to run each experiment with more than 8 trials, semi-superivsed machine learning algorithms are extremely slow to train: one run of FixMatch takes $20$-GPU hours on CIFAR-10, and over five days on STL-10.
context: The paper reports that even eight trials per condition produce an evaluation costing hundreds of GPU-days.
uncertainty: This is an explicit resource constraint, not evidence of a general statistical stopping rule.

claim: Carlini explicitly wants to avoid a defense cycle in which simple attacker transformations defeat a fixed similarity metric, motivating a move beyond direct dataset geometry.
quote: However, if the adversary inserted examples that applied color-jitter, or small translations, this defense would no longer able to identify the cluster of poisoned examples. This is a cat-and-mouse game we want to avoid.
context: This criticism of clustering precedes the training-dynamics defense.
uncertainty: The passage states an anticipated evasion and design preference; it does not provide a quantitative evaluation of those transformed attacks.

claim: His proposed defense workflow combines automated triage with limited human inspection, preserving much of the cost advantage of unlabeled data.
quote: we believe that by combining automatic techniques to identify potentially-malicious examples, and then manually reviewing these limited number of cases, it may be possible to prevent this attack.
context: Rather than requiring full relabeling, the defense isolates a small subset for review or removal.
uncertainty: The human-review component is proposed; the paper's numerical evaluations primarily concern automated identification and removal.

claim: Carlini tests a standard clustering implementation before developing a more specialized defense, finding that the inserted poisons form a removable cluster under the evaluated distance representation.
quote: Indeed, running a standard implementation of agglomerative clustering [45] is effective at identifying the poisoned examples in our attacks. Thus, by removing the largest cluster, we can completely prevent this attack.
context: The clustering defense groups examples by similarity, including pixel-space distance.
uncertainty: The paper immediately identifies distance-function dependence as a significant limitation; largest-cluster removal is not established as generally safe.

claim: To make the large source-target grid feasible, he reduces both dataset size and training duration and explicitly reports the associated reduction in attack success.
quote: To reduce training time, we remove half of the unlabeled examples (and maintain a $0.1\%$ poison ratio of the now-reduced-size dataset) and train for a quarter the number of epochs.
context: The reduced setup produces 51% attack success, compared with more than 80% in the full-training baseline.
uncertainty: Dataset size and training duration change together, so this experiment does not isolate their individual effects.

claim: Carlini offers stronger extraction of information from unlabeled data as a hypothesis for increased vulnerability, while acknowledging that concentrating development on newer methods could have favored those attacks.
quote: We hypothesize this is caused by the better techniques extracting more “meaning” from the unlabeled data. (It is possible that, because we primarily experimented with recent techniques, we have implicitly designed our attack to work better on these techniques. We believe the simplicity of our attack makes this unlikely.)
context: This qualifies the observed relationship between algorithm accuracy and attack success.
uncertainty: The explanation remains a hypothesis; the paper's appeal to simplicity does not rule out attack-development bias.

claim: Giving the attacker additional power to inject one correctly labeled poison does not outperform choosing a good ordinary source in the tested strategies.
quote: We attempted various strategies to do this, ranging from inserting out-of-distribution data [48] to mounting a Poison Frog attack [51]. However, none of these ideas worked better than just choosing a good source example as determined in Figure 3.
context: The joint labeled/unlabeled extension is reported as a negative result. The paper says good source examples cannot yet be predicted except by brute-force training.
uncertainty: The result does not establish that all possible joint attacks are ineffective.

claim: Carlini attributes the failed density searches to interactions among poisoned examples: individual-example influence could not be treated independently, and greedy optimization became trapped in worse solutions than a simple density.
quote: Unfortunately, each of these attempts failed for the same reason: the presence or absence of one particular example is not independent of the other examples. Therefore, it is difficult to accurately measure the true influence of any particular example, and greedy searches typically got stuck in local minima
context: The paper reports that the resulting local minima required more insertions than a constant-density construction with fewer starting examples.
uncertainty: This explains failures of the attempted searches, not impossibility of optimizing the density by other methods.

claim: Despite strong measured defense performance, he expects future counterattacks and positions the method as a promising baseline rather than a final solution.
quote: No defense is full-proof, and this defense is no different. It is likely that future attacks will defeat this defense, too.
context: The following sentence argues that training-dynamics defenses provide a strong baseline and a direction for extension.
uncertainty: Future defeat is a forecast, not an attack demonstrated in this paper.

claim: He chooses the default interpolation density empirically from eleven candidate functions, using a distribution that samples three times more heavily near the source than near the target.
quote: Unless otherwise specified, in this paper we use the sampling function $\rho(x)=1.5-x$. This is the function that we found to be most effective in an experiment across eleven candidate density functions—see Section 3.2.7 for details.
context: The density controls where a fixed budget of poisoned examples is placed along the interpolation path.
uncertainty: Best among the tested candidates does not imply a globally optimal density.

claim: Despite prioritizing recent high-performing algorithms, he includes four older methods to broaden the evaluation.
quote: Nevertheless, for completeness we consider older methods as well: we include evaluations of Virtual Adversarial Training [39], PiModel [31], Mean Teacher [59], and Pseudo Labels [33].
context: The older algorithms are less accurate in the paper's benchmark setting.

claim: He draws a conditional deployment conclusion: training on unlabeled data from untrusted sources requires poisoning defenses rather than indiscriminate ingestion.
quote: Training semi-supervised learning algorithms on real-world data will require defenses tailored to preventing poisoning attacks whenever collecting data from untrusted sources.
context: The conclusion connects the experimental attack to production systems collecting available unlabeled data.
uncertainty: This is a security recommendation derived from the studied threat model, not a deployment evaluation.

claim: He responds to unstable label selection in the zero-knowledge attack by adding support paths into the source example.
quote: These additional interpolations make it more likely for $x^{\prime}$ to be labeled correctly as $y^{*}$, and when this happens, then more likely that the attack will succeed.
context: Additional images are connected to the chosen source to help it acquire the desired label before propagation reaches the target.
uncertainty: This is an explicitly described modification within one project, not evidence of a career-level methodological change.

claim: Carlini tests semantic interpolation with a pretrained DC-GAN and reports nine successes in ten trials while using a larger poisoning budget than the headline baseline.
quote: We use a DC-GAN [46] pre-trained on CIFAR-10 to perform the interpolations. We again perform the same attack as above, where we poison $1\%$ of the unlabeled examples by interpolating in between the latent spaces of $z^{\prime}$ and $z^{*}$. Our attack succeeds in $9$ out of $10$ trials.
context: The extension addresses conspicuous pixel-space blends and uses 1% poisoning rather than the baseline's highlighted 0.1%.
uncertainty: These trials establish attack feasibility under their settings, not measured indistinguishability under human inspection.

claim: For the training-dynamics defense, he uses a much faster approximation rather than established sophisticated influence-function machinery.
quote: We further find that it is not necessary to resort to such sophisticated approaches, and a simpler (and $10-100\times$ faster) method is able to effectively recover influence.
context: The approximation compares one example's prediction changes with another example's changes in the following epoch.
uncertainty: Recover influence is operationalized by the paper's approximation and should not be read as exact causal identification.

claim: He proposes that better techniques are more vulnerable because they extract more meaning from unlabeled data, while explicitly considering whether attack development was biased toward recent methods.
quote: We hypothesize this is caused by the better techniques extracting more “meaning” from the unlabeled data. (It is possible that, because we primarily experimented with recent techniques, we have implicitly designed our attack to work better on these techniques. We believe the simplicity of our attack makes this unlikely.)
context: The paper finds higher poisoning success for the more accurate training techniques.
uncertainty: The mechanism is labeled a hypothesis, and simplicity does not experimentally rule out development bias.

claim: Carlini chooses a simpler, faster approximation to influence rather than applying more sophisticated influence-function machinery when the approximation suffices for the detection task.
quote: We further find that it is not necessary to resort to such sophisticated approaches, and a simpler (and $10-100\times$ faster) method is able to effectively recover influence.
context: The task concerns how unlabeled training examples influence one another, rather than how training points influence a test prediction.
uncertainty: Recovering influence here refers to the paper's operational proxy, not exact recovery of causal influence.

claim: To investigate why stronger techniques are more vulnerable, he deliberately degrades modern methods when improving the older methods is unavailable.
quote: Because it is not possible to artificially increase the accuracy of worse-performing techniques, we artificially decrease the accuracy of the state-of-the-art techniques.
context: He trains FixMatch, UDA, and MixMatch for fewer steps with a smaller model, reducing accuracy to roughly 70–80%.
uncertainty: This intervention changes training duration and model size together and establishes a relationship rather than isolating accuracy as a sole causal variable.

claim: Attack evaluation randomly selects both the target test example and an incorrect desired label, instead of reporting only hand-selected target-label combinations.
quote: To perform our experiments, we randomly select $x^{*}$ from among the examples in the test set, and then sample a label $y^{*}$ randomly among those that are different than the true label $c(x^{*})$.
context: Success requires the poisoned model to assign the selected example the particular desired incorrect label.
uncertainty: Random selection does not remove the uncertainty associated with the small number of trials used in many experiments.

claim: He extrapolates the study into a broader concern about training on data without regard to provenance or quality, while framing this as a possible source of vulnerabilities.
quote: More broadly, we believe that or analysis highlights that the recent trend where machine learning systems are trained on any and all available data, without regard to its quality or origin, might introduce new vulnerabilities.
context: The conclusion anticipates related vulnerabilities in other forms of unlabeled training, including self-supervised learning.
uncertainty: This is a broader hypothesis and research agenda; the paper's direct experiments concern semi-supervised image classification.

claim: He addresses uncertainty about source-target selection with a 40-by-40 grid of separately trained models, balancing image selection across all ten classes.
quote: In order to ensure our attack remains consistently effective, we now train an additional $40\times 40$ models. For each model, we construct a different poison set by selecting $40$ source (respectively, target) images from the training (testing) sets, with $4$ images from each of the $10$ classes.
context: This experiment examines heterogeneity hidden by aggregate attack success rates.
uncertainty: The grid uses a reduced training regime, so its absolute success rate is not directly equivalent to the full-training baseline.

claim: Before settling on a density sweep, he attempts more adaptive optimization through binary-search placement, pruning a dense bridge, and estimating local propagation distances.
quote: Initially, we attempted to analytically compute the optimal density function, however this did not end up succeeding. Our first attempt repeatedly trained classifiers and performed binary search to determine where along the bridge to insert new poisoned examples.
context: Another attempt begins with 500 interpolated examples and removes examples while the attack still succeeds.
uncertainty: The paper describes unsuccessful strategies but does not supply complete algorithms or quantitative comparisons for each.

claim: He generalizes the concern to indiscriminate data collection while presenting vulnerability in other unlabeled-learning settings as an expectation for future investigation.
quote: We expect that other forms of unlabeled training, such as self-supervised learning, will be similarly vulnerable to these types of attacks.
context: The conclusion calls for studying other settings where models train on uncurated data and raises data quality and origin as security concerns.
uncertainty: Self-supervised vulnerability is a forward-looking hypothesis here, not an empirical result of this paper.

claim: Despite strong measured defense results, he anticipates future counterattacks and positions the defense as a baseline for further work.
quote: No defense is full-proof, and this defense is no different. It is likely that future attacks will defeat this defense, too.
context: The following discussion describes training-dynamics defenses as a promising direction that can be extended.
uncertainty: This is an explicit expectation about future attacks, not evidence that a counterattack had already succeeded.

claim: The transfer-learning experiment separates initial training data from subsequently poisoned data and explicitly provides the initial weights to the attacker.
quote: We initialize our model with a semi-supervised learning model trained on the first $50\%$ of the unlabeled dataset to convergence. Then, we provide this initial model weights $\theta_{\text{init}}$ to the adversary.
context: The attacker inserts poisons into the second half, modifies 0.1% of the unlabeled dataset, and succeeds in eight of ten reported trials after training resumes.
uncertainty: This is a controlled fine-tuning experiment, not evidence that all pretrained-model workflows have the same susceptibility.

claim: He standardizes the main experimental setup around a widely used, relatively small architecture and checks that targeted poisoning preserves ordinary test accuracy.
quote: This model has become the standard benchmark model for semi-supervised learning [42] due to its relative simplicity and small size while also reaching near state-of-the-art results [53]. In all experiments we confirm that poisoning the unlabeled dataset maintains standard accuracy.
context: The main setup uses a 1.4-million-parameter ResNet-28; a later diagnostic experiment deliberately uses a smaller model.

claim: He evaluates the more visually plausible interpolation with a pretrained DC-GAN and reports nine successes in ten trials at a 1% poisoning ratio.
quote: We use a DC-GAN [46] pre-trained on CIFAR-10 to perform the interpolations. We again perform the same attack as above, where we poison $1\%$ of the unlabeled examples by interpolating in between the latent spaces of $z^{\prime}$ and $z^{*}$. Our attack succeeds in $9$ out of $10$ trials.
context: The extension demonstrates that the attack need not rely exclusively on direct pixel blends.
uncertainty: The experiment establishes attack success, not measured indistinguishability from benign images under human review.

claim: He quantifies the defense's operational tradeoff as an extra training run and checks whether removing falsely flagged examples harms clean accuracy.
quote: Thus, at cost of doubling the training time—training once with poisoned examples, and a second time after removing them—it is possible to completely prevent our attack.
context: The paper reports no statistically significant clean-accuracy reduction from retaining 99.9% of the unlabeled data after false-positive removals.
uncertainty: Complete prevention is claimed for the attack presented; details of the statistical test are not supplied in this passage.

claim: Carlini concentrated experiments on the most accurate techniques because he expected those techniques to be more useful, while still testing four older methods for broader coverage.
quote: We perform most experiments on the three most accurate techniques: MixMatch [3], UDA [66], and FixMatch [53], with additional experiments on VAT [39], Mean Teacher [59], Pseudo Labels [33], and Pi Model [31].
context: The following sentences justify this emphasis by the leading methods' accuracy advantage and anticipated future usefulness.
uncertainty: Expected usefulness is the paper's stated prioritization rationale, not independently established deployment prevalence.

claim: He reports an unexpected outcome in the zero-knowledge experiment: connected endpoints often receive a label belonging to neither endpoint's true class.
quote: Unexpectedly, we found that while the final label the model assigned was rarely $y^{*}=c(x^{\prime})$ (our attack objective label), and instead most often the final label was a label neither $y^{*}$ nor $c(x^{*})$.
context: Connecting two unlabeled examples still couples their eventual labels but does not reliably determine which label wins.

claim: The team used temporal visualizations as an independent behavioral check on the request-classification heuristic. Requests following a dataset's random index order supported the interpretation that clients were downloading that dataset.
quote: Indeed, because the ordering of URLs in the dataset index is random (instead of, say, alphabetical), a dataset download appears to be the only explanation for why the URLs would be linearly accessed in this particular order.
context: Plots ordered controlled URLs by their positions in the original index and colored requests by source IP.
uncertainty: The exclusion of other explanations is the authors' interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: The download-counting method explicitly trades sensitivity for confidence. It assumes one IP address per download and applies precision and recall conditions to distinguish dataset retrieval from unrelated crawling.
quote: To begin our analysis, we make a (significant) simplifying assumption that anyone downloading one of these datasets does so from a single IP address. We may thus underestimate the true rate at which each dataset is downloaded.
context: A counted download must retrieve at least 90% of controlled dataset URLs, touch all six domains, and devote at least 50% of its requests to dataset URLs.
uncertainty: Distributed downloads, changed IP addresses, and partial downloads may be missed.

claim: The live-domain experiment was designed to demonstrate control and observe exposure without introducing malicious training examples. Acquired URLs returned missing-content responses.
quote: We do not actually poison any datasets. For all URLs we own, we return a 404 Not Found response; so from the perspective of a dataset downloader our purchasing of the domain is completely transparent.
context: The study also provided an explanatory landing page and a contact address for former domain owners.
uncertainty: This statement concerns public datasets and live downloads; separate model experiments used locally modified training data.

claim: The project follows vulnerability reporting with implementation work: the authors contact maintainers, implement optional SHA-256 verification in a widely used downloader, and provide backup hashes for datasets with near-original data.
quote: We additionally implemented an option in img2dataset to verify SHA-256 image hashes upon download, thus preventing our attack for anyone using this tool, and provide our own backup of hashes
context: Section VI-B reports that six affected datasets had begun releasing image-content hashes at the time of writing.
uncertainty: Protection depends on using the verification option and appropriate trusted hashes; availability of the option alone does not establish universal adoption.

claim: The authors recognized that measuring old datasets could overstate exposure for users who downloaded them earlier, and used the release of COYO-700M during the project to test vulnerability immediately upon publication.
quote: Fortunately, the COYO-700M dataset was released during the writing of this research paper, on 30 August 2022. On that same day, we computed the fraction of the dataset that was vulnerable to our poisoning attack
context: The day-zero measurement found 0.1% of images hosted on expired domains purchasable for less than $1,000.
uncertainty: This establishes an example of release-day vulnerability, not a measurement of every dataset on its release date.

claim: Compute cost materially shaped the experiment: all selected targets and both attack objectives were evaluated within one combined CLIP training run.
quote: The key technical constraint in our experiment is that all attacks need to be done in parallel to minimize costs, as retraining CLIP is quite expensive.
context: Appendix B reports training a ViT-B-32 model for 32 epochs with batch size 3072 on 16 A100 GPUs.
uncertainty: The combined design does not provide independent retraining replications for each target or objective.

claim: The timing defenses are derived from the attack’s prerequisite: forcing malicious content to survive long enough for moderation makes opportunistic snapshot timing less useful.
quote: This can be achieved in one of two ways: (1) curators can randomize the snapshot order
context: The alternatives are randomized, sufficiently extended snapshotting or delayed release with trusted moderators’ corrections applied before finalization.
uncertainty: Effectiveness depends on moderation latency and trusted correction handling; these are proposed defenses rather than reported deployments.

claim: The frontrunning analysis changes the attack assumptions explicitly: it relinquishes sustained control of content in exchange for an ability to predict when the content will be collected.
quote: Our second attack removes the assumption that the adversary has sustained control over the web data in a training set. To do this we make a new assumption: that we can predict precisely when the web content will be downloaded.
context: Section V studies Wikipedia snapshots, where malicious edits may be quickly reverted on the live site but persist in a static snapshot.
uncertainty: This is a change between threat models within the paper, not evidence of a change in Carlini's personal research views.

claim: The passive monitoring sample combines high-coverage and randomly selected domains: three domains hosting the most images and three randomly selected buyable domains per dataset.
quote: For each dataset, we purchase the three most popular expired and buyable domains (that is, the domains available for purchase that hosted the most images), and three randomly selected domains that were available for purchase.
context: Requests were logged with access time, a hash of the IP address, requested URL, and supplied headers.

claim: To investigate possible prior exploitation, the authors require a conjunction of changed image content and changed domain ownership, then examine candidates rather than labeling every content change malicious.
quote: We search for a signature of a domain-purchasing attack by looking for domains that (1) host images that have been modified since the initial dataset release and (2) have changed ownership since the initial dataset release.
context: Section IV-D combines image comparisons with domain purchase information from whois records.
uncertainty: This signature detects only a subset of possible poisoning mechanisms and cannot establish the absence of all attacks.

claim: The multilingual annotation method expands seed terms through manual inspection and then checks candidate terms for both newly captured reversions and false positives.
quote: We then sample comments with each of these newly identified words to verify that they capture new instances of reversions (that is, they are used to uniquely tag reversions in the language’s Wikipedia), and do not produce too many false positives.
context: The authors start from automated and manual reversion markers and words resembling revert or undo.
uncertainty: They explicitly state that no author is an active contributor to any language’s Wikipedia and do not claim a perfect reversion lexicon.

claim: The downstream experiment tested whether real purchase constraints still permitted consequential poisoning when captions could not be changed. The two objectives were targeted ImageNet misclassification and erroneous NSFW classification.
quote: For each of these attack objectives, we first identify appropriate text captions in LAION 400M for which the corresponding image domains can be purchased for a total of $1,000 USD. Then, we locally replace these images with poisoned samples to simulate the effect of an attack, without any potential to cause harm to others.
context: Section IV-E bridges measured domain control to model behavior using local replacements.
uncertainty: This was a local simulation of downstream impact, not an end-to-end poisoning of unsuspecting users.

claim: When exact article snapshot timestamps are unavailable, the authors reconstruct intervals from edit histories and tighten them using the sequential order in which articles are processed.
quote: For each article, we thus know that the snapshot time $t_{i}$ was in-between the times of the article’s last included edit (top-most blue point) and the first non-included edit (bottom-most orange point).
context: Section V-B uses neighboring articles' included and excluded edits to narrow initially loose intervals, then fits crawl timing within each worker's sequence.
uncertainty: The reconstructed intervals bound unknown times; they are not direct observations of exact snapshot timestamps.

claim: The attack-surface measurement required repeated evidence of domain expiration across both geography and time, rather than classifying a domain from a single failed lookup.
quote: To measure this, we perform an nslookup on every domain name in the dataset from two geographically distinct data-centers in May 2022 and August 2022 and report the domain as expired if all four lookups result in a NXDOMAIN response.
context: Section IV-B operationalizes expiration before separately checking whether a registrar offers the domain for sale.
uncertainty: Expiration is the study's DNS-based operational definition; buyability is checked separately.

claim: The local attack construction selects targets that are compatible with the existing, unmodifiable captions and a real domain budget. Ten ImageNet target classes must each appear sufficiently often in captions associated with cheaply buyable domains.
quote: We pick 10 classes as target labels for poisoning, such that captions containing the label appear at least 1000 times in the captions linked to cheap buyable domains; see Table I.
context: Appendix B replaces 1,000 images per selected target while keeping captions fixed and constraining the total domain cost.
uncertainty: Target selection is constrained by available captions; the result does not establish equal feasibility for arbitrary desired classes.

claim: Manual follow-up changes the interpretation of suspicious CC3M domains: one serves advertisements after squatting, while two additional exact-hash candidates reflect lapsed DNS records and re-encoded images without changed ownership.
quote: However, further investigation reveals the ownership of these domains has not changed and the DNS record simply lapsed, and images were re-encoded.
context: Section IV-D does not treat the initially detected attack signature as sufficient proof of malicious dataset poisoning.

claim: The attack-timing optimization explicitly models opposing failure modes rather than treating earlier or later edits as uniformly better.
quote: This induces a tradeoff: the attacker should make edits early enough to ensure they do not miss the snapshot time, but late enough to maximize the chance of frontrunning editors.
context: The success bound uses conservative ends of the reconstructed snapshot intervals and sweeps an adjustment to predicted edit times.

claim: The authors imposed operational limits on their measurement activity and reported institutional ethics review, connecting practical feasibility work to explicit collection constraints.
quote: When searching for expired domains, we limit our DNS requests to 500/second, we only ask for the cost of purchasing the top-10,000 domains in each dataset, and only eventually purchase six. This research study was deemed “exempt” by our institution’s IRB.
context: Section IV-C's ethical considerations describe the collection as minimally invasive.
uncertainty: The IRB determination is reported by the authors; no review documentation is supplied.

claim: The authors report testing the noninterference behavior communicated to affected downloaders.
quote: We have tested that the 404 response we send will cause all standard image downloading tools to skip the image entirely.
context: The landing page explains that requests would otherwise have failed because the domain was expired, and says users need not specially exclude the research domains.
uncertainty: The supplied text does not enumerate the tested tools or provide their test results.

claim: The snapshot evaluation distinguishes uncertainty in reconstructing historical times from uncertainty in predicting the next snapshot.
quote: This provides an upper bound on the true estimation error—bounded by 27 minutes on average.
context: The first evaluation uses the maximum error relative to a ground-truth interval; the second compares extrapolated predictions with times estimated retrospectively for the next snapshot.
uncertainty: Twenty-seven minutes is an average upper bound for the historical fitting stage, not a universal per-article prediction guarantee.

claim: For immediate mitigation, the authors retain existing trust in dataset maintainers, curators, and downloaders rather than requiring a wholesale redesign before defenses can be deployed.
quote: These assumptions mirror the existing trust that clients place in maintainers, curators, and downloaders and thus represent the quickest, short-term path to enacting defenses.
context: Section VI-A distinguishes near-term defenses from later proposals that reduce trust assumptions.
uncertainty: These defenses do not address compromised or malicious trusted operators.

claim: Unexpectedly low complete-download counts for billion-image datasets lead the authors to examine usage patterns. They attribute some high-precision, low-recall traffic to users downloading subsets derived from larger datasets.
quote: We found that the reason for this is that these datasets are rarely downloaded in their entirety; instead, they serve as an upstream source for smaller subsets.
context: Examples include the Public Multimodal Dataset and LAION-Aesthetics, whose images are drawn largely from LAION-2B-en.
uncertainty: The paper supplies examples and traffic-pattern interpretation rather than a comprehensive accounting of all partial downloads.

claim: The local model experiment supplies behavioral evidence beyond infrastructure vulnerability, reporting success on both targeted classification objectives.
quote: The object-misclassification attack works for 60% of the targets: the chosen image gets classified as the target label by a zero-shot CLIP classifier. The NSFW attack works for 90% of targeted images.
context: The appendix describes ten target classes and ten benign images, with 1,000 replacement images per target.
uncertainty: These are results for selected targets in the reported shared training run. The main text and appendix contain inconsistent percentage representations of the 1,000-image poisoning count.

claim: For LAION-400M, the team constrained its historical comparison to the evidence actually preserved. Lacking original image bytes, it used original CLIP embeddings and qualified the negative finding as no evidence at present.
quote: We find no domain with such a signature in LAION-400M, and thus have no evidence at present that this attack would have been exploited against this dataset. Because we only have the original CLIP embeddings for this dataset (the original raw bytes were not saved), we only perform this comparison.
context: The analysis compared the original release with two later downloads and manually examined a sample of domains with modified images.
uncertainty: Embedding comparison and sampled investigation can miss changes or attacks; the finding is not an exhaustive absence claim.

claim: The team bounded the project around mechanisms specific to dataset poisoning rather than enlarging the attack surface with generic network interception or website exploitation.
quote: We focus our attacks on mechanisms that are unique to our study of dataset poisoning. Other potential security vulnerabilities (e.g., the ability of an adversary to interfere with unencrypted network requests, or to exploit website vulnerabilities to inject new content) are out of scope and would only improve our attack success rates.
context: Section III-C states the scope before presenting the two attack scenarios.

claim: The team broadened the analysis beyond English but restrained its takeaway: multilingual editions often appeared more vulnerable, while very large calculated poisoning fractions were not presented as realistic operational expectations.
quote: We reiterate that such large poisoning rates are unlikely to ever happen, due to IP bans or rate limiting.
context: Of 35 analyzed non-English editions, 22 had higher estimated vulnerability than English. Three editions lacked accessible checkpoints and Tagalog lacked sufficient data.
uncertainty: Sparse editing can also widen timing intervals and make the method especially conservative for some small editions.

claim: The multilingual extension used language-specific manual validation and explicitly acknowledged limited community expertise. The team checked newly identified terms for both additional true reversions and excessive false positives.
quote: We then sample comments with each of these newly identified words to verify that they capture new instances of reversions (that is, they are used to uniquely tag reversions in the language’s Wikipedia), and do not produce too many false positives.
context: Appendix A-A starts with automated reversion markers and terms resembling revert or undo; no author was an active contributor to any language's Wikipedia.
uncertainty: The authors do not claim complete or perfectly accurate reversion vocabularies.

claim: The study’s public-facing communication makes concrete commitments about data retention and participant withdrawal.
quote: Any data we have logged will be deleted upon completion of our study. If you would prefer not to participate in this study, please contact us via the email address below and we will delete any data you may have contributed to our study.
context: This text appeared on the landing pages of purchased domains, alongside an explanation of the study and an offer to return domains to their original owners.
uncertainty: The corpus documents the commitments, not independent verification that every promised deletion or domain disposition occurred.

claim: In responding to reviewers, the authors explicitly defend research on failures to deploy known protections as valuable security research.
quote: Performing research on areas where perfect defenses exist, but are rarely used, is still valuable.
context: The response challenges a program-committee concern that the attack depends on absent standard integrity protections, using SQL injection and memory-corruption defenses as analogies.
uncertainty: The response is coauthored; the critical meta-review itself is third-party speech and should not be attributed to Carlini.

claim: The threat model makes practical feasibility demanding by excluding insider knowledge, dishonest infrastructure operators, label modification, and alteration of the published URL index.
quote: We further assume all maintainers, curators and downloaders behave honestly and do not assist the adversary in any way. As such, the adversary has no control over the auxiliary data
context: The modeled adversary is relatively unskilled and resource constrained, and can modify only content served at a small number of existing dataset URLs.

claim: The download-counting method favored conservative identification over maximal recall. It assumed a single IP per download and required both broad coverage of controlled dataset URLs and a substantial fraction of requests matching the dataset.
quote: To begin our analysis, we make a (significant) simplifying assumption that anyone downloading one of these datasets does so from a single IP address. We may thus underestimate the true rate at which each dataset is downloaded.
context: A qualifying download needed at least 90% of controlled URLs, representation from all six domains, and at least 50% of requests directed to dataset URLs.
uncertainty: Distributed downloads, changing IP addresses, and subset downloads can escape these criteria.

claim: The study imposes operational limits on its measurement activity: bounded DNS request rates, price checks restricted to a subset of domains, and only six domain purchases per dataset.
quote: Our data collection is minimally invasive. When searching for expired domains, we limit our DNS requests to 500/second, we only ask for the cost of purchasing the top-10,000 domains in each dataset, and only eventually purchase six.
context: The paper reports that the institution's IRB deemed the study exempt.
uncertainty: The characterization as minimally invasive is the authors' assessment; the concrete limits are explicitly reported.

claim: The public study design included an ownership-restoration and closure plan: former owners could request their domains back, and the team said it would let acquired domains expire when the study ended.
quote: If you are the original owner of this domain, we would be happy to return it to you at your request to the above email address. We will let this domain expire when we have finished our research study.
context: Appendix C's landing-page FAQ addresses former domain owners directly.
uncertainty: This is a stated plan and conditional offer, not confirmation of completed transfers or expirations.

claim: The delayed-snapshot proposal included a trust restriction on subsequent changes: only trusted moderators' corrections should be applied, so attackers cannot exploit the review window through selective deletion or reversion.
quote: (Subsequent edits must be accepted from trusted moderators so as to avoid selective deletion or reversion by attackers.) Even a reasonable grace period of one day could have a significant impact on the number of malicious edits that will be caught.
context: The paper estimates that extending the review window from five minutes to one day would increase the observed reversion fraction from 50% to 90%.
uncertainty: This is a proposed defense evaluated through historical reversion statistics, not a reported deployment trial.

claim: The live-domain experiment demonstrates exposure without inserting poisoned content into other researchers’ downloads.
quote: We do not actually poison any datasets. For all URLs we own, we return a 404 Not Found response; so from the perspective of a dataset downloader our purchasing of the domain is completely transparent.
context: Root pages explain the study and offer to return accidentally expired domains to their original owners.
uncertainty: The statement concerns the live measurement study; separate poisoning experiments modify local dataset copies.

claim: The authors reject centralizing every distributed dataset as an immediately practical defense because deployment constraints matter alongside technical simplicity.
quote: While the simplest defense to split-view poisonings attack would be to convert the distributed dataset
context: The same sentence identifies monetary, privacy, and legal challenges as making this unrealistic. The proposed alternative attaches cryptographic hashes to the dataset index and checks downloaded content.
uncertainty: This is a conditional assessment of the studied ecosystem, not a claim that centralized datasets are always infeasible.

claim: The study addresses the alternative explanation that vulnerability is merely an artifact of dataset age by measuring a newly released dataset on its release day.
quote: On that same day, we computed the fraction of the dataset that was vulnerable to our poisoning attack and found that already $0.1\%$ of the images were hosted on expired domains that cost fewer than $1,000 USD to purchase.
context: COYO-700M appeared during the research process on 30 August 2022; the authors connect its immediate exposure to the time required to collect the dataset.

claim: In responding to reviewers, the authors defended the value of studying widespread failures to deploy known defenses. Their criterion of research importance included practical exposure, even when the underlying security mechanism was already understood.
quote: Performing research on areas where perfect defenses exist, but are rarely used, is still valuable.
context: Appendix E responds to a program-committee criticism that the attacks work only where standard integrity protection is absent, using SQL injection and memory corruption as analogies.
uncertainty: The reviewer criticism is external speech; only the authors' response is attributed to this collaborative work.

claim: The timing-defense design targets the attack's necessary duration of control. One proposed approach delays finalization and incorporates trusted moderators' later corrections into the snapshot.
quote: For our second approach which is more comprehensive, Wikipedia could create an initial snapshot of an an article, hold it for a period
context: Section VI-C proposes either randomized snapshot order over a longer period or a grace period followed by back-applied moderator reversions; subsequent edits must come from trusted moderators.
uncertainty: These are proposed mitigations, not reported deployed changes to Wikipedia.

claim: For transient content control, the team reframed the problem around snapshot timing. Static dataset snapshots can preserve a malicious edit even after the live source has been repaired.
quote: An attacker who can predict when a Wikipedia page will be scraped for inclusion in the snapshot can perform poisoning immediately prior to scraping. Even if the edit is quickly reverted, the snapshot will contain the malicious content— forever.
context: The frontrunning analysis separates prediction of an article's snapshot time from the time required for moderators to revert an edit.
uncertainty: Successful timing is a condition of this mechanism, not guaranteed by every malicious edit.

claim: The study connects security failures to how datasets are distributed in practice. Its attack selection follows from the economic, privacy, and legal constraints that make datasets mutable collections of URLs or periodic snapshots rather than fixed artifacts.
quote: Our attacks exploit critical weaknesses in the current trust assumptions of web-scale datasets: due to a combination of monetary, privacy, and legal restrictions, many existing datasets are not published as static, standalone artifacts.
context: The two resulting attack settings are distributed dataset downloads and centralized snapshots.

claim: Manual follow-up distinguishes suspicious measurements from malicious exploitation instead of treating every changed hash and renewed domain as an attack.
quote: If we instead compare cryptographic hashes of images, we find two additional domains that have been repurchased. However, further investigation reveals the ownership of these domains has not changed and the DNS record simply lapsed, and images were re-encoded.
context: In CC3M another flagged domain served a squatter’s advertisement; the broader investigation reports no evidence of the proposed poisoning attack in the wild.
uncertainty: Failure to find evidence in the examined data does not establish that exploitation never occurred.

claim: The authors explicitly trade measurement accuracy for avoiding harm, rejecting experimental vandalism as a way to measure moderation speed.
quote: Note that while the most accurate methodology would be to inject malicious edits and measure the distribution of reversion times, we believe this would be unethical. Instead, we take an entirely passive—albeit less accurate—approach as discussed in Section V-F.
context: They analyze historical Wikipedia edits and make no edits to Wikipedia themselves.
uncertainty: This is a shared methodological and ethical judgment in the paper, not separately attributable speech by Carlini.

claim: The public-facing study notice makes specific commitments about participant agency and data retention: deletion of collected data after the study and deletion of an individual's contributions on request.
quote: Any data we have logged will be deleted upon completion of our study. If you would prefer not to participate in this study, please contact us via the email address below and we will delete any data you may have contributed to our study.
context: Appendix C reproduces the landing page placed on purchased domains; it also promises to return domains to original owners and let them expire after the study.
uncertainty: The source documents commitments, not independent verification that deletion or domain return subsequently occurred.

claim: The authors explicitly distinguish the error profiles of exact and perceptual image comparisons. Exact hashes detect all byte changes but flag benign transformations; perceptual comparisons reduce such false positives while permitting adversarial false negatives.
quote: Comparing images with cryptographic hashes has no false-negatives (i.e., any change is detected) but gives false-positives for “benign” changes, e.g., if a domain re-encodes or resizes its images.
context: The choice of comparison method affects the retrospective search for evidence of domain-purchasing attacks.
uncertainty: The no-false-negatives statement concerns detecting content changes under the hash comparison, not detecting every possible poisoning attack.

claim: The threat model deliberately excluded insider assistance and privileged knowledge. The attacker could change hosted content but could not change the published URL index or its labels and captions, making those restrictions part of the feasibility test.
quote: We assume the adversary has no specialized or insider knowledge about the curator, downloader, or maintainer—other than knowledge of the set of URLs
context: Section III-B assumes honest maintainers, curators, and downloaders, with attacker access limited to content at some indexed URLs.

claim: The authors bound the investigation around dataset-specific mechanisms, explicitly excluding other security vulnerabilities that could make attacks easier.
quote: We focus our attacks on mechanisms that are unique to our study of dataset poisoning. Other potential security vulnerabilities (e.g., the ability of an adversary to interfere with unencrypted network requests, or to exploit website vulnerabilities to inject new content) are out of scope and would only improve our attack success rates.
context: The resulting demonstrations use expired-domain purchases and predictable snapshots rather than website exploitation or network interference.

claim: The authors seek corroborating evidence for their traffic classification by visualizing request order against dataset index order. Sequential access to an otherwise randomly ordered index supports the interpretation that the traffic comes from dataset downloaders.
quote: Indeed, because the ordering of URLs in the dataset index is random (instead of, say, alphabetical), a dataset download appears to be the only explanation for why the URLs would be linearly accessed in this particular order.
context: Section IV-C also compares user-agent strings with a hardcoded string in the img2dataset downloader.
uncertainty: This is observational corroboration, not direct identification of the users or their downstream training jobs.

claim: The combined training experiment produced targeted effects under fixed-caption constraints: six of ten object targets were assigned the intended incorrect class, and nine of ten benign NSFW targets were mislabeled.
quote: The object-misclassification attack works for 60% of the targets: the chosen image gets classified as the target label by a zero-shot CLIP classifier. The NSFW attack works for 90% of targeted images.
context: Appendix B reports the results of the single combined model-training experiment.
uncertainty: The source gives inconsistent percentage conversions for 1,000 poisoned images in the main text and appendix, and the main text says above 90% for the NSFW result. The count-based appendix description is retained here.

claim: Compute cost materially shapes the experiment: the authors combine the selected targets and both poisoning objectives into one CLIP training run rather than retraining independently for every attack.
quote: The key technical constraint in our experiment is that all attacks need to be done in parallel to minimize costs, as retraining CLIP is quite expensive.
context: Appendix B reports a ViT-B-32 model trained for 32 epochs with batch size 3072 on 16 A100 GPUs.
uncertainty: The combined run does not supply independent retraining replicates for each target or objective.

claim: The defense strategy distinguishes immediately deployable improvements under existing trust assumptions from longer-term designs requiring less trust.
quote: These assumptions mirror the existing trust that clients place in maintainers, curators, and downloaders and thus represent the quickest, short-term path to enacting defenses.
context: The proposed immediate defenses assume honest maintainers, curators, and downloaders; the transparency discussion subsequently revisits those assumptions.
uncertainty: The defenses do not protect against every compromised participant in the data supply chain.

claim: The study corroborates its request-filtering heuristics using the order of URL accesses, exploiting the dataset index’s arbitrary ordering as an independent signature.
quote: While our strict precision and recall requirements already give strong evidence that the IP addresses we logged were indeed downloading the dataset, the linear ordering of URL requests from these addresses all but confirms this.
context: Time-versus-index plots reveal sequential downloads, parallel chunks, pauses, and substantial variation in download speed; user-agent evidence provides another cross-check.
uncertainty: This is corroborative observational evidence rather than direct confirmation from every downloader.

claim: The paper declines to treat perceptual hashing as an adequate security-preserving fix for exact hashing's utility cost, because attackers can optimize poisoned images to evade a perceptual comparison.
quote: Switching to a perceptual hash function (which aims for invariance to small image changes) would lead to higher utility, but would not meaningfully prevent our poisoning attacks
context: Section VI-B concludes that qualitatively new defense ideas are needed to avoid the high utility cost.
uncertainty: This assessment relies partly on cited work concerning attacks on perceptual hashes; those papers are not independently examined in this chunk.

claim: The short-term defense was chosen around deployment constraints. Rather than requiring centralized redistribution of all content, the team proposed cryptographic hashes over original raw data and rejection of mismatching downloads.
quote: While the simplest defense to split-view poisonings attack would be to convert the distributed dataset
context: Section VI-B immediately explains that centralization is unrealistic because of monetary, privacy, and legal constraints, and proposes SHA-256 integrity checks instead.
uncertainty: The defense assumes a trusted, unpoisoned original index and correctly implemented verification.

claim: The project deliberately targets an upstream feasibility question that much poisoning research assumes away: whether an adversary can actually place poisoned data into a training dataset.
quote: Our paper does not address any of these questions as there are already hundreds of papers already dedicated to each. We focus on the preliminary question: is it actually possible for an adversary to actually poison a dataset?
context: The preceding questions concern attack impact, stealth, defenses, and attacks on defenses.
uncertainty: This is the coauthored paper’s stated problem selection, not evidence of Carlini’s individual role in choosing it.

claim: The paper stopped short of claiming a general solution for uncurated web data. It suggested cross-site consensus but deferred application-specific defenses because their validity depends on how training consumes and resolves content.
quote: However, any solution in this space requires downstream knowledge of how URL content is consumed, vectorized, and deconflicted during training. We leave application-specific solutions to general poisoning to future work.
context: Section VI-D contrasts Common Crawl with settings that have either a trusted original snapshot or trusted moderators.
uncertainty: This is a stated boundary of the paper's contribution, not a personal stopping rule.

claim: The paper qualifies its 6.5% Wikipedia poisoning estimate by acknowledging omitted operational defenses and hindsight in parameter selection.
quote: In reality, of course, a number of factors beyond our analysis would likely prevent us from reaching this fraction, such as rate limiting of edits or IP bans. We also “cheat” in choosing the optimal value of the adjustment value
context: The authors also note that only one attempt per article is modeled and suggest historical data could improve prospective parameter selection.
uncertainty: The estimate is model based and was not validated through live malicious edits; it should not be presented as an achieved poisoning rate.

claim: The authors stop short of claiming a general poisoning solution when trust and downstream consumption cannot be specified adequately.
quote: However, any solution in this space requires downstream knowledge of how URL content is consumed, vectorized, and deconflicted during training. We leave application-specific solutions to general poisoning to future work.
context: The discussion considers consensus across websites for datasets such as Common Crawl, which lack a trusted original snapshot or a universal moderator.
uncertainty: This is an explicit scope boundary, not evidence of a personal stopping heuristic.

claim: Rather than equating a vulnerable dataset index with actual exposure, the authors measure whether researchers and practitioners still download the affected datasets.
quote: As a result, in order to measure the potential impact of a split-view poisoning attack it is necessary to study the rate at which these datasets are actually still being actively downloaded by researchers and practitioners today.
context: Split-view poisoning only affects clients downloading after the attacker gains control, so continued dataset use is load-bearing evidence.
uncertainty: Observed downloading establishes exposure opportunity, not that downloaded data was subsequently used in model training.

claim: The authors broaden the analysis beyond English while documenting both missing data and annotation limitations. They analyze 35 of 39 non-English Wiki-40B languages and avoid presenting the reversion detector as exhaustive.
quote: Again our analysis here is loose: we identify only a subset of (often automated) reversions; however for the same reason as above we believe this represents a lower bound of the mean reversion time.
context: German, Chinese, and Czech checkpoints were inaccessible for the studied times; Tagalog lacked enough data for reliable analysis.
uncertainty: Cross-language comparisons depend on incomplete language-specific reversion detection and interval widths.

claim: The team explicitly bounded its timing defenses by moderator availability and ability to recognize malicious changes. Quiet articles, lightly moderated languages, and changes that mislead models while appearing valid to people remain concerns.
quote: Furthermore, our defenses hinge on the existence of a trusted curator who can detect malicious edits—something that may be difficult if an attacker intentionally introduces imperceptible changes over time that impact only machine understanding, but appear valid to human review.
context: Section VI-C states that the proposed measures make attacks harder but cannot eliminate them entirely.
uncertainty: The imperceptible-change scenario is a discussed limitation, not an attack experimentally demonstrated in this study.

claim: The authors connect the economic feasibility analysis to model experiments while containing experimental harm through local simulation.
quote: For each of these attack objectives, we first identify appropriate text captions in LAION 400M for which the corresponding image domains can be purchased for a total of $1,000 USD. Then, we locally replace these images with poisoned samples to simulate the effect of an attack, without any potential to cause harm to others.
context: The simulation preserves the published text captions and replaces only image content that the modeled attacker could control.
uncertainty: This is not an end-to-end malicious deployment against external clients.

claim: The split-view study deliberately uses ordinary domain expiration rather than depending on website exploitation, coercion, or interference with network traffic. This makes the demonstrated attack pathway concrete and accessible.
quote: While more sophisticated attacks may accomplish the same goal—such as exploiting a website, coercing a website’s owner to modify content, or modifying unencrypted network traffic in flight—we focus on the natural phenomenon of domain expiration in this work.
context: Section III-C explains the choice of expired-domain acquisition as the mechanism for controlling indexed content.

claim: The reversion-speed estimate intentionally uses an assumption that can understate how long malicious content remains: each identified reversion is attributed to the immediately preceding edit.
quote: We then conservatively assume that the edit being reverted was the immediately preceding edit, and so measure the reversion time as the elapsed interval between these two edits.
context: The underlying corpus contains Wikipedia edits from January 2021 through June 2022; reversions are identified using recurring comment strings.
uncertainty: The method does not directly link every reversion to the original offending edit and can miss reversions not captured by the string rules.

claim: The authors qualify their estimated 6.5% Wikipedia poisoning rate by acknowledging operational defenses omitted from the calculation and hindsight in selecting the optimal timing adjustment.
quote: In reality, of course, a number of factors beyond our analysis would likely prevent us from reaching this fraction, such as rate limiting of edits or IP bans. We also “cheat” in choosing the optimal value of the adjustment value
context: Section V-D calls the estimate conservative with respect to timing bounds but recognizes that it is optimistic with respect to omitted deployment constraints.
uncertainty: The 6.5% figure is a model-based estimate absent other defenses, not an achieved live attack rate.

claim: Language-specific reversion annotation is developed iteratively: recognizable automated or manual reversion comments seed candidate terms, and further sampled comments are used to check whether each term identifies new reversions without excessive false positives.
quote: We then sample comments with each of these newly identified words to verify that they capture new instances of reversions (that is, they are used to uniquely tag reversions in the language’s Wikipedia), and do not produce too many false positives.
context: Appendix A-A explains construction of the multilingual reversion vocabulary.
uncertainty: The authors state that none is an active contributor to any language's Wikipedia and do not expect perfect term lists.

claim: The project follows disclosure with implementation work intended to make defenses usable in the actual download ecosystem.
quote: We additionally implemented an option in img2dataset to verify SHA-256 image hashes upon download, thus preventing our attack for anyone using this tool, and provide our own backup of hashes in a Google Cloud Bucket
context: The paper reports contacting every studied maintainer and six datasets subsequently releasing SHA-256 image-content hashes.
uncertainty: Protection requires suitable hashes and use of the verification option. The source does not identify which coauthor implemented the changes.

claim: The attack-timing calculation explicitly balances two failure modes: editing too late to enter the snapshot and editing so early that moderation removes the content first. An adjustment parameter also accommodates prediction bias.
quote: This induces a tradeoff: the attacker should make edits early enough to ensure they do not miss the snapshot time, but late enough to maximize the chance of frontrunning editors.
context: Section V-D sweeps a timing adjustment and combines snapshot intervals with measured reversion-time distributions.
uncertainty: The source's descriptions of the direction of timing bias are not fully consistent; the need to adjust for bias is clear.
