context: Section 3 introduces quality, error rates, robustness, unforgeability, message support, and efficiency.

claim: The survey warns that low distortion at the token level need not remain small over long outputs or multiple responses.
quote: Multiple or long watermarked responses may jointly exhibit greater degradation, and therefore low-distortion is fairly weak.
context: Section 3.1.2 evaluates guarantees that constrain individual token distributions in language-model watermarking.

claim: The paper argues that watermark policy must track technical differences, capabilities, and limitations rather than assume all watermarking systems provide interchangeable guarantees.
quote: The future of watermarking depends not only on technological advancements but also on cohesive policy efforts across international boundaries. It is important that these policy efforts are aligned with state-of-the-art watermarking schemes, cognizant of their differences, capabilities, and limitations [56].
context: This connects the survey's formal distinctions and technical critiques to its intended policy audience.

claim: The paper distinguishes recovering secret keys from defeating a watermark, explicitly noting that removal and forgery can succeed without key extraction.
quote: In most cases, if an adversary successfully extracts the secret keys, they can easily remove or forge watermarks. However, it is important to note that extracting the secret keys is not a prerequisite for executing removal or forging attacks.
context: Section 4.1 lists secret extraction as an additional, harder adversarial objective.

claim: The survey treats watermarking as a potential privacy threat as well as a provenance tool, illustrating how embedded user identifiers could connect anonymous public accounts to real users.
quote: If that user later posts that image on an anonymous but public social media account, anyone with detector access can link this account to the user’s identity.
context: The example assumes a provider has embedded a user’s ID in generated images. The same passage discusses whistleblower tracking and warns that undetectable watermarks can make tracking imperceptible.
uncertainty: The identity-linkage example is a hypothetical misuse scenario, not an allegation of a documented provider practice.

claim: The survey separates theoretical progress in pseudorandom-code text watermarking from practical readiness, explicitly recording the absence of a practical LLM implementation.
quote: Further advancements in PRCs are discussed in [119, 74, 120], although PRCs have yet to be implemented for a practical LLM watermarking scheme.
context: Section 6.1 discusses constructions combining undetectability with robustness to token substitutions.
uncertainty: The implementation-status statement is limited to the time and scope of the supplied paper.

claim: The authors propose an image analogue of downsampling while explicitly distinguishing the proposal from previously evaluated attacks.
quote: A similar approach could be considered for image watermarks, although we are unaware of such an attack being evaluated in prior work. For example, the attacker could ask for a generation of “an image with object X on the left and object Y on the right”, and then simply crop half of the output.
context: The proposed attack tests whether prompting for a composite image and extracting a subset weakens its watermark.
uncertainty: This is a proposed test, not an experimentally established vulnerability.

claim: The paper treats the importance of watermark properties as application-dependent instead of assuming one universal ordering of requirements.
quote: There are many different properties one might desire of a watermarking scheme, the relative importance of which depends on the application scenario. In this section, we will outline what we view as the most important of these properties.
context: The framework considers quality, detection errors, robustness, unforgeability, message embedding, and efficiency.

claim: The authors require false-positive guarantees that do not depend on a particular natural-content distribution, linking this requirement to detector credibility and unequal flagging across content types.
quote: Note that the above definition is agnostic to the distribution of natural content. This is absolutely essential for the interpretability and credibility of the watermark detector. If the false positive rate only holds for content generated under certain conditions, then it is possible that the detector will disproportionately flag some kinds of content.
context: Section 3.2 defines false positives for fixed content with probability taken over the detection key.

claim: The paper allows non-robust watermarks to be useful when users have little incentive to remove them, giving exclusion of AI-generated images from training datasets as an example.
quote: The utility of non-robust watermarks is especially apparent for watermarking applications where the user does not suffer any negative consequences when caught: For example, one may wish to detect AI-generated images online in order to omit them from training datasets.
context: Section 3.3 distinguishes usefulness in low-adversarial-pressure settings from robustness against deliberate removal.
uncertainty: The argument depends on assumptions about user incentives, not a reported measurement of removal behavior.

claim: The paper challenges Gaussian Shading's claim of lossless performance by examining whether its single-image proof covers correlations across multiple generated images.
quote: Yang et al. [69] claim “lossless performance,” supported by a proof that the distribution of a single watermarked image matches that of an un-watermarked image. However, this proof does not account for correlations across multiple generated images, which are critical for metrics such as FID [92], CLIP Score [93], and Inception Score [94].
context: Section 6.2 applies the earlier distinction between single-response and multi-response quality guarantees to a concrete published claim.
uncertainty: This is a technical critique in the survey, not an independently reproduced experiment in the supplied source.

claim: The paper considers low distortion at the token level a weak quality guarantee because degradation can accumulate over longer or multiple responses.
quote: Multiple or long watermarked responses may jointly exhibit greater degradation, and therefore low-distortion is fairly weak.
context: Section 3.1.2 discusses language-model schemes whose guarantees concern individual token distributions.

claim: The false-positive definition is deliberately independent of the distribution of natural content, because distribution-specific guarantees could conceal disproportionate flagging of particular content types.
quote: Note that the above definition is agnostic to the distribution of natural content. This is absolutely essential for the interpretability and credibility of the watermark detector. If the false positive rate only holds for content generated under certain conditions, then it is possible that the detector will disproportionately flag some kinds of content.
context: Section 3.2 explains why the guarantee is formulated for any fixed content, with probability over the detection key.

claim: The copyright discussion expands the adversary model to include a dishonest model owner, showing why revealing a key after seeing disputed content may fail as proof of generation.
quote: However, for many existing schemes, a malicious model owner could take a user-generated image, and manufacture a fake watermark key under which the image is watermarked! Therefore, revealing this key is not convincing proof.
context: Section 7 considers an owner trying to prove that an image claimed by a user actually came from its model.
uncertainty: The criticism applies to many existing schemes as described, not to every possible watermark construction.

claim: Within text watermarking, the authors choose to emphasize methods integrated into generation rather than concentrate on post-processing approaches.
quote: In this paper, we focus more on advanced watermarking approaches that integrate watermarking directly into text generation process. Below, we discuss recent representative works in this domain.
context: Section 6.1 briefly reviews format, lexical, and syntactic post-processing before turning to generation-time schemes. Section 6.2 makes a parallel scope choice for images.
uncertainty: This is the survey's emphasis, not evidence that the authors reject all post-processing methods.

claim: The authors identify a fundamental incompatibility between robust detection and verbatim-output unforgeability: tolerance of edits can allow harmful modifications to retain a watermark and be falsely attributed to the model.
quote: The first thing to observe is that this definition of unforgeability is fundamentally incompatible with robustness. If a detector is robust, then it is possible to generate a response from the model, modify it slightly to make it problematic, and then falsely attribute the problematic content to the watermarked model
context: The incompatibility concerns the paper's strict definition requiring attributed content to have been output verbatim.
uncertainty: It is not a claim that every possible definition of unforgeability is incompatible with robustness.

claim: The coauthored paper frames watermarking as a potentially useful intervention against misinformation and deception while explicitly limiting its role: it is not a comprehensive solution to generative-AI risks.
quote: While watermarking is not a silver bullet for addressing all risks associated with GenAI, it can play a crucial role in enhancing AI safety and trustworthiness by combating misinformation and deception.
context: The abstract establishes the motivation and limits of the research program.
uncertainty: This is the paper's collective framing, not an individually attributable statement of Carlini's priorities.

claim: The image-evaluation framework conditions metric choice on where watermarking enters the pipeline, distinguishing post-generation degradation from generative fidelity and perceptual similarity.
quote: The quality evaluation of watermarked images depends on whether the watermark is applied during or after the image generation process. Metrics such as Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) are commonly used to measure quality degradation in post-generation watermarking.
context: The following discussion lists FID, CLIP, Inception Score, and LPIPS for generative-model quality assessment.

claim: The authors propose Pareto-optimal performance across multiple watermark properties, supported both empirically and theoretically and resting on minimal assumptions, as a research objective.
quote: Optimal watermarking schemes should aim to achieve a Pareto-optimal balance among these dimensions, both empirically and theoretically, while relying on minimal assumptions. Existing studies [143, 144] claim optimality within certain restricted settings.
context: Section 7 explicitly qualifies existing optimality claims by their restricted settings.

claim: The authors describe a literature-review method spanning more than 100 peer-reviewed papers, multiple research communities, and recent preprints to accommodate the field's rapid development.
quote: To construct this SoK, we conducted an extensive review of over 100 peer-reviewed papers published from the early 2000s to the 2020s. Our sources include top venues in security (e.g., USENIX Security, IEEE S&P), AI (e.g., NeurIPS, ICML), and multimedia (e.g., CVPR, ACM Multimedia), as well as relevant arXiv preprints reflecting the fast-paced development of the field.
context: Section 1.1 gives the paper's stated methodology for systematizing knowledge.
uncertainty: The supplied passage does not report a reproducible search protocol or identify which review tasks Carlini performed.

claim: The robustness framework accounts for adversarial knowledge, since watermark keys and detector or decoder access can enable stronger removal attacks.
quote: Robustness may depend on the knowledge provided to the channel. It is sometimes possible to use the watermarking keys or detector/decoder access to craft stronger watermark removal attacks [70, 71, 72].
context: This is one of the reasons the authors give for using a broad, conditional definition of robustness.
uncertainty: The stronger attacks are attributed to prior studies, not new attacks performed in this survey.

claim: The authors recommend complementing formal detection bounds with empirical measurements because guarantees can depend on content statistics and implementation-level randomness can reduce detectability.
quote: First, bounds on the false negative rate (i.e., the likelihood that watermarked content is undetected) often depend on statistical characteristics of the content, such as the entropy of a piece of text. Second, inherent randomness in machine learning models and system components (e.g., GPUs) can slightly reduce the detectability of a watermark.
context: Section 5.1 explains why analytically derived error bounds do not remove the need for empirical validation.
uncertainty: This is evaluation guidance, not a report of a particular GPU-related debugging incident.

claim: The paper treats universal detection as an organizational coordination problem as well as a technical one: fragmented adoption leaves providers primarily able to recognize their own outputs.
quote: For watermarking to be universally effective in identifying AI-generated content, it requires widespread adoption by all organizations offering generative AI services. A unified watermarking scheme would enable comprehensive detection of AI-generated content across platforms. Without such standardization, detection efforts are likely to be fragmented, with model owners only capable of identifying outputs generated by their own systems.
context: The final open-problems discussion connects deployment to industry collaboration, legislation, and international policy.
uncertainty: This is the paper's governance framing; the passage does not establish that a single unified scheme is the only possible route to interoperable detection.

claim: The paper makes detectability conditional on available randomness: a model required to emit a fixed response cannot also embed a watermark without relaxing fidelity to that response.
quote: For example, if the model is prompted to output a fixed response, one cannot hope to embed the watermark, unless one gives up distortion-free ness (which means not faithfully following instructions in the “fixed-response” case).
context: Section 3.3 explains why provable false-negative bounds often require sufficiently random content.

claim: The paper includes computational cost as a first-class deployment requirement, covering computation, memory, and throughput rather than security properties alone.
quote: The watermarked generation process should impose minimal computational overhead, ensuring that the computational efficiency remains comparable to that of the unwatermarked generation process in terms of computation, memory usage, and throughput. Significant computational complexity can hinder real-world deployment, making the model less appealing for practical applications.
context: Section 3.6 also asks that detection, decoding, and attribution remain inexpensive.

claim: The paper requires explicit specification of adversary information and system access because these assumptions determine attack feasibility and strength.
quote: It is essential to explicitly define what systems and information an adversary is assumed to have access to. These capabilities determine the feasibility and success of various attack strategies.
context: Section 4.2 enumerates generator access, sample access, white-box access, chosen-key access, verifier access, and surrogate models.

claim: Computational efficiency is an explicit deployment requirement, covering generation compute, memory, throughput, and the cost of subsequent verification.
quote: The watermarked generation process should impose minimal computational overhead, ensuring that the computational efficiency remains comparable to that of the unwatermarked generation process in terms of computation, memory usage, and throughput.
context: Section 3.6 also calls for minimizing detection, decoding, and attribution requirements.
uncertainty: This is a stated system-design priority of the paper.

claim: The paper recommends matching quality measurements to the downstream task, including execution-based correctness for generated code rather than relying solely on generic text similarity.
quote: For task-specific evaluations, metrics such as ROUGE [87], BLEU [88], BERTScore [89], BARTScore [90], and InstructScore [91] are used to measure the semantic and lexical alignment for summarization and translation tasks. In the context of code generation, executable accuracy metrics like Pass@k are used to determine the correctness of generated code.
context: Section 5.3.1 extends watermark quality assessment to summarization, translation, and code generation.

claim: The survey’s criticism of post-hoc detection concerns the strength and scope of its evidence: limited empirical datasets, absent theoretical false-positive guarantees, and out-of-distribution limitations.
quote: Additionally, post-hoc detection methods cannot provide theoretical guarantees for the false positive rates and face fundamental limitations when handling out-of-distribution data [21].
context: Section 2.1 contrasts passive detection of statistical signatures with deliberately embedded watermark signals.
uncertainty: This is the survey’s characterization of prior detection methods, not a new experiment reported in this source.

claim: The paper recommends empirical checks even when theoretical detection bounds exist, identifying content-dependent entropy assumptions and machine-learning system randomness as reasons theory alone may not predict realized detectability.
quote: First, bounds on the false negative rate (i.e., the likelihood that watermarked content is undetected) often depend on statistical characteristics of the content, such as the entropy of a piece of text. Second, inherent randomness in machine learning models and system components (e.g., GPUs) can slightly reduce the detectability of a watermark.
context: Section 5.1 explicitly recommends complementing formal bounds with empirical measurements.
uncertainty: This is an evaluation prescription, not a report of a particular GPU-related debugging incident.

claim: The paper assesses recording every generated output as an alternative detection strategy and identifies storage, organizational coordination, privacy, and open-source applicability as concrete limitations.
quote: This solution suffers from a number of limitations: (1) it requires substantial storage and cross-organizational coordination; (2) it raises privacy concerns as the record could expose private interactions with AI models; and (3) it cannot be applied to open-source models.
context: The introduction considers retrieval from a record of all generated content before presenting watermarking.
uncertainty: This is an analytical comparison, not evidence that Carlini personally implemented or abandoned the alternative.

claim: The authors avoid the loose label “publicly detectable” because it obscures which keys are public and which security properties survive disclosure.
quote: Such watermarking schemes are sometimes referred to as simply “publicly detectable” in the literature, but we avoid this terminology here as it does not specify which keys can be published, or which properties are preserved when they are.
context: Section 3.4 instead uses the more specific term unforgeable public attribution and distinguishes other possible public-key guarantees.

claim: The open-problems section identifies a gap between public-attribution constructions and systems combining strong robustness with practical efficiency.
quote: However, present constructions either lack strong robustness or concrete efficiency. It remains open whether schemes with public attribution and strong robustness can be efficiently instantiated or if more powerful robustness notions can coexist with public attribution in theory.
context: The discussion considers who should have access to watermark verification and compares public attribution to digital signatures.
uncertainty: This is the paper’s time-bounded statement of an open problem; its exact interpretation depends on the attribution and robustness definitions.

claim: The paper rejects unqualified robustness claims: robustness must specify the transformation channel, and a low-false-positive watermark cannot survive every possible channel.
quote: Importantly, it is not possible to be robust to every channel. For instance, any scheme with a low false positive rate cannot be robust to any channel which is input-independent.
context: Section 3.3 models environmental changes and adversarial modifications as channels; its broader definition also accommodates adversary knowledge and response entropy.

claim: The paper includes attacks that manipulate generation instructions before deleting unwanted portions, illustrating how the structure of the requested output can become an attack surface.
quote: A notable example is the Emoji Attack (or Pineapple Attack), where the attacker prompts a language model to embed special symbols (e.g., emojis) between words. Removing these special words after generation significantly disrupts watermarks
context: Section 5.2.1 classifies this as downsampling rather than ordinary substitution or regeneration.
uncertainty: The paper describes an attack example; it does not report an original measurement of its success.

claim: The survey allows useful deployment without adversarial robustness when users have little incentive to remove the watermark, such as identifying generated images for exclusion from training data.
quote: The utility of non-robust watermarks is especially apparent for watermarking applications where the user does not suffer any negative consequences when caught: For example, one may wish to detect AI-generated images online in order to omit them from training datasets.
context: Section 3.3 separates usefulness against unmodified content from resilience against deliberate evasion.
uncertainty: This is an application-dependent argument, not evidence that removal incentives were empirically measured.

claim: The authors identify evasion as the primary watermark threat and state that it should always receive rigorous evaluation.
quote: The primary threat faced by watermarks and which should always be evaluated rigorously is an evasion attack, where an adversary removes the watermark from a piece of AI generated content.
context: Section 5.2.1 divides evasion tests into edit, regeneration, and downsampling attacks.

claim: The paper distinguishes the theoretical appeal of pseudorandom error-correcting codes from demonstrated practical readiness for language-model watermarking.
quote: Further advancements in PRCs are discussed in [119, 74, 120], although PRCs have yet to be implemented for a practical LLM watermarking scheme.
context: The preceding analysis describes PRCs as supporting both undetectability and robustness to a constant fraction of token substitutions.
uncertainty: This is a time-bound assessment within the supplied paper, not a claim about the current implementation landscape.

claim: The review gives semantic sentence watermarks qualified credit: it identifies inefficiency in sequential sampling, describes a clustering-based improvement, and retains their research value despite missing theoretical guarantees.
quote: However, its sequential sampling process is inefficient and fails to utilize prior semantic information. k-SemStamp [122] improves robustness by replacing LSH with k-means clustering, incorporating clustering results as intrinsic semantic information. Despite lacking theoretical guarantees, these methods offer insights for advancing semantic text watermarking.
context: Section 6.1 assesses SemStamp and k-SemStamp.
uncertainty: These are evaluations of external work; the passage does not establish personal endorsement of either method by Carlini.

claim: The authors identify a concrete trade-off in extending distortion-free guarantees across responses: using multiple key pairs can improve the guarantee but increases detection costs and false positives.
quote: By simply using multiple pairs of generation and detection/decoding keys, it is possible to make any distortion-free scheme satisfy a low-distortion notion for multiple responses. However, this comes at the expense of the detector’s computational efficiency and the false positive rate.
context: The discussion distinguishes preserving one response distribution from preserving behavior across multiple generations.

claim: NES is tuned to use only two samples per confidence estimate because that retains useful attack success while reducing detectability.
quote: We found that the attack remains reasonably successful even when $s$ is reduced to $s=2$, and the attack becomes harder to detect, so we used $s=2$ in our experiments.
context: The appendix explores the tradeoff against s=50: additional samples can improve attack success but require more queries and trigger more detections.
uncertainty: The appendix comparison also uses different query budgets for the two sample counts, so it is not an isolated estimate of sample-count effects.

claim: The team distinguished regimes where the learned similarity encoder added little value from those where it substantially improved detection.
quote: Against these higher-distortion transformations, the similarity encoder is more effective at detecting attacks compared to $\ell_{2}$ distance on images, resulting in 6–8$\times$ more detections.
context: Low-distortion transformations remained below the raw-distance detector's threshold, so the encoder offered little benefit there. Higher-distortion transformations exposed the encoder's advantage.
uncertainty: These are results for the evaluated transformations and settings, not a general robustness guarantee.

claim: The neighbor-count choice balanced stronger detection thresholds against latency and computation; the team selected 50 neighbors where further threshold gains began to flatten.
quote: However, $k$ is the minimum number of queries before our defense could possibly flag a possible attack, so smaller values of $k$ can potentially enable faster detection of attacks; and smaller values of $k$ reduce the computational cost of calculating the $k$-neighbor distance.
context: The threshold curve rose sharply until approximately k=50 and then plateaued, motivating the selected value.

claim: The authors distinguish protecting a specified image's neighborhood from preventing an attacker from finding any classification error.
quote: If the adversary were content with finding any image that is misclassified, then an adversary could simply generate random candidate inputs and wait until a test error randomly occurred (ford2019adversarial, ).
context: For their 92%-accurate classifier, they estimate that an attacker seeking any error would need only about 13 random images.
uncertainty: That estimate depends on sampling from a distribution with the stated error rate.

claim: The team separates finding an adversarial example near a specified image from finding any classification error, acknowledging that its defense does not solve the latter problem.
quote: If the adversary were content with finding any image that is misclassified, then an adversary could simply generate random candidate inputs and wait until a test error randomly occurred (ford2019adversarial, ).
context: With the paper's 92%-accurate CIFAR-10 classifier, it estimates that an attacker seeking any error would need only about 13 images.
uncertainty: The estimate assumes candidate inputs exhibit the classifier's stated error rate.

claim: The team addressed its inability to detect transfer attacks by combining the detector with ensemble adversarial training, while explicitly acknowledging an accuracy-versus-robustness tradeoff.
quote: In practice, the defender may tune $\epsilon$ according to their demands between accuracy and robustness.
context: Transfer attacks were evaluated using a holdout architecture trained on the same dataset and training parameters. The EAT model reduced transfer success but increased clean error from 7.8% to 14.6%.
uncertainty: The combined system was tested against selected attacks; this does not establish universal protection against zero-query attacks.

claim: The autoencoder attack's distance target is selected experimentally to balance evading similarity detection against preserving useful classifier outputs.
quote: We found that in practice $d=10$ is well-balanced between being big enough so the detector is fooled, but not so big that $f(\alpha(x;r))$ is substantially different from $f(x)$.
context: They try target distances from 2 through 20 and select the setting most effective at fooling the detector.
uncertainty: This is a reported empirical tuning outcome, not a general optimality claim.

claim: Combining the detector with ensemble adversarial training exposed an explicit accuracy–robustness tradeoff that the authors left to deployment requirements.
quote: In practice, the defender may tune $\epsilon$ according to their demands between accuracy and robustness.
context: The EAT model reduced transfer-attack success while its clean error increased from 7.8% to 14.6%.
uncertainty: The reported tradeoff is specific to the trained models and tested attacks.

claim: The defense's success criterion was economic friction rather than an assertion that attacks could never succeed: detections were translated into accounts an attacker would need to create.
quote: A key metric for the effectiveness of our defense is the number of accounts that an attacker must create to successfully craft an adversarial example.
context: The threat model assumes account creation has a practical cost and detected accounts are cancelled.
uncertainty: The economic interpretation depends on those account-cost and enforcement assumptions.

claim: The team explicitly bounded what query monitoring could accomplish and proposed combining it with a separate defense against attacks generated entirely offline.
quote: we envision combining our defense (to detect query-based attacks) with an existing defense (to detect zero-query attacks).
context: Transfer attacks can arrive without a detectable attack-generation query history.
uncertainty: Combining defenses does not itself establish robustness against every black-box attack.

claim: The economic analysis considered both time-limited and query-limited histories, translating detections into waiting time or paid buffer-flushing queries.
quote: Then an attacker who knows which queries will trigger a detection could avoid detection by flushing the buffer (by making $N$ extra random queries) just before being detected.
context: The thought experiment grants knowledge of impending detections and uses contemporaneous service prices to illustrate attacker and defender costs.
uncertainty: These are conditional cost estimates using historical prices, not measured deployment economics or current prices.

claim: For the hybrid surrogate attack, the team deliberately granted the attacker knowledge unavailable under the stated deployment model to strengthen the evaluation.
quote: but in our experiments we artificially give the attacker the extra power to know the optimal $D$, to give the attacker every possible advantage.
context: D controlled how far from the original image to sample queries while avoiding detection; the actual similarity encoder was assumed secret.
uncertainty: This advantage applies to the evaluated sampling parameter, not literally every possible attacker capability.

claim: When training a learned query-blinding attack, the team avoided access to the exact victim function by using a separately trained classifier on a smaller data subset.
quote: In order to ensure that we are not “cheating” by training on the exact function $f(\cdot)$ which we will be attacking, we train a new classification neural network $f^{\prime}(\cdot)$ on $10\%$ of the CIFAR-10 training data.
context: The randomized autoencoder was trained to preserve predictions while separating transformed versions of an image.

claim: Attack tuning explicitly traded estimation quality and attack success against query count and detection risk, rather than leaving default attack parameters fixed.
quote: Additionally, a higher value of $s$ increases the chance that the attack will succeed, at the cost of increasing the number of detections due to the corresponding higher number of queries.
context: The experiments compared two versus fifty samples per confidence estimate; the lower-sample variant was used to make attacks harder to detect.
uncertainty: The comparison also used different query budgets, so it should not be interpreted as an isolated single-variable experiment.

claim: The team rejected raw pixel distance as the sole similarity measure because simple transformations could evade it and storing complete queries imposed storage and privacy costs.
quote: This could pose a significant cost to the hosting service in storage costs, and storing user queries for longer than strictly necessary introduces potential privacy risks.
context: A learned low-dimensional perceptual encoder was intended to improve transformation resistance while reducing retained data.
uncertainty: The paper identifies privacy risks from retention but does not establish a formal privacy guarantee for the encodings.

claim: The detector's threshold is calibrated against an explicit benign-data false-positive target rather than chosen solely to maximize attack detection.
quote: In particular, we set the threshold so that if the entire training set were to be randomly streamed as queries, $0.1\%$ of the training set would be flagged as attacks (i.e. the false positive rate would be $0.1\%$).
context: Detection uses the mean distance to nearest prior queries in a learned encoding space.
uncertainty: The calibration uses randomly streamed training images; it does not establish the same false-positive rate for real user query sequences. A footnote acknowledges that deployment may require a lower rate.

claim: Choosing a learned similarity encoding addresses both attack evasion and the storage/privacy costs of retaining full user images.
quote: This could pose a significant cost to the hosting service in storage costs, and storing user queries for longer than strictly necessary introduces potential privacy risks.
context: The authors also find that small rotations or translations can evade a detector based on raw-image Euclidean distance; lower-dimensional perceptual encodings are intended to address both problems.
uncertainty: Reduced storage is not demonstrated to provide a formal privacy guarantee.

claim: The team strengthened query-blinding attacks by addressing collisions among transformed queries, using both greedy resampling and a graph-based selection formulation.
quote: By the birthday paradox, we should expect that as we generate increasingly many images, an increasingly large fraction will be similar to each other, which might cause the attack to be detected. We improve our attacks so they avoid querying multiple blinded images that are too similar.
context: For a simplified distance detector, candidate queries became graph nodes and nearby pairs became edges. Approximate independent-set selection yielded larger diverse subsets than greedy querying.
uncertainty: The graph formulation was analyzed under simplifying assumptions; the implemented defense used a learned encoder.

claim: The paper treats success against unmodified attacks as insufficient evidence and requires attacks specifically adapted to the proposed defense.
quote: While showing that our proposed defense can detect existing attacks is a useful first step, it is not sufficient for a complete evaluation. We must also evaluate whether our defense can detect future attacks.
context: The team developed query blinding to test whether transformed queries could conceal attack generation.
uncertainty: Testing adaptive attacks does not exhaust all possible future attacks.

claim: The paper considers delayed enforcement as a conditional mitigation for information leaked through account cancellation.
quote: If necessary, a defender could further reduce the amount of information revealed by the side channel by delaying account cancellation.
context: The analysis trades reduced information about the secret encoder against additional free attack queries, including an example with at most 10% more queries.
uncertainty: This is a proposed analytical mitigation, not reported evidence from a deployed system.

claim: The attack evaluation deliberately grants a larger perturbation allowance than common white-box CIFAR-10 evaluations to compensate for the difficulty of black-box attacks.
quote: we choose this slightly larger distortion because black-box attacks are known to be more difficult to generate and so we give the adversary slightly more power to compensate.
context: Targeted attacks use an infinity-norm bound of 0.05 instead of approximately 0.031, with randomly chosen original images and target classes.
uncertainty: This is an evaluation choice within the paper's threat model, not evidence that all relevant attacker capabilities were exhausted.

claim: Dataset selection explicitly trades scale for experimental breadth: CIFAR-10 is familiar in adversarial research and permits substantially more experiments than ImageNet.
quote: Finally, training a network for CIFAR-10 is significantly less computationally expensive than for ImageNet, allowing for us to perform a wide range of experiments.
context: The other stated reasons are CIFAR-10's popularity and the authors' assessment that ImageNet defenses were beyond then-current capabilities.
uncertainty: This choice limits the direct evidence to a small-image benchmark; the historical assessment is not a present-day claim.

claim: The initial experiments place the detector over a non-robust classifier to make the contribution of the detector easier to measure.
quote: In our paper we study our defense on top of a non-robust model for simplicity and to accurately measure the value of this type of defense.
context: Later experiments add ensemble adversarial training to address transfer attacks.

claim: After targeted hybrid attacks failed to obtain enough examples of the target class, the team changed this evaluation to untargeted attacks focused on the next-most-likely class.
quote: Therefore, for the evaluation of this attack, we focus on untargeted attacks and exclusively target the next-most-likely class, instead of a random class.
context: The hybrid attack achieved modest success with fewer detections; the paper left improved sampling strategies to future work.
uncertainty: Its results are not directly equivalent to the randomly targeted attacks used elsewhere in the paper.

claim: The encoder's value was assessed against a simpler distance-based ablation, and the paper reported that its advantage depended on the distortion regime.
quote: Against these higher-distortion transformations, the similarity encoder is more effective at detecting attacks compared to $\ell_{2}$ distance on images, resulting in 6–8$\times$ more detections.
context: At lower transformation distortion, the paper reports little benefit from the learned encoder over raw image distance.
uncertainty: The multiplier concerns the evaluated higher-distortion transformations, not all attacks.

claim: Baseline attack trials stop on the first qualifying adversarial example, and the reported defensive benefit is repeated detection before that eventual success.
quote: We terminate each attack as soon as it finds such an example. Each attack does eventually succeed at a high rate, but is detected frequently with at least 200 detections on average.
context: The unmodified NES and Boundary attacks both achieve 100% success in the table while triggering hundreds or thousands of detections.
uncertainty: Detection counts should not be confused with preventing eventual adversarial-example generation when attacks are permitted to continue.

claim: The authors distinguish protecting a specified input from preventing discovery of any model error, conceding that random search can succeed quickly at the latter.
quote: If the adversary were content with finding any image that is misclassified, then an adversary could simply generate random candidate inputs and wait until a test error randomly occurred (ford2019adversarial, ).
context: For their 92%-accurate classifier, the paper estimates about thirteen random images to find an error.
uncertainty: The estimate assumes samples with the stated error probability and concerns a different attack objective.

claim: The team investigated why brightness blinding hurt the boundary attack and attributed the failure to corrupted local-geometry estimates that caused premature convergence.
quote: the preprocessing causes the attack to misapproximate the local boundary geometry and reduce the step size too drastically, causing the attack to converge prematurely before finding a point within distance $\epsilon$ from the original image $x$ and fail to make further progress.
context: The original boundary attack outperformed the tested variants; larger steps also prevented convergence, and Perlin noise did not help at the evaluated higher query counts.
uncertainty: The causal explanation is the authors' experimental diagnosis.

claim: The team strengthened its attack by filtering candidate queries for diversity, including a graph-based approximation that improved on greedy selection.
quote: While the maximum independent set in general is NP-hard to approximate, we find that simple approximation algorithms identify sub-graphs with a cardinality on average twice as large as greedy querying.
context: Similar candidate queries were connected in a graph; selecting mutually separated candidates reduced detection opportunities.
uncertainty: The graph analysis used a simplified pixel-distance detector, though the authors report benefits against their learned encoder as well.

claim: The hybrid surrogate attack is intentionally given knowledge unavailable under the stated deployment model to make the defense evaluation more favorable to the attacker.
quote: in our experiments we artificially give the attacker the extra power to know the optimal $D$, to give the attacker every possible advantage.
context: D controls how far sampled points lie from the original image so that queries are less likely to trigger the secret similarity encoder.
uncertainty: The quoted phrase describes this particular advantage; it does not establish that the evaluation grants every conceivable attacker capability.

claim: The team explicitly treated success against existing attacks as insufficient evidence and required adaptive attacks designed around the proposed defense.
quote: While showing that our proposed defense can detect existing attacks is a useful first step, it is not sufficient for a complete evaluation. We must also evaluate whether our defense can detect future attacks.
context: This motivated query blinding, which transforms queries to conceal their similarity while retaining information about the classifier's output.
uncertainty: The adaptive attacks explored cannot exhaust all possible future attacks.

claim: The team considered account cancellation itself an information channel and proposed delayed cancellation as a conditional mitigation, while recognizing that delay gives attackers extra queries.
quote: If necessary, a defender could further reduce the amount of information revealed by the side channel by delaying account cancellation.
context: The paper analyzes schedules that bound cancellation-timing information and quantifies the accompanying increase in allowed attack queries.
uncertainty: The side-channel analysis is theoretical; a successful end-to-end encoder-extraction attack is not demonstrated.

claim: The evaluation deliberately gave black-box attackers a larger perturbation budget than commonly used in white-box CIFAR-10 work and stopped an attack once it met the specified success criterion.
quote: We terminate each attack as soon as it finds such an example. Each attack does eventually succeed at a high rate, but is detected frequently with at least 200 detections on average.
context: Success required the chosen target class within an L-infinity distortion of 0.05, compared with the approximately 0.031 white-box bound discussed in the paper. Both unmodified attacks achieved 100% success but triggered many detections.
uncertainty: Detection was treated as a cost event in these experiments; the results do not mean the attacks were mathematically prevented from succeeding.

claim: For learned query blinding, the authors avoid training directly against the inaccessible victim and instead train a substitute classifier on a restricted data subset.
quote: In order to ensure that we are not “cheating” by training on the exact function $f(\cdot)$ which we will be attacking, we train a new classification neural network $f^{\prime}(\cdot)$ on $10\%$ of the CIFAR-10 training data.
context: A randomized autoencoder learns transformations intended to preserve classification while separating transformed queries.

claim: When training a learned query-blinding attack, the team avoided training on the exact target classifier and instead used a separate classifier trained on 10% of CIFAR-10.
quote: In order to ensure that we are not “cheating” by training on the exact function $f(\cdot)$ which we will be attacking, we train a new classification neural network $f^{\prime}(\cdot)$ on $10\%$ of the CIFAR-10 training data.
context: The randomized autoencoder was intended to produce mutually distant images while preserving classification. Its distance target was separately tuned to balance evasion against output preservation.

claim: The team translated detections into two different operational costs: waiting for a time-bounded history to expire, or spending extra queries to flush a query-bounded history.
quote: Then an attacker who knows which queries will trigger a detection could avoid detection by flushing the buffer (by making $N$ extra random queries) just before being detected.
context: The economic thought experiment grants the attacker knowledge of impending detection. It estimates more than a year for the best attack with a 100-hour history, or roughly $1,500 with a 10,000-query buffer under the quoted API prices.
uncertainty: These are conditional calculations using prices and assumptions in the supplied 2019 paper, not current costs or empirically measured attacker behavior.

claim: The appendix reports a successful attack outside the main hard-label setting, providing concrete counterevidence to an unrestricted interpretation of the defense.
quote: We experimentally verified that this type of attack approach is effective and allows the soft-label variant of NES [22] to succeed against our query-based detector.
context: The attack estimates outputs from displaced queries using local linearity and can average estimates across directions.
uncertainty: The supplied text does not provide detailed success-rate measurements for this appendix experiment.

claim: The authors retain a simple CNN for the initial similarity encoder despite acknowledging that greater architectural complexity could improve results.
quote: A more complex architecture might yield stronger results, but to keep our initial design simple we use this CNN.
context: They initialize from an image classifier, replace its last layer with a 256-dimensional encoding layer, and fine-tune using contrastive loss.
uncertainty: The statement supports a simplicity choice in this prototype, not a universal preference against complex models.

claim: A failed targeted hybrid attack leads to a narrower revised evaluation using untargeted attacks directed toward the next-most-likely class.
quote: In our experiments, we found that targeted version of this attack did not succeed, as it was difficult to find enough points with the target class through random sampling.
context: The revised attack succeeds at a modest rate with fewer detections, motivating further investigation of surrogate-assisted attacks.
uncertainty: Its results are not directly comparable to the randomly targeted attacks without accounting for the changed objective.

claim: The detector's threshold was calibrated against benign training-data queries to target a 0.1% false-positive rate, rather than chosen solely to maximize attack detection.
quote: We choose the detection threshold so that benign use of the classifier is not flagged.
context: The following specification sets the threshold so that randomly streaming the entire training set flags 0.1% of its examples. A footnote acknowledges that practical deployments may require an even lower rate.
uncertainty: Calibration on randomly streamed training examples does not demonstrate the same false-positive rate under actual user query distributions.

claim: When brightness blinding harms the Boundary attack, the authors diagnose a mechanism: distorted local-geometry estimates cause overly small steps and premature convergence.
quote: the preprocessing causes the attack to misapproximate the local boundary geometry and reduce the step size too drastically, causing the attack to converge prematurely before finding a point within distance $\epsilon$ from the original image $x$ and fail to make further progress.
context: The original Boundary attack outperforms the tested variants; simply increasing its step size also prevents convergence.
uncertainty: The mechanism is the authors' reported diagnosis within these implementations and experiments.

claim: The team knowingly retained a simple CNN similarity encoder for the initial design despite the possibility that a more complex architecture would improve results.
quote: A more complex architecture might yield stronger results, but to keep our initial design simple we use this CNN.
context: The encoder reused a classifier's architecture and weights, replaced its last layer with a 256-dimensional encoding layer, and was fine-tuned with contrastive loss.
uncertainty: The stronger-results alternative is a possibility raised by the authors, not an experimentally demonstrated improvement.

claim: Adaptive evaluation included tuning attack parameters for stealth, even when that meant reducing the samples available for confidence estimation.
quote: We found that the attack remains reasonably successful even when $s$ is reduced to $s=2$, and the attack becomes harder to detect, so we used $s=2$ in our experiments.
context: The original NES setting used 50 samples. The appendix compares the detection and success consequences of using 2 versus 50 samples and states that reported metrics average over successful attacks.
uncertainty: The appendix also uses different maximum query budgets for the two sample settings, which limits a simple isolated causal comparison.

claim: The paper explicitly limits its defense to settings where model weights remain inaccessible; successful model extraction invalidates that protection.
quote: Our defense assumes that the model can be kept secret. If the attacker can learn the model weights (e.g., through a model extraction attack (ModelExtraction, )) then our proposed defense again is not effective.
context: Query monitoring cannot observe the attacker's offline white-box computations.

claim: CIFAR-10 was selected to make extensive experimentation feasible, alongside its prevalence in adversarial-example research and the team's assessment that ImageNet defenses were then beyond available capabilities.
quote: Finally, training a network for CIFAR-10 is significantly less computationally expensive than for ImageNet, allowing for us to perform a wide range of experiments.
context: This was one of three explicit dataset-selection reasons, rather than a claim that CIFAR-10 alone establishes deployment robustness.

claim: The team selected hard-label access as its main threat model because it considered that interface especially realistic, while acknowledging evidence that confidence-score access could be harder to defend.
quote: Our approach would extend naturally to other settings, but as argued in prior work (Biggio, ) we believe the hard-label setting is the most realistic black-box threat model.
context: Hard-label queries return only the predicted category; the appendix separately demonstrates a successful soft-label attack.
uncertainty: The realism judgment is the authors' stated assessment, not independently established here.

claim: After targeted hybrid attacks failed because random sampling rarely found enough target-class points, the team changed that evaluation to a weaker objective focused on the next-most-likely class.
quote: In our experiments, we found that targeted version of this attack did not succeed, as it was difficult to find enough points with the target class through random sampling.
context: The paper describes the resulting evaluation as untargeted. It achieved modest success with fewer detections and was presented as a promising direction rather than a complete defeat of the defense.
uncertainty: Its success rates are not directly comparable to the randomly targeted attacks elsewhere in the paper.

claim: Neighbor-count selection balanced stronger detection thresholds against detection delay and computation; the team selected 50 where threshold gains began to plateau.
quote: However, $k$ is the minimum number of queries before our defense could possibly flag a possible attack, so smaller values of $k$ can potentially enable faster detection of attacks; and smaller values of $k$ reduce the computational cost of calculating the $k$-neighbor distance.
context: Larger neighborhoods allowed a larger threshold at the same calibrated false-positive rate.

claim: The project reframes adversarial-example defense around detecting the process of attack generation across queries, making query-sequence distinguishability its central hypothesis.
quote: The central hypothesis we evaluate is whether the sequence of queries used to generate a black-box adversarial example is distinguishable from the sequence of queries when under benign use.
context: The proposed defense retains state rather than independently judging whether each submitted image is malicious.
uncertainty: This is a coauthored project's framing, not independently attributable as Carlini's personal research philosophy.

claim: For the hybrid surrogate attack, the team deliberately granted the attacker knowledge beyond the nominal threat model to make the test more favorable to the attacker.
quote: in our experiments we artificially give the attacker the extra power to know the optimal $D$, to give the attacker every possible advantage.
context: The sampling-distance parameter would normally be unknown because the similarity encoder was private.
uncertainty: This grants one specific additional capability; it does not mean the evaluation covered every conceivable attacker advantage.

claim: The coauthored stateful-detection project reframed the defense problem around recognizing the process of constructing an adversarial example, using query sequences rather than classifying individual inputs as malicious.
quote: This paper studies the problem of detecting the generation of adversarial examples, as opposed to trying to (statelessly) detect whether or not any individual input is malicious—which has proven to be difficult (carlini2017adversarial, ).
context: The central hypothesis was that black-box attack query sequences could be distinguished from benign usage.
uncertainty: This is a collaborative project choice, not evidence that Carlini individually originated the reframing.

claim: The encoder's benefit is evaluated against a simpler Euclidean detector and is found to depend on attack strength: little benefit at low distortion, substantially more detections at high distortion.
quote: Against these higher-distortion transformations, the similarity encoder is more effective at detecting attacks compared to $\ell_{2}$ distance on images, resulting in 6–8$\times$ more detections.
context: The low-distortion attacks remain below the raw-distance detector's threshold, making both detectors similarly effective in that regime.
uncertainty: The multiplicative comparison concerns the tested high-distortion transformations, not every adaptive attack.

claim: The team investigated why an adaptive boundary attack became weaker: brightness preprocessing corrupted its estimate of local boundary geometry and caused excessively small steps and premature convergence.
quote: We found that the success rate decreases because the boundary attack adjusts its step size according to the local geometry of the boundary (estimated from past queries); the preprocessing causes the attack to misapproximate the local boundary geometry and reduce the step size too drastically,
context: Larger boundary-attack steps also failed to converge, and Perlin-noise sampling did not help at the larger query budgets tested. The original boundary attack outperformed the studied variants.
uncertainty: The passage reports the authors' diagnosis of the observed failure.

claim: The authors deliberately focus on label-only black-box access, which they regard as realistic, while explicitly recognizing that confidence-score access may make defense harder.
quote: Our approach would extend naturally to other settings, but as argued in prior work (Biggio, ) we believe the hard-label setting is the most realistic black-box threat model. (We have some evidence (see Appendix E) that solving the soft-label setting may be more challenging.)
context: The main experiments return a categorical prediction without a numerical confidence score.
uncertainty: The supplied appendix ultimately demonstrates a successful soft-label attack, so the suggested extension is not established robustness.

claim: The appendix reports a successful counterexample to extending the defense to confidence-score access: a blinding attack lets soft-label NES evade the detector.
quote: We experimentally verified that this type of attack approach is effective and allows the soft-label variant of NES [22] to succeed against our query-based detector.
context: The attack estimates the victim's output from two displaced queries using local near-linearity, optionally averaging over multiple directions.
uncertainty: This is a limitation of the presented defense, not a proof that all stateful soft-label defenses are impossible.

claim: The team considered the detector's own information leakage and proposed delayed account cancellation as a conditional mitigation, acknowledging that delay also gives direct attacks more queries.
quote: If necessary, a defender could further reduce the amount of information revealed by the side channel by delaying account cancellation.
context: The paper analyzes cancellation schedules that reduce information about the secret encoder, including a schedule allowing at most 10% additional free queries.
uncertainty: The side-channel analysis is theoretical within the paper's account and query model, not a demonstrated deployment result.

claim: To isolate the detector's contribution, the team initially evaluated it on a non-robust classifier rather than attributing a combined defense's performance entirely to the new method.
quote: In our paper we study our defense on top of a non-robust model for simplicity and to accurately measure the value of this type of defense.
context: A later experiment added ensemble adversarial training. The paper also announces release of the defense and attack source code.

claim: The evaluation deliberately allowed a larger perturbation than commonly used in white-box CIFAR-10 work to compensate for the difficulty of black-box attack generation.
quote: we choose this slightly larger distortion because black-box attacks are known to be more difficult to generate and so we give the adversary slightly more power to compensate.
context: Targeted success required the selected target class within an infinity-norm distance of 0.05; an attack was terminated when it first found such an example.
uncertainty: This is a project-specific evaluation choice, not evidence of a universal evaluation rule.

claim: The paper states model secrecy as a necessary assumption and explicitly concedes that learning the model weights defeats this defense.
quote: Our defense assumes that the model can be kept secret. If the attacker can learn the model weights (e.g., through a model extraction attack (ModelExtraction, )) then our proposed defense again is not effective.
context: Offline attack generation bypasses query-history monitoring.

claim: The team explicitly selected hard-label black-box access as its main setting, while limiting the detector's scope to attacks that interact with the service.
quote: We focus on the hard-label setting, where each query to the model returns only the categorical label assigned by the classifier, but not a numerical confidence score associated with it.
context: The paper argues that hard-label access is realistic and separately acknowledges that monitoring queries cannot detect zero-query transfer attacks.
uncertainty: The realism claim is the paper's assessment; the corpus does not establish that this access model dominates deployed services.

claim: The evaluation operationalizes defensive success as increasing an attacker's account-creation cost, rather than requiring that adversarial examples become impossible to generate.
quote: A key metric for the effectiveness of our defense is the number of accounts that an attacker must create to successfully craft an adversarial example.
context: Accounts are cancelled when attacks are detected; the threat model assumes that obtaining replacement accounts has a practical cost.
uncertainty: The practical security interpretation depends on the account-cost and enforcement assumptions.

claim: The authors standardize transformation strength before comparing different query-blinding transformations.
quote: The parameters for each transformation are normalized so that the expected $\ell_{2}$ distortion from each transformation is equal to $2.32$; exact values are given in Appendix B.
context: The distortion target matches the enlarged sampling radius used in a parameter-adjusted NES baseline; a subsequent evaluation raises expected distortion to 5.10.
uncertainty: Equal expected pixel-space distortion does not imply equal perceptual change or equal classification preservation.

claim: Combining stateful detection with ensemble adversarial training introduces an explicit clean-accuracy versus transfer-robustness tradeoff that the defender may tune.
quote: In practice, the defender may tune $\epsilon$ according to their demands between accuracy and robustness.
context: Stateful monitoring cannot detect zero-query transfer attacks. The combined model's clean error rises from 7.8% to 14.6%, while the tested transfer attacks become substantially less successful.
uncertainty: The combination does not establish complete black-box robustness; the evidence concerns the tested attack families.

claim: The authors translate detection counts into operational attacker costs, analyzing both waiting out a time-bounded history and flushing a query-bounded history.
quote: Then an attacker who knows which queries will trigger a detection could avoid detection by flushing the buffer (by making $N$ extra random queries) just before being detected.
context: The thought experiment grants the attacker detection knowledge and estimates elapsed time, query charges, and defender storage cost under illustrative buffer settings.
uncertainty: The economics use historical service prices and idealized assumptions; they are not current cost estimates or measured attacker behavior.

claim: The paper explicitly limits its defense to settings where model parameters remain secret; successful model extraction would invalidate the proposed protection.
quote: Our defense assumes that the model can be kept secret. If the attacker can learn the model weights (e.g., through a model extraction attack (ModelExtraction, )) then our proposed defense again is not effective.
context: The authors identify stateful detection of model extraction as a possible future direction.

claim: Attack construction includes avoiding collisions among blinded queries, with graph-based filtering outperforming a greedy query-selection procedure in their experiments.
quote: While the maximum independent set in general is NP-hard to approximate, we find that simple approximation algorithms identify sub-graphs with a cardinality on average twice as large as greedy querying.
context: Candidate queries are graph vertices, and pairs closer than a threshold are connected. The exact independent-set reduction is described for a simplified Euclidean detector with k=2.
uncertainty: The full detector uses learned encodings and k=50; the authors report that promoting diversity still reduces detections, rather than claiming the simplified reduction exactly models deployment.

claim: The team reframed adversarial-example defense around detecting the process of attack generation, testing whether query sequences reveal malicious activity that individual-input inspection misses.
quote: The central hypothesis we evaluate is whether the sequence of queries used to generate a black-box adversarial example is distinguishable from the sequence of queries when under benign use.
context: The proposed defense retains query history and looks for unusually similar queries.

claim: The paper explicitly rejects successful detection of existing attacks as sufficient evidence and requires attacks adapted to the proposed defense.
quote: While showing that our proposed defense can detect existing attacks is a useful first step, it is not sufficient for a complete evaluation. We must also evaluate whether our defense can detect future attacks.
context: The authors develop query blinding specifically to challenge defenses that monitor query sequences.
uncertainty: Adaptive experiments test concrete attacks; they cannot establish coverage of all future attacks.

claim: The team operationalized defensive success as increasing an attacker's account-creation cost, rather than requiring that an adversarial example never be found.
quote: A key metric for the effectiveness of our defense is the number of accounts that an attacker must create to successfully craft an adversarial example.
context: The threat model assumes accounts have a practical creation cost and are cancelled when an attack is detected. Detection counts therefore serve as an attacker-cost proxy.
uncertainty: The economic interpretation depends on account creation being meaningfully costly and cancellation being enforceable.

claim: For the initial defense, the team consciously favored a simple encoder architecture over pursuing potentially stronger architectural complexity.
quote: A more complex architecture might yield stronger results, but to keep our initial design simple we use this CNN.
context: The encoder reused a trained CNN and replaced its final layer with a 256-dimensional encoding layer.
uncertainty: The statement does not establish that a more complex architecture would actually improve results.

claim: The detector threshold was calibrated against benign data, with an explicit acknowledgment that its experimental false-positive target might still be too high in practice.
quote: we set the threshold so that if the entire training set were to be randomly streamed as queries, $0.1\%$ of the training set would be flagged as attacks
context: A footnote states that a lower false-positive rate may be necessary in deployment.
uncertainty: Randomly streamed training images are a calibration proxy, not evidence about every real user's query distribution.

claim: The neighborhood-size decision balances detection strength against detection delay and computation, using an observed plateau to choose 50 neighbors.
quote: We can see that this threshold increases sharply until about $k=50$, where the distance begins to plateau and marginally continues to increase as $k$ increases. Therefore, we select $k=50$.
context: A larger neighborhood permits a larger threshold at the same false-positive rate, but requires more queries before detection and more distance computation.

claim: The appendix supplies a concrete counterexample to extending the hard-label defense to probability outputs: a locally linear query-blinding construction enabled a soft-label NES attack to succeed.
quote: We experimentally verified that this type of attack approach is effective and allows the soft-label variant of NES [22] to succeed against our query-based detector.
context: The attack queries displaced points and extrapolates classifier probabilities back toward the desired input, optionally averaging over multiple directions.
uncertainty: The appendix reports success without detailed quantitative results in the supplied text.

claim: CIFAR-10 was selected partly to make broad experimentation affordable, alongside its prevalence in adversarial-example research and the authors' assessment of ImageNet defense difficulty.
quote: Finally, training a network for CIFAR-10 is significantly less computationally expensive than for ImageNet, allowing for us to perform a wide range of experiments.
context: The defense was evaluated on low-resolution image classification.
uncertainty: The choice limits direct evidence for larger images and other application domains.

claim: The team rejected raw pixel distance for both adversarial and operational reasons: simple transformations could evade it, and retaining complete queries imposed storage costs and privacy risks.
quote: This could pose a significant cost to the hosting service in storage costs, and storing user queries for longer than strictly necessary introduces potential privacy risks.
context: The chosen replacement was a learned perceptual-similarity encoder producing lower-dimensional representations, intended to resist transformations while reducing storage.
uncertainty: The paper identifies privacy risks of storing queries; it does not establish that storing encodings eliminates those risks.

claim: The paper's broader security lesson emphasized interactions among ordinary product features, linking the attack to the combined behavior of logit bias and returned log probabilities.
quote: Our attack also highlights how small design decisions influence the overall security of a system. Our attack works because of the seemingly-innocuous logit-bias and logprobs parameters made available by the largest machine learning service providers, including OpenAI and Google—although both have now implemented mitigations to prevent this attack or make it more expensive.
context: The authors call for practitioners to understand how system-level design choices affect the security of the full product.
uncertainty: Provider mitigation status is reported historically in the paper and has not been independently updated.

claim: The defense discussion treated security measures as functionality and deployment tradeoffs, including privacy costs for stateful rate limiting.
quote: Unfortunately this has several significant drawbacks: the threshold has to be independent of $h$ (or learning the threshold would reveal $h$); the system would need to maintain state of all user queries to the API; and preventing Sybil attacks requires a global pool of user queries, which can present significant privacy risks (Debenedetti et al., 2023).
context: Other discussed options included removing useful logit-bias functionality, replacing it with a token block-list, and architectural changes with computational costs.
uncertainty: These are analyzed tradeoffs and proposed defenses, not evidence that the team deployed all of them.

claim: The normalization-layer detector required empirical numerical adjustments before its theoretically motivated procedure worked at lower precision.
quote: We found that the technique required two adjustments before it worked on models with lower than 32-bit precision (it always worked with 32-bit precision).
context: The authors replaced subtraction of one reference output with subtraction of the mean output and computed that mean in lower precision before casting to 64-bit precision for SVD.
uncertainty: The claim concerns the tested architectures and precisions, not a universal guarantee for arbitrary numerical implementations.

claim: The multi-token logprob-free attack maintained explicit feasible intervals and stopped according to a chosen query budget, returning the tightest bounds then available.
quote: After $T$ rounds (where $T$ is chosen based on the total query budget for the attack), we return the tightest known bounds on each logit.
context: Each observed output added linear inequalities to the feasible set; minimum and maximum values over that set bounded the unknown logit differences.
uncertainty: Finite-budget bounds need not reach any particular precision unless the corresponding conditions are met.

claim: Advance permission materially determined the production-model sample, rather than the sample being selected solely for technical representativeness.
quote: We selected these models because these were the only production models which were able to receive advance permission to attempt an extraction attack; we are exceptionally grateful to OpenAI for allowing us to perform this research using their models.
context: The evaluation focused on five OpenAI models available on 1 January 2024: ada, babbage, babbage-002, gpt-3.5-turbo-instruct, and gpt-3.5-turbo-1106.
uncertainty: This permission-constrained sample does not establish empirical coverage of every production provider discussed in the paper.

claim: The defense discussion treats removing logit bias as a security-functionality tradeoff because the same control supports legitimate applications.
quote: Perhaps the simplest defense would be to outright remove the logit bias parameter from the API. Unfortunately, there are several legitimate use cases of this parameter.
context: Examples include constrained generation and proxy-based generation adjustments; the paper also considers replacing numerical bias with a token block-list.

claim: The authors evaluated rate limiting as a system-level defense and identified information leakage, statefulness, and privacy costs in its implementation.
quote: Unfortunately this has several significant drawbacks: the threshold has to be independent of $h$ (or learning the threshold would reveal $h$); the system would need to maintain state of all user queries to the API; and preventing Sybil attacks requires a global pool of user queries, which can present significant privacy risks (Debenedetti et al., 2023).
context: The proposed defense limited logit-bias queries for each prompt to stop an attacker from learning enough logits to infer hidden width.

claim: The work prioritizes high-fidelity recovery and identifies several concrete reasons why prior ReLU-network extraction techniques do not directly scale to production language models.
quote: In this paper, we focus on high-fidelity attacks. Most prior high-fidelity attacks exploit specific properties of deep neural networks with ReLU activations.
context: The listed obstacles include discrete token inputs, non-ReLU activations, transformer components, much greater scale, and limited-precision outputs.
uncertainty: High fidelity describes the extraction objective; the paper recovers one layer up to symmetries, not full-model functional equivalence.

claim: The authors validated recovered weights against ground truth after accounting for the transformation ambiguity inherent in their extraction method.
quote: For the six models considered previously, we evaluate the attack success rate by comparing the root mean square (RMS) between our extracted matrix $\tilde{\mathbf{W}}=\mathbf{U}\cdot\mathbf{\Sigma}$ and the actual weight matrix, after allowing for a $h\times h$ affine transformation.
context: They solve a least-squares alignment problem before reporting RMS error and compare reconstruction error with a random-initialization reference.
uncertainty: Small aligned error does not mean the raw recovered matrix is elementwise identical to the original weights.

claim: The production experiments used the four-logprob method because it performed best on both precision and query efficiency, and omitted alternative-method ablations because of their cost.
quote: Given the results from the prior section, we chose to implement the improved 4-logprob attack (Section 5.3) because it is both the most query efficient attack and also the most precise attack. Switching to a different attack algorithm would increase our total experiment cost significantly, and so we do not perform these ablation studies.
context: The decision followed comparative logit-recovery measurements rather than theoretical query counts alone.
uncertainty: Alternative algorithms were not all rerun against the production targets.

claim: The paper frames its result as an existence proof while acknowledging that immediate practical harm from the extracted layer was not established.
quote: We give an existence proof that it is possible to steal one layer of a production language model. While there appear to be no immediate practical consequences of learning this layer, it represents the first time that any precise information about a deployed transformer model has been stolen.
context: The conclusion asks whether such attacks pose greater hazards than existing black-box access and approximate extraction methods.
uncertainty: The historical priority claim is the paper's own claim and has not been independently verified from this corpus.

claim: The project selected high-fidelity extraction and explained why existing techniques did not directly scale to production language models.
quote: In this paper, we focus on high-fidelity attacks. Most prior high-fidelity attacks exploit specific properties of deep neural networks with ReLU activations.
context: The paper identifies discrete token inputs, non-ReLU activations, transformer components, model scale, and limited output precision as obstacles to prior extraction methods.
uncertainty: The achieved recovery concerns a model component up to symmetries, not a complete functionally equivalent language model.

claim: The team changed the direction of extraction relative to prior bottom-up methods, targeting the final layer and exploiting its low-rank structure.
quote: Our attack departs from prior approaches that reconstruct a model in a bottom-up fashion, starting from the input layer. Instead, our attack operates top-down and directly extracts the model’s last layer.
context: The final projection maps a comparatively small hidden state into a larger vocabulary-logit vector, making its output subspace observable through suitable queries.
