quote: What's the pattern that this 1 falls into? Okay. Here's the pattern. You know, it turns out that the gradients are not flowing because the softmax is saturated to 1. What do you do? Make sure the softmax doesn't saturate.
context: At 10:21, describing an adversarial-example defense he says he broke in roughly an hour or two.
uncertainty: He explicitly characterizes this familiar-domain result as engineering rather than new science.

claim: Carlini allows that sufficiently powerful offensive capabilities could justify restricting distribution, while immediately considering whether the same capability could enable comprehensive defense.
quote: If you did give me the magic box that could break into any government system in the world that anyone could have if they have the tools, I probably would say that shouldn't be something we distribute to everyone in the world.
context: His subsequent counterconsideration is that running the hypothetical tool defensively might reveal bugs that could then be patched.
uncertainty: An explicitly hypothetical boundary case, not a claim that such a tool exists.

claim: Carlini explicitly favors open source in worlds resembling the present, but treats that stance as revisable in response to compelling contrary evidence.
quote: In any world that looks noticeably like our world we're living in today, I think open source is objectively a good thing. And is the thing I would be biased towards until I see a very compelling evidence to the contrary.
context: He grounds this inclination in his assessment of open source's historical benefits for computer security and safety.
uncertainty: He explicitly says he cannot currently specify the evidence that would change his mind; the claimed benefit is his assessment.

claim: For noisy or discontinuous defenses, he looks for ways to obtain a smoother optimization signal, including straight-through estimators. His visualizations focus on making the loss surface usable for optimization.
quote: And so you can, for example, use this thing called a straight through estimator and make gradients become nicer for just discontinuous or ugly objective functions.
context: 55:28; describing the progression from accidental gradient masking to defenses deliberately making gradients difficult.
uncertainty: He gives a family of techniques, not a guarantee that one estimator defeats every such defense.

claim: He explicitly attributes some of his concentration in breaking image-classifier defenses to enjoying the activity and pursuing it before others do.
quote: And probably mostly just because this is a thing that I, for some reason, enjoy doing and just will do before other people get to it, and so other people just don't do it as much.
context: 5:59; explaining his unusually large contribution within this narrow research area.
uncertainty: His explanation for other researchers' participation is speculative.

claim: He favors limited proof-of-concept work that demonstrates an attack is easy, because otherwise defenders may not learn what malicious actors can readily do. He contrasts that with spending a year building a specialized attack agent, which he says could go too far.
quote: if you sort of just put minimal work in, in order to prove the proof of concept is easy, This is important to do to show people how easy it is because the people who know it's easy are not gonna write the papers and say it's easy.
context: At 2:12:22, giving his current rationale for attack-automation research and a boundary based on development effort and weaponization.
uncertainty: He presents a contextual judgment, not a precise duration-based rule that determines whether any project is acceptable.

claim: His practical stopping heuristic is that exhausting roughly five to ten promising ideas without success often means he will not find an attack. In familiar image-classifier cases, he says the first one or two ideas usually work.
quote: I feel like if it's not in the top 5 or top 10, then, it's usually I can't think of something else.
context: 50:31; asked how many conceptual strategies he tries before one succeeds.
uncertainty: He stresses that this varies by problem and familiarity; it is not a fixed stopping policy or evidence that an unbroken defense is secure.

claim: Carlini usually favors the simplest attack objective because ease of debugging outweighs mathematical elegance and captures most of the attainable performance.
quote: the simplest possible objective is usually the best 1. Even if you can have a better objective function that seems mathematically pure in some sense, the fact that it's easy to debug simple loss functions means that you can get 90% of the way there
context: At 13:27, discussing lessons learned across gradient-based attacks.
uncertainty: Presented as a practical heuristic, not a universal optimization theorem.

claim: His extraction experiments leave substantial unexplained variation: some diffusion-training images repeated around a hundred times could be recovered, while some repeated around ten thousand times could not. He does not claim to understand where or why memorization occurs.
quote: some images were inserted a 100 times that we could extract and some images were inserted like 10,000 times and we couldn't.
context: 1:11:37; connecting language-model memorization research begun with LSTMs to later image-model extraction work.
uncertainty: The counts are conversational approximations, and failure to extract is not itself proof that an image was not memorized.

claim: Despite the leverage he obtains from advising, he explicitly tries to reserve at least half his time for papers he technically drives. He associates personal ownership with doing experiments and knowing the paper in fine detail.
quote: I think the balance for me is that I try also to spend at least half of my time only on papers that I'm technically driving.
context: At 7:26, contrasting technically led projects with an industry role resembling a professor advising graduate students.
uncertainty: This is a stated allocation target, not a measured time-use record.

claim: He offers a conditional rationale for targeting universal jailbreaks: preventing easy copy-and-paste proliferation can be useful even if attackers can still develop separate attacks for individual prompts.
quote: I'm willing to say like straight out that like this is not going to solve the entire problem completely, but it will make some things harder for some people.
context: 2:17:05; proposing why someone might design the particular jailbreak challenge discussed by the interviewer.
uncertainty: He explicitly says he does not know the organizers' actual rationale. The supplied source ends before the exchange is complete.

claim: Carlini does not treat adversarial vulnerability as refuting partial interpretability. He distinguishes explaining some correlated features from claiming a complete account of every mechanism in a model.
quote: I think if someone were to tell me, I have a perfect explanation of what's going on in every part of the model, then I might question what's going on here.
context: At 1:34:15, responding to the interviewer's suggestion that adversarial-feature arguments undermine sparse-autoencoder interpretations generally.
uncertainty: His defense is of limited interpretability claims, not a validation of every feature label or sparse-autoencoder method.

claim: He connects attacks on fine-tuning-resistant models to earlier failures of gradient-obstructing image defenses. In the collaborative work he describes, changes to learning rates, restarts, and warmup could restore effective optimization.
quote: it fails in the exact same way of you change the learning rate a little bit, you add some random restarts and you add some warmups so that things work a little better.
context: At 55:28, explaining how the same diagnostic intuition carried from image perturbations to updating model weights.
uncertainty: He previously identifies his role in the fine-tuning attack work as advisory; the quotation does not establish that he personally implemented these changes.

claim: Carlini reports a practical exhaustion point after roughly five to ten plausible attack ideas fail. In familiar image-classifier settings, his first or second idea usually works; less familiar domains require more exploration.
quote: I feel like, usually if if you've exhausted the top, like, 5 or 10 things and it hasn't you haven't gotten a successful attack, then you're not gonna get 1.
context: At 50:31, answering how many conceptual strategies he tries before finding an effective attack.
uncertainty: He immediately limits this to his own experience and ability to generate further ideas; it is not a robustness certificate.

claim: Carlini says his default approach is driven by empirical model behavior rather than speculative analogies to human cognition, while acknowledging that human-inspired reasoning has helped others make progress.
quote: I tend to be much more driven empirically and not by, like, what might be if humans kind of thing.
context: At 1:37:59, discussing time-limited human susceptibility to adversarial images and possible benefits of additional reasoning.
uncertainty: He explicitly allows that his preference could be a disadvantage in some research directions.

claim: The unfine-tunable-model attacks reused the diagnosis that difficult gradients do not necessarily imply real robustness; learning-rate changes, restarts, and warmups could make optimization effective again.
quote: And it fails in the exact same way of you change the learning rate a little bit, you add some random restarts and you add some warmups so that things work a little better.
context: At 55:28, relating recent weight-editing defenses to gradient-obfuscation arguments used in image defenses around 2017.
uncertainty: Earlier in the interview he attributes the technical work on unfine-tunable models to students.

claim: He deliberately limits confidence in brain analogies because deep-learning expertise does not establish biological expertise. He treats his own proposed neural explanations as uncertain thought experiments.
quote: That's why I tend to just assume that I don't know anything what's going on in the brain and I'm probably just wrong.
context: 1:42:20; after speculating that recursive processing might precede a conscious feeling that something is wrong.
uncertainty: This is domain-specific epistemic caution, not a general claim that his model-security intuitions are unreliable.

claim: He uses three-dimensional visualization while warning that it can produce false confidence about high-dimensional defenses. Familiarity with previously misleading geometric intuitions helps him identify defenses worth investigating.
quote: I I do the let's think of 3 dimensions and then just, like, imagine that things roughly go like this. But this can be really deceptive because there are so many defenses that are predicated on the belief that things are working in 3 dimensions.
context: At 43:49, discussing visualization and the failure of low-dimensional intuitions when moving to spaces with many dimensions.
uncertainty: His nearby claims about distances and hyperplanes are explicitly informal and later qualified; they should not be treated as general geometric theorems.

claim: He separates permissive intuition generation from rigorous execution. A fuzzy geometric picture is acceptable for proposing an attack, but he returns to numerical and mathematical details when implementing it.
quote: And then once you have to go actually go do the attack, now you have think about it rigorously.
context: 47:48; explaining that a wrong attack intuition can simply fail, whereas a defensive guarantee requires ruling out alternatives.
uncertainty: This is an account of his workflow, not a claim that intuition establishes security results.

claim: Carlini wants policy discussions to incorporate the technical limitation that models could not then be locked down to the degree some decision-makers wanted, while placing broader societal judgments outside his own primary expertise.
quote: I think the thing I want these people to understand is that at least right now and presumably for the near future, we probably can't lock these things down to this degree that they would want.
context: Responding to a question about open model weights, concentration of power, and whether testing could justify model release.
uncertainty: A time-specific assessment from the February 2025 interview, with an explicitly uncertain near-term projection.

claim: Carlini gives a hypothetical capability threshold that could make unrestricted distribution unacceptable: a tool anyone could use to break into any government system. He immediately complicates that example by considering whether the same tool could enable comprehensive defensive patching.
quote: If you did give me the magic box that could break into any government system in the world that anyone could have if they have the tools, I probably would say that shouldn't be something we distribute to everyone in the world.
context: Exploring circumstances that might overturn his open-source default.
uncertainty: A deliberately hypothetical example, not a claim that such a system exists or a settled release policy.

claim: Carlini treats small theoretical cryptographic breaks as meaningful early warnings because attack methods can improve, and he approves of generous security margins.
quote: So this is technically a break. And the reason why they do this is because attacks only get better.
context: At 1:54:34, correcting the interviewer's view that cryptographic failure is simply binary and immediately practical.
uncertainty: The surrounding compute examples are illustrative, and this does not establish an identical stopping threshold for his machine-learning attack work.

claim: He describes the preceding year's agenda as primarily investigating attack feasibility, real-world vulnerability, and general privacy properties, rather than disproving individual defenses.
quote: We spent most of our time on other areas trying to understand to what extent attacks are possible, to understand the real world vulnerability of models to certain types of attacks, to do some general privacy analysis
context: 9:11; correcting the impression that his recent publication output mainly consisted of breaking particular defenses.
uncertainty: The description concerns his collaborative portfolio during the period he calls the last year; it does not establish a permanent change in agenda.

claim: He has a strong presumption in favor of open source in worlds resembling the present, but explicitly leaves that position open to compelling contrary evidence.
quote: In any world that looks noticeably like our world we're living in today, I think open source is objectively a good thing. And is the thing I would be biased towards until I see a very compelling evidence to the contrary.
context: He contrasts historical security benefits with hypothetical future systems capable of much more powerful exploitation.
uncertainty: He says he cannot yet specify exactly what evidence would change his mind; no actual reversal is reported.

claim: Despite the leverage of advising, Carlini explicitly tries to reserve at least half his time for papers he technically drives. His strongest sense of ownership attaches to work where he performs experiments and understands the paper in fine detail.
quote: I think the balance for me is that I try also to spend at least half of my time only on papers that I'm technically driving.
context: At 7:26, distinguishing personally driven research from his industry-based analogue of faculty advising.
uncertainty: An intended allocation, not a measured time budget.

claim: Carlini distinguishes meaningful machine-learning progress from security adequacy: a defense with 70% accuracy under attack can be a major advance over zero while still being easy to defeat through repeated attempts.
quote: So on 1 hand, it's much, much higher than 0, very good progress. On the other hand, 70% is very, very far away from 99.999.
context: At 52:57, rejecting the simple framing that image adversarial defenses either work or do not work without specifying the standard.
uncertainty: The accuracy range and retry example are illustrative; no independence assumption for repeated attempts is established.

claim: He usually avoids spending substantial time on modest variants of adversarial training because he trusts their foundation and expects limited gains from attacking them. He instead selects qualitatively unusual defenses, while acknowledging that this selection inflates his observed attack success rate.
quote: this artificially inflates the attack success rates because I'm biasing my search for the ones that I feel like I have a good prior probably are not going to be effective.
context: At 51:15, discussing adversarial training combined with extra data, loss terms, or smoothing, versus novel defense classes.
uncertainty: His belief that many adversarial-training variants are broadly correct is a prior guiding effort allocation, not a claim that they provide complete security.

claim: He favorably contrasts a simpler projected-gradient approach with his own earlier, more elaborate attack formulation. He accepts slightly worse optimization performance when a constraint-based formulation makes the method much simpler and adequate for evaluating a defense.
quote: This algorithm is called PGD and this is the 1 everyone remembers because it's the right way of doing it. Like, you know, you can squeeze epsilon more performance out of it if you do things like a lot fancier.
context: At 16:41, discussing constraining image perturbations to a small region instead of adding a separate distance-minimization term.
uncertainty: His historical account is informal; the evidence supports his evaluation of the simplicity tradeoff, not a verified priority history.

claim: The unfinetunable-model collaboration transferred lessons from image defenses: changing optimization settings could overcome intentionally difficult gradients. Carlini explicitly says students did the technical work while he helped reason about the attacks.
quote: And it fails in the exact same way of you change the learning rate a little bit, you add some random restarts and you add some warmups so that things work a little better.
context: 10:21 and 55:28; discussing attacks on models intended to resist later modification of their weights.
uncertainty: The specific implementation work should not be attributed to Carlini personally.

claim: He qualifies his skepticism about protecting locally released models by identifying indistinguishability obfuscation as a possible theoretical exception. He distinguishes this possibility from practical feasibility and from solving behavioral jailbreaks.
quote: So the argument I've given that it shouldn't be possible maybe breaks down if IO actually ends up working. But then it's not clear again, now I'm gonna jailbreak the thing.
context: At 1:01:56, describing a cryptographic route to making local computation behave like a query-only black box under assumptions and without useful performance.
uncertainty: He says the approach is nowhere near practical for the machine-learning models under discussion.

claim: Carlini supports separating security evaluation from development because adversarial assessment involves different skills and incentives, which organizations can accommodate even when individuals struggle to switch roles.
quote: they understand that there is a different set of skills for security and there is a different set of incentives. And so it's valuable for splitting these things up.
context: Explaining the value of red teams and multiple independent security analysts.

claim: He distinguishes demonstrating a security capability from weaponizing it. That distinction underlies his view that capability research can often be justified without building a highly developed offensive system.
quote: in security, there is the knowledge of what you can do and then there's the weaponization of it. And in most papers people write, they just don't weaponize it
context: At 2:12:22, addressing risks from research that uses language models to construct attacks.
uncertainty: His surrounding historical examples and broad claims about security practice are not independently verified in the supplied corpus.

claim: He attributes much of his attack intuition to repeated practice, remembering failure modes, and recognizing analogous cases. He distinguishes predicting that a defense will fail from identifying the specific mechanism that breaks it.
quote: having done this a lot for many different defenses and having seen all of the ways that things can fail and then you just remember this and you pattern match to the next closest thing.
context: At 49:19, responding to the interviewer's suggestion that his intuition is unusually reliable.
uncertainty: This is his retrospective explanation of expertise, not an experimentally established account of his cognition.

claim: Carlini identifies attachment to a defense after months of development as one reason its creators may struggle to attack it effectively.
quote: it's very hard after you've spent 6 months building something that you really want to work to actually change your frame of mind and be like, now I really want to break it.
context: Answering why outside attackers often break a published defense more easily than its original developers; he also discusses publication incentives against reporting a failed idea.
uncertainty: This is his explanatory assessment, not a quantified experimental result.

claim: He distinguishes making a system secure from making its bugs harder to discover. Although he allows that restricted access and rapid changes might become a practical fallback, he regards actual robustness as preferable.
quote: I would rather have things that just actually work as opposed to things that are insecure, but we just lock them down and just make it harder to find the bugs because those they're still insecure.
context: At 27:02, considering a possible world in which deep learning proves too difficult to secure and providers instead restrict access.
uncertainty: This is a security-design preference, not an unconditional endorsement of releasing every model.

claim: For familiar image-classifier defenses, he often treats attack development as engineering diagnosis against a catalog of known failure modes. His example is recognizing saturated softmax outputs as the cause of vanished gradients and restoring a usable optimization signal.
quote: I'm just like going through like, I have these long list of things I've broken before. What's the pattern that this 1 falls into? Okay. Here's the pattern. You know, it turns out that the gradients are not flowing because the softmax is saturated to 1.
context: At 10:21, explaining why one recently published adversarial-example defense took him only roughly an hour or two to break.
uncertainty: He explicitly confines this familiarity to a particular class of defenses; it should not be generalized to all his research.

claim: Carlini wants policy deliberations about model release to begin from the technical limitation that models cannot currently be locked down to the degree some decision-makers would desire.
quote: I think the thing I want these people to understand is that at least right now and presumably for the near future, we probably can't lock these things down to this degree that they would want.
context: Asked about reconciling open model release, misuse prevention, and concentrated control of model weights.
uncertainty: A time-bounded assessment in the supplied February 2025 interview, expressed probabilistically.

claim: His diagnosis of the distillation defense led to simple numerical repairs: higher precision or rescaling logits could restore useful gradients and make the attack succeed.
quote: And all I need to do to attack it is, for example, this 1 failed if you just did the gradients in floating point 64. You get enough signal that everything works out.
context: At 55:28, describing how numerical zero gradients created a false appearance of robustness.
uncertainty: The supplied interview does not include code or a reproduced experiment.

claim: When pressed to clarify his geometry intuition, Carlini distinguishes random-search difficulty from actual distance to a decision boundary: a nearby adversarial direction can coexist with apparently long distances along random directions.
quote: And so maybe this is the more precise version of what I'm trying to say is things are close, but when you search for them randomly, it looks like they're far away.
context: At 45:35, refining an earlier broad statement that points are close to hyperplanes in high dimensions.
uncertainty: He subsequently stresses that this is an informal intuition rather than a proof or fully specified mathematical statement.

claim: He rejects a simple inference from parameter sparsity to elimination of adversarial directions. Efficient use of weights and restricted activation-space behavior are different properties.
quote: what these models are doing is these models are not wasting any weights, which is different than not wasting any directions and activation space.
context: At 1:26:58, responding to the interviewer's suggestion that small, highly sparse models should prevent the repeated creation of new attack directions.
uncertainty: He does not claim to settle the exact proposed toy-model experiment and begins his response with uncertainty.

claim: He prefers security that survives public scrutiny to security dependent on keeping mechanisms hidden. His desired trajectory is disclosure, broad analysis, and substantive robustness, while acknowledging that locked-down systems might be the best attainable fallback.
quote: But I would rather have things that just actually work as opposed to things that are insecure, but we just lock them down and just make it harder to find the bugs because those they're still insecure.
context: 27:02; discussing proprietary models and drawing a comparison with openly analyzed cryptographic algorithms.
uncertainty: This is a preference about the basis of security, not an unconditional endorsement of releasing every model's weights.

claim: Carlini's loss-surface visualization is operational: he asks how to replace or work around discontinuous, noisy gradients so optimization can proceed, including through straight-through estimators.
quote: And so you can, for example, use this thing called a straight through estimator and make gradients become nicer for just discontinuous or ugly objective functions.
context: At 55:28, describing gradient masking and his recurring visualization of smoothing an irregular mountain-like surface.
uncertainty: These are examples of attack techniques, not a claim that every irregular loss surface can be overcome this way.

claim: The empirical strength of human-written jailbreaks conflicts with Carlini's expectation that direct optimization of a differentiable model should be stronger. This unresolved discrepancy motivates investigation rather than a settled explanation.
quote: it feels to me like the optimization attacks should be just strictly stronger, but empirically they're not right now.
context: At 1:06:21, contrasting interactive security probing with the mathematical accessibility of neural networks.
uncertainty: He says he has no research results on this question yet and does not endorse either explanatory story as established.

claim: He identifies a tradeoff between resisting manipulation and remaining responsive to legitimate correction. He wants a coding assistant to take a user's report of failure seriously, while recognizing that credulity can also be exploited; refusal can sometimes provide another option.
quote: I would want the model to say like, oh, okay, let me go back and look. Like, I believe you actually ran the code and I made a mistake.
context: At 2:05:26, responding to a discussion of alignment-faking behavior and models' willingness to accept user-provided premises.
uncertainty: He explicitly says he does not know the optimal operating point; he offers no complete resolution of corrigibility and manipulation resistance.

claim: The adversarial-suffix work used an affirmative-response prefix as a simple surrogate objective for obtaining a substantive answer. This avoided requiring advance knowledge of the desired answer and was presented as a simpler starting point than optimizing a latent refusal direction.

quote: I think the thing that I just want to make sure that people do is that they base whatever they're thinking about on true technical facts.
context: At 1:04:42, giving a hypothetical requirement to use a supposedly fine-tuning-resistant defense that actually fails.
uncertainty: He explicitly says the broader sociotechnical questions are outside his main area of work.

claim: He corrects claims of one-shot memorization by distinguishing a document appearing once in a dataset from a string appearing repeatedly within that document and being encountered over multiple training epochs.
quote: oftentimes it's not that it's seen that string exactly once, but like that string is contained many times in a single document and the document seen seen once.
context: At 1:11:37, responding to the interviewer's claim that extracted training strings may have been seen only once.
uncertainty: He says 'oftentimes'; he does not rule out all genuine single-exposure memorization.

claim: He often begins attack design with a visual, high-level account of what should happen, temporarily suppressing implementation details before working out a concrete construction.
quote: For me, I guess, for many of these attacks that I try and think about, I tend to think about them visually, but I think ignoring the details is, like, is entirely fine.
context: 41:02; explaining how he reasons about embedding-space attacks after clarifying that the particular poisoning paper under discussion was not his.
uncertainty: The visual method is his self-description; the motivating poisoning construction belongs to other researchers.

claim: He argues that security evaluation must test finding the important mechanism inside a messy real system, not only solving an already isolated technical exercise. As academic knowledge becomes less limiting, he wants more end-to-end evaluation.
quote: oftentimes when we test models, we test them on the thing that we think is hard for humans, but is not like the actual thing that represents the real task. And I would like to see more people trying to understand the end to end nature of things.
context: At 2:07:17, connecting the repository-attack experiments to differences between benchmark scores and agentic performance.
uncertainty: He does not reject academic benchmarks categorically; he says measures such as MMLU were useful when those capabilities were still limiting.

claim: His organizing framework for many attacks separates two design choices: the scalar objective and the optimization procedure. He applies this framing across image perturbations, poisoning, and attacks that alter model weights.
quote: 1 is what is the objective that you're maximizing or minimizing? Like, is the specific loss function you're using? And the other is what is the optimization technique that you are using to make that number go up?
context: 13:27; he explicitly sets aside human-written social-engineering jailbreaks before giving this framework.
uncertainty: The framework is scoped to optimization-based attacks, not offered as a complete taxonomy of all security attacks.

claim: His tentative central forecast is that models may remain substantially vulnerable, requiring systems designed around the possibility of model mistakes. He draws on human organizational checks, such as review by another person, as a system-design analogy.
quote: maybe it's like my median prediction is these models remain roughly as vulnerable as they are now. And we just have to build systems that understand that models can make mistakes.
context: At 1:44:46, discussing whether useful deployed systems require perfect model-level robustness.
uncertainty: He presents this as a tentative prediction and retains hope that new reasoning or robustness techniques could change it.

claim: He deliberately limits the evidential role of biological analogy because he does not regard himself as knowledgeable about brain mechanisms. He treats such ideas as thought experiments rather than an established foundation for his results.
quote: That's why I tend to just assume that I don't know anything what's going on in the brain and I'm probably just wrong.
context: At 1:42:20, after speculating about recursive processing that might precede conscious reasoning.
uncertainty: The following sentence in the transcript appears grammatically corrupted; this item relies on the clear statement of epistemic caution quoted here.

claim: He is skeptical that a broadly useful, user-controlled model can be restricted to benign applications in the same way one might wish to restrict a general-purpose physical or software tool. He regards where responsibility should be assigned as a separate question from what restrictions are technically achievable.
quote: We don't have a C compiler that has the ability to only write benign software and not attacks. Every tool that you have can be used in both of these ways.
context: At 1:01:56, responding to the prospect of open-weight models that remain useful but cannot be adapted for dangerous tasks.
uncertainty: This is an analogy supporting skepticism, not an impossibility proof or a settled position on liability.

claim: Carlini interpreted repeated successful obfuscation attacks on language-model defenses through earlier image-classifier evidence of many distinct adversarial directions. A result initially surprising in the older setting became an expectation in the newer one.
quote: If you believe this paper from 2016, then this recent paper makes complete sense to me. It's saying the exact same thing is true, but in the case of language models defeating the circuit breaker paper
context: At 1:24:13, discussing an older transferable-adversarial-examples paper and a newer obfuscated-activations paper.
uncertainty: These are other researchers' results, used as evidence for his expectations; he recalls dates and direction counts approximately.

claim: Carlini separates permissive intuition-building from rigorous execution. He allows fuzzy mental models during exploration, then returns to explicit numerical and mathematical operations when implementing an attack.
quote: And then once you're done thinking about that, you can go back to the numbers and start looking like, mechanically, what's going on?
context: At 47:48, contrasting informal visualization with the rigor required to make an actual attack work.

claim: The Protect AI detector results exclude tasks where detector redaction removed the secret that the attacker was supposed to exfiltrate.
quote: Some injection tasks are not achievable with PI Detector because the secret to be exfiltrated by the attacker is mistaken as an attack and so are redacted. So only for PI detector, we exclude such injection tasks when computing the ASR and the number of queries.
context: This footnote is attached to Protect AI in Table 7.
uncertainty: The exclusion changes the task denominator for this detector and limits direct comparison with other defenses.

claim: The authors explicitly harmonized the paper's reported human attack criterion with the automated criterion, even though the competition interface required a stricter combination of task successes.
quote: In the main paper, we report the number of attacks that succeeded solely on the attacker task, rather than the user task as well: this is inline with how we ran the automated attacks.
context: Competition success required completion of both the legitimate user task and the injected attacker task.
uncertainty: Competition scores and the main paper's attack counts therefore measure different success conditions.

claim: The team deliberately separated changing attack history from the fixed system prompt to enable caching and reduce search costs.
quote: We deliberately place the past attempts in the user messages as they vary each optimization step. On the other hand, the system prompt remains fixed throughout so we can cache them to save cost.
context: The controller sampled both random and elite candidates to supply as history to the mutator.

claim: For Data Sentinel, the team selected sentiment analysis and spam detection and required attacks to redirect the actual task while also bypassing the detector.
quote: Following their protocol, we selected two tasks, sentiment analysis and spam detection, from their evaluation suite. In each trial, the target model is instructed to perform one task (e.g., sentiment analysis), while the adversary must supply a prefix to the input data that causes the model to instead perform the other task (e.g., spam classification).
context: The RL objective used average accuracy on the intended malicious task; reported accuracy exceeded 80% on both tasks.
uncertainty: These results concern the two selected tasks, not every possible Data Sentinel deployment.

claim: The StruQ experiment adapts the attack to the defense’s own target-phrase task by letting the RL attacker prepend adversarial prefixes to task data.
quote: We followed their setup, allowing our RL attacker to prepend adversarial prefixes to the data portion of each task in order to elicit the target term instead of the correct answer. This approach succeeds in every case we tested.
context: The intended failure is a model producing a specified target term instead of performing the legitimate task.
uncertainty: The appendix separately identifies a reward-hacking risk in target-term experiments; reported success should be interpreted alongside that limitation.

claim: For RPO, the team retained the original HarmBench evaluation protocol and tested both RL and gradient attacks, reporting 98% and 96% attack success respectively.
quote: To evaluate this defense, we followed the same evaluation protocol as the original work and use HarmBench with our RL and gradient-based attacks. We observed that the RL method was able to achieve $98\%$ ASR. Similarly, the gradient method achieved $96\%$ ASR.
context: RPO optimizes a defensive prompt using adversarial inputs; Carlini is explicitly credited elsewhere with the gradient experiments.
uncertainty: The result does not establish that gradient attacks are equally effective against other defenses.

claim: The MELON experiment varies attacker knowledge: search reportedly achieves 76% success without explicit defense knowledge, while supplying the paper and implementation enables a conditional strategy that raises success to 95%.
quote: When we simulate a stronger adversary with perfect knowledge of the MELON paper and implementation, the mutator quickly discovers a “conditional” strategy such as:
context: MELON compares tool calls in a real-user run and a second run with a substituted summarization request; the adaptive strategy distinguishes those runs.
uncertainty: The exact example following this sentence is absent from the supplied rendering; the reported rates remain available in the surrounding text.

claim: The paper defines convincing worst-case robustness evaluation around an attacker who adapts to the defense and whose computational budget is not artificially restricted.
quote: the metric that matters is how well the defense stands up to the strongest possible attacker—one that explicitly adapts their attack strategy to the defense design Kerckhoffs (1883) and whose computational budget is not artificially restricted.
context: This standard motivates the critique of fixed attack datasets and generic low-budget optimization.
uncertainty: It is the paper's evaluative position, not independently attributable personal speech.

claim: The authors distinguish cryptographic computational hardness from defenses that merely require a modest, fixed hardware budget to defeat.

context: They acknowledge that computational complexity can provide practical security while rejecting a few days of commodity GPU work as comparable evidence.

claim: The paper reports manual verification of attacks to check that apparent success did not merely exploit the scoring mechanism.
quote: We manually verified all attacks to ensure they were not exploiting weaknesses in our scoring mechanism.
context: This assurance appears in the main experimental overview and is especially relevant to the later discussion of reward hacking.
uncertainty: The supplied text does not detail a manual-review rubric, reviewer agreement, or an audit trail for every verification.

claim: The team excluded plan-then-execute defenses because their data-independent planning would guarantee attack failure in most selected scenarios, acknowledging a defense class outside the paper's headline break results.
quote: We skip “plan-then-execute” defenses, such as Tool Filter, CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2025), IPIGuard (An et al., 2025), because the attack is guaranteed to fail in most of the selected scenarios as the planning phase is done independently of the triggers, i.e., control flow is data-independent.
context: The authors also argue these defenses have task-applicability and utility limitations.
uncertainty: The paper's results cannot support a claim that all prompt-injection defenses fail; the omitted class is explicitly described as resisting these selected attacks.

claim: The StruQ evaluation followed its target-phrase task and restricted the RL attacker to prepending adversarial prefixes to the data portion; the authors report success in every tested case.
quote: We followed their setup, allowing our RL attacker to prepend adversarial prefixes to the data portion of each task in order to elicit the target term instead of the correct answer. This approach succeeds in every case we tested.
context: The intended failure is diversion from the legitimate task to a fixed target phrase.
uncertainty: The appendix separately identifies reward hacking in a variant where the attacker could choose the target term, so the validity of scoring remains a material concern.

claim: The study frames automated adaptive attacks as a response to the cost and uneven skill of human red-teaming, while retaining humans as an important source of strong attacks.
quote: Human red-teamers remain the most effective source of these tailored attacks, but large-scale human testing is expensive. (Moreover, not all humans are equally strong.) This creates a need to use automated gradient-based or LLM-assisted attacks as adaptive attackers to enable rigorous, scalable evaluation.
context: This tradeoff motivates studying multiple automated methods alongside a human competition.
uncertainty: The comparative claim is the paper's framing, not a universal result across all security settings.

claim: Carlini helped produce the initial paper draft, wrote an attack section, and participated in the collective editing and final framing.

uncertainty: These credits do not identify which broader evaluative statements Carlini personally authored.

claim: Across RL sessions, the team updated the attacker policy with GRPO and used 32 independent sessions per sample with an unaligned closed-source base model.

All experiments use a closed-source base model with no safety alignment; for each sample we perform 32 independent sessions.

uncertainty: The statement about all experiments appears within the RL subsection and should not be generalized to the separate search and human experiments.

claim: The paper defines a convincing robustness evaluation around the strongest adaptive attacker rather than a fixed collection of attacks or a conveniently limited compute budget.

uncertainty: This is the paper’s stated evaluation philosophy, not proof of Carlini’s position in every security setting.

claim: The mutator prompt is initially generated by another LLM and then manually edited, combining machine-generated scaffolding with human intervention.

claim: The Data Sentinel evaluation requires a substantive task takeover as well as detector evasion, using sentiment analysis and spam detection as interchangeable legitimate and adversarial objectives.
quote: Unlike most other defenses, Data Sentinel evaluates not only whether an adversary can bypass the detector, but also whether the adversary can simultaneously force the model to perform a different task. Following their protocol, we selected two tasks, sentiment analysis and spam detection, from their evaluation suite.
context: The RL attack optimizes accuracy on the attacker’s replacement task. The paper reports over 80% accuracy on both replacement tasks, comparable to an undefended model.
uncertainty: The result concerns these selected classification tasks, not every form of task takeover.

claim: The paper recommends giving human red-teamers information about deployed defenses rather than relying on obscurity during testing.

uncertainty: The paper's own competition concealed model identities and defense deployment, so this recommendation exceeds that study's information access.

claim: The paper's response to reward hacking is to align scores with real success criteria and inspect attack behavior qualitatively, not rely on a single automated metric.

context: This follows the StruQ repetition example.
uncertainty: The passage states the methodological lesson but does not fully specify the corrective scoring changes used in subsequent runs.

claim: The gradient implementation follows the original GCG method, is applied only to RPO, and scores candidates using negative model loss.
quote: We followed implementation of GCG as detailed in the original paper Zou et al. (2023). We only applied this attack on RPO defense approach and we used the -loss of the model as the score mechanism in our implementation.
context: Carlini is explicitly credited with the gradient attack and its experiments.
uncertainty: The supplied appendix does not provide a detailed account of his implementation debugging or hyperparameter choices.

claim: The paper makes defense-aware adaptation and substantial optimization resources central requirements for a convincing robustness evaluation.
quote: Instead, we should evaluate defenses against adaptive attackers who explicitly modify their attack strategy to counter a defense’s design while spending considerable resources to optimize their objective.
context: The authors contrast this standard with static harmful strings and weak optimization methods not designed for the defense.

claim: Carlini's specifically assigned technical contribution was the gradient-based attack work; the contribution list separately states that he ran the gradient experiments.
quote: Nicholas worked on the gradient version of the attacks.
context: Other named collaborators developed and ran the reinforcement-learning, search-based, and human attack components.
uncertainty: The source identifies responsibility but does not describe Carlini's individual reasoning or implementation process.

claim: Although the detectors fail strong adaptive evaluation, the paper preserves a narrower practical role for them against unsophisticated or opportunistic attacks.
quote: That said, detectors are relatively easy to deploy and can still provide practical value by blocking some unsophisticated or opportunistic attacks, making them a useful–but limited–component of a broader defense strategy.
context: This qualification prevents the robustness critique from becoming an assertion that detectors have no operational value.
uncertainty: The study does not quantify that narrower practical benefit.

claim: The AgentDojo attack evaluation selected 80 samples from Slack, Travel, and Workspace and excluded Banking because the authors judged it less realistic for contemporary agentic use.
quote: The subset comprises of 80 samples from the Slack, Travel, and Workspace suites. The Banking suite is skipped as we deem it to be relatively less realistic for agentic tasks today.
context: Both automated search and human red-teaming used AgentDojo tasks.
uncertainty: The realism judgment is a study-selection rationale, not independently established evidence about banking agents.

claim: The human study reports voluntary informed participation, avoidance of sensitive personal data, anonymization, and communication with the API providers used in the event.
quote: All participation was voluntary, and individuals were informed about the purpose of the exercise, the scope of their role, and the potential risks. No personally identifiable or sensitive data were collected. All data was anonymized prior to analysis and reporting.
context: A subsequent sentence states that all providers whose APIs were used were informed of the event's purpose and scope.
uncertainty: The contribution statement credits other collaborators with organizing the human study; these practices cannot be assigned to Carlini individually.

claim: The Data Sentinel experiment required a functional task substitution, not merely detector evasion: the model had to perform the alternative classification task accurately.
quote: In each trial, the target model is instructed to perform one task (e.g., sentiment analysis), while the adversary must supply a prefix to the input data that causes the model to instead perform the other task (e.g., spam classification).
context: The RL objective used average accuracy on the maliciously requested task; the authors report over 80% accuracy on both substitutions and detector bypass in every case.

claim: Reported median queries measure time to first success only among successful scenarios; failures at the 800-query limit are excluded.
quote: “Median Num. Queries” is median of the number of queries needed to find the first successful trigger (the unsuccessful scenarios, i.e., no successful trigger found after 800 queries, are excluded from the median calculation).
context: This definition accompanies the detailed AgentDojo results table.
uncertainty: These medians are conditional on success and should not be interpreted as unconditional attack cost.

claim: For the 29 overlapping human/search scenarios, human success was defined collectively: a scenario counted as broken if any participant succeeded within the query budget.
quote: Here, we compute the ASR for the human attack by treating all participants collectively as one entity, i.e., if any participant succeeds on a given scenario (with a particular query budget), we count that as a success.
context: Under this aggregation, humans reached 100% scenario success and the search attack reached 69% with 800 queries.
uncertainty: The collective scenario-level metric is different from the submission-level ASR reported in the competition tables.

claim: The researchers evaluate defenses individually and select an attack family they judge likely to work against each defense, rather than applying an identical attack indiscriminately.
quote: We systematically evaluate each defense in isolation and choose an attack from our set of attacks that we believe is most likely to be effective.
context: The study includes 12 defenses spanning prompting, adversarial-data training, filtering, and secret-knowledge mechanisms.
uncertainty: This selection strategy does not produce an exhaustive attack-by-defense comparison.

claim: The reported search configuration used Gemini-2.5 Pro at its maximum thinking budget and sampled eight candidates per mutation step.
quote: We use Gemini-2.5 Pro with the maximum thinking budget as LmMutator and randomly sample eight candidates for each mutation/iteration.
context: This operationalizes the study's willingness to allocate substantial attacker computation.
uncertainty: The source does not establish that this configuration is optimal or necessary.

claim: Despite including gradient experiments, the paper generally recommends direct text-space attacks because current gradient attacks are unreliable in discrete prompt spaces.
quote: As such, current gradients-based attacks are still unreliable, and we generally recommend attacks that operate in the text space directly like the three following methods.
context: The stated difficulties are the vast discrete input space and large behavioral changes caused by small wording changes.
uncertainty: This is a recommendation about methods at the time of the paper, not evidence that Carlini abandoned gradient research.

claim: The individual-participant comparison gives a more qualified picture than collective human success: the best participant beats search, but search beats the other two people who attempted every scenario.
quote: The best participant who attempted all 29 scenarios achieves ASR of 75% still surpassing 69% of the search attack. However, the search attack surpasses the other two participants who attempted all 29 scenarios.
context: The authors add that humans distribute their effort unevenly across scenarios and that equalized attempt counts would make the comparison more reliable.
uncertainty: Only three participants attempted all scenarios, and their effort was not standardized.

claim: For illustrative successful triggers, the authors specify a simple scenario-order selection rule rather than claiming the examples are random or representative.
quote: We select the first scenario from the Workspace suite in AgentDojo (user task 0 and injection task 0) if possible. If this scenario fails, we select the next successful one.
context: The rule applies to examples using Gemini-2.5 Pro and GPT-5 Mini as base models.
uncertainty: The examples are selected conditional on success and therefore cannot establish the typical distribution of attack behavior.

claim: The authors articulate a falsification-oriented evidence standard: an empirical evaluation should seriously attempt to break a defense, while recognizing that failure to break it is not proof of robustness.
quote: Overall, empirical evaluations cannot prove that a defense is robust; all it can (and should) do is fail to prove that the defense is broken! A defense evaluation should try as hard as possible to break the defense and ultimately fail.
context: The same lesson warns against turning the current automated attacks into fixed targets for defense design.

claim: The authors acknowledge weaker search results against GPT-5 Mini and some PIGuard combinations, while predicting that additional parallel trials might raise success.
quote: Our search algorithm has >80% ASR on most combinations of models and defenses except for GPT-5 Mini with any defense and PIGuard when combined with the more robust models.
context: The next sentence expresses the belief that scaling the adversary's budget could produce high success against GPT-5 Mini.
uncertainty: The improved success under a larger budget is not demonstrated in the supplied results.

claim: The authors identify a contextual classification tradeoff: triggers that are not obviously malicious in isolation may be hard to block without increasing false positives.
quote: Hence, the detectors cannot flag such triggers as unsafe, especially out of context, without significantly raising the false positive rate on benign data (which is already higher than the other defenses, see Table 7).
context: This explanation follows observations of successful triggers without an obvious instruction-overwriting intent.
uncertainty: The passage is an interpretation of observed attacks rather than a formal impossibility result.

claim: The selected MAP Elites controller preserves strong candidates across different regions of the search space to pursue multiple effective and diverse attacks.
quote: Our final attack algorithm uses a controller based on the MAP Elites algorithm (Mouret & Clune, 2015), which heuristically partitions the search space according to some pre-defined characteristics and tries to find the best performing candidates (called “elites”) for each of the partitions to discover multiple strong and diverse solutions.
context: Candidates were stored in islands and grid cells characterized by length and diversity; OpenEvolve's empirical successes motivated the choice.
uncertainty: The paper does not isolate the causal contribution of every controller component.

claim: The authors explicitly limit the study's interpretation: its robustness numbers are not necessarily comparable, and its purpose is to expose evaluation failures rather than rank defenses comprehensively.
quote: As a result the robustness numbers are not necessarily comparable across defenses. In other words, the goal of this section is not to provide a full evaluation of defenses across all attacks or to compare the effectiveness of multiple defenses.
context: This qualification accompanies the main experimental results.

claim: The paper recommends that defense authors personally attempt manual attacks and lower the barriers for outside red-teamers by releasing code and usable interfaces.
quote: For academic researchers, we recommend (1) spending some time trying to break the defense manually yourself (when you propose a new defense, you are often in the best position to find its weaknesses) and (2) making it as easy as possible for others to red-team the defense
context: The source gives open-source code and easy human interaction as examples and recommends disclosing defense details to industry red-teamers.
uncertainty: This is a collective recommendation rather than evidence that Carlini follows the same procedure in every project.

claim: The experimental design evaluates defenses individually and selects an attack family judged likely to work against each particular defense.
quote: We systematically evaluate each defense in isolation and choose an attack from our set of attacks that we believe is most likely to be effective.
context: The study targets 12 defenses spanning prompting, adversarial training, filtering, and secret-knowledge mechanisms.
uncertainty: This is not an exhaustive cross-product evaluation of every attack against every defense.

claim: The authors identify a contextual ambiguity problem for detectors: blocking apparently innocuous attack text can also raise false positives on benign inputs.
quote: Hence, the detectors cannot flag such triggers as unsafe, especially out of context, without significantly raising the false positive rate on benign data
context: The observation concerns successful triggers that are not obviously harmful and do not clearly announce an attempt to override instructions.
uncertainty: This is the authors' interpretation of the observed triggers, not a formal impossibility result.

claim: Detector evaluations made the search adaptive by returning both confidence scores and detection flags to the attacker.
quote: Our search-based adaptive attack (with the detector’s confidence score and detection flag fed back to the attacker) achieves ASR of $>90\%$ against Protect AI, PromptGuard, and Model Armor (with Gemini-2.5 Pro as the base model).
context: The section reports PIGuard as more resistant, with 71% ASR.
uncertainty: The narrative says greater than 90%, while Table 7 lists exactly 90% for Protect AI and Model Armor with Gemini-2.5 Pro.

claim: The comparison methodology warns that averaging over an open competition's participants can understate human attack capability because skill and submission behavior vary substantially.
quote: Human attackers, especially in open competition events, range from highly skilled to largely inexperienced. Thus, the vast majority of attacks may be submitted by less experienced hackers or those who repeated spam the submission (with potentially an automated script), neither of which is an effective attack.
context: The authors use this concern to motivate alternatives to a simple average-human success metric.
uncertainty: The passage describes a potential comparison bias rather than measuring the skill distribution of this competition.

claim: The detector experiments make attacks adaptive by feeding detector confidence and flags back into search, rather than testing whether a previously generated attack happens to pass the filter.
quote: Our search-based adaptive attack (with the detector’s confidence score and detection flag fed back to the attacker) achieves ASR of $>90\%$ against Protect AI, PromptGuard, and Model Armor (with Gemini-2.5 Pro as the base model). PIGuard is somewhat more resistant but still reaches $71\%$ ASR.
context: The attack must bypass the guardrail and induce the undesired behavior in the underlying system.
uncertainty: The main-text greater-than-90% wording differs slightly from Table 7, which lists 90% for Protect AI and Model Armor with Gemini-2.5 Pro.

claim: The paper recommends making human red-teaming easier through accessible defenses and strong information access, including giving industry red-teamers details of deployed defenses.
quote: We therefore encourage industry labs to continue exploring human red-teaming efforts under the strongest threat model (i.e., human attackers should be given details of any defenses that are part of the system).

quote: For score functions, for RPO and CircuitBreakers we used perplixity of the model on the target malcious tokens summed with harmbench classifier safety score.

claim: The RL experiments updated the attacker with GRPO and used 32 independent sessions per sample with an unaligned, closed-source base model.

All experiments use a closed-source base model with no safety alignment; for each sample we perform 32 independent sessions.

uncertainty: The base model is not named in the supplied passage; 'all experiments' is situated within the RL discussion.

claim: Despite including gradient-based experiments, the paper generally recommends attacks operating directly in text because discrete prompt optimization makes current gradient attacks unreliable.

context: The preceding explanation cites the vast discrete input space and unpredictable behavioral changes from small wording edits.

claim: The paper resists equating query count with overall efficiency when comparing humans and automation.
quote: This metric is difficult to compare across human and automated methods because the latter will often have orders of magnitude more attempts, but this does not mean the attack is worse than humans: it could be more efficient than humans in other ways such as wall time or number of breaks found.
context: The metric under discussion is the number of attempted attacks before the first successful break.
uncertainty: The paper does not resolve these competing cost measures into one normalized comparison.

claim: The human experiments paired defended and undefended versions of a scenario while hiding model identities and whether a defense was deployed.
quote: For every defense tested, we selected a user and injection task pair (i.e., a scenario) from an AgentDojo suite, and ran two challenges with the task pair, one with the defense, and one without the defense as a baseline. The name of the model is replaced with a pseudonym, and participants are unaware of defenses potentially being deployed.
context: This differs from the paper's recommendation that strong industry red-teamers receive defense details.
uncertainty: The competition therefore does not implement the strongest knowledge condition advocated by the authors.

claim: On 29 overlapping scenarios, the paper compares collective human success against one search run, reports 100% versus 69% success, and explicitly acknowledges that many independent humans have an advantage over a search process without restarts.
quote: One caveat that complicates the comparison here is that there are a number of humans attempting each scenario independently (usually fewer than 500 as not every participant attempts every scenario) whereas the search attack essentially has one attempt (i.e., no random restart).
context: Collective human success means that any participant succeeds on a scenario; search was evaluated with up to 800 queries.
uncertainty: The reported superiority of the collective does not establish superiority under equal numbers of independent runs or equal total resources.

claim: The qualitative attack analysis does not claim discovery of wholly new attack strategies; the authors observe familiar encodings, languages, formats, and disguises emerging from automated search.
quote: At a glance, we do not notice a completely new strategy that does not exist in the literature or on the internet.
context: The listed patterns include encoded text, multilingual prompts, structured formats, and fake completions or logs.
uncertainty: The authors explicitly frame this as an informal inspection rather than an exhaustive novelty audit.

claim: The paper cautions that query counts do not by themselves determine whether human or automated attacks are more efficient, because time and number of discoveries can favor different methods.
quote: This metric is difficult to compare across human and automated methods because the latter will often have orders of magnitude more attempts, but this does not mean the attack is worse than humans: it could be more efficient than humans in other ways such as wall time or number of breaks found.
context: The metric under discussion is attempts until the first successful break.
uncertainty: The study does not present a fully standardized cost comparison across these dimensions.

claim: The study deliberately excludes plan-then-execute defenses because separating planning from injected data makes attacks fail in most selected scenarios.
quote: We skip “plan-then-execute” defenses, such as Tool Filter, CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2025), IPIGuard (An et al., 2025), because the attack is guaranteed to fail in most of the selected scenarios as the planning phase is done independently of the triggers, i.e., control flow is data-independent.
context: This establishes an important boundary on the paper's claim that the evaluated defenses were bypassed.
uncertainty: The reported results do not support a claim that all architectural approaches to prompt-injection defense fail.

claim: The team evaluated defenses individually and selected an attack family judged likely to work against each defense, rather than applying an identical attack mechanically to every defense.
quote: We systematically evaluate each defense in isolation and choose an attack from our set of attacks that we believe is most likely to be effective.
context: The study covers 12 defenses spanning prompting, training, filtering, and secret-knowledge mechanisms.
uncertainty: The source does not describe an exhaustive comparison of every possible attack against every defense.

claim: The researchers assess legitimate-task utility as well as attack success and question whether filter defenses’ limited robustness would survive calibration to an acceptable false-positive rate.
quote: All of the model filtering defenses substantially harm utility of the system. While some of them show a small sign of robustness, it is unclear whether this will still be the case when the detectors are tuned to have a practically acceptable false positive rate.
context: Utility is measured on all AgentDojo scenarios, rather than only the attack subset. Prompting defenses generally preserve utility but show little robustness benefit in the authors’ assessment.
uncertainty: The paper does not report the proposed recalibration experiment at a matched acceptable false-positive rate.

claim: The project deliberately prioritizes whether defenses can be broken over measuring the minimum cost of breaking them.
quote: our aim is not to study how hard it is to break any particular defense, but rather whether or not any particular defense is effective or not.
context: The threat models grant substantial computational resources. The paper distinguishes cryptographic-scale hardness from attacks requiring days of commodity GPU time and leaves improved attack efficiency as future work.
uncertainty: This experimental priority does not establish that attack cost is irrelevant to all practical deployments.

claim: The human interface exposed the agent's reasoning stream, tool calls, and final success feedback to support iterative attack debugging.
quote: They are able to watch a stream of reasoning and tool calls as the agent interacts with the environment. After the agent stops running, the environment automatically checks if the agent has been tricked, and reports this information to the user.
context: Participants crafted replacement untrusted tool-output text and could revise it after observing execution.

claim: The AgentDojo attack evaluation selected 80 Slack, Travel, and Workspace samples and omitted Banking because the authors judged it less realistic for contemporary agent use.
quote: The subset comprises of 80 samples from the Slack, Travel, and Workspace suites. The Banking suite is skipped as we deem it to be relatively less realistic for agentic tasks today.
context: Both automated search and human red-teaming used AgentDojo.
uncertainty: The realism judgment belongs to the authors and narrows the study's coverage.

claim: Carlini’s explicitly assigned technical contribution was the gradient-based attack work; the contribution list separately credits him with running the gradient-based experiments.

claim: The human study uses a substantial incentive-backed competition rather than only internal expert testing.

claim: Because defenses used different evaluation procedures, the authors followed each original paper's approach and added benchmarks while expressly limiting cross-defense comparisons.

claim: The study measures utility across all AgentDojo scenarios and questions whether detector robustness would survive tuning to acceptable false-positive rates.

claim: The search implementation used Gemini-2.5 Pro with its maximum thinking budget as the mutator and sampled eight candidates per iteration.

claim: The competition rewards shorter successful attacks and allows other participants to displace the current winner, intentionally encouraging continued iteration.

claim: The final search controller used MAP Elites, with the choice motivated by its use in OpenEvolve and empirical successes in other optimization tasks.

uncertainty: The cited successes motivate the choice but are not evidence from this paper about security evaluation performance.

claim: The search analysis reports diminishing gains after roughly 100–200 queries and proposes independent or parallel exploration as a better use of additional budget than simply extending a sequential run.

claim: The authors limit novelty claims about discovered prompts: automated search explored many familiar encodings, languages, formats, and disguises, but they did not notice a wholly new strategy.

uncertainty: The comparative risk assessment is the authors' judgment, not an experimentally measured outcome.

claim: The authors ask defense researchers to support external scrutiny through accessible code and interfaces that humans can readily probe.

claim: Carlini's specifically assigned technical contribution was the gradient-based attack work; the contribution statement separately says he ran the gradient-based experiments.

claim: The human study reports voluntary informed participation, avoidance of personally identifiable or sensitive data, and anonymization before analysis.

claim: The RL attacker used iterative feedback within each session, revising a candidate after observing both the target's response and a defense-specific score.

uncertainty: The contribution statement attributes the RL implementation and experiments to Milad, not Carlini individually.

claim: MELON provided an explicit test of attacker knowledge: disclosing the defense paper and implementation enabled a conditional strategy that improved reported ASR from 76% to 95%.
quote: When we simulate a stronger adversary with perfect knowledge of the MELON paper and implementation, the mutator quickly discovers a “conditional” strategy such as:
