claim: The authors identified an unused source of evidence: testing had white-box access, but their exposure measure used only input-output behavior.
quote: Currently, we only make use of the input-output behavior of the model to compute the exposure of sequences. When performing our testing, we have full white-box access including the actual weights and internal activations of the neural network. This additional information might be used to develop stronger measures of memorization.
context: This appears among limitations and future work, alongside the restriction to generative models or other models with an appropriate perplexity measure.
uncertainty: Using internals for stronger measurement is proposed future work, not an implemented result in this paper.

claim: The word-level language-model experiments framed configuration selection as a tradeoff between utility and memorization, highlighting a Pareto frontier rather than selecting only by accuracy.
quote: The highest utility model memorizes the canary to such a degree it can be extracted. Other models that reach similar utility exhibit less memorization. A practitioner would prefer one of the models on the Pareto frontier, which we highlight.
context: The authors kept the released model implementation unchanged, inserted a canary five times, and varied hyperparameters on WikiText-103.
uncertainty: The recommendation is the paper's stated selection criterion, not evidence of Carlini's private preferences across unrelated projects.

claim: The project explicitly scoped its attacker to adaptive, repeated black-box queries with access to output probabilities or logits.
quote: This work assumes a threat model of curious or malevolent users that can query models a large number of times, adaptively, but only in a black-box fashion where they see only the models’ output probabilities (or logits).
context: The threat model concerns disclosure of rare character sequences and uncommon word combinations from generative models.
uncertainty: Black-box access here includes probability information; it is not equivalent to access only to generated text or the top label.

claim: The initial demonstration trained to minimum validation loss, explicitly controlling against overtraining as an explanation for memorizing a single inserted secret.
quote: We augment the PTB dataset with a single out-of-distribution sentence: “My social security number is 078-05-1120”, and train our LSTM model on this augmented training dataset until it reaches minimum validation loss, carefully doing so without any overtraining (see Section 2.3).
context: A small character-level LSTM subsequently completed the inserted number when supplied with part of its prefix.
uncertainty: This stopping choice concerns the reported experiment; it does not establish a general personal stopping rule.

claim: The paper makes canary selection conditional on the evaluation objective: highly out-of-distribution canaries for approximate worst-case bounds, and in-distribution canaries for more average-case bounds.
quote: To approximate worst-case bounds, highly out-of-distribution canaries should be inserted; for more average-case bounds, in-distribution canaries can be used.
context: The testing methodology says that the randomness space matters substantially even when the exact surrounding format often matters less.
uncertainty: These are proposed testing choices, not formal guarantees that the resulting measurements bound all real secrets.

claim: Canary selection is conditional on the evaluation objective: the authors recommend strongly out-of-distribution canaries for approximate worst-case bounds and in-distribution canaries for more average-case bounds.
quote: To approximate worst-case bounds, highly out-of-distribution canaries should be inserted; for more average-case bounds, in-distribution canaries can be used.
context: The setup section identifies the randomness space as a consequential testing choice even when the fixed format has little effect.
uncertainty: These are empirical testing recommendations, not a theorem that the selected canaries bound every possible secret.

claim: The context experiment separated a change in detectability from a change in memorization by measuring the same model under different amounts of known context.
quote: For the first four rows of Table 6, we use the same model, but compute the exposure using different levels of context. This ensures that it is only our ability to detect exposure that changes.
context: Additional surrounding or internal context increased measured exposure; changed canary formats required separate training runs.

claim: The authors used quantization as a control against the explanation that the model merely stored a complete compressed copy of its training corpus.
quote: To demonstrate the model is not storing a complete copy of the training data, we show that the model can be compressed to be much smaller while maintaining the same exposure and test accuracy.
context: Reducing weights from 32-bit to 8-bit representations left validation loss nearly unchanged and the inserted canary extractable.

claim: The authors delimit extraction as a metric-validation instrument and acknowledge assumptions that weaken its realism as an attack.
quote: However, this algorithm has assumptions that make it ill-suited to real-world attacks. To begin, real-world models usually only return the most likely (i.e., the arg max) output. Furthermore, we assume knowledge of the surrounding context and possible values of the canary, which may not hold true in practice.
context: The experimental threat model gives access to output probabilities or logits and uses known canary formats.
uncertainty: These are limitations stated by this paper; the passage does not assess later extraction methods or deployments.

claim: To validate exposure against actual extraction, the authors vary canary frequency and training regime while holding final test accuracy fixed, then attempt recovery from every resulting model.
quote: We train multiple models on the PTB dataset inserting a canary (drawn from a randomness space $|\mathcal{R}|\approx 2^{30}$) a varying number of times with different training regimes (but train all models to the same final test accuracy).
context: In these experiments, extraction always succeeds above estimated exposure 33 and never succeeds below 31.
uncertainty: Those numerical thresholds belong to this search space and experimental setup, not all models or secrets.

claim: When extending exposure to translation, the authors used correct target tokens during perplexity computation to prevent early decoding errors from contaminating later measurements, repurposing an existing test-accuracy implementation.
quote: If one of the early words is guessed incorrectly and we feed it back in to the next layer, the errors will compound and we will get an inaccurate perplexity measure. By always feeding in the correct output, we can accurately judge the perplexity when changing the last few tokens.
context: They used a TensorFlow English–Vietnamese model trained on 100,000 sentence pairs and inserted matching canary translations.

claim: To observe memorization dynamics at fine resolution, the authors fixed the canary's position by disabling shuffling and measured exposure after every minibatch.
quote: We insert the canary near the beginning of the Penn Treebank dataset, and disable shuffling, so that it occurs at the same point within each epoch. After every mini-batch of training, we estimate the exposure of the canary.
context: Exposure spiked after minibatches containing the canary and fluctuated or decreased during other minibatches.
uncertainty: Disabling shuffling is an experimental control here, not a general recommendation for training.

claim: To distinguish actual changes in memorization from changes in an observer's ability to detect it, the authors varied known context while holding the model fixed.
quote: For the first four rows of Table 6, we use the same model, but compute the exposure using different levels of context. This ensures that it is only our ability to detect exposure that changes.
context: Additional prefix, suffix, or internal-format knowledge increased detectable exposure; formats requiring different training data were tested in separate models.

claim: The Enron study is explicitly designed to challenge the alternative explanation that observed memorization is an artifact of artificial canary insertion.
quote: It is possible (although unlikely) that we detect memorization only because we have inserted our canaries artificially. To confirm this is not the case, we study a dataset that has many naturally-occurring secrets already in the training data.
context: The authors preprocess email bodies, separate them by sender, and train character models for users whose emails contain pre-existing secrets.
uncertainty: The selected users and small per-user corpora do not establish population-wide extraction rates.

claim: Batch-size experiments controlled for final predictive performance and repeated each configuration, then exposed a practical tradeoff between lower memorization and training efficiency.
quote: While this does give a method of reducing memorization for some models, it unfortunately comes at a significant cost: training with a small batch can be prohibitively slow, as it may prevent parallelizing training across GPUs (and servers, in a decentralized fashion).
context: Across batch sizes from 16 to 1024 and different capacities, the authors averaged ten runs per setting and compared models with nearly identical final losses.
uncertainty: The paper describes this as useful for some models, not a universal monotonic batch-size law.

claim: The authors used concrete extraction demonstrations both to validate risk and to communicate its practical significance to practitioners.
quote: Such empirical extraction has proven useful in convincing practitioners that unintended memorization is an issue of serious, practical concern, and not just of academic interest.
context: The surrounding discussion describes extracting credit card numbers from a language model trained on Enron email.
uncertainty: The paper reports practitioner persuasion without identifying the practitioners or separately measuring the communication effect.

claim: The project selected a practical measurement problem: enabling practitioners to assess disclosure risk and choose training procedures using empirical evidence about memorization.
quote: Our testing methodology enables practitioners to choose model-training approaches that best protect privacy—basing their decisions on the empirical likelihood of training-data disclosure and not only on the sensitivity of the training data.
context: The paper compares training approaches that achieve similar accuracy while producing substantially different exposure of inserted secrets.
uncertainty: This is the collaborative project's stated purpose, not evidence that Carlini individually originated the problem or methodology.

claim: The dropout evaluation sweeps a wide range of rates and repeats training ten times per rate to reduce sensitivity to stochastic variation.
quote: We vary the probability to drop a neuron from $0\%$ to $90\%$, and train ten models at each dropout rate to eliminate the effects of noise.
context: The authors find no statistically significant reduction in unintended memorization; rates above 30 percent reduce test accuracy in their model.
uncertainty: Repeated runs reduce uncertainty from randomness but do not literally eliminate all noise, despite the source's wording.

claim: The batch-size experiments identified an operational tradeoff: smaller batches could reduce memorization at similar final accuracy, but could make training prohibitively slow by limiting parallelism.
quote: While this does give a method of reducing memorization for some models, it unfortunately comes at a significant cost: training with a small batch can be prohibitively slow, as it may prevent parallelizing training across GPUs (and servers, in a decentralized fashion).
context: The authors varied batch sizes from 16 to 1024 and model capacity, training ten models per configuration and averaging results.
uncertainty: The observed relationship is scoped to these experiments and is not strictly monotonic at every batch size in the reported table.

claim: The Enron study was explicitly designed to challenge the alternative explanation that observed leakage was an artifact of artificially inserted canaries.
quote: It is possible (although unlikely) that we detect memorization only because we have inserted our canaries artificially. To confirm this is not the case, we study a dataset that has many naturally-occurring secrets already in the training data.
context: They removed attachments, quoted replies, automated emails, and company-wide messages, then trained sender-specific character models on emails containing pre-existing secrets.
uncertainty: This validates naturally occurring leakage in the selected dataset and model setup; it does not establish prevalence across all email models.

claim: The project evaluated utility and privacy jointly, identifying a Pareto frontier rather than treating maximum predictive performance as the sole model-selection objective.
quote: The highest utility model memorizes the canary to such a degree it can be extracted. Other models that reach similar utility exhibit less memorization. A practitioner would prefer one of the models on the Pareto frontier, which we highlight.
context: The word-level WikiText-103 experiment varied hyperparameters while measuring test perplexity and exposure of a canary inserted five times.
uncertainty: The tradeoff is demonstrated for the tested models and hyperparameters, not established as an invariant relationship.

claim: The architecture comparison approximately matched parameter counts to test whether unintended memorization extended beyond one architecture without simply comparing different theoretical capacities.
quote: All models have 620K (+/- 5K) parameters and so have the same theoretical capacity. Convolutional neural networks (CNN/WaveNet) perform less well at the language modeling task, and memorize the canary to a lesser extent.
context: The comparison included GRU, LSTM, CNN, and WaveNet variants on PTB; all exhibited unintended memorization.
uncertainty: Matched parameter counts do not make architectures behaviorally equivalent, and predictive performance differed.

claim: The methodology requires the test model to reproduce the intended training configuration, because architecture, optimizer, training duration, and hyperparameters can all affect memorization.
quote: This training process should be identical: applying the same model using the same optimizer for the same number of iterations with the same hyper-parameters.
context: The authors insert canaries at different frequencies and report exposure against insertion count under the actual intended training setup.

claim: The privacy experiments distinguish negligible measured memorization from a strong formal privacy guarantee, highlighting a gap between empirical behavior and large-epsilon bounds.
quote: Even with a vanishingly-small amount of noise, and values of $\varepsilon$ that offer no meaningful theoretical guarantees, the measured exposure is negligible.
context: Clipping and noise suppressed exposure in tested models even at privacy-budget values too large to provide meaningful theoretical protection.
uncertainty: The measured canary result does not establish strong privacy for all records or attacks at those epsilon values.

claim: For highly exposed canaries that ordinary sampling rarely brackets, the authors moved from sampling-based interpolation to distribution-based extrapolation.
quote: To solve it, we can attempt to use extrapolation as a method to estimate exposure, whereas our previous method used interpolation.
context: They fit a skew-normal distribution to candidate log-perplexities. The resulting exposure estimate can exceed the upper bound of exact exposure.
uncertainty: The extrapolation relies on a distributional approximation; estimated exposure and exact rank-based exposure must be distinguished.

claim: The authors require memorization tests to reproduce the intended production training setup because architecture, optimization, duration, and hyperparameters can each change exposure.
quote: This training process should be identical: applying the same model using the same optimizer for the same number of iterations with the same hyper-parameters.
context: The test model is trained on a dataset augmented with canaries before exposure is measured.

claim: GPU batching improved extraction speed but sacrificed the guarantee that the first completed sequence was optimal; the authors compensated with an explicit additional-search stopping heuristic.
quote: Applying this optimization violates the guarantee that the first leaf node found is always the best. We compensate by counting the number of iterations required to find the first full-length sequence, and continuing that many iterations more before stopping.
context: They processed multiple priority-queue nodes simultaneously, then sorted completed sequences by log-perplexity after the extra iterations.
uncertainty: The compensation is a heuristic; the passage does not claim that it restores the original optimality guarantee.

claim: The paper reports a failed sanitization approach rather than implying that intuitive data filtering solved the problem.
quote: We attempted to construct an algorithm that could automatically identify potential secrets by training two models on non-overlapping subsets of training data and removing any sentences where the perplexity between the two models disagreed. Unfortunately, this style of approach missed some secrets (and is unsound if the same secret is inserted twice).
context: The authors still endorse sanitization as a best practice but reject it as a complete privacy defense.
uncertainty: This documents failure of the described approach, not impossibility of every sanitization method.

claim: In the Smart Compose application, exposure measurements were intended to inform limits on unique-sequence incidence and sampling, together with clipping and privacy noise.
quote: Informed by these results, limits can be placed on the incidence of unique sequences and sampling rates, and clipping and differential-privacy noise (see Section 9.3) can be added to the training process, such that privacy is empirically protected by eliminating any measured signal of exposure.
context: The study inserted canaries between one and 10,000 times into a commercial model's training data and observed negligible exposure for very rare secrets.
uncertainty: The passage describes controls that can be applied; it does not specify every deployed setting. Absence of measured exposure is an empirical result, not a universal privacy proof.

claim: The private-training results separate empirical leakage measurements from formal guarantees: negligible measured exposure can occur even when the reported privacy parameter offers no meaningful theoretical protection.
quote: Even with a vanishingly-small amount of noise, and values of $\varepsilon$ that offer no meaningful theoretical guarantees, the measured exposure is negligible.
context: The authors interpret clipping and carefully selected noise as attenuating the signal from unique examples, while discussing gaps between measured privacy loss and analytic upper bounds.
uncertainty: Low exposure for the tested canary does not itself supply a differential-privacy guarantee or rule out other leakage.

claim: The private-training experiments adapt existing DP-SGD code to recurrent networks and replace plain SGD with RMSProp after observing better baseline performance.
quote: We slightly modified this code to adapt it to recurrent neural networks and improved its baseline performance by replacing the plain SGD optimizer with an RMSProp optimizer, as it often gives higher accuracy than plain SGD [48].
context: Most subsequent private-training experiments use RMSProp; the implementation is reported as 10–100 times slower than standard training.
uncertainty: The authors did not tune either optimizer's hyperparameters and acknowledge that SGD's tuning requirements may explain its poorer results.

claim: To isolate when memorization changes during training, the authors fix the canary's position, disable shuffling, and measure exposure after every minibatch.
quote: We insert the canary near the beginning of the Penn Treebank dataset, and disable shuffling, so that it occurs at the same point within each epoch. After every mini-batch of training, we estimate the exposure of the canary.
context: Exposure spikes when the canary-containing minibatch is processed and fluctuates or decreases between those encounters.
uncertainty: Disabling shuffling is an experimental control here, not a general training recommendation.

claim: To test whether clipping alone offers privacy, the authors choose a black-box attack because the corresponding white-box experiment would expose unmasked gradient information directly.
quote: Of course, it doesn’t make sense to audit clipping alone in a white-box access threat model; no noise is added and so the dot-product value we compute to find type I and type II error rates (as described in Section˜5.1 and Section˜5.2) will not be masked by any noise.
context: They instead insert a canary, train a CIFAR-10 WRN-16 model, and evaluate the final model.

claim: The insufficient-noise experiment varies the magnitude of an implementation error and evaluates sensitivity to relatively small violations of the claimed privacy bound.
quote: We train models with decreasing scales of noise, implying larger values of $\epsilon$ than the claimed upper bound. Results are shown in Figure˜9, where we find auditing with $f$-DP closely follows the true upper bound, meaning we can detect a violation to reported $\epsilon=1.27$ when the true value is $\epsilon=1.57$.
context: The paper reports that the other tested approaches fail to detect a violation even when the true upper bound reaches 2.17.

claim: The augmentation-multiplicity experiment reports a null trend rather than asserting that this accuracy-improving training choice systematically increases or decreases empirical privacy leakage.
quote: In Fig.˜19, we measure lower bounds at different Augmult values, and observe no clear trend between lower bounds and the value for Augmult.
context: Appendix D.3 studies a technique that averages gradients across multiple augmentations of one example before clipping.
uncertainty: No clear trend in the reported lower bounds does not establish exact equality of true privacy leakage across augmentation settings.

claim: The private black-box experiment used two populations of independently trained models and transformed the canary’s label probability into log odds before estimating privacy bounds.
quote: We select a canary example, then we train 1,000 models with the canary point (+ training set), and 1,000 models with only the training set (canary excluded).
context: Section 6.4 compares distributions of log(p/(1-p)), where p is the probability assigned to the canary’s label, using the functional-DP estimator.
uncertainty: This black-box protocol retains a high training cost despite the paper’s two-run white-box result.

claim: The experimental setup explicitly distinguishes confidence intervals from credible intervals and states both the nominal uncertainty level and the default attacker model.
quote: Unless otherwise stated, all lower bounds are given with a 95% confidence (Clopper-Pearson as in Nasr et al. [21]) / credible interval (Zanella-Béguelin et al. [30]), and we audit in the White-box access with Gradient Canaries threat model using Algorithm˜2.
context: These defaults govern the reported comparisons unless individual experiments specify otherwise.
uncertainty: Nominal interval levels should be read alongside the paper's disclosed threshold-selection caveat.

claim: The team limits additional observation generation once existing training steps already yield tight bounds, rather than increasing training solely to collect more audit data.
quote: Of course, we could increase the number of training steps to create a larger number of observations, but we found our method is strong enough to produce tight bounds for large $\varepsilon$ with as little as a few hundred observations
context: Appendix B describes two-model white-box experiments and the default canary sampling rate of one.
uncertainty: This is a justification for experimental sufficiency, not a formal adaptive stopping rule.

claim: The authors resist attributing the entire black-box auditing gap to reduced attacker access because subsampling also affects the correspondence between theoretical and observed tradeoffs.
quote: However, it is difficult to separate the effects of the black-box threat model from the effect that sub-sampling has on privacy leakage estimation
context: For CIFAR-10 with Wide ResNet, the black-box audit obtains an epsilon lower bound around 1.6 for models trained to a theoretical epsilon of eight.
uncertainty: The experiment does not independently identify the contribution of each factor.

claim: The comparison attributes the principal improvement to the functional-DP representation rather than to the choice between Bayesian credible intervals and Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals.
quote: Regardless of if we use Zanella-Béguelin et al.’s method for finding credible intervals, or use the Clopper-Pearson confidence interval, the main gain in estimating $\epsilon$ comes from auditing with $f$-DP.
context: Section 6.2 compares both statistical estimators under the different auditing frameworks.
uncertainty: This is an interpretation of the experiments reported in the paper.

claim: The first injected bug reverses clipping and averaging. Every tested audit detects a violation, but functional-DP auditing quantifies substantially greater leakage, changing the assessment of severity.
quote: All methods are able to detect a violation but only $f$-DP auditing can show the implementation is completely broken, as we can show $\epsilon>35$.
context: The implementation claims epsilon 1.27; conventional approaches produce lower bounds below 10 in the described experiment.
uncertainty: The phrase 'completely broken' is the authors' characterization; the concrete reported evidence is a lower bound above 35.

claim: For implementation debugging, the team deliberately includes the canary at every iteration to isolate the privacy mechanism from subsampling behavior.
quote: If the trainer sets $q_{c}=1$, the canary is selected in all iterations, and the audit focuses on the privacy mechanism without data sub-sampling. This modification allows us to identify bugs in DP-SGD that are not due to batch sampling.
context: Algorithm 2 allows separate sampling rates for ordinary examples and canaries.
uncertainty: This design isolates one class of failures and does not audit the correctness of batch sampling.

claim: The threshold analysis shows why an analytically optimal decision threshold can be operationally useless at a finite observation budget.
quote: Furthermore, the optimal threshold for ($\epsilon$, $\delta$)-DP auditing (given by Eq.˜18) with Clopper-Pearson gives a lower bound of zero since there aren’t a sufficient number of observations to cover this region of the observation space.
context: Appendix C evaluates thresholds with 5,000 observations and contrasts finite-sample behavior with large-sample theory.

claim: The black-box experiment was included to measure what happens as adversarial access is progressively removed, even though final-model-only access differs from the threat model used in standard DP analysis.
quote: We choose to evaluate it because it allows us to compare how the incremental removal of adversarial access to model updates and gradients affects the tightness of our lower bound for $\epsilon$.
context: The black-box adversary inserts an example before training and observes only the completed model.
uncertainty: A weaker lower bound under reduced access need not by itself establish the true privacy leakage in that setting.

claim: The third injected bug tests sensitivity to modest noise-scale errors, demonstrating detection when true epsilon is 1.57 against a claimed 1.27.
quote: We train models with decreasing scales of noise, implying larger values of $\epsilon$ than the claimed upper bound.
context: Functional-DP auditing detects the 1.57-versus-1.27 discrepancy; the other listed approaches fail even when the true upper bound reaches 2.17.
uncertainty: These detection thresholds are experimental results for the reported setup, not universal sensitivity guarantees.

claim: The paper adapts a prior Bayesian estimation approach to f-DP rather than treating the new privacy formalism and the uncertainty estimator as inseparable.
quote: Recently, Zanella-Béguelin et al. [30] showed it is also possible to compute credible intervals for $\epsilon$ using a Bayesian method which can significantly reduce the number of observations to estimate a tight bound. Here, we show it is possible to extend their approach to lower bound in $f$-DP
context: Experiments compare both Bayesian and Clopper-Pearson estimators under f-DP and standard epsilon-delta formulations.
uncertainty: The paper retains its earlier caveats about interpreting and comparing the uncertainty statements.

claim: The principal methodological choice was to exploit knowledge of the specific privacy mechanism rather than retain a universal mechanism-agnostic audit.
quote: We show that “opening the black box” and tailoring our scheme to the specific privacy mechanisms used in DP-SGD results in much tighter empirical privacy estimates and with significantly fewer observations (i.e., training runs).
context: The authors explain why their approach can improve both statistical tightness and computational efficiency.
uncertainty: The efficiency gain depends on mechanism-specific knowledge and its applicability.

claim: For the input-canary experiment, the authors restrict observations to the first 250 updates because including later training updates weakens their estimated per-step lower bound.
quote: Note that for this experiment we only use the first 250 iterations of DP-SGD to collect observations and estimate the per-step $\epsilon$ lower bound.
context: The surrounding text compares this window with the full 2,500-update run and reports weaker input-space auditing toward the end of training.
uncertainty: This is an observation-window choice, not evidence that training itself was stopped after 250 updates; weaker audit bounds do not alone prove lower true leakage.

claim: The biased-noise comparison credits another method with also detecting the bug, while identifying two conventional epsilon-delta approaches that miss it.
quote: We can detect violations when auditing with $f$-DP; the auditing method introduced by Lu et al. [17] also successfully detects the bug.
context: The following sentence reports failure to detect a violation using direct epsilon-delta auditing with either Clopper-Pearson or the Zanella-Béguelin et al. method.
uncertainty: Detection outcomes apply to the specified biased-noise experiment.

claim: The team used agreement with established auditing methods at large sample sizes as a cross-check on the new mechanism-specific approach.
quote: We also verify experimentally that our results agree with existing auditing techniques [21, 30] after sufficiently many training runs.
context: This verification accompanies the introduction of Gaussian DP and functional DP as more informative auditing frameworks.
uncertainty: Agreement in the evaluated settings is not a general proof of validity for every mechanism or implementation.

claim: The audit uses a functional-DP guarantee close to the mechanism's actual error tradeoff curve to avoid looseness introduced by auditing only a conventional epsilon-delta guarantee.
quote: we instead use an $f$-DP guarantee that is as close as possible to the true trade-off function of the mechanism.
context: Section 4 explains why mechanisms with identical epsilon-delta guarantees can nevertheless support different false-positive and false-negative tradeoffs.

claim: The black-box DP audit compares distributions of canary-label log odds from 1,000 models trained with the canary and 1,000 trained without it.
quote: We select a canary example, then we train 1,000 models with the canary point (+ training set), and 1,000 models with only the training set (canary excluded).
context: Section 6.4 converts model probabilities to log odds and uses functional DP to estimate a lower bound from the resulting distributions.
uncertainty: The two-training-run efficiency claim concerns the white-box procedure and does not describe this black-box experiment.

claim: The clipping-only experiment uses balanced training-with-canary and training-without-canary groups and interprets its strongest result relative to the maximum measurable lower bound at that sample size.
quote: In total, we train 2,000 models: 1,000 when the canary input was in training and 1,000 when the canary wasn’t included.
context: For clipping norm ten, the reported epsilon lower bound is 41.0 against a maximum attainable lower bound of 44.0 at that observation count.
uncertainty: The paper's broad phrase that clipping provides no privacy should be read as a conclusion from these tested settings, not a proof about every possible clipping-only algorithm.

claim: Conversion from stepwise audits to end-to-end privacy estimates relies on a tight characterization of each step and corresponding composition results.
quote: For instance, if we assume that each step is tightly characterized by Gaussian DP, then the tightness of Gaussian DP composition allows us to infer that the end-to-end training procedure is also tightly characterized by Gaussian DP
context: Section 5.5 uses Gaussian composition for the appropriate setting and more general functional DP with PLD when subsampling is present.
uncertainty: The quoted inference is conditional on the per-step characterization; it is not a generic rule for composing arbitrary empirical lower bounds.

claim: The clipping-only study empirically searches over canary inputs and selects blank white and mislabeled images because their losses separate most clearly according to training membership.
quote: We experimented with a range of different canary inputs, but found that blank (white) and mislabeled images produced the strongest lower bounds for $\epsilon$. In other words, these two canary types had losses that were easily separable depending on if they were included in training or not.
context: This selection concerns black-box auditing of a model trained with gradient clipping but no added privacy noise.

claim: The team analyzed threshold choice as a source of auditing inefficiency, showing that GDP bounds become threshold-independent with sufficient observations while conventional epsilon-delta auditing requires a particular threshold to maximize the bound.
quote: That is, given two Gaussian distributions, the lower bound derived from GDP is independent of the threshold. Given a sufficient number of observations from $\mathcal{O}$ and $\mathcal{O}^{\prime}$, our lower bounds found through GDP will be approximately equal,
context: Appendix C.1 combines a derivation with threshold experiments, including a comparison where conventional auditing requires roughly 250 million observations to reach the GDP-based result.
uncertainty: The threshold-independence claim is tied to the Gaussian setting and sufficient observations; it is not a claim about arbitrary mechanisms or tiny samples.

claim: The strongest audit grants access to every privatized update and permits an arbitrary canary gradient, making the adversary’s capabilities explicit rather than treating the resulting bound as access-independent.
quote: The adversary has access to the privatized gradient and model parameters in every update step and can choose an arbitrary gradient at each update step [4], which we refer to as a canary gradient.
context: The paper identifies this as its gradient-canary white-box threat model and connects it to standard DP-SGD analysis.
uncertainty: The adversary still lacks the randomness used for noise addition and batch selection.

claim: The second injected bug restricts random seeds to 100 possibilities, creating a finite set of noise vectors; the authors motivate this synthetic failure with a related real seed-reuse error.
quote: We train a model where the seed can only take on 100 different possible values, meaning there are only 100 different possible Gaussian noise vectors.
context: The paper links the motivation to a JAX DP-SGD example that reused a random seed across parameter sets.
uncertainty: The experimental bug is analogous to the cited real error, not a reproduction established by this passage.

claim: The authors explicitly decide that additional training steps are unnecessary for their demonstrated large-epsilon estimates once a few hundred observations already provide tight bounds.
quote: Of course, we could increase the number of training steps to create a larger number of observations, but we found our method is strong enough to produce tight bounds for large $\varepsilon$ with as little as a few hundred observations
context: Appendix B describes training two models per dataset in the white-box setting, normally with the canary included in every update.
uncertainty: This is a project-specific sufficiency judgment, not a general stopping rule or an adaptive stopping procedure.

claim: Computational feasibility was a central problem-selection criterion: audits requiring thousands of complete training runs would be impractical for expensive large models.
quote: Existing auditing techniques do this by running the training algorithm thousands of times—which is prohibitively expensive for large models that can cost millions of dollars to train even once.
context: This motivates the second research question, concerning tight estimation with few training runs.

claim: To test whether gradient clipping alone offers meaningful protection, the team uses a black-box audit because an unnoised white-box gradient would expose the canary signal directly.
quote: Instead, we audit in the black-box threat model by creating a canary point, inserting it into the training set, and then training a CIFAR-10 WRN-16 model.
context: The preceding discussion explains why white-box auditing without noise would be uninformative for this question.

claim: The team nevertheless adapts Bayesian estimation to functional DP, showing willingness to use an empirically effective approach while separately discussing its statistical interpretation.
quote: Here, we show it is possible to extend their approach to lower bound in $f$-DP (and then convert to a lower bound for $\epsilon$).
context: Section 4.2 extends the Zanella-Béguelin et al. method alongside the paper's Clopper-Pearson implementation.
uncertainty: This is a parallel methodological option, not evidence of a chronological reversal in Carlini's personal beliefs.

claim: The team explicitly accounted for numerical approximation looseness and checked how a small number of approximation lines compared with an optimal trade-off curve.
quote: We approximate the trade-off function using Algorithm 4, which will give us a looser bound for $\epsilon$, however, the difference is in the order of $10^{-1}$.
context: Appendix A reports that even ten approximations give a good estimate in Figure 13 and distinguishes single-step GDP experiments from multistep PLD experiments.
uncertainty: The stated approximation quality is reported for the illustrated analysis, not established as a universal error bound.

claim: The audit was designed around a trade-off function close to the mechanism’s actual hypothesis-testing behavior, to avoid information loss from working only with a single epsilon-delta guarantee.
quote: While it is possible to audit any algorithm to lower bound its privacy with an $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP guarantee, we instead use an $f$-DP guarantee that is as close as possible to the true trade-off function of the mechanism.
context: Different mechanisms with identical epsilon-delta guarantees can permit different combinations of false positive and false negative rates.

claim: For implementation debugging, the team intentionally isolated the privacy mechanism from subsampling by including the canary in every iteration in most experiments.
quote: When using auditing to debug an implementation of DP-SGD, we focus on the auditing of the privacy mechanism itself, rather than the sub-sampling process. We therefore set $q_{c}=1$ throughout most of the experiments in Section˜6.
context: The separate canary sampling rate allows this diagnostic intervention without requiring the same sampling rate for ordinary training examples.
uncertainty: This choice excludes some sampling-related implementation failures from the audit’s scope.

claim: The paper scrutinizes the statistical interpretation of a competing Bayesian audit, distinguishing numerical approximation issues from the different meanings of Bayesian credible intervals and frequentist confidence intervals.
quote: Equation˜11 cannot be evaluated in closed form, and so we must approximate it, and it is not clear how this approximation translates into a statistically sound lower bound. Moreover, the comparison between bounds found through this method and through Clopper-Pearson may be slightly unfair, as they are distinct statements about uncertainty of an estimate.
context: Despite these reservations, the paper acknowledges the Bayesian method’s empirical improvements and extends it to functional DP.
uncertainty: The passage raises unresolved validity and comparability concerns; it does not establish that all Bayesian estimates are unsound.

claim: The clipping-only experiment invests in 2,000 model trainings and explicitly compares the achieved bound with the maximum measurable at that observation count.
quote: In total, we train 2,000 models: 1,000 when the canary input was in training and 1,000 when the canary wasn’t included.
context: Reported epsilon lower bounds are 23.4, 26.8, and 41.0 for clipping norms 0.1, 1.0, and 10.0; the observation-limited maximum is 44.0.
uncertainty: The authors describe clipping alone as providing no privacy; the experiment directly establishes large lower bounds in the tested settings, not every possible sense of zero protection.

claim: The noise-scale debugging experiment tested sensitivity to relatively small privacy-budget violations, not just catastrophic failures.
quote: Results are shown in Figure˜9, where we find auditing with $f$-DP closely follows the true upper bound, meaning we can detect a violation to reported $\epsilon=1.27$ when the true value is $\epsilon=1.57$.
context: The team progressively reduced noise scale. The other compared auditing methods failed to identify a violation even when the true upper bound reached epsilon 2.17.
uncertainty: The detection thresholds are experimental results for the evaluated setup, not guaranteed sensitivities for arbitrary models or sample budgets.

claim: The paper explicitly connects methodological improvements to software testing and recommends integrating privacy audits into development pipelines.
quote: We show that our improved auditing scheme can surface bugs that would not have been captured by prior methods [21, 30, 17, 12]. We thus encourage developers of differentially private learning algorithms to incorporate our auditing tools into their testing pipeline.
context: The recommendation follows experiments on incorrect clipping, biased noise generation, and insufficient noise.
uncertainty: This is a recommendation made by the coauthored paper, not individually attributed speech.

claim: After testing multiple datasets, the collaboration narrows most subsequent experiments to CIFAR-10 because its strongest attack produced largely dataset-independent tightness.
quote: Given that our results show that tight lower bounds are largely independent of the choice of dataset if the adversary audits in a white-box threat model with canary gradients, our remaining experiments will focus primarily on the CIFAR-10 dataset unless stated otherwise.
context: The preceding comparison includes CIFAR-10, Purchase, and random pixels with random labels.
uncertainty: The scope reduction is justified only for the stated gradient-canary threat model.

claim: The clipping-only study searched across canary inputs and retained blank and mislabeled images because they produced the most separable losses; it then used 1,000 models with and 1,000 without the canary.
quote: We experimented with a range of different canary inputs, but found that blank (white) and mislabeled images produced the strongest lower bounds for $\epsilon$.
context: The reported lower bounds were 23.4, 26.8, and 41.0 for clipping norms 0.1, 1.0, and 10.0 respectively, against a maximum attainable bound of 44.0 at that observation count.
uncertainty: These large attack-based lower bounds support substantial leakage in the tested clipping-only systems; they are not a universal numerical characterization of every clipping-only model.

claim: The model-size comparison was used to show that a weak auditing method can reverse a substantive empirical conclusion: functional DP found slightly greater leakage for WRN-40, whereas a non-functional-DP audit suggested the opposite ranking.
quote: Interestingly, if one was to use a non $f$-DP auditing method, one would make an incorrect conclusion that the WRN-16 leaks more than the WRN-40. Using our $f$-DP auditing method, we identify that, indeed, the larger WRN-40 model leaks slightly more than the WRN-16 model.
context: Appendix D.2 asks whether the relationship between model size and memorization also appears under DP-SGD.
uncertainty: The evidence is a comparison of two architectures and their achieved privacy lower bounds, not a universal law relating size to privacy loss.

claim: Input-space canary construction targets gradients orthogonal to ordinary training gradients, but the team explicitly avoids using private non-noisy batch gradients because doing so would violate the attacker assumptions.
quote: However, we cannot use the example in the training batch directly to craft such an example as it will violate the DP-assumptions (the adversary cannot have access to non-noisy gradients).
context: Appendix C.3 instead assumes access to examples from the same distribution to estimate the relevant gradient direction and craft a distinguishable canary.
uncertainty: The replacement procedure still assumes distribution-matched auxiliary data.

claim: The authors identify subsampling as a setting where their convenient threshold behavior breaks down and tighter auditing may require more precise error-rate estimates and threshold optimization.
quote: This suggests that to accurately audit a sub-sampled privacy-preserving mechanism, it may be necessary to use attacks with more precise false positive rates and optimal thresholds in order to achieve tight bounds.
context: The observation follows an experiment with canary sampling probability one quarter and 10,000 observations.
uncertainty: The paper presents this as a suggested requirement, not a proved necessary condition.

claim: For input-space canaries, the team chooses the first 250 training iterations because they yield stronger per-step lower bounds than pooling observations from the whole training run.
quote: Note that for this experiment we only use the first 250 iterations of DP-SGD to collect observations and estimate the per-step $\epsilon$ lower bound.
context: Section 6.4 compares this early window with a complete 2,500-step run and reports weaker auditing from later updates.
uncertainty: A stronger estimated per-step lower bound from early observations does not mean the total privacy loss of a longer run is smaller.

claim: The white-box audit turns each update into a scalar distinguishability observation by taking a dot product between the privatized gradient sum and the canary gradient.
quote: For each batch, the trainer computes the dot product between the privatized gradient sum and the canary gradient (or the gradient from the canary input), resulting in a score (which we again refer to as an observation).
context: Algorithm 2 collects observations from batches corresponding to datasets with and without a canary.

claim: End-to-end estimates were constructed by composing stepwise privacy estimates under an explicit characterization assumption, rather than directly observing every end-to-end distinguishing event.
quote: For instance, if we assume that each step is tightly characterized by Gaussian DP, then the tightness of Gaussian DP composition allows us to infer that the end-to-end training procedure is also tightly characterized by Gaussian DP and that we can sum up the privacy parameters.
context: Section 5.5 uses Gaussian composition for the Gaussian case and more general functional DP with PLD when subsampling must be accounted for.
uncertainty: The inference depends on the stated stepwise characterization and composition assumptions.

claim: The authors choose an f-DP guarantee close to the mechanism's actual hypothesis-testing tradeoff to avoid looseness introduced by converting through standard privacy guarantees.
quote: we instead use an $f$-DP guarantee that is as close as possible to the true trade-off function of the mechanism. By doing so, we can avoid any looseness that appears in converting between this $f$-DP guarantee and its collection of many $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-DP guarantees.
context: Different mechanisms can share the same epsilon-delta guarantee while having different achievable false-positive and false-negative tradeoffs.

claim: The authors explain their sample-efficiency strategy as inference about rare outcomes from common outcomes, justified by structural knowledge of the privacy mechanism.
quote: However, we can make inferences about these rare outcomes from common outcomes by leveraging our knowledge about the privacy mechanism. As an analogy, if we know that data follows a Gaussian distribution, then we could estimate the mean and variance from a few samples, and make inferences about the tails of the distribution without ever observing those tails.
context: Direct empirical estimation of rare events in the standard differential privacy formulation can require prohibitively many observations.
uncertainty: The inference depends on the mechanism assumptions; it is not a distribution-free shortcut.

claim: The white-box audit uses alignment with a canary gradient as its distinguishing statistic, collecting observations from batches with and without the possible canary contribution.
quote: For each batch, the trainer computes the dot product between the privatized gradient sum and the canary gradient (or the gradient from the canary input), resulting in a score (which we again refer to as an observation).
context: The attack tries to determine whether a batch came from the original dataset or the neighboring dataset containing the canary.

claim: The authors use convex-model theory to motivate an empirical question about deep models while explicitly declining to claim the same theorem applies.
quote: The analysis for this result is specific to convex models; and we cannot prove such properties for the deep models. However, when can evaluate if a similar phenomenon holds empirically.
context: Appendix D.1 investigates whether later training steps exhibit less measurable leakage, motivated by prior privacy-loss plateau results for convex models.
uncertainty: The quoted grammatical error is present in the supplied source.

claim: The black-box evaluation was selected to measure the effect of progressively removing adversarial access, despite differing from the intermediate-update visibility assumed in the paper's account of standard DP analysis.
quote: We choose to evaluate it because it allows us to compare how the incremental removal of adversarial access to model updates and gradients affects the tightness of our lower bound
context: The black-box attacker inserts one example before training and observes the completed model.

claim: The main natural-dataset comparison reported variability across repeated experiments, not just a single successful audit.
quote: Results are given in Figure˜6, where we report the average lower bound found over ten independent executions of the experiment along with standard deviation, and the theoretical upper bound for $\epsilon$ given by the privacy accountant.
context: The comparison audits a CIFAR-10 model with 79% test accuracy at epsilon 8 and delta 10^-5 against contemporary auditing methods.

claim: The collaboration declines to rely on a convenient central-limit approximation where it can underestimate privacy cost, choosing Privacy Loss Distribution accounting for DP-SGD instead.
quote: Dong et al. [9] suggest to use a Central Limit Theorem for DP to compute a closed form solution, unfortunately, this can lead to significant underestimation of the privacy cost in general settings [16]. Therefore, to analyze DP-SGD we use an empirical approach called the “Privacy Loss Distribution (PLD)”[16] to approximate the trade-off function
context: The choice addresses the combination of subsampling and composition over many training updates.

claim: For implementation debugging, the authors deliberately include the canary in every update to isolate the privacy mechanism from subsampling behavior.
quote: When using auditing to debug an implementation of DP-SGD, we focus on the auditing of the privacy mechanism itself, rather than the sub-sampling process. We therefore set $q_{c}=1$ throughout most of the experiments in Section˜6.
context: Experiments with subsampled canaries are retained for black-box privacy-leakage analysis.
uncertainty: This design leaves subsampling bugs outside the scope of most debugging experiments.

claim: The authors scrutinize statistical guarantees in earlier Bayesian auditing work, distinguishing practical improvement from unresolved approximation validity and from differences between confidence and credible statements.
quote: it is not clear how this approximation translates into a statistically sound lower bound. Moreover, the comparison between bounds found through this method and through Clopper-Pearson may be slightly unfair, as they are distinct statements about uncertainty of an estimate.
context: The related-method discussion also acknowledges that the Bayesian approach improves empirical tightness and reduces required runs.
uncertainty: The passage raises methodological concerns; it does not establish that the earlier Bayesian method is invalid.

claim: Restricting the attacker to input canaries reveals an architectural dependence that was much less apparent under gradient-canary auditing.
quote: Specifically, we can get an (almost) tight lower bound when using Wide Resnet architecture regardless of the datasets. Moreover, when we compare the CIFAR-10 dataset results between Wide Resnet and ConvNet models, we see a large gap which further emphasizes the significance of the model architecture on privacy leakage.
context: The authors report tight input-space bounds for epsilon below ten and contrast Wide ResNet with ConvNet.
uncertainty: These are attack-derived lower bounds; differences can reflect both privacy leakage and the effectiveness of the available audit.

claim: After finding largely dataset-independent tightness under the gradient-canary white-box threat model, the team narrows subsequent experiments primarily to CIFAR-10.
quote: Given that our results show that tight lower bounds are largely independent of the choice of dataset if the adversary audits in a white-box threat model with canary gradients, our remaining experiments will focus primarily on the CIFAR-10 dataset unless stated otherwise.
context: Table 1 compares CIFAR-10, Purchase, and random data across several privacy budgets and auditing methods.
uncertainty: The dataset-independence conclusion is explicitly restricted to this powerful threat model.

claim: The team used theory about convergent convex models to motivate a deep-model experiment while explicitly separating empirical analogy from proof.
quote: The analysis for this result is specific to convex models; and we cannot prove such properties for the deep models. However, when can evaluate if a similar phenomenon holds empirically.
context: Appendix D.1 investigates whether early and late training iterations differ in their input-space audit bounds, motivated by prior results on privacy-loss plateaus.
uncertainty: The paper does not prove a privacy-loss plateau for the deep networks it evaluates.

claim: Input-canary evaluation compares the new construction against several substantively different baselines instead of only one convenient alternative.
quote: We evaluate four different canary strategies: (1) a random sample from the dataset distribution with a wrong label, (2) using a blank sample, (3) an adversarial example, and (4) and our new canary crafting approach given in Algorithm˜3 and discussed in Section˜C.3.
context: Appendix C specifies projected gradient descent for the adversarial-example baseline and orthogonality-based optimization for the new construction.

claim: Input-canary construction aims for gradient orthogonality while respecting the attacker's information restrictions; the authors avoid directly using private batch gradients and estimate them from same-distribution data.
quote: However, we cannot use the example in the training batch directly to craft such an example as it will violate the DP-assumptions (the adversary cannot have access to non-noisy gradients). Therefore, we assume the adversary has access to an example from the same distribution as the training dataset
context: Algorithm 3 crafts an input whose gradient differs from the estimated gradients of ordinary training examples.
uncertainty: Access to suitable same-distribution data is an explicit additional attacker assumption.

claim: The team treated the cost of repeatedly training large models as a substantive obstacle to privacy measurement, motivating a reduction from thousands of training runs to two.
quote: Existing auditing techniques do this by running the training algorithm thousands of times—which is prohibitively expensive for large models that can cost millions of dollars to train even once.
context: The introduction asks whether DP-SGD’s privacy leakage can be tightly estimated with a small number of training runs.
uncertainty: The two-run result concerns the paper’s white-box auditing approach; its black-box experiments still train thousands of models.

claim: GDP's threshold robustness is explicitly conditional on Gaussian observations and enough data; the authors contrast it with conventional auditing that needs a particular threshold for tightness.
quote: That is, given two Gaussian distributions, the lower bound derived from GDP is independent of the threshold.
context: Appendix C.1 derives threshold independence and then discusses approximate empirical equality with sufficiently many observations.
uncertainty: The analytical statement does not establish equal finite-sample precision at every threshold.

claim: The experimental reporting standard explicitly distinguished 95% frequentist confidence intervals from 95% Bayesian credible intervals and specified a default adversary model.
quote: Unless otherwise stated, all lower bounds are given with a 95% confidence (Clopper-Pearson as in Nasr et al. [21]) / credible interval (Zanella-Béguelin et al. [30]), and we audit in the White-box access with Gradient Canaries threat model using Algorithm˜2.
context: The benchmark suite includes CIFAR-10, Purchase, multiple architectures, and a randomly generated dataset.
uncertainty: The paper’s separately disclosed threshold-selection issue qualifies the interpretation of nominal interval coverage.

claim: The team checked gradient-canary design choices through a controlled comparison of sparse, constant, and Gaussian canaries, normalizing their norms and testing whether to refresh them at each step.
quote: In each setting, gradient values are re-scaled such that the canary gradient has a maximum norm equal to the clipping norm. We also measure if there is a difference between using the same canary gradient at each iteration of DP-SGD or creating a new canary gradient.
context: Appendix C.2 reports that a refreshed Dirac canary performs best, while the figure caption describes only a small advantage for Dirac canaries and little difference between static and moving canaries.
uncertainty: The reported advantage should not be inflated into a large or universal performance difference.

claim: The authors resist a simple causal interpretation of the weaker black-box bounds because removing intermediate access also leaves subsampling-related estimation effects difficult to disentangle.
quote: However, it is difficult to separate the effects of the black-box threat model from the effect that sub-sampling has on privacy leakage estimation
context: For a CIFAR-10 Wide ResNet trained to theoretical epsilon 8, the reported black-box lower bound is approximately 1.6.
uncertainty: The measured gap does not by itself show how much is genuine additional privacy versus audit looseness.

claim: The debugging experiments reported single-step bounds and explicitly acknowledged that composing those bounds would not turn the audit into a detector for every implementation bug.
quote: For example, a bug that is caused by implementing a biased sub-sampling method from the training dataset will likely not be captured by our audit.
context: Section 6.3 audits implementations claiming epsilon 1.27 and explains why it does not present the results as a complete end-to-end correctness check.
uncertainty: The audit is a targeted empirical diagnostic, not a proof that all parts of an implementation are correct.

claim: The input-space attack was evaluated against several concrete alternatives rather than only against no attack: mislabeled data, blank inputs, and adversarial examples.
quote: We evaluate four different canary strategies: (1) a random sample from the dataset distribution with a wrong label, (2) using a blank sample, (3) an adversarial example, and (4) and our new canary crafting approach given in Algorithm˜3 and discussed in Section˜C.3.
context: Appendix C.3 specifies projected gradient descent for the adversarial-example baseline and an orthogonality objective for the new crafted canary.

claim: The early-versus-late training pattern does not reproduce on random data, and the authors leave the explanation of weakening later-iteration audit bounds unresolved.
quote: We find that indeed, the first part of training does leak more information than later in training on the CIFAR-10 dataset. However, when we evaluate the random dataset we do not see the same behavior
context: Appendix D.1 also warns that fewer than 100 iterations provide too few observations for confident estimates and identifies the later-iteration behavior as future work.
uncertainty: The evidence consists of input-space attack lower bounds; their weakening alone does not prove a corresponding reduction in true leakage.

claim: The collaboration directly challenges an earlier dataset-dependence interpretation and offers insufficient attack strength as an alternative explanation.
quote: Lu et al. also suggest that empirical privacy leakage is dataset dependent. Our work directly contradicts this claim; we argue that their observations were mostly due to using weaker attacks than are permitted under the DP threat model.
context: The paper supports this challenge using stronger white-box attacks with gradient canaries across several datasets.
uncertainty: The challenge is conditional on adversarial capabilities; the paper later reports dataset and architecture dependence under more restricted attacks.

claim: The paper's central methodological decision was to exploit knowledge of the specific privacy mechanism rather than retain the mechanism-independent approach of earlier audits.
quote: We observe that existing auditing techniques are universal: they make no assumption about the privacy mechanism. We show that “opening the black box” and tailoring our scheme to the specific privacy mechanisms used in DP-SGD results in much tighter empirical privacy estimates and with significantly fewer observations (i.e., training runs).
context: The approach uses Gaussian and functional differential privacy to characterize DP-SGD more precisely.
uncertainty: This is a project-specific methodological choice, not evidence that Carlini universally prefers specialized methods.

claim: The black-box results include a negative finding on random data and identify achieved accuracy as a potentially relevant difference across configurations.
quote: Specifically, when examining the random dataset, no non-trivial lower bounds for auditing can be achieved. One of the key factors that distinguishes these experiments is the final accuracy the model is able to attain.
context: The paper compares stronger bounds for CIFAR-10 Wide ResNet with weaker results for ConvNet, Purchase, and random data.
uncertainty: Accuracy is an observed distinguishing factor, not established here as the causal explanation; failure to obtain a bound is not proof of no leakage.

claim: A second controlled bug reduced Gaussian-noise randomness to only 100 possible seeds, motivated by an actual category of PRNG-reuse implementation error.
quote: We train a model where the seed can only take on 100 different possible values, meaning there are only 100 different possible Gaussian noise vectors.
context: The paper relates the constructed bug to a JAX example that reused a random seed. Functional DP auditing and Lu et al.’s method detected the constructed violation, while the tested direct epsilon-delta methods did not.
uncertainty: The 100-seed experiment is a constructed analogue, not a reproduction of the exact JAX bug.

claim: For the central CIFAR-10 comparison, the authors report repeated experiments, dispersion, and the theoretical accountant bound together rather than only a single successful audit.
quote: Results are given in Figure˜6, where we report the average lower bound found over ten independent executions of the experiment along with standard deviation, and the theoretical upper bound
context: The audited model achieves 79% test accuracy at a theoretical epsilon of 8 and delta of 10^-5.

claim: The authors explicitly recognize a tradeoff between strong audits and realistic attacker assumptions, and therefore evaluate multiple threat models.
quote: We similarly study multiple threat models, as there is inevitably a trade-off between the power of the audit (with a powerful adversary) and generalizability of the audit to practical machine learning applications
context: Section 3 orders three threat models by decreasing attacker power.

claim: The study deliberately compared several adversary models because more powerful auditing access improves detection but can reduce relevance to practical deployments.
quote: We similarly study multiple threat models, as there is inevitably a trade-off between the power of the audit (with a powerful adversary) and generalizability of the audit to practical machine learning applications (where the assumptions we make to instantiate a powerful adversary may be unrealistic).
context: Section 3 organizes experiments into white-box gradient canaries, white-box input canaries, and black-box access.

claim: The black-box results include a negative finding on random data and examine final predictive accuracy as a possible explanatory factor across datasets and architectures.
quote: Specifically, when examining the random dataset, no non-trivial lower bounds for auditing can be achieved. One of the key factors that distinguishes these experiments is the final accuracy the model is able to attain.
context: The paper contrasts higher-accuracy CIFAR-10 Wide ResNet results with weaker bounds for other evaluated settings.
uncertainty: The comparison suggests an association; it does not isolate accuracy as a causal mechanism.

claim: The project selected two connected shortcomings of existing privacy audits: tight estimates depended on extreme datasets, and obtaining statistically useful estimates required prohibitively many training runs.
quote: First, they only give tight estimates under implausible worst-case assumptions (e.g., a fully adversarial dataset). Second, they require thousands or millions of training runs to produce non-trivial statistical estimates of the privacy leakage.
context: The abstract frames both shortcomings as the problems the new auditing scheme addresses.

claim: The paper flags insufficient statistical power as a reason extremely short training windows produce loose privacy bounds.
quote: if we only look at a very small number (<100) of the iterations we get a very loose bound on $\epsilon$ because we do not have enough observations to have a sufficiently confident estimation
context: This caveat accompanies the experiment comparing leakage estimates across early training windows.
uncertainty: The fewer-than-100 threshold describes this experimental setting, not a universal sample-complexity boundary.

claim: The biased-noise test deliberately restricts the random seed space, and the authors motivate this synthetic failure with a related seed-reuse error in a real DP-SGD example.
quote: We train a model where the seed can only take on 100 different possible values, meaning there are only 100 different possible Gaussian noise vectors.
context: The surrounding passage relates the constructed bug to a JAX example that reused a random seed across sets of model parameters.
uncertainty: The experiment models a related failure mode; it is not described as reproducing the JAX bug exactly.

claim: The evaluation includes natural image and purchase datasets, more than one image-model architecture, and a random dataset control, with uncertainty intervals specified as part of the default setup.
quote: We experiment with two commonly used datasets in the privacy literature: CIFAR-10 (with Wide ResNet (WRN-16) [29] and ConvNet architectures) and Purchase. In addition we also evaluate our experiment on a randomly initialized dataset.
context: Section 6.1 states that lower bounds use 95% confidence or credible intervals unless otherwise stated.
uncertainty: Confidence intervals and Bayesian credible intervals are distinct uncertainty statements, as the paper itself notes.

claim: The project targeted a limitation of prior tightness results: they required an adversary to choose the entire training dataset, leaving open whether tight privacy estimates were possible on natural datasets.
quote: However, their tightness result only holds in a narrow and very strong adversarial model, where the adversary chooses the entire training dataset. This leads to a natural follow-up question:
context: The introduction motivates its first research question by examining the scope of the earlier Nasr et al. result.

claim: The main natural-dataset comparison reports variation over ten independent executions and attributes most of the improvement to using f-DP rather than to the choice of interval estimator.
quote: we report the average lower bound found over ten independent executions of the experiment along with standard deviation, and the theoretical upper bound for $\epsilon$ given by the privacy accountant. Regardless of if we use Zanella-Béguelin et al.’s method for finding credible intervals, or use the Clopper-Pearson confidence interval, the main gain in estimating $\epsilon$ comes from auditing with $f$-DP.
context: The experiment audits a CIFAR-10 model with 79% test accuracy at a theoretical epsilon of eight.

claim: The team limited the black-box experimental scope when stronger white-box canary methods did not have a straightforward extension.
quote: Unfortunately, it is not trivial to extend either the adversarial example or our crafting approach to the black-box setting and therefore we do not use them in the black-box experiments.
context: Appendix C.3 reports tighter white-box bounds from the new crafted canaries before explaining their omission from black-box tests.
uncertainty: Omission for implementation difficulty does not show that these approaches cannot work in black-box settings or that the tested black-box attacks are optimal.

claim: The collaboration selected two concrete limitations of existing privacy audits as its central research problems: dependence on implausibly adversarial datasets and the cost of thousands or millions of training runs.
quote: But these auditing techniques suffer from two limitations. First, they only give tight estimates under implausible worst-case assumptions (e.g., a fully adversarial dataset). Second, they require thousands or millions of training runs to produce non-trivial statistical estimates of the privacy leakage.
context: The abstract frames the project around making tight empirical privacy estimates applicable to natural datasets and affordable to compute.

claim: The early-versus-late training investigation preserved a counterexample to its emerging pattern: CIFAR-10 showed stronger early leakage estimates, but the random dataset did not.
quote: We find that indeed, the first part of training does leak more information than later in training on the CIFAR-10 dataset. However, when we evaluate the random dataset we do not see the same behavior
context: The same discussion warns that fewer than 100 iterations yield loose bounds because there are too few observations for a sufficiently confident estimate.
uncertainty: These are attack-derived estimates whose strength depends on the observation count and canary construction.

claim: The black-box results retained a substantial gap between the theoretical budget and the achieved attack bound, and the team declined to attribute that gap solely to reduced attacker access.
quote: However, it is difficult to separate the effects of the black-box threat model from the effect that sub-sampling has on privacy leakage estimation,
context: For CIFAR-10 with Wide ResNet trained to epsilon 8, functional DP with Bayesian estimation achieved a lower bound of approximately 1.6. The paper identifies subsampling-related trade-off approximation as a confounding factor.
uncertainty: The experiment does not isolate the causal contribution of access restrictions versus subsampling to the remaining gap.

claim: The paper openly acknowledges a statistical-validity tension in its comparative experiments: it selects thresholds on the same observations used to report lower bounds, following prior practice despite recognizing that this makes the bound technically invalid.
quote: Note that if thresholds we use are found using the same observation data that we compute the lower bound on, the bound is technically not valid. However, it has become common to report lower bounds on the same set of observations that one uses to find an optimal decision threshold [30, 18],
context: Section 5.2 says each method will use the threshold maximizing its reported lower bound; Appendix C.1 separately explains the held-out-data requirement.
uncertainty: The paper’s asymptotic threshold-independence argument for GDP does not itself remove every finite-sample concern about adaptive threshold selection.

claim: The model-size experiment demonstrates that the choice of audit can reverse the apparent ordering of privacy leakage between architectures.
quote: Interestingly, if one was to use a non $f$-DP auditing method, one would make an incorrect conclusion that the WRN-16 leaks more than the WRN-40. Using our $f$-DP auditing method, we identify that, indeed, the larger WRN-40 model leaks slightly more than the WRN-16 model.
context: The authors compare WRN-16 and WRN-40 to test whether larger models' memorization tendencies also appear under DP-SGD.
uncertainty: The evidence concerns the tested architectures and audit bounds; it does not establish a universal size-leakage law.

claim: The central methodological choice was to exploit knowledge of DP-SGD’s privacy mechanism rather than retain a universally applicable, mechanism-agnostic audit.
quote: We show that “opening the black box” and tailoring our scheme to the specific privacy mechanisms used in DP-SGD results in much tighter empirical privacy estimates and with significantly fewer observations (i.e., training runs).
context: The paper explains that assumptions about the mechanism permit inference about rare outcomes from more common observations.
uncertainty: The resulting efficiency depends on the mechanism-specific characterization being appropriate.

claim: The collaboration reports that its crafted input canary strengthens white-box bounds but explicitly limits its use when extension to black-box access is not straightforward.
quote: As can be seen, using our canary crafting approach we can achieve significantly tighter bounds on DP-SGD compared to other canary crafting strategies. Unfortunately, it is not trivial to extend either the adversarial example or our crafting approach to the black-box setting and therefore we do not use them in the black-box experiments.
context: The result is illustrated for CIFAR-10 using a Wide ResNet architecture.
uncertainty: The absence of these attacks in black-box experiments is a methodological limitation, not evidence that such extensions are impossible.

claim: The authors quantify the loss introduced by approximating the PLD tradeoff function rather than presenting their numerical approximation as exact.
quote: We approximate the trade-off function using Algorithm 4, which will give us a looser bound for $\epsilon$, however, the difference is in the order of $10^{-1}$.
context: Appendix A also compares the approximation with the optimal tradeoff curve and reports useful estimation with ten approximations.
uncertainty: The quoted approximation accuracy is reported in the paper's evaluated setting.

claim: The team evaluates its crafted input against mislabeled, blank, and adversarial examples, but excludes the adversarial and newly crafted approaches from black-box experiments because transferring them is nontrivial.
quote: Unfortunately, it is not trivial to extend either the adversarial example or our crafting approach to the black-box setting and therefore we do not use them in the black-box experiments.
context: Appendix C.3 reports stronger white-box bounds for the new crafting procedure before stating this scope limit.
uncertainty: The exclusion is a limitation of the evaluated methods, not evidence that effective black-box extensions are impossible.

claim: A practical motivation for the Gaussian formulation is that its inferred privacy lower bound becomes independent of the decision threshold under the stated mechanism and observation assumptions.
quote: A benefit of auditing with $q_{c}=1$ and GDP is that the lower bounds we derive with GDP are agnostic to our choice of decision threshold used to compute type I and type II errors (in the limit of number of observations)
